en: The *Dharmasūtras* composed by Gautama,
together with the commentary *Mitākṣarā* written by Haradatta;
therein, the first chapter of the first book.
Salutation to Rudra.
This concise commentary (*mitākṣarā*) on the Dharmaśāstra composed by Gautama is being produced by Haradatta.
The Veda is the root of Dharma. 1.1.

Dharma is a quality of the self (*ātman*) produced by action, which is the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and is designated as *apūrva*. Its source (*mūla*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The Veda, consisting of the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*, is that source. The singular number is used in reference to the genus; thus, the four Vedas—namely the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*—are themselves the authority regarding Dharma. Neither the direct perception of a yogi, nor inference, nor presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), nor the scriptures of the Śākyas and others [is the authority]. Therefore, it will be explained that duties such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) have that [Veda] as their source, and not practices such as bowing to shrines (*caityavandana*) or plucking out the hair (*keśolluñcana*). The mention of "Dharma" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*); for Adharma as well, the Veda alone—consisting of prohibitions—is the source. For prohibitory injunctions turn one away from engaging in objects such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). And one who has engaged in an object through passion, hatred, and so forth cannot be turned away from it [by anything else]. If that object were performed and yet were not a cause of demerit (*pratyavāya*), then the prohibitory injunction itself makes known its status as a cause of demerit. (1.1)

Now, where a directly perceived Veda serving as a source is not available, how is it to be understood? [The answer is: "In such cases, it is by the tradition and conduct of those who know that [the Dharma is established]. (1.2)

The *smṛti*—the traditional law codes composed by those such as Manu who know that [Veda] and know the Veda—and their *śīla*, which is their practice; these two, *smṛti* and *śīla*, are the authority for people like us. Furthermore, it is impossible that their practice is without a foundation. And while there is indeed an experience of the Veda among those belonging to the Vedic tradition even when the texts have been lost, because those [ancient sages] existed at that time and because the lineage of transmission was uninterrupted, the Vedic practice of theirs is rooted in the Veda itself. As Āpastamba has said: "Their lost readings are inferred from usage. (1.2)

If conduct (*śīla*) were the authority, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). How so? Kata and Bharadvāja exchanged their wives; Vasiṣṭha [approached] Caṇḍālī Akṣamālā; Prajāpati [approached] his own daughter; and by Rāma, following his father’s word and without deliberation, his mother’s head was severed—such acts of violence (*sāhasa*) would also become authoritative. To this he says: "No; transgression of Dharma and violence are seen even among the great. (1.3)
Even such audacity on the part of the great is seen as merely a transgression of dharma and not as dharma itself, because it is rooted in passion and hatred. 1.3.
Nor does the same consequence apply to people such as ourselves merely because such [perception] has not been seen among them; why? Because of the weakness of their faculties (avaradaurbalyāt). 1.4.

Because those who are inferior, such as ourselves, are weak; and thus it is heard in scripture: "For them, there is no transgression due to their particular splendor; but the inferior person, employing [the mantra] after merely observing that [splendor], comes to grief. (1.4)

Now, when two contradictory means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) of equal strength come into conflict—for example, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," and "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice"; or "One offers the oblation after sunrise," and "One offers the oblation before sunrise"—and the Smṛti: "Food contaminated by hair or insects is always unfit to be eaten" (Gautama Dharmasūtra 17.8–9); or:
"That which has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or trodden upon, as well as that contaminated by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth" (Manu Smṛti 5.125).
Thus says Manu. In that case, what should be done?
When there is a conflict between two rules of equal force, there is an option (*vikalpa*). 1.5.

There is an option (*vikalpa*) between two such objects that have been established as having equal authority; it consists in accepting one or the other, such as "this is it" or "that is it. There is no possibility of a combination (*samuccaya*), because it is impossible. However, when there is a conflict between *śruti* and *smṛti* regarding the communication of excellence, the meaning of the *smṛti* is not to be respected, because they do not possess equal strength. For this very reason, Jābāli said: "But when there is a conflict between *śruti* and *smṛti*, *śruti* alone is more authoritative.
When there is no conflict, the practice prescribed by *smṛti* should always be performed just like that which is Vedic. (1.5)
Now, intending to explain the duties (dharma), and because they are preceded by the initiation ceremony (upanayana), he first describes that initiation:
"The initiation for a Brāhmaṇa is in the eighth [year]. (1.6)

The mention of "Brāhmaṇa" here refers to the state of being a Brāhmaṇa that occurs immediately after the *upanayana* (initiation). However, the inclusion of the term "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of making it known that initiation belongs only to one who is already a Brāhmaṇa by birth, and that Brāhmaṇahood is not something produced by the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) such as initiation. Furthermore, scriptural prohibitions such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" and "A Brāhmaṇa must not drink liquor" would not apply to one who has not been initiated. The eighth year is the primary time for the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa. By explaining the *upanayana* while bypassing the previously occurring sacraments such as *garbhādhāna* (conception), he demonstrates its preeminence. Consequently, even if *garbhādhāna* and the others are not performed due to some unforeseen circumstance, the *upanayana* still takes place. It is established, however, that if it is not performed, there is no entitlement to marriage and other rites. (1.6)
The optional [rite] is performed on the ninth or the fifth day. 1.7.
The *kāmya* is that which has desire as its motive. It occurs either in the ninth or the fifth year. Āpastamba states: "In the ninth year, for one desiring splendor" (ĀpDh 1.1.23).
Manu states: "For a Brahmin desiring sacred luster (*brahmavarcasa*), it should be performed in the fifth year" (MDh 2.37). 1.7.
The number of years begins from conception. 1.8.
The calculation of years begins with conception and so forth, not with birth and so forth. || 1.8 ||
That is the second birth. 1.9.
That initiation is his second birth; here, the Sāvitrī is his mother and the teacher is his father. Through this, his status as a twice-born is established. 1.1.9.
Therefore, for that reason, he is the teacher (ācārya). 1.10.
Therefore, in the absence of the father, that man from whom the initiation (upanayana) takes place is the teacher (ācārya). 1.10.
But not from initiation alone. Why then? From the study of the Vedas as well. 1.11.
Reciting after [the teacher] means teaching. Regarding this, Manu says:
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpa and the Rahasya, him they call an Ācārya" (MDh 2.140). || 1.11 ||
The eleventh and twelfth [stages] are for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya [respectively]. || 1.12 ||
This rule regarding these two [the king and the Vaiśya] is obligatory; however, that which is for the sake of a desired object has been shown by Manu:
"For a king seeking power, it is on the sixth day; for a Vaiśya seeking wealth, on the eighth" (MDh 2.37). || 1.12 ||
Now he states the rules for times of distress:
"The Sāvitrī does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year. (1.13)

The prefix *ā* denotes a limit inclusive of the whole. Up to the sixteenth year from birth, the *sāvitrī* of a Brāhmaṇa is not fallen, that is, not lost. By the word *sāvitrī*, the initiation (*upanayana*) which is the cause for its instruction is indicated. The meaning is that this is the time for that initiation. (1.1.13)
For a Kṣatriya, [the period of impurity lasts] twenty-two days; for a Vaiśya, two more [than that]. || 1.14 ||

In both cases, the prefix *ā* is understood [from the previous rule]. The elision of the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is to be observed. The *Sāvitrī* [initiation] does not lapse for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second year, nor for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth year. 1.14.
The girdles are made of muñja grass, of bowstring (murvī), and of hemp (sautrī), respectively. 1.15.

Muñja is a specific type of *darbha* grass; a girdle (*mauñjī*) is made from its product. *Mūrvā* is a specific wild medicinal herb (known as *saralī* in the Dravidian language); a cord (*maurvī*) is made from its product. The term "bowstring" (*jyā*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that which is both a bowstring and made of *mūrvā*. By the word "bowstring," it is implied that it is to be taken from a bow. A cord made of thread is *sautrī*. These are the girdles according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*). 1.15.
The skins of the black antelope, the spotted deer, and the goat. || 1.16 ||

The *kṛṣṇa* is the black antelope; the *ruru* is a spotted deer; the *basta* is a goat. Their skins serve as upper garments in that respective order, according to the view of Āpastamba in [ĀpDh 1.3.10]: “But one should wear an animal skin as an upper garment. || 1.16 ||
The garments of hemp, linen, bark, and blankets are for all.

*Śāṇa* is a product of hemp (*śaṇa*). *Kṣauma* is a product of *kṣumā* (linseed) or *atasī*; others say it is white cotton cloth (*śvetapaṭṭa*). *Cīra* is bark-cloth made from *darbha* grass and similar materials. A blanket (*kambala*) made of wool (*ūrṇā*) is called *kutapa*. These four types of garments are permitted for all [ascetics]. 1.17.
Or cotton that has not been processed. 1.18.
Unprocessed cotton cloth is [permitted] for all; "unprocessed" means free from that alteration which consists of producing a different color by means of dyeing substances such as safflower. 1.18.
He states the inferences: "Some [say] even the saffron robe. 1.19.
However, some teachers maintain that even [a garment] dyed with a decoction (kaṣāya) may be worn. 1.19.
In that regard, there is also a restriction:
the garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of tree-bark; those of the other two [castes] should be dyed with madder and turmeric, respectively.

That which is dyed with the decoction of trees is *vārkṣa*; that belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. That which is dyed with *mañjiṣṭhā* is *māñjiṣṭha*; that which is dyed with turmeric is *hāridra*. These two belong to the other two—that is to say, to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. (1.20)
The staffs of a Brāhmaṇa are made of *bailva* or *pālāśa* wood. || 1.21 ||
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; it is not, however, the case that both may be used together.
The *aśvattha* and *pīlu* [are used] for the remainder. || 1.22 ||
The *pīlu* is a specific type of tree, commonly known as the *utā*. The remainder refers to the case of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya castes. 1.22.
Or rather, [the fire] of all [is fit for sacrifice]. 1.23.
If none of those mentioned are available, the staff shall be made of a tree suitable for sacrifice, or of any sacrificial wood. 1.23.
Unpressed, curved like sacrificial posts, and with their bark intact. || 1.24 ||

"Uninjured" means not damaged by insects or the like. "Bent like a sacrificial post" (yūpavakra) means bent at the top like a sacrificial post. "With bark" (saśalka) means having the bark intact. Staves of this kind are for all [classes]. 1.24.
They are equal in measure to the crown of the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose.

In this context, they are intended to correspond respectively: the staff of a Brāhmaṇa should reach the top of the head; that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead; and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose. (1.25)
And those with shaven heads, matted hair, topknots, and tangled locks. || 1.26 ||

In this context, there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). "Shaven-headed" (*muṇḍāḥ*) means those whose hair has been entirely removed. "Wearing matted locks" (*jaṭilāḥ*) means those who maintain their hair; *jaṭā* is a mass of hair. Those for whom the *jaṭā* consists of only a crest-lock are "those with matted locks as a crest" (*śikhājaṭāḥ*). This is a common attribute applicable to all. The term "shaven-headed" is employed here with reference to the *Chandogas*. (1.26)
If one has something in hand and is impure from food remnants, one should sip water for purification after setting it down. 1.27.

The functions of voiding urine and excrement, as well as eating and so forth, are the causes for becoming *ucchiṣṭa* (ritually impure from remnants). If one who holds an object in his hand becomes *ucchiṣṭa*, he should perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping) without setting that object down. If, while already *ucchiṣṭa*, he comes to hold an object in his hand, he should set the object down and then perform *ācamana*. Thus says Manu:
"But if one who holds an object in his hand is somehow touched by someone who is *ucchiṣṭa*, he shall attain purity by performing *ācamana* without even setting that object down. [MDh 5.143]

Furthermore, regarding substances such as food and drink, one should perform the act of voiding urine or feces upon that very substance, then set that vessel aside and sip water for purification (ācamana). However, regarding objects such as clothing or a staff, one should sip water for purification without setting them aside at all. 1.27.
Now, the purification of substances is described:
the purification of objects made of metal, clay, wood, and woven cloth consists of wiping, burning, scraping, and washing, respectively. 1.28.

The purifications for metallic and other substances are, in their respective order, scrubbing and so forth. "Metallic" refers to bronze (*kāṃsya*) and the like; "earthen" refers to clay vessels and the like; "wooden" refers to those made of wood and the like; and "textile" refers to those made of thread and the like. For these, the purification is scrubbing in sequence: therein, bronze is purified with ash, gold and silver with cow-dung, and copper with acid. This applies to those [vessels] smeared with food-remnants. Kaṇva states: "For metallic objects of this kind, [purification is] by means of ash and so forth. For those touched by a woman in her courses, a *caṇḍāla*, or similar persons, purification occurs by immersing them in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one day and scrubbing twenty-one times. For earthen vessels, purification is by thorough burning. "Thorough burning" is a burning such that a change of color occurs; such a burning is the means of purification. This refers to those [vessels] defiled by contact. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:

"An earthen vessel that has been touched by liquor, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears, or blood is not purified at all except by being fired again. [VaDh 3.59] For wooden objects, purification is achieved by planing; this applies to those that have been permeated by impure substances (amedhya) and the like, whereas in other cases, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), washing, and so forth suffice. For woven cloth (tāntava), purification is achieved by washing; this applies to those defiled by contact. For those defiled by dirt and the like, there is either scrubbing or the excision of that specific portion. For many items defiled by contact, purification is achieved by sprinkling. || 1.28 ||
As in the case of fire, [the same applies] to stones, gems, conch-shells, and pearls. || 1.29 ||
The purification of stones and similar objects is by wiping, just as it is for metallic objects. 1.29.
As in the case of wood, [the same applies] with respect to the bones and the earth. 1.30.

Bone refers to elephant tusks and the like; earth refers to houses and the like. The purification of these two is by planing, just as with wood. Although one should have said "like wood" (*dāravavat*), the use of the term "like wood" (*dāruvat*) indicates that whatever purification applies to the modification (*vikāra*) also applies to the material substance (*vikārin*). || 1.30 ||
And sowing [is a duty] toward the earth. 1.31.
Bringing soil from elsewhere to fill it constitutes an additional purification of the ground. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says:
"The ground is purified by four means: by digging, by burning, by sprinkling with water, and by the treading of cows; but fifthly, by smearing. (VaDh 3.57) || 1.31 ||
As with cloth, so it is with ropes, split bamboo, and leather. || 1.32 ||

*Vidala* refers to that which is made from the split-bamboo, cane, reed, and so forth; others say it also includes that made from a broom (*piccha*). Regarding the three beginning with rope, purification is by washing, just as for clothes. But Paiṭhīnasi says: "Ropes, split-bamboo, and skins, when touched by those who are untouchable, are purified by sprinkling. (1.32)
Or there is the discarding of those that are utterly corrupted. 1.33.
This refers to the same subject matter as that [passage] by Vasiṣṭha beginning with "with liquor, urine, or feces" (VaDh 3.59). The word "vā" (or) serves to set aside the alternative position. 1.33.
One should begin the purification facing either the east or the north. 1.34.

Because of the statement that "one may begin the ritual action according to one's wish," there is no restriction regarding direction for acts such as washing the feet. However, Āpastamba says, "The washing of the feet is toward the west" (ĀpDh 1.31.2). The mention of "purification" is intended to indicate the rule of direction not only for sipping water (ācamana) but also for purification after voiding urine, excrement, and so forth. (1.34)

Seated in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, having washed his hands up to the wrists, and remaining silent, he should sip water three or four times so that it touches his heart. 1.35.

This is one sentence. At the time of sipping water (ācamana), the phrase "seated in a clean, unpolluted place" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the rule "seated, standing, or bent forward. Having placed the right arm between the knees—that is, in the middle of the two knees—[the left hand is not necessarily required], because only the "right arm" has been mentioned. The term "wearing the sacred thread" (*yajñopavītī*) is stated here even though it was already established in its proper place, for the purpose of ensuring it remains in its position, or rather, for the purpose of arranging the upper garment. Thus says Āpastamba: "In the service of teachers, elders, and guests; during the fire-oblation (*homa*), the act of recitation (*japa*), eating, sipping water, and Vedic study, one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder. And: "Or else, the thread alone serves the purpose of the *upavīta*" [ĀpDh 1.15.1; 2.4.22]. Having washed both hands up to that point from which the jewel is bound—that is, up to the wrist (*maṇibandha*)—one should remain silent, refraining from making noise. The phrase "touching the heart" is intended to define the quantity: one should sip as much water as reaches the heart, namely, as much as a bean sinks in; this should be done three or four times. Where the sipping is prescribed with a mantra, there it is performed four times along with that mantra; elsewhere, the option is three times. || 1.35 ||
It is wiped twice. || 1.36 ||
After each [sipping], one should wipe both lips with the hand using water.
And he should sprinkle water on his feet. || 1.37 ||
And by the word "ca" (and), the head [is also included]. 1.37.
And he should touch the cavities of the head. 1.38.

"Head-born" (*śīrṣaṇyāni*) means those located on the head; that is to say, those originating from the head. "Apertures" (*khāni*) refers to the sense organs. One should touch them. Here, the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate that one should touch each individual sense organ. (1.38)
And one should place it upon the head. || 1.39 ||
By the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that one should touch both the navel and the head with all the fingers. || 1.39 ||
Having slept, having eaten, and having sneezed, once again. || 1.40 ||
Furthermore, on account of sleep and other such causes, one should sip water twice; this is the meaning. 1.40.
In the case of things stuck between the teeth, they are treated like the teeth themselves, except when touched by the tongue. (1.41)
Regarding food particles stuck between the teeth or smears of leavings, there is no impurity, except when touched by the tongue; otherwise, they are treated like the teeth themselves. 1.41.
Regarding that as well—some say [it lasts] until death. 1.42.
Even when there is contact with the tongue, as long as the remnants do not fall from their place, there is no impurity. || 1.42 ||
One should know that regarding those who have fallen [from their vows], it is like [the case of] the outflows; one remains pure even while swallowing them.

"Exudation" (āsrāva) refers to saliva. "Swallowing" (nigaraṇa) refers to its entry into the interior. Regarding the statement that one is pure even while swallowing what has been spat out, the expression "one should know it to be like exudation" is intended to indicate that, in the case of exudation, one is pure precisely because of swallowing. [1.1.43]
Drops that do not fall upon the body do not make one impure with remnants; they do not constitute leavings. 1.44.

"Oral" (*mukhya*) means pertaining to the mouth. "Drops" (*vipruṣaḥ*) are droplets of saliva. When they fall upon the ground or other such surfaces, they do not cause one to become ritually impure through leavings (*ucchiṣṭatām*).
The removal of stains and odors from an impure substance constitutes purification. 1.45.
"Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, snot, nails, phlegm, tears, and rheum from the eyes—these twelve are the impurities of men.

Thus says Manu. All of this is intended by the term *amedhya* (impure). Purity is attained by removing that odor and that stain to the extent that they are eliminated. In this regard, for that impurity which consists of odor alone, there must be the removal of that odor; for that which consists of both odor and stain, there must be the removal of both. (1.45)
That [cleansing] is first performed with water and with clay. 1.46.

First, there is the removal of odor and stains with water; then, the removal of adhering odor and stains with both earth and water. This is the purification for hands, feet, and so forth when smeared with impurities, since specific rules for metallic objects and the like have already been stated previously.
And [the same applies] in cases of contact with urine, feces, oil, exudations, and food. || 1.47 ||

The word "ca" (and) serves to include what was previously mentioned. "Sneha" means semen. "Visraṃsana" means the discharge or removal of urine, feces, and oily secretions. "Abhyavahāra" refers to an inedible substance; contact with such a substance is intended. On these occasions, purification is to be performed as before with earth and water. (1.47)
And where the sacred tradition (āmnāya) would enjoin [it]. 1.48.

In whatever matter a particular purification the tradition (āmnāya) may prescribe, that alone shall apply there; as, for example, the washing with water at the Mārjālīya fire of the *camasa* cups that have been smeared with remnants. 1.48.

Now follows the rule for approaching the teacher: having grasped the left hand [of the teacher] except for the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying, "Recite, sir! Thereupon, with his eyes fixed on the teacher and his mind concentrated, he should touch his vital breaths (prāṇas) with *darbha* grass. 1.49.

With his own right hand—since the word "left" is used as a qualification, it is understood that [he uses] the right—he should grasp the teacher's left foot, excluding the big toe (*anaṅguṣṭha*, i.e., with the toes). Having grasped it, he should address the teacher, saying, "Recite, sir! In this regard, having fixed his mind and eyes upon the teacher, he should remain attentive. His vital breaths are the sense organs located in the head; the student must perform the ritual rinsing (*upasparśana*) of those [organs] with *darbha* grass according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*). 1.49.
The three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) consist of fifteen measures (mātrās). || 1.50 ||

The word "should be performed" (*kāryā*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Having rubbed [the hands] along the sides of the knees, one should make a single snap; that constitutes one *mātrā*. One should hold the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) for as long a time as it takes to complete those fifteen [snap-counts]; that is one *prāṇāyāma*. Three of these should be performed. Manu says:
"One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while the breath is restrained; that is called *prāṇāyāma*. Thus it is said.
And the seat is [placed] on blades of grass with their points directed eastward. 1.51.
He made his seat upon darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward; "must be done" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 1.51 ||
The five vyāhṛtis preceded by Oṃ and ending with Satya [are the five Brahma-mantras]. || 1.52 ||

The *vyāhṛtis* are five: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *satyam*, and *puruṣaḥ*. However, in this context, the fourth should be called the *puruṣa-vyāhṛti* and the fifth the *satya-vyāhṛti*. Furthermore, each of these should be preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*). (1.52)
In the morning, one should perform the clasping of the teacher's feet. 1.53.
Every day at dawn, one must perform the clasping of the teacher’s feet. Manu says:
"The clasping of the teacher’s feet should be performed with crossed hands;
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand" (MDh 2.72). 1.53.
And at the beginning and end of the recitation of the Brahman, [the *praṇava* is uttered]. 1.54.
"Brahman" refers to the Veda; "recitation" means teaching it. In that regard, one must perform the clasping of the teacher's feet both at the beginning and at the end.
Having been permitted, he should sit facing east; the disciple should sit to his right, facing either east or north. 1.55.
Permitted by the teacher, he should sit to the teacher's right, facing either east or north; the choice depends on the requirements of the task at hand. 1.55.
And the recitation of the Sāvitrī verse. 1.56.
"This [verse] beginning with 'tat savitur vareṇyam' is the one dedicated to the deity Savitṛ, and no other; it must be recited at every study session as part of the *anuvacana*. (1.56)
In the case of taking [something] from a Brahmin, it is the same as from the beginning. 1.57.

That which has been stated beginning with “having grasped the left hand with his own hand” [GDh 1.49] and ending with the recitation of the Sāvitrī verse must be performed at the very beginning, at the time of receiving the Veda—the *brahman*—from the teacher (*guru*). This applies immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*) and at the time of the instruction on the Sāvitrī. However, on a daily basis, one should perform the grasping of the teacher’s feet and sit down only when permitted, both at the commencement and the conclusion of the morning study. || 1.57 ||
The syllable *oṃ* [is used] elsewhere as well. 1.58.
The syllable *oṃ* should be uttered even on occasions other than the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*; the meaning is that it should be done every day at the time of study. || 1.58 ||
But if he returns in the interval, there must be a renewed initiation. 1.59.

"Going between" refers to passing between the teacher and the pupil. Upon anyone passing between them, the formal approach (*upasadana*) must be performed again. The formal approach consists of the rites beginning with "with the left hand" [GDh 1.49] and ending with "the syllable *Oṃ* even elsewhere" [GDh 1.58]. || 1.59 ||
For [killing] a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a cat, there shall be a fast for three days and staying away from home. 1.60.

If dogs or other such animals pass between [the teacher and the student], a three-day fast and a stay away from home must be observed; "stay away from home" means dwelling elsewhere than at the teacher’s household. Manu, however, states:
"In the case of cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, and mongooses passing between, one should know that there is no study for a day and a night" (MDh 4.126).
That [rule] concerns the study for the purpose of retention; however, the rule of Gautama concerns the study for the purpose of acquisition. 1.60.
For others, there shall be breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the consumption of clarified butter (ghṛtaprāśana).

For others—meaning animals such as cattle and the like, excluding dogs and so forth—if they enter between [the teacher and the disciple], three *prāṇāyāmas* must be performed and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) must also be performed. All of this is an expiation for the disciple, not for the teacher; however, according to others, it applies to both. 1.61.
And likewise when studying near a cremation ground. 1.62.

Regarding *abhi* in the sense of "above," such as over a cremation ground, and likewise in the case of studying [the Veda], the penance is as follows: breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). The repetition [of the rule] is for the purpose of concluding the section on teaching. 1.62.
Thus ends the first chapter in the first book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrī-Gautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the second chapter.
In connection with the subject of initiation, the duties of one who has not been initiated are stated:
before initiation, there is freedom of action, freedom of speech, and freedom of eating. 2.1.

The rule "for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth [year]" refers to the subject of initiation (*upanayana*) in times of distress. "Acting according to desire" means acting according to one's own will. "He may even sell things that should not be sold; he may live even by the 'dog's livelihood' (*śvavṛtti*). "Speaking according to desire" means speaking vulgarities, falsehoods, and so forth. "Eating according to desire" refers to eating garlic, stale food, and the like, or eating four or five times a day—one who does this is so described. However, there is no over-extension to such acts as killing a Brāhmaṇa or drinking liquor. (2.1)
From what has not been offered as an oblation. 2.2.

The *hutaśeṣa* consists of the remnants of the sacrificial oblation, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake. One who eats that is called *hutāt*; one who is the opposite of that is *ahutāt*. For it is said: "One who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) should not eat the *huta*. (2.2)
A celibate student. || 2.3 ||

This is an exception to the general rule regarding sexual conduct and the like; for since it has been stated that [the period lasts] until the sixteenth year, there is the possibility of attachment to women. Therefore, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should be one who has conquered his senses. And so it is said in another *Smṛti*: "The penance for a transgressor (*avakīrṇin*) is lost; he becomes pure by means of the vow of the *avakīrṇin*, but after [the sixteenth year], neither by the initiation nor by the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. (2.3)
He becomes one whose urine and excrement have been properly disposed of. 2.4.

He for whom urine and feces occur as they happen is so described; thus, one may perform the act even facing east or another direction. Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding the location, such as the rule "not on the ground without having covered it" (GDh 9.38). 2.4.
For him, no rule for sipping water exists. || 2.5 ||
Because mental visualization is prohibited, sipping water (ācamana) is permitted for him, just as it is for women and Śūdras. 2.5.
Except for wiping, sprinkling with water, and washing. 2.6.

Excluding *apamārjana* and the like, there is no ritual for sipping water (*ācamana*). This means that *apamārjana* and so forth do exist [as alternatives]. Although *apamārjana* and the rest are not included within the ritual for sipping water, they are nevertheless prescribed by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). *Atramārjana* (here, *apamārjana*) is the wiping with a hand moistened with water of that which is smeared with food remnants and the like. *Pradhāvana* is the washing with water and clay of that which is smeared with impurities and the like. *Avokṣaṇa* is the sprinkling [of water] upon one who has been touched by a woman in her courses and so forth. This applies to those who are extremely young; for those over six years of age, they require a bath. For such an uninitiated child, this much is the highest limit of penance (*prāyaścitta*) in the event of transgressing the rules regarding acting according to one's own will and so forth. Regarding this, another *Smṛti* states:
A child who is less than sixteen years old, as well as one who is eighty years of age,
women, and those who are ill, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five years old,
the teacher and likewise a friend shall perform the penance for the sake of purification.
Therefore, for this most ignorant one, there is neither offense nor sin;
consequently, neither royal punishment nor penance is prescribed for him. (2.6)
There is no impurity resulting from touching that [corpse]. 2.7.

Because of that touching (*upasparśana*), there would be no impurity even from the touching of one who has not yet performed the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), or one touched by a woman in her courses (*udakyā*) and the like. "Touching" (*upasparśana*) here means the contact of one who has been touched with one who has not been touched; therefore, bathing is not to be performed. Furthermore, there is no sipping of water (*ācamana*) even from touching one who is defiled by food remnants or one who has just voided urine or feces. This also applies only prior to the age of six. For what purpose, then, is purification prescribed for him? It is certainly not for the sake of performing religious rites, nor for the sake of fitness for touch, since he remains fit for touch even without having performed purification. We say it is for the sake of protection. And so says another *Smṛti*:
"For the sake of protecting a child, one should practice purification from the fifth year onwards. (2.7)
But one should certainly not employ him for the Agnihotra sacrifice or for the offering of bali-oblations. 2.8.

One should not employ this [boy] who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) in the *agnihotra*, the *aupāsana-homa*, and so forth, nor in the *bali-haraṇa*, the *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth; that is to say, one must not employ him. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is implied that he should not be employed even in other rites accompanied by mantras. The particle "only" (*eva*) is used for emphasis. Now, Āśvalāyana says: "From the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) onwards, one should perform the domestic rites (*gṛhya*) oneself, or the wife, or the son, or a daughter, or a resident pupil. And the followers of the Sāmaveda (*chandoga*) state that the wife should offer the oblation; thus, in this alternative permitted for the wife, daughter, and others, the meaning is "but certainly not him [the uninitiated boy]. (2.8)
He should not utter the word "Brahman," except when offering the *svadhā* libation. 2.9.

"Brahman" refers to the Veda. One should not cause this [Veda] to be recited by, nor should one utter it oneself, for one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). Is this so without exception? No, he says; "except for the pouring of the *svadhā*. This is an elliptical expression for all ancestral rites (*pitrya-karman*). This is because it is seen in the *Vasiṣṭha-dharma-sūtra*: "Except for water-rites and those connected with the *svadhā* and the ancestors" (VaDh 2.7). Furthermore, there is the rule: "A son who has not yet mastered the syllables is worthy of the sacraments of his parents," and so forth. If no other [initiated person] is available, then all ancestral rites should be performed at that time by having him learn the mantras first. 2.9.
The rule [of conduct] begins with the initiation ceremony (upanayana). 2.10.

The restriction concerning fire, fuel, and so forth that will be stated hereafter applies precisely to those who have undergone initiation (*upanayana*) and the like; since [the rules] are interrupted for one not initiated, this [section] is intended for the sake of the qualification of the initiated. 2.10.
The religious life has been explained. 2.11.

The practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) that was prescribed for one who has not been initiated is the same for one who has been initiated as well. Now, it may be objected that a prohibition will be stated later in the rule, "gazing at and touching women" (GDh 2.16). Nevertheless, this present verse is intended to prohibit such acts as recollecting them or speaking of them. 2.11.
Regarding fire, fuel, eating, and conduct. || 2.12 ||

The kindling of the fire, the fuel, and the oblation; the collection of alms is *bhaikṣa*; wandering from house to house for that purpose is *bhaikṣacaraṇa*. These two must be performed daily. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having brought the fuel from afar, he should place it in the open air;
and evening and morning, he should offer oblations into the fire with them, remaining unwearied."
“Having failed to go on alms-round and having failed to kindle the fire, one who is not ill shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* for seven nights.
[MDh 2.186–87] But Āpastamba says: “Some say that the worship of the fire should take place only in the evening. [ĀpDh 1.4.17] || 2.12 ||
Truthful speech. 2.13.
One who has been initiated must speak only the truth. 2.13.
Sipping water. 2.14.
"Upasparśana" means bathing; that too must be performed day after day. 2.14.
Some [say it consists of] the gift of a cow and so forth. 2.15.

The vow called *godāna* is to be performed in the sixteenth year; it is the second among the vows. Some teachers of the *Chandoga* school maintain that the ritual bathing (*snāna*) begins with the *godāna*, because even for this [period], he is bound by the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), just like one who has been initiated previously. This is a prohibition against the daily bath (*nityasnāna*); however, the occasional bath (*naimittika*) must be performed. In that case, the immersion is done like [holding] a staff, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "One should not bathe in water while boasting" (ĀpDh 1.2.30). || 2.15 ||
And there is the state of being external to the junctions. 2.16.

He for whom the two twilights—morning and evening—occur outside the village is one whose twilights are external (*bahiḥsaṃdhya*); his state is such that the twilight worship must be performed only outside the village. (2.16)
Regarding when he should tell that story, he says:
"He should stand during the first watch and sit during the last, remaining silent as long as the stars are visible, or until the stars have disappeared. (2.17)

One should stand during the morning twilight and sit during the evening twilight. The accusative case is used here to denote duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*). He explains the commencement and conclusion of standing and sitting: beginning at a time when light is still present, until another light is no longer seen. That is to say, in the morning, beginning with the light of the stars until the light of the sun is seen; and in the evening, beginning with the light of the sun until the stars are seen. During that entire time, one should remain restrained in speech. And so says Manu:
"One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the appearance of the sun."
"But one should sit facing the west when the stars have clearly appeared," thus [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.101]. 2.17.
One should not look at the sun. 2.18.

This prohibition regarding the constant looking at the sun applies to the religious student (*brahmacārin*); however, for the graduate (*snātaka*), there is this rule: "One should never look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun; nor at the eclipsed sun, nor at the sun reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky" (MDh 4.37). 2.18.

One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, anointing the body, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, speaking, playing musical instruments, bathing, brushing the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear. 2.19.

One should avoid honey and the rest. Honey is that produced by bees. Meat is that of deer and other animals. Fragrance refers to sandalwood and the like. Garlands are flowers. Day-sleep is sleeping during the day. Eye-ointment is for the eyes. Anointing is the rubbing of oil on the body. A vehicle is a cart and so forth. An umbrella and a parasol are well known. Desire is sexual union with women. Anger is wrath. Greed is the longing for material objects. Delusion is the absence of discernment. Idle talk is excessive chatter. Playing musical instruments refers to the lute and others. Bathing for pleasure is the washing of the body from the neck downwards with warm water and such. Cleaning the teeth is the removal of dental impurities. Exultation is an overflow of the mind resulting from the attainment of what is desired. Dancing and singing are well known. Slander is the recounting of the faults of others. Fear is the cause of fear, such as entering a forest wilderness; this [category] should also be understood to include exultation. (2.19)
Upon seeing the teacher, one should cover the neck, refrain from leaning on a support, and avoid stretching out the feet. 2.20.

"Gurus" refers to fathers, teachers, and so forth. In a place suitable for seeing them, one should avoid such things as covering the neck with a cloth. "Covering the neck" (*kaṇṭhaprāvṛtam*) means wrapping the neck with a garment or similar item. "Squatting on the thighs" (*avasakthikā*) means remaining in a position with one foot placed upon the thigh. "Leaning against" (*apāśrayaṇam*) means sitting while leaning against a wall, pillar, or the like. "Stretching out the feet" is well known. The meaning is that one should remain in the presence of elders with the restraint of modesty. (2.20)
Spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. || 2.21 ||
"One should avoid" means: spitting is the noisy expulsion of phlegm from the throat; laughing is mirth; yawning is a gape; and cracking the knuckles is the noisy rubbing of the finger joints. (2.21)
Looking at or touching a woman when there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse. || 2.22 ||

The "beholding" of women is the detailed examination of their limbs, not a mere chance glance; "touching" is physical contact. He should avoid these as well. Because of the statement "when there is suspicion of sexual intercourse," there is no fault in the case of young girls, the elderly, or those who are ill, nor for one who himself is in such a state [of incapacity].
Gambling, service to the base, taking what is not given, and violence. || 2.23 ||

"One should avoid gambling. Gambling is of two kinds, distinguished by whether it involves living beings (*prāṇin*) or non-living things (*aprāṇin*). Gambling with living beings includes, for example, fighting rams; gambling with non-living things includes, for example, playing with dice. "Service to the base" means service to those of low birth and so forth; it is both base and a form of service, such as carrying water and performing other menial tasks. "Taking what is not given" is the taking of that which has not been given by anyone, even if it is discarded or ownerless. "Violence" is the infliction of pain upon living beings. (2.23)
The names of the teacher, his son, his wife, and the initiated disciple. || 2.24 ||

One should avoid using the names of one's teacher, his son, or his wife, as well as the name of one who has been initiated. Even when out of sight, one should employ a name that is not based on their personal attributes. 2.24.
The syntactical connection of this sūtra is also with the verb "one should avoid," extending from honey and meat up to this point.
A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid intoxicating liquor. (2.25)

A *brāhmaṇa* [should avoid] harsh, indecent words that cause distress to others; "intoxicant" (*madya*) refers to substances that produce intoxication. He should always avoid both those and that. Because of the expression "always for a *brāhmaṇa*," there is no transgression for *kṣatriyas* and *vaiśyas* who are householders in the consumption of intoxicants other than those made from flour (*paiṣṭī*). (2.25)
He should sleep on a low bed or seat, rise before [others], and go to rest after [others]. 2.26.
The meaning of this is clear in the *Mānava* (Manusmṛti):
"In the presence of his guru, his bed and seat must always be low;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him" (MDh 2.194). || 2.23 ||
Restrained in speech, arms, and belly. || 2.27 ||
Restraint of speech is the avoidance of excessive chatter; restraint of the arms is the absence of actions such as crushing clods of earth; restraint of the belly is moderation in eating. || 2.27 ||
One should mention the name and lineage of the teacher with respect. || 2.28 ||

One should mention one's own name and lineage after having bowed to the teacher. "After having bowed" means having properly bowed, that is, without concealment. Another says: one should mention the teacher’s name and lineage after having bowed—that is, having become properly bowed down or humble. (2.28)
And likewise, when one has honored that which is most excellent. || 2.29 ||

"Honored" means worshipped in the world; "superior" means excelling through knowledge and other qualities. Regarding those two as well, one should likewise bow down properly. On this point, there is another traditional text (*smṛti*):
"The teacher, his son, his wife, an initiated person, a guru, a father, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, and likewise a mother."
A wise man should not speak harshly even when bowed down to by his well-wishing father-in-law, his husband, his mother, or his sister.

The word "and so forth" (ity-evaṃśabdaḥ) in the phrase "in worship and in what is beneficial" extends by analogy everything that has been said regarding the teacher, both in its specific form and in its full extent. By this, even the bed, seat, and so on, must be low when in their presence. (2.29)
Leaving behind his bed, seat, and dwelling place, he gave his assent. || 2.30 ||
When the teacher issues a command, the pupil, giving his assent with a reply, should rise from his bed, seat, or standing place and go toward him. 2.30.
Approaching [the teacher] is [required] because of the verbal instruction, even when [the teacher] is not seen. || 2.31 ||
If the teacher, standing outside, speaks without having seen the disciple, then the disciple must approach and go toward him; he must not show disrespect by thinking, "I am not being seen. || 2.31 ||
One should remain standing with feet placed on the ground when seeing a teacher, as well as when attending to the lateral movement of breath. 2.32.

When the teacher occupies a lower place or seat while one is oneself situated on a high place or seat, then, upon seeing the teacher, one should rise. One should also rise upon seeing the teacher when attending to crosswinds or during the voiding of urine and feces. The word "ca" (and) serves to connect these instances with the preceding rule. (2.32)
One should follow him as he walks. || 2.33 ||
One should follow after the teacher when he is walking. 2.33.
Karma is that which is called "that which makes known. 2.34.

The meaning is that, having informed the teacher, "I shall perform this as atonement for whatever duty remains to be done by this disciple," he should understand for himself what is required of the teacher—such as fetching water-jars and so forth—and having performed it, he should live by reporting to him, "It has been done. 2.34.
When summoned, he remains meditative. || 2.35 ||
"Being summoned by the teacher, one should study, but one should not initiate the lesson on one's own accord. (2.35)
One should be intent upon what is pleasant and beneficial. (2.36)

One should be devoted and intent upon that which is both pleasing and beneficial to the teacher. "Pleasing" means that which causes satisfaction at the present time; "beneficial" means that which produces [satisfaction] at a later time. || 2.36 ||
And the same applies to his wife’s sons. 2.37.
The wife and sons of that teacher—toward them also one should behave in this same manner as toward the teacher himself. (2.37)
The exception to this is as follows: eating the leavings of food, bathing [him], adorning him, washing his feet, massaging him, and clasping his feet [are not permitted]. (2.38)

"Eating the remnants" means eating what remains after [the teacher] has eaten. "Bathing" is the sprinkling with water for ablution preceded by the massaging of the head and limbs with bathing powders and the like. "Adorning" means decorating. "Washing the feet" is well known. "Massaging" refers to anointing with oil, rubbing the body, and so forth. "Greeting by clasping the feet" is as previously described [at MDh 2.72], beginning with "with crossed hands. These acts are not to be performed toward the teacher's wife or sons; therefore, it is established that they are to be performed only toward the teacher himself. (2.38)
Now follows the counter-exception regarding the clasping of the feet:
one must clasp the feet of the wives of one's gurus upon returning from a journey abroad. 2.39.
Having returned from a journey after having gone abroad, one should perform the salutation by clasping the feet of the wives of one's teachers. (2.39)
Even there, it is not [the case] for many young women who have entered into worldly affairs. 2.40.

However, some teachers maintain that for young wives of gurus, even if they have been away from home, a student who has reached the age of sixteen and is engaged in formal conduct should not perform the salutation by clasping the feet. 2.40.

It has been stated [above] regarding the maintenance of the sacred fires and the practice of begging for alms. Since the fuel for the fires is restricted to each individual household, he now prescribes the rule for the common practice of begging for alms:
"The practice of begging for alms from all social classes (varṇas), with the exception of those accused of grave sins and those who have fallen from their caste. (2.41)

"Sārvavarṇika" means occurring among all castes. One should wander for alms among all castes, excluding those who have been formally accused and those who have fallen from their caste. "Those who have been accused" refers to those guilty of minor offenses (upapātakin). 2.41.
The word "existence" (bhava) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of each section] according to the sequence of the letters. 2.42.

In the two words "bhikṣāṃ dehi" (give alms), the word *bhavat* (your honor) should be employed in the vocative case at the beginning, middle, and end according to the sequence of syllables. In the case of women, it takes the feminine gender. For a Brāhmaṇa: *brāhmaṇasya bhavan bhikṣāṃ dehi* (O honorable Brāhmaṇa, give alms). For a Brāhmaṇī: *brahmaṇyāṃ bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi* (O honorable Brāhmaṇī, give alms). For a Kṣatriya: *kṣatriyasya bhikṣāṃ bhavan dehi* (O honorable Kṣatriya, give alms); *bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*. For a Vaiśya: *vaiśyasya bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavan* (O honorable Vaiśya, give alms); *bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*. 2.42.
If [the aforementioned] teachers, kinsmen, gurus, or one's own [relatives] are not available, [one may seek them] elsewhere. 2.43.

The teacher has said: "kinsmen" refers to paternal uncles and others who are *sapiṇḍas*; "elders" refers to maternal uncles and others; "one's own" means those belonging to oneself. "In the absence of alms elsewhere," one should go for alms to the houses of the teacher and others. (2.43)
Among these, one should avoid each preceding one more than the following.

Among those [categories], such as the teacher and others, one should avoid whichever is mentioned first. In the absence of [a place] elsewhere, [one may stay] in one's own house; in its absence, among the gurus; in its absence, among kinsmen; and in its absence, in the teacher’s house. 2.44.
Having offered [the food] to the teacher and being permitted by him, he should eat. 2.45.
Having announced to the teacher, "This alms-food has been brought," he should eat it when permitted by him; if the teacher should take it himself, then he should bring something else. 2.45.
In his absence, [the debt shall be paid] by his wife, his son, or his fellow student. || 2.46 ||
In the absence of the teacher, having informed the teacher’s wife or others as appropriate, he should eat with their permission. 2.46.
Restraining his speech, being satisfied, and not being greedy,
he should set down water nearby.

He remained silent for as long as he was eating; being satisfied by the mere sight of the food, rejoicing, and not being distracted—meaning not forming excessive desire—he "placed near," which, with the causative sense internalized, means "having caused to be placed near," namely water or a water-vessel. 2.47.
He states the method for instructing a disciple: "The instruction of a disciple is by means of non-punishment. (2.48)
"Killing" means striking. A disciple should be disciplined by the teacher through means such as rebukes, even if not struck. (2.48)
If one is unable [to do so], [one may strike] with thin strips of rope or split bamboo. || 2.49 ||

If he cannot be disciplined by means of threats and the like, then he should be punished by striking him with a thin rope or with a split bamboo cane; for even though these two are mentioned in a copulative compound, there is an option between them, as seen in the *Mānava* [Manusmṛti 8.229]: "With a rope or with a split bamboo cane. Even after striking him with those two, which are weak, he may still be disciplined. 2.49.
One who strikes with anything else shall be punished by the king. || 2.50 ||
If he strikes with his hand or other means out of a fit of anger, the teacher is to be punished by the king; thus has the residence of the disciple in the teacher's family been described. 2.50.
To the question "For how long a time? he says:
"He should observe the life of a student (brahmacarya) for twelve years regarding one Veda. (2.51)

Although each Veda has many branches—namely, the Rigveda in twenty-one divisions, the Yajurveda in one hundred branches, the Sāmaveda with a thousand paths, and the Atharvaveda in nine divisions—nevertheless, in this context, by the word "Veda" is intended only as many branches of each Veda as have been adopted by former authorities through study and ritual practice. He who studies one Veda shall observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) at the teacher's house for twelve years. (2.51)
Or, in all cases, there should be twelve for each. 2.52.

But he who is capable of studying the four Vedas—meaning twelve years for each Veda, totaling forty-eight years—is as Āpastamba has stated: "For one who has been initiated, the period of residence as a student in the teacher's household is forty-eight years" (ĀpDh 1.2.11–12). 2.52.
Or [the rule applies] up to the point of grasping. 2.53.
For as long a time as it takes to be able to master one, two, three, or four Vedas—such is the duration [of the vow]. || 2.53 ||
At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with a gift of wealth. || 2.54 ||
Upon the completion of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with wealth as the purpose; he is to be asked: "O Teacher, please accept this wealth. (2.54)
Or, having performed [the ritual], he may bathe with permission. 2.55.

Then, having done what was commanded by the teacher—"Bring [the materials]!"—he should perform his bath. Or, when permitted by him with the words, "My child, I am satisfied with your virtues alone; enough with wealth," he should perform the bath, which is the *samāvartana* ceremony. (2.55)
"The teacher is the best of gurus; some say the mother, others say the mother. (2.56)

Among teachers such as one's father and others, the teacher (ācārya) possessing the aforementioned characteristics is the most excellent. For he indeed produces him through knowledge; that is the superior birth. Therefore, when there is a gathering of many teachers, he alone is to be honored first. However, some teachers consider the mother to be the most excellent. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"Ten times more venerable than a sub-teacher (upādhyāya) is a teacher; a hundred teachers are equal to a father;
and a mother exceeds the father tenfold in terms of respect. (VaDh 13.48)

Āpastamba also states: "The mother undertakes many tasks for the sake of her son's status; therefore, service toward her is obligatory even if she has fallen from her caste. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is intended to mark the completion of the chapter. 2.56.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the third chapter.
Some state that there is an alternative classification of these stages of life. 3.1.

Regarding this student who has thus studied the Veda, some teachers say that the four stages of life (*āśrama*) to be described hereafter are to be chosen optionally; others, however, say they are to be practiced cumulatively. On this point, Āpastamba states: “Among all of these, one who conducts himself without distraction according to the instructions attains security” (ĀpDh 2.21.2), and also: “Having understood the duties, he may undertake whichever he desires” (ĀpDh 2.21.5). Likewise, after describing the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya-āśrama*), Baudhāyana says: “From this very stage, one who remains a student goes forth into the wandering life” (ĀpDh 2.21.8). But by Manu, their cumulative practice is shown.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who seeks liberation without having discharged them falls downward. All these stages, moreover, when entered upon in due order according to the scriptures, [lead to the goal].
"They lead the Brahmin who acts according to what has been taught to the supreme goal. (MDh 6.88) Thus ends [verse] 3.1.
What, then, are those stages of life? The student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller. (3.2)

Although this stage was previously mentioned as the *brahmacarya-āśrama*, what is intended here is the state of a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*) who desires to enter it. A *bhikṣu* is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*); a *vaikhānasa* is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Because he conducts himself according to the path taught by the *Vaikhānasas*, that stage of life is indicated here as the primary one. In other scriptures, the *vaikhānasa* is the third and the *bhikṣu* is the fourth stage of life; however, the change in order here is for the purpose of excluding the *vaikhānasa* from the category of "the three previously mentioned stages of life" (GDh 28.49). 3.2.
Among them, the householder is the source of the others, because they do not produce offspring on their own. 3.3.

Among those residing in all four stages of life (*āśrama*), the householder is the source and the place of origin. It is only by being produced by a householder that one becomes eligible for the other four stages of life, because procreation is forbidden for those residing in stages of life other than that of the householder. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"Caṇḍālas, those who have fallen from their vows, wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), and ascetics (*tāpasa*)—the offspring born of these should be made to dwell together with the Caṇḍālas. (3.3)
Now, intending to explain the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma), he speaks first of the student (brahmacārin), who was mentioned at the outset:
"In that regard, [the duties] of the student have been stated" (3.4).

In that regard, among those [types of students], it is stated that for the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) as well, the same rules apply as those prescribed for the temporary student (upakurvāṇa), beginning with the statement: "The rule begins with the initiation ceremony" (GDh 2.10). || 3.4 ||
In this regard, the distinction is that dependence on the teacher lasts until the end. 3.5.5
Until his end, until the fall of the body, he should remain in the teacher’s family alone, devoted to service. 3.5.
He should recite [the mantra] with the remainder of the teacher's ritual duties. || 3.6 ||

Since the word *guru* is used here in reference to the *ācārya*, it is intended to include the parents as well. Therefore, while serving his *ācārya* and his parents, he should recite the Veda during the time remaining after that; he must not remain idle. (3.6)
In the absence of the guru, the livelihood is that of his offspring; in his absence, it is with an aged fellow-student or with the sacred fire. 3.7.

The conduct that has been prescribed toward the teacher is to be observed toward his son in his absence; in the absence of his son, toward an elder—whether superior in learning or in age; in the absence of an elder, toward a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*); and in the absence of a fellow student, it is to be performed toward the sacred fire. Toward the fire, the conduct consists of the offering of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) and other such rites. (3.7)
One who conducts himself thus, having conquered his senses, attains the world of Brahmā.
The meaning is clear. The state of having conquered the senses has been shown by Manu:
"That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled, neither rejoices nor becomes dejected, should be known as one who has conquered his senses" (MDh 2.98). 3.8.
And this is not in conflict with the subsequent [sections]. 3.9.

For the subsequent stages of life (*āśrama*) as well, whatever is not in conflict with this mode of conduct (*vṛtta*) is common to them; for example, the avoidance of gambling and similar activities. That which is in conflict is as follows: the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) for the wandering ascetic (*pravrajita*), residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukulavāsa*) for the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), and celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for the householder—this is another mode of conduct. Furthermore, the entire collection of duties (*dharmajāta*) belonging to the subsequent stages of life should be understood as applying to this one as well. Is this without distinction? No; it is that which is non-conflicting. That which does not conflict with the duties of this stage of life—such as "one should not converse with Mlecchas, the impure, or the unrighteous" (GDh 9.16)—applies to him too. (3.9)
Because there is much to be said, [the author] bypasses the householder, even though he is the one who follows in order, and speaks of the duties of the mendicant:
"A mendicant is one who has no accumulation" (3.10).
A store is a collection of material things; he would be devoid of that. || 3.10 ||
One whose semen is drawn upward. || 3.11 ||

Regarding the statement, “And this is not inconsistent with the following [rules]” (GDh 3.9), although mastery over the senses has already been established, the phrase “one whose semen flows upward” (ūrdhvaretas) is intended to mean that one should exert effort in such a way that the flow of the seminal fluid is brought to a halt. || 3.11 ||
He should remain fixed in one place during the rainy season.
The word *varṣā* is always used in the plural. When the rainy season has arrived, one should be firm in conduct and remain in one place. || 3.12 ||
One who seeks alms should go to the village. 3.13.
One should enter the village only at the time for alms; at all other times, one should dwell in temples and the like, or at the roots of trees. (3.13)
He should perform the lowest penance until he has ceased [the offense].

If, at the time for alms, one has been delayed by failing to reach a house, he should not enter that same house again on that day. Regarding this, Manu says: "A mendicant should always go for alms when the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed" (MDh 6.56). 3.14.
One whose desires have ceased. || 3.15 ||
One should not be intent on pronouncing blessings in the homes of others for the sake of obtaining an excessive amount of alms. || 3.15 ||
Restrained in speech, sight, and action. || 3.16 ||

Restraint of speech is silence. Restraint of the eyes is the non-engagement of the eyes on any spot other than the place where one steps. Restraint of action is for a mendicant not to transgress the prescribed duties. Regarding this, there is another Smṛti text concerning the contradiction of restraint of speech: "One does not censure even an ascetic who asks about the path, engages in the yoga of dharma, performs his private recitation (svādhyāya), or speaks the words 'give, please' for the sake of alms. (3.16)
Or he may wear a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts. (3.17)

*Kaupīna* is the name for the private parts; one should wear only as much clothing as is required to cover them. One should not wear anything more than that, such as upper garments or the like. (3.17)
Some say it is discarded after being washed. 3.18.
Some think that even that loincloth, if it has been discarded, worn out, and likewise abandoned by others, may be washed and worn. (3.18)
One should not take a limb of herbs or trees that is not detached. 3.19.

One should not take—that is, one should not accept—the limb of trees, creepers, and so forth that is not separated from its fruit, leaves, and so on, nor fallen from it; however, one may take what has fallen of its own accord. || 3.19 ||
He shall not dwell in a village for more than one night during the non-seasonal period. 3.20.

Excepting that season in which the rule of permanent residence has been prescribed—namely, the rainy season—in other seasons, he should not stay for a second night in a village where he has stayed for one night; thus it is said: "He should stay only one night in a village. (3.20)
He may be either shaven-headed or wear a topknot. || 3.21 ||

One should have all the hair shaved together with the top-knot (*śikhā*), or one may shave it except for the top-knot. By stating the alternative "either shaven-headed or wearing a top-knot," the option between adopting the single staff (*ekadaṇḍa*) or the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) is also indicated. Regarding this, there are *śruti* and *smṛti* texts:
"He whose top-knot consists of knowledge, and no other, like that of fire—he is called a wearer of the top-knot (*śikhin*), the wise man; not others who merely wear their hair. [Brahma Upaniṣad 87]
Having shaved his head including the top-knot, the wise man should discard the external thread;
then, taking up the single staff, he should practice the dharma of a mendicant—
whether he possesses the top-knot and the sacrificial thread, or whether he is fully awakened.
Having taken up the triple staff, he should practice the dharma of a mendicant.
One should avoid the destruction of seeds. 3.22.

Seeds are rice and so forth. Their "destruction" is threshing with a pestle and other tools; one should not perform that. By this, even the preparation of rice into cooked grain is implied, because he has ownership only over food that has been prepared. 3.22.
For he is equal toward all beings in both harming and favoring them. 3.23.
He who is the same toward injury and favor regarding living beings—remaining unchanged whether one causes harm or another bestows favor—is [the wise man]. (3.23)
One who does not initiate [action]. || 3.24 ||
One should not undertake any undertaking pertaining either to this world or the next. As Āpastamba has said: “One should live without desire for this world or the next. (3.24)
Now he speaks of the Vaikhānasa:
"The Vaikhānasa dwells in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, and is devoted to austerity. (3.25)

A *vaikhānasa* is a forest-dweller who, living in the forest, should eat roots and fruits, whether raw or cooked, but not boiled rice. Austerity consists in the emaciation of the body; therefore, he should consume even roots and fruits only in very small quantities. (3.25)
Having established the sacred fires according to the Śrāvaṇaka rite. 3.26.

The *Śrāvaṇaka* is a treatise (*śāstra*) concerning the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*). The remainder of the sense is that, having established the sacred fire according to the method prescribed therein, one should offer oblations in the evening and in the morning. (3.26)
He shall not eat vulgar food. 3.27.
One should not eat even fruits and roots that grow in cultivated fields. 3.27.
He is a worshiper of the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages. || 3.28 ||
Day after day, he should perform the five great sacrifices with wild fruits and roots alone. Regarding this, Manu says:
"With various pure forest products, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should offer these very same great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule" (MDh 6.5). 3.28.
He should be hospitable to all guests, with the exception of those who are prohibited. 3.29.

All those who approach him are his guests; however, there is no such restrictive rule as that "for a Brahmin, one who is not a Brahmin is not a guest" (GDh 5.39). Even in that case, he should avoid thieves, outcasts, and the like, with the exception of those whose exclusion is specifically forbidden. 3.29.
One may also consume [the meat] of a wild boar. 3.30.

*Vaiṣka* refers to meat killed by wild beasts such as tigers and the like; that too he may consume. The word *api* (also/even) has a secondary sense, meaning that even such meat is edible in the absence of fruits, roots, and so forth. Even in that case, one must exclude anything other than those [five] specified in the rule, "Five five-toed animals are edible. The phrase "excluding what is forbidden" (*pratiṣiddhavarjam*) is connected to both parts [of the verse] according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). 3.30.
He should not stand upon ground that has been ploughed by a ploughshare. || 3.31 ||
Dwelling in the forest, he should not occupy a place that has been ploughed with a plow. || 3.31 ||
And he should not enter a village. 3.32.
Even for one dwelling in the forest, entering a village at will is forbidden. (3.32)
He has matted hair and is clothed in bark and deerskin. || 3.33 ||

The *jaṭila* is one who maintains his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails; he wears a garment made of bark or *darbha* grass and an upper garment of deerskin, as is seen in the established rules of other *smṛtis*. (3.33)
One should not eat more than once a year.
When a year has passed, or even more than a year, he should not eat even forest-grown food. Regarding this, Manu says:
"In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard what was previously collected and produced during the year, as well as worn-out clothes, flowers, roots, and fruits" (MDh 6.15). 3.34.
The stages of life (āśrama) have been described, and both their optional alternatives and their combination have also been shown. [The author] now demonstrates their relative importance:
"But the teachers [maintain] the single stage of life, because the householder's state is directly enjoined. (3.35)

The word *tu* expresses a distinction. In all the Vedic scriptures, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, the duties of the householder alone—such as the Agnihotra and others—are prescribed most extensively. Therefore, all teachers consider the state of the householder to be the sole stage of life (*ekāśramya*) and the primary one. For those who are incapable [of fulfilling these], the duties of the other stages of life are prescribed; this is because the other stages are directly enjoined and because they depend for their existence upon the householder stage. The repetition [of the verse] has been explained. (3.35)
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The duties of the householder are now declared:
A householder shall take a wife who is of equal caste, not previously married to another, and younger than himself. (4.1)

"Householder" (*gṛhastha*) is a designation used for one who is about to become so. Alternatively, it is intended to show that those duties which belong to a householder apply equally to a *snātaka* even before marriage. He should take—that is, marry—a wife who is his equal in birth and family, who has not been promised to another even by word of mouth, and who is of younger age. [4.1]
Marriage is [permitted] with those who do not share the same *pravara*. 4.2.

There is no marriage with those who share a single common *pravara*. For example, among the descendants of Aṅgiras—namely Harita, Kutsa, Piṅga, Śaṅkha, Darbha, Haimaka, and Bhava—the *pravaras* are Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva. The detailed enumeration of *pravaras*, such as "Hārīta should not marry a Kautsī," is to be found in the *Āpastamba-śrautasūtra* (4.2).
Beyond the seventh degree from paternal relatives and beyond the fifth degree from maternal relatives on the side of the progenitor. 4.3.

When counting the circle of paternal relatives starting from the father, one may marry a girl born beyond the seventh degree; when counting the circle of maternal relatives starting from the mother, one may marry a girl born beyond the fifth degree. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "beyond the seventh from the progenitor," this is established. For example, a husband who is barren or diseased may request his brother-in-law, saying, "Procreate a son in my field (womb). Or, when the lineage is in danger of extinction, elders may appoint a widow, as was seen when Vyāsa procreated Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others in the field of Vicitravīrya at the command of Satyavatī. As Yājñavalkya has said:

"A son begotten by appointment in the field of one who is childless belongs, according to the law, to the inheritance of both and is the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for both. This refers to that case [of the verse], namely, "and of the progenitor" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.127). 4.3.
Now, the varieties of marriage:
In the *brahma* rite, one should give away the daughter, having clothed and adorned her, to a man endowed with learning, good conduct, kinship, and virtue. 4.4.

*Vidyā* is knowledge of the Vedas; *cāritra* is the performance of prescribed duties; *bandhavaḥ* are kinsmen, such as maternal uncles and others; and *śīla* is faith in what is enjoined. To one endowed with these qualities, having clothed him in a pair of garments and adorned him according to his means, he should give his daughter. Such a marriage is designated as *brāhma*. (4.4)
The mantra for the formal union in the Prājāpatya rite is: "Let dharma be practiced together. (4.5)

In the marriage known as Prājāpatya, the formula for the giving [of the bride] is: "Let dharma be practiced together. Although the practice of dharma together occurs even in the Brāhma and other forms of marriage, nevertheless, by means of this mantra, an agreement is made that dharma must be practiced with her alone until death; one must not enter another stage of life, nor should another woman be taken as a wife. This is the distinction of the Prājāpatya from the Brāhma and others. "Having clothed and adorned her" is the same [as in the preceding rule]. (4.5)
In the r̥ṣi-rite, he should give a pair of cattle to the one who provides the maiden. 4.6.

In the marriage known as the Ārṣa, one should give a pair of cattle, consisting of a cow and a bull, to the father of the girl; the groom, or some relative of his, gives them. "Having clothed her and adorned her" is the same [as in the previous rule]. 4.6.
Giving to a priest within the sacrificial altar is the divine rite; it is performed after having adorned [the bride]. 4.7.

Within the altar, at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), when the officiating priest performs his ritual duties, the giving of a girl after having adorned her is the *daiva* marriage. Regarding the phrase "having clothed and adorned her," the mention of "having adorned her" in this context is for the purpose of adorning the groom as well with rings and other ornaments. (4.7)
The Gāndharva marriage is the union of two who desire each other of their own accord. 4.8.
The Gāndharva marriage is the union of a willing bride and a willing groom; from the word "herself," the desire of the groom is understood. (4.8)
The Āsura [form] consists of the bending down [of the bridegroom] by means of wealth on the part of those who possess women. || 4.9 ||

The Āsura marriage is that in which the father or other relatives of the girl—who possesses brothers—acquire honor through the payment of wealth or the giving of riches. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states: "The Āsura [arises] from the taking of wealth" (YDh 1.61). And Manu says:
"The giving away of a daughter by one's own will, after having given wealth to the kinsmen and according to one's ability to the girl herself, is called the Āsura dharma" (MDh 3.31).
Because of the expression "of those who have women," the giving of wealth to a maiden alone is not the basis for the Āsura form of marriage. And so says another Smṛti:
"That the kinsmen do not take a bride-price (śulka) from them is not a sale;
it is merely an honorarium for the maidens, out of kindness and not solely for its own sake. (4.9)
The Rākṣasa [form of marriage] is from taking by force. || 4.10 ||
The taking of a maiden by force after defeating her kinsmen is the Rākṣasa form of marriage. || 4.10 ||
The Paiśāca [form of marriage] results from approaching [the bride] while she is unconscious. 4.11.
When one approaches a woman while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged, without her conscious consent, that is the Paiśāca form of marriage. 4.11.
Thus the eight forms of marriage have been described; among them, the first four are lawful.
From the beginning, the four forms of marriage are lawful for all castes; they do not deviate from dharma and are praised. (4.12)
"Some say there are six. 4.13.
Some authorities say that six [forms of marriage] are lawful; they maintain that even the Gāndharva and Āsura forms do not deviate from the Dharma. 4.13.
