He states the specific designations prescribed in the scriptures for the sons born to Brāhmaṇas and others from Kṣatriya and other women through purchase or marriage: "Those born of women one degree, two degrees, or three degrees lower [than their fathers] are known as Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Dauṣmanta, and Pāraśava. (4.14)

From a Brāhmaṇa and his next-lower wife, a Kṣatriya woman, a son born is a Savarṇa. From a Kṣatriya and his next-lower wife, a Vaiśya woman, a son born from her is an Ambaṣṭha. From a Vaiśya and his next-lower wife, a Śūdra woman, a son born from her is an Ugra. From a Brāhmaṇa and his wife separated by one caste, a Vaiśya woman, a son born from her is a Niṣāda. From a Kṣatriya and his wife separated by one caste, a Śūdra woman, a son born from her is a Dauṣmanta. From a Brāhmaṇa and his wife separated by two castes, a Śūdra woman, a son born from her is a Pāraśava. The detailed exposition regarding the determination of castes should be sought in other Smṛtis. || 4.14 ||
He speaks of those born in the inverse order: "But those born in the inverse order are the Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka,
and Caṇḍāla" (4.15).

The phrase "born from those [women] separated by one, two, or three [classes]" is understood to carry over. From a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇī woman is the next [in rank]; from him, upon her, is born a Sūta. From a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriyā woman is the next; from him, upon her, is born a Māgadha. From a Śūdra, a Vaiśyā woman is the next; from him, upon her, is born an Āyogava. From a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇī woman is separated by one [class]; from him, upon her, is born a Kṛta. From a Śūdra, a Kṣatriyā woman is separated by one; from him, upon her, is born a Vaidehaka. From a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇī woman is separated by two; from him, upon her, is born a Caṇḍāla. (4.15)
According to the opinion of others, he states the distinctions of their names by grouping them according to each caste: "The Brāhmaṇī bore sons from the castes in order:
the Brāhmaṇa, the Sūta, the Māgadha, and the Caṇḍāla. (4.16)
The meaning is clear. Here, the mention of "succession" (*anupūrvya*) refers to the intention to express the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*), and not to the forward order (*anuloma*). 4.16.

From those very [Kṣatriyas] were born the Mūrdhāvasikta-Kṣatriyas, Dhīvaras, and Pulkasas; from those very [Kṣatriyas] were born the Vaiśyas: the Bhṛjjakaṇṭhas, Māhiṣyas, Vaiśyas, and Vaidehas, as well as the Pāraśavas, Yavanas, Karakas, and Śūdras.
"Some say [he should address him] as 'chūdra'. (4.17)

Some traditionalists (smartas), following the sequence already stated beginning with "the Brāhmaṇī gave birth," maintain that there are distinct designations for those born respectively from Brāhmaṇas and the other castes upon Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, and Śūdrā women. (4.17)
The transition to another caste occurs through either advancement or decline in the seventh or fifth generation, according to the teachers. (4.18)

The phrase "they consider" (*manyante*) is the completion of the sentence. For those very *anuloma* offspring, such as the *savarṇā* and others, there is an elevation through the father’s line, resulting in the attainment of a higher caste after the seventh generation; and there is a degradation through the mother’s line, resulting in the attainment of a lower caste after the fifth generation. For example: A daughter born from a Brāhmaṇa who has married a Kṣatriya woman is a *savarṇā*; she too, when married by a Brāhmaṇa and bearing a child in that union, and this process continues until the seventh—when the seventh-generation descendant born of a Brāhmaṇa-married wife produces an offspring, that offspring belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste itself. Similarly, a son produced by a Brāhmaṇa on a Kṣatriya woman is a *savarṇā*; he too, having married a Kṣatriya woman, produces a son, and that son likewise marries a Kṣatriya woman, continuing thus until the fifth—when the fifth-generation descendant produces an offspring on a Kṣatriya woman, that offspring belongs to the Kṣatriya caste itself. Such is the meaning of the alternative rule (*vikalpa*). Even in that case, regarding the transition to another caste, if there is an abundance of virtuous conduct and Vedic study, one becomes elevated in the fifth generation; but if there is a low occupation, one becomes degraded in the fifth generation. This should be understood to apply similarly for a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman, and for a Vaiśya on a Śūdra woman. (4.18)
And [the same applies] to those born in other creations. 4.19.

Apart from the four primary castes (*cāturvarṇya*), there also occurs a mutual transition between different castes among those born of *anuloma* unions—such as the *savarṇa*, *ambaṣṭha*, and others—through the processes of elevation (*utkarṣa*) and degradation (*apakarṣa*). For example: a daughter produced by a *savarṇa* man on an *ambaṣṭhī* woman is married again by a *savarṇa* man; the daughter produced by him on her in turn is likewise married by a *savarṇa*. When this process continues until the seventh generation, the offspring of the seventh woman who is married by a *savarṇa* man becomes that very caste itself. Similarly, if that same [daughter] bears a daughter on an *ambaṣṭha* man, and she too on an *ambaṣṭha*, then the offspring of the seventh woman who is married by an *ambaṣṭha* becomes an *ambaṣṭha* himself. This should be understood to apply to the *ambaṣṭhas* as well. (4.19)
But those born in the inverse order are devoid of dharma. || 4.20 ||

Those born from inverse unions, such as Sūtas and others, are devoid of dharma; that is, they are devoid of dharma such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth. Among them, in another scripture, the mere initiation ceremony is accepted for the Sūta alone. (4.20)
And [the same applies] regarding a Śūdra woman. 4.21.

Even one born from a Śūdra woman in the direct order (ānulomyena), such as a Pāraśava and others, is devoid of dharma. Thus, it is established that those born in the direct order, beginning with those of equal caste (savarṇa), are entitled to dharma. And so says Manu:

"Six sons—those born of women of their own caste and those born of other castes—are considered to possess the dharma of the twice-born; however, all those born of Śūdra women through transgression (apadhvaṃsaja) are declared to share the dharma of Śūdras. (MDh 10.41) || 4.21 ||
But from a Śūdra woman who is not of equal status, he has the livelihood of an outcaste. || 4.22 ||

One born from a Śūdra to a woman of a different caste, such as a Vaiśya woman and so forth, is an Āyogava and others; his occupation is that of an outcast, and like an outcast, he is to be avoided in matters such as being seen, touched, or receiving gifts. Likewise, one born from a Vaiśya to a Kṣatriya woman, or from a Kṣatriya to a Brāhmaṇa woman, does not have the occupation of an outcast. (4.22)
The last one is the most wicked. 4.23.

Among those born from a Śūdra of a different caste, he who is the last-born—that is, the Caṇḍāla born of a Brāhmaṇa woman—is the most sinful and must be strictly avoided. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "One should avoid a Caṇḍāla even from as far away as a cow’s tail-fan. (4.23)
Now he praises the marriages under discussion: "Virtuous sons purify. (4.24)
Virtuous sons of good conduct, born of us, purify the lineage of their progenitor. 4.24.
In this regard, there is a distinction:
[the lineage] from the Ṛṣi extends through three generations. 4.25.
A son born of a woman wedded according to the Ārṣa rite purifies three generations of ancestors by delivering them from hell. (4.25)
Ten from the divine [sacrifice], and ten indeed from that of Prajāpati.
In this context, the word *puruṣa* (person), though forming a compound, is also connected with the word *daśa* (ten). The particle *eva* (only) is intended for restriction. 4.26.
A son of Brahmā saves ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself—such is a son of Brahmā. 4.27.

A daughter wedded by the Brāhma rite is called a Brāhmī; a son born of her purifies ten ancestors—ten preceding generations beginning with the father—and ten descendants—beginning with the son—who are yet to be, as well as himself as the twenty-first. Therefore, the Brāhma marriage is most excellent. (4.27)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
He introduces the time for conception: "One should approach [the wife] during her season. (5.1)

The period of sixteen days and nights beginning from the appearance of the menses is the *ṛtu* (fertile season) for women, the time for conception; during that time, one should approach one’s wife. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Āpastamba-dharma-sūtra*: “Starting from the fourth day up to the sixteenth, they teach that approaching the wife on each successive even night leads to the excellence of progeny. However, the *Mānava-dharma-śāstra* states: “The natural fertile season (*ṛtu*) of women is recorded as sixteen nights, together with those four days [at the beginning and end] which are censured by the virtuous.”
Of these, the first four are censurable, as is the eleventh;
the thirteenth also is censurable, while the remaining ten nights are recommended.
[The same applies to] the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon day, and the fourteenth. [MDh 3.46–47]
"A twice-born man who has completed his studies (snātaka) should always remain a celibate student (brahmacārī), even during the fertile period. Thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya, however, states:
"Approaching his wife in this manner when she is emaciated, he should avoid the Maghā and Mūla constellations. [YDh 1.80]

And as it is said: "Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights" (MDh 3.48). Therefore, among the sixteen nights, the first three must be avoided under all circumstances. By approaching his wife on the remaining nights—abandoning the prohibitions enjoined by all the *smṛtis*—he procreates an excellent son. Conversely, by failing to approach her during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) out of hatred or other such motives, he incurs sin. Thus says Devala:
"He who, being in good health, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses..."
"He incurs the sin of killing an embryo by destroying a fetus that has been conceived. And another Smṛti states:
"But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him..."

"In her menses, his ancestors lie within that month. Thus, although this [duty] is obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*), it is of two kinds because of the scriptural injunction regarding transgression (*pratyavāya*) for its non-performance. Furthermore, according to the opinion of some, it is also a restrictive rule (*niyama*), as in: "One should approach her only during the fertile period (*ṛtu*)," and "One must certainly approach her. (5.1)
The Teacher, however, sets forth an enumeration:
"Or rather, in all cases, with the exception of what is forbidden. (5.2)

Or he may approach her at all times—both during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and outside of it—avoiding the prohibited days; or he may act according to his desire, keeping in mind the boon granted to women: "May we unite even until the birth of a child. And as for that boon: "Let us come together at will until the birth of a son. Furthermore, even though he himself has conquered his senses, it is recorded in the Smṛti: "One's lawful wife must always be protected," and "Guard this lineage with vigilance; let not the seed of another be sown in your field" (VaDh 17.9). 5.2.
Now follow the five great sacrifices:
he who honors the gods, the ancestors, human beings, the spirits, and the seers. || 5.3 ||

Here, the word *pūjaka* (worshipper) is connected with each member of the compound, beginning with "gods. A term heard at the end of a *dvandva* compound is connected with each individual member. Thus, a householder should always be a worshipper of the gods and the others. In this context, "worship of the gods" refers to the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, the complete *homa*, and other fire-rituals (*agnikārya*). Regarding the worship of the ancestors, Manu says: "One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the fivefold sacrifice (*pāñcayājñika*);
however, one should not feed any twice-born person there for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*. (MDh 3.83)

"One should offer the *śrāddha* day after day with food and water, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors" (MDh 3.82). Thus it is said. Worship of humans is the worship of guests; worship of beings is the offering of oblations (*bali*); worship of the seers (*ṛṣi*) is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). "Sacrifice to the seers" and "sacrifice to Brahman" are synonyms. (5.3)
And these are explained here; the sequence is not intended to be significant. But as for the *brahmayajña*, it is the daily private recitation (*nityasvādhyāya*). (5.4)

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Its specific procedure is set forth in the *Taittirīyaka*, beginning with the passage, "One who is about to perform the *brahmayajña*. Here, by the use of the word "constantly" (*nitya*), it is shown that one should study whenever the opportunity arises, even at times other than those specifically designated for the *brahmayajña*. (5.4)
But the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) consists of the offering of water to the ancestors, and other [offerings] according to one's ability. 5.5.

One should always offer water to the ancestors. Other things, such as food, fruits, roots, and so forth, should be offered according to one’s enthusiasm and according to one’s ability. Here, by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods and the sages must also be performed regularly. Regarding this, Manu, speaking of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), says: "Having bathed daily and being pure, one should perform the libation for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. (MDh 2.176). Kātyāyana says:
"One should offer water-libations to the deities and the ancestors in the water;
one should offer water-libations for those who have died without the proper funeral rites on dry land," so says Bhṛgu.
Water that is not poured upon the ground does not serve [the ancestors], whether it be in water-vessels, in bowls, offered while angry, or with only one hand.
Uśanas says: "The waters are all the hosts of gods, and the waters are remembered as the hosts of ancestors;
therefore, water should be offered into the waters, for what is given to the ancestors therein becomes inexhaustible."
Bhṛgu states another method:
"Standing in water reaching up to the navel, with his mind directed upwards and reflecting, [he should say]:
'May my ancestors come; may they accept this handful of water.'"
"Three times each, the wise man, facing south and remaining silent, should cast water into the air while speaking loudly and ever more loftily," thus [it is said]. (5.5)

Since the fire-ritual is the foundation of the sacrifice to the gods, he first states the time for the formal adoption of the sacred fires: "The fire begins with the wife, or it begins with the inheritance. (5.6)

By the word "wife" (*bhāryā*), marriage is indicated. One should tend the sacred fire, beginning either from the day the wife is led to that fire, or from the day the partition of the inheritance is made by the father, brothers, or others. The tending begins in the evening. There is no transgression for one who lives off the work of his father or eldest brother prior to the partition of the inheritance. (5.6)
In that [fire], the domestic rituals are performed. 5.7.152.
When the domestic fire has been thus consecrated, the rites pertaining to human beings, such as the *puṃsavana* and others, are to be performed. (5.7)
The sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the private recitation of scripture and the offering of oblations. 5.8.

The word *tasmin* (in that) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. In this regard, the connection of the *devayajña* with fire is well known; however, for the *pitṛyajña*, *manuṣyayajña*, and *bhūtayajña*, food is cooked in this domestic (*gṛhya*) fire for their sake. Regarding the *brahmayajña*, its connection with fire has been shown by Uśanas in one view: "Some say [it should be performed] near the fire. Since the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) is prescribed even for one who does not maintain a consecrated fire (*aparigṛhītāgni*), these [sacrifices] are to be performed in the common (*laukika*) fire.
Now he states the procedure for the *devayajña* and the *vaiśvadeva*: Agni, Agni Dhanvantari, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati...
The oblation known as the *sviṣṭakṛt* is performed. 5.9.

In this context, the word *homa* refers to the utterance of *svāhā*, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "The injunctions for *juhuti* [offerings] have the utterance of *svāhā* as their primary element. One should offer [the oblation] into the fire with [mantras] beginning with *agnaye* and ending with *svāhā*. Furthermore, the term *sviṣṭakṛt* should be understood as having *agni-* as its prefix (*agnisviṣṭakṛt*). Since the fire is already established by the fact that it is a *homa*, the explicit mention of "in the fire" is intended to indicate that it should not be performed on the ground, as is the case with the *baliharaṇa* offerings. Therefore, the ritual feature of *homa*, namely the utterance of *svāhā*, also applies to the *baliharaṇas*. Accordingly, Āśvalāyana states: "Then, with 'svāhā,' the *baliharaṇa* [is performed]. For the followers of Āpastamba, the mantras are recited precisely ending with *svāhā*. (5.9)
Now he describes the offering of the sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña) and the presentation of the bali:
"And to the deities of the directions, each according to their own [quarter]. (5.10)

The offering (bali) for each deity should be presented in the direction assigned to that deity. Starting from the east and proceeding clockwise up to the northeast, one should perform the rite, saying "Svāhā to Indra" and so forth. || 5.10 ||
To the great ones at the doors. 5.11.
In as many doors as there are in the house, one should offer oblations with the formula: "Svāhā to the great ones! (5.11).
Having entered for the sake of the household deities. || 5.12 ||

Having entered [the house], one should offer the bali-oblation to the household deities with the formula "svāhā. Because of the word "having entered," this must not be performed by one standing outside the door. (5.12)
To Brahmā, in the center. || 5.13 ||

In the middle of the house, an offering (bali) should be presented with the formula "To Brahmā, svāhā. By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that offerings should also be made to the deities of the directions; furthermore, following the mention of Brahmā, offerings must be presented to the deities specified by the author of the Sūtra—namely Pṛthivī, Vāyu, Prajāpati, and the Viśvedevas. 5.13.
Saying "To Ākāśa," the bali offering should be thrown into the intermediate space.
"And one should cast the bali offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night," so says Manu (MDh 3.90). 5.14.
And in the evening, [he should offer it] to the night-walkers. 5.15.

In the evening bali-offering, this is the distinction: the bali should be offered with the words, "Svāhā to the night-walkers. By the use of the word "and," it is also [offered] to those previously mentioned. 5.15.
The giving of alms after reciting a blessing is unprecedented. 5.16.

After the offering of the *bali*, the giving of alms (*bhikṣā*) should be performed. Having uttered the words of benediction, "May there be well-being," one first gives water into the hand of the mendicant. There is a specific rule regarding the wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*):
having given water into the hand of the ascetic (*yati*), one gives the alms, and then water again.
It is said: "The alms may be as large as a mountain, while that water is like the ocean."

This gift of alms, in the absence of honoring guests, shall constitute the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*). These five great sacrifices, excluding the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), are to be performed both evening and morning. Why? Because of the traditional teaching of Āśvalāyana: “Now, one should offer what has been prepared as an oblation, both evening and morning,” and because of the statement in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: “It is said that [the sacrifice] is performed evening and morning,” and so forth. (5.16)
And likewise regarding righteous acts of giving. 5.17.
Regarding those who give gifts—those gifts which are righteous and not motivated by fear or other such causes—in their case, it is likewise "giving unprecedentedly" (appūrvadāna). 5.17.
In connection with the topic of giving, he states the specific results [of gifts]:
"The fruits for non-Brahmins, Brahmins, Vedic scholars, and those who have mastered the Vedas are equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite, respectively. (5.18)

A non-Brāhmaṇa is one of the Kṣatriya or other castes; a Brāhmaṇa is one who possesses the mere birth-status. A Śrotriya is one who has studied the Veda. One who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), its ritual manuals (kalpas), and its secret doctrines (rahasyas) is a Vedapāraga (one who has mastered the Veda). A gift given to these [recipients] yields, respectively, fruit that is equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite. Thus says Manu: "A gift given to a non-Brāhmaṇa is equal [in merit]; to one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa it is double; to a Śrotriya it is a hundred-thousandfold; and to a Vedapāraga it is infinite. (MDh 7.85) || 5.18 ||
In connection with the topic of giving, he states the specific cases where something must necessarily be given and where there is sin in not giving:

"A distribution of wealth outside the sacrificial altar is required for the sake of one's teacher, for a bride, for medicine, for one whose livelihood is exhausted, for one who is about to sacrifice, for one engaged in study, for one on a journey, and for a Vaiśvajita. (GDhS 5.19)

That gift which is given to the members of the sacrificial assembly (*sadasyas*) at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) during a sacrifice is "within the altar" (*antarvedi*). Other than that, it is "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*). The distribution of goods (*dravyasaṃvibhāga*) refers to the giving of gold and other items; this must necessarily be performed for the sake of one's teacher and others. It is for the sake of the teacher regarding one who has completed his Vedic study and for the sake of the sacrificial fee. "Marriage" (*niveśa*) means wedding; it is for the sake of that first [marriage]. "For medicine" (*auṣadhārtha*) means for the sake of a remedy for one who is ill. "Deprived of livelihood" (*vṛttikṣīṇa*) means one who lacks a means of subsistence for that day. "About to sacrifice" (*yakṣyamāṇaḥ*) means one who is about to perform a sacrifice. "Connection with study or travel": he whose connection is with study is "connected with study" (*adhyayanasaṃyoga*); he whose connection is with a journey is "connected with travel" (*adhvasaṃyoga*). These are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. "The performer of the Vaiśvajit" (*vaiśvajitaḥ*) is one who has performed the Viśvajit sacrifice and is thus destitute of wealth due to having given away all his possessions. When requested by these [persons], one must certainly give gold and so forth according to one's ability. By stating "one incurs sin by not giving," and by the mention of "outside the altar," this rule applies specifically to those initiated for a sacrifice; however, within the altar, gifts should be given even to others. (5.19)
When others are begging, one should give prepared food. || 5.20 ||

To others—those other than those already mentioned—who are begging for alms, cooked food (kṛtānna) must necessarily be given. There is no fault in not giving money or other such items. Regarding cooked food as well, Vasiṣṭha states:

"The king should punish that village where twice-born men who do not observe vows, who do not study, and who wander about begging for alms reside; for he is bound by the same rule as the punishment for a thief" (VaDh 3.4). 5.20.
Now follows the refutation of the doctrine that giving is unnecessary:
even after having given his word, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness. 5.21.

Even after having promised "I will give," one need not give in a matter connected with unrighteousness (*adharma*), if one should know that the recipient will use that wealth for unrighteous purposes such as visiting prostitutes and the like. By the expression "connected with unrighteousness," it is shown that one incurs sin by not giving what was promised in any other case. (5.21)
He states a specific rule regarding the matter of making a promise:
"The words of one who is angry, delighted, frightened, afflicted, greedy, a child, an elderly person, one of dull intellect, intoxicated, or insane—though they may be false—are not sinful. (5.22)

Words spoken when one is angry and so forth—though false and not corresponding to the facts—do not produce sin, for they do not constitute a transgression. "Angry" means possessed by anger; "joyful" means possessed by joy; "frightened" means possessed by fear. Because these states are permeated by other [emotional] qualities, the speech is not authoritative. Therefore, even in the case of failing to give after having promised, there is no fault on their part. (5.22)
Now he states those who must be fed before the householder:
"One should first feed the guest, the child, the sick person, the pregnant woman, the newly married daughter living in the father's house, the elderly, and those of lower status. (5.23)

The guest (atithi) is one who will be described [later]. The children (kumāra) are the young. The sick (vyādhita) is one in whom disease has arisen. The pregnant women (garbhiṇyaḥ) are well known. The women living in their own homes (svavāsinyaḥ) are daughters and sisters. The elderly (sthavira) are the aged. The dependents (jaghanya) are the servants and so forth. One should feed these before oneself and eat afterwards. The separate mention of the dependents is for the purpose of indicating their immediate succession. 5.23.
And having informed one's teacher, father, and friends, one should carry out their command.

If the teacher and others should arrive at the time of eating, then, having offered the prepared food to them, the ritual acts regarding that food should be performed according to their wish; the meaning is that while they are present, one should not act independently. 5.24.
The honey-mixture (madhuparka) is offered upon the arrival of a sacrificial priest, a teacher, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle. 5.25.
When officiating priests and others have arrived at the house, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered. || 5.25 ||
Again, after a year. || 5.26 ||
If they, having been honored, should return after a year, the madhuparka must be offered again; not before that. (5.26)
Before [the completion of] a sacrifice or a marriage. 5.27.

Even before the lapse of a year, the madhuparka must be offered to those who have arrived for a sacrifice or a wedding; the procedure for the madhuparka is to be understood as that prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras. 5.27.
And [the same applies] to a king who is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya). || 5.28 ||
In this same manner, the madhuparka should be offered to a king who is also a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya). || 5.28 ||
One should not offer a seat or water to one who is not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya). 5.29.
For a king who is not a śrotriya, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) consists merely of a seat and water. 5.29.
But for a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), he should provide water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and various kinds of food. || 5.30 ||

The word "tu" (but) does not exclude the Brāhmaṇa. For a learned Brāhmaṇa guest, one who is capable should provide *pādya*—water for washing the feet—and *arghya*—such as fruits, offerings, betel, and so forth—as well as various kinds of food, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and cakes (*apūpa*), in an excellent manner. 5.30.
But if it is incapable, it is either eternal or distinguished by its refinement. 5.31.
Whatever is always available in his house, that very thing he should prepare, distinguished by seasonings such as long pepper and cumin. || 5.31 ||
The gift of food to one who is of good conduct but not a learned scholar is of middling merit. || 5.32 ||
But when a guest who, though lacking in learning, is of virtuous conduct arrives, food should be given to him with the intermediate preparation. 5.32.
Even toward those who are hostile, he maintains a welcoming attitude toward grass, water, and earth, and extends them honor and respect to the very end. 5.33.

One who is perverse and lacks knowledge is not of virtuous conduct; therefore, one should offer him ground, grass, a seat, and water, saying, "Please sit here. One should offer a welcome immediately upon his arrival and subsequently employ the greeting "Welcome. Worship should be performed with hospitable conversation. And it should not be excessive. Excessive hospitality (*atyāśa*) refers to a distinguished sequence of offerings such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and cakes (*apūpa*); other than that, it should be performed according to the moderate way. *Āśa* means eating (food). 5.33.
Lying down, sitting, following after, and attending upon are the same for both an equal and a superior. 5.34.

Whether a guest is equal to oneself in terms of learning, conduct, and so forth, or superior to oneself—in both these cases, bedding, seating, and other such things should be given that are equivalent to one's own. A *āvasatha* is a specific place within the house. Since following [the guest] and attending upon him are impossible for oneself, equality in those respects is not possible; however, the meaning is that even those two duties must be performed. (5.34)
Even to a small degree, [one should not dwell] upon what is inferior. || 5.35 ||

Some say that when even a guest who is slightly inferior to oneself arrives, one should give them bedding and other such things exactly as one would to an equal. We, however, say this: when an inferior guest arrives, bedding and other items should be given even in small measure; but one should not, on the grounds that the guest is inferior, practice total omission. (5.35)
He states the definition of a guest:
"A guest is one who does not belong to the same village, stays for only one night, and waits under a tree or at the threshold. (5.36)

One from a different village is a *asamānagrāma* (a guest from another village). One who stays for a single night is a *aikarātrika*. When the sun is above the trees, that is the time known as *adhivṛkṣasūrya*, namely midday; or else, when the rays of the sun are above the trees, that is the time, or evening. A guest who has arrived at such a time is in every way most worthy of honor. 5.36.
An inquiry after one's welfare, health, and freedom from disease. 5.37.

Among the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, when they have encountered one another on the road and so forth, questions concerning their welfare and the like should be made in the following order: a Brāhmaṇa should be asked, "Is it well with you, long-lived one? a Kṣatriya, "Is there freedom from illness for your honor? and a Vaiśya, "Are you free from disease? (5.37)
The last [is] for the Śūdra. || 5.38 ||
Among the auspicious and other [types of water], that which is last should be used by a Śūdra, even when he is free from disease. (5.38)
A non-Brāhmaṇa is not a guest for a Brāhmaṇa. 5.39.

A non-Brahmin, such as a Kṣatriya or others, does not become a guest of a Brahmin. The duties pertaining to a guest mentioned previously are not to be applied in that case; he is to be received only by the offering of water, food, and so forth. (5.39)
If he is covered during a sacrifice. 5.40.
If summoned at the time of a sacrifice, he should be honored like a guest. || 5.40 ||
In that regard as well: "But the meal for the Kṣatriya is after the Brāhmaṇas. (5.41)
Even when he is on the side of hosting guests, food should be given to the Brahmins after they have finished eating. 5.41.
Others, together with their servants, for the sake of compassion—for the sake of compassion. (5.42)

Others, such as Śūdras and the like, who arrive at the time of hospitality, he should feed together with his servants, laborers, and so forth, provided that he has the means. Even though they do not possess the status of guests (*atithi*), he should still feed them for the sake of compassion (*anṛśaṃsya*). Cruelty (*nṛśaṃsatā*) is manifest harshness; this is for the purpose of being free from that. "Compassion is the supreme duty"—thus, compassion is indeed the highest duty. [The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the chapter. 5.42.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The worship of guests has been described. He now states the manner of worship for others as well: "In a gathering, one should perform the clasping of the feet every day. (6.1)

When there is an assembly or meeting with the mother and others who are about to be mentioned, one must perform the clasping of the feet every day, according to the previously described method: "It should be done with crossed hands" (MDh 2.72). 6.1.
But having approached [the teacher] after being away from home; || 6.2 ||

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the previously mentioned case. Having gone abroad oneself—that is, having undertaken a journey—or when they [the parents] have gone abroad, one should go to where those [elders], such as mother and father, are staying and perform the clasping of their feet. (6.2)
He mentions his mother, father, and so forth:
"of his mother, father, their relatives, his ancestors, his teachers of knowledge, and their teachers. (6.3)

Mother and father are well known. Their kinsmen are the maternal uncle, the maternal aunt, the paternal uncle, the paternal aunt, and so forth. Elder siblings are the older brothers. Teachers of learning are the *ācāryas*, *upādhyāyas*, and so forth. Their teachers are the *ācāryas* and others. The two preceding sūtras refer to these [categories]. (6.3)
In the case of a combination [of causes], it belongs to the other. 6.4.

When one's mother and other elders meet together simultaneously, the highest-ranking person must be saluted first. The superiority of the teacher has been stated previously: "The teacher is the best among gurus; some say the mother" (GDh 2.56). However, Āpastamba has prescribed the salutation as follows: "In the case of a meeting between the teacher and the sub-teacher, having saluted the sub-teacher, one should desire to salute the teacher," and so forth (ĀpDh 1.8.19). || 6.4 ||
He states the rule for salutation: "In the presence of those who know [the ritual], one should perform a salutation by announcing one's own name, saying, 'I am so-and-so. (6.5)

When meeting someone who is capable of returning a greeting, one should perform the salutation (*abhivāda*) by first stating one's own name—that which is used in common worldly practice—and then clearly and loudly saying, "I am so-and-so. The term *abhivāda* means the act of saluting; it is derived from the root *vad* with the prefix *abhi* and the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *ac*. Thus, for those who understand the meaning, when a group of elders is assembled, the salutation should be performed according to the proper order by stating one's secret name, saying, "I am so-and-so. This refers to cases where the person being saluted is not inferior [to the speaker]. For example: "O sir, I am Haradattaśarman by name; I salute you. When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one. Furthermore, at the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as a protracted (*pluta*) vowel.

The meaning of this is as follows: By the word *vipra*, this refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa. A Brāhmaṇa who offers a salutation (*abhivādayitā*) is to be addressed with the words, “May you be long-lived, O gentle one (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya*”). At the end of his name, the vowel *a* (of the vocative ending) preceded by the penultimate syllable is to be protracted (*pluta*). The phrase “preceded by the penultimate syllable” is an adjective qualifying the *a*. Because it is that which precedes the final syllable, it is to be protracted; therefore, this occurs even when there is an intervening consonant. For example: “*āyuṣmān bhava saumya haradattā3a*” (where the *a* is protracted despite the intervening *t*). Or, with an intervening consonant: “*āyuṣmān bhava saumyāgni3da*” (where the *a* is protracted despite the intervening *g*). Such is the usage. Vasiṣṭha, however, states a specific rule regarding diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*): “In a vocative, the final vowel is protracted; they say that a diphthong is not subject to the *apragṛhya* rule. This means that the diphthongs *e* and *o* undergo a change. According to the grammarians: “When a non-*apragṛhya* diphthong (*ec*) is used in calling from a distance, the first half becomes *ā* and the second half becomes *i* or *u* respectively. When the *a* is applied at the end, then according to the rule “*tayor yvāv aci saṃhitāyām*,” the *y* and *v* are substituted. Thus, the forms “*āyuṣmān bhava saumya pinākapāṇā3ya*” and “*viṣṇā3ve*” are the resulting usages. However, this manner of salutation does not apply under the view that it concerns an assembly of ignorant people. Regarding that, there is another Smṛti text: [i] *ā u bhāvaṃ cāpadyata iti* | “*eco ‘pragṛhyasyādūrād dhūte pūrvasyārdhasyād uttarasyedutau*” iti vaiyākaraṇaḥ | tatrānte ‘kāre prayukte tayor yvāv aci saṃhitāyām iti yakāravakārau | āyuṣmān bhava saumya pinākapāṇā3yeti viṣṇā3veti ca prayogaḥ | ajñasamavāya iti pakṣe nāyam abhivādanaprakāraḥ | tatra smṛtyantaram || [i] “It becomes *ā* and *u*. According to the grammarians: “When a non-*apragṛhya* diphthong (*ec*) is used in calling from a distance, the first half becomes *ā* and the second half becomes *i* or *u* respectively. When the *a* is applied at the end, then according to the rule “*tayor yvāv aci saṃhitāyām*,” the *y* and *v* are substituted. Thus, the forms “*āyuṣmān bhava saumya pinākapāṇā3ya*” and “*viṣṇā3ve*” are the resulting usages. However, this manner of salutation does not apply under the view that it concerns an assembly of ignorant people. Regarding that, there is another Smṛti text: [The following verse is provided: “*āyuṣmān bhava saumyeti vācyo vipro ‘bhivādane | akāraś cāsya nāmno ‘nte vācyaḥ pūrvākṣaraplutaḥ ||*” “‘May you be long-lived, O gentle one’ is what should be said to a Brāhmaṇa upon greeting; and the vowel *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced with the preceding syllable protracted. [The following verse is provided: “*bhoḥśabdaṃ kīrtayed ante svasya nāmno ‘bhivādane | nāmnāntyākṣaraṃ yac ca tat plaveta svare pare ||*” “One should utter the word *bhoḥ* at the end of one’s own name when greeting; and whichever is the final syllable of the name, that should be protracted before a following vowel. [The following verse is provided: “*nāmadheyasya yad antyam akṣaraṃ tat plaveta vai | svaravidhiḥ sa vijñeyo vyañjane parataḥ sadā ||*” “That which is the final syllable of the name should indeed be protracted; this is to be understood as the rule for vowels, always when followed by a consonant. [The following verse is provided: “*yo vāpy asya paro varṇas tam evāhur dvijottamāḥ | saṃyoge prathamaṃ varṇaṃ plavanta iti niścayaḥ ||*” “Or rather, the best of the twice-born say that the very next letter after it [the final syllable] should be protracted; such is the certainty regarding the first letter in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). [The following verse is provided: “*yadi hy asya paraṃ varṇaṃ plāvayanti dvijātayaḥ | saṃyogādau sthitaṃ varṇaṃ tadā taṃ plāvayanty uta ||*” “If the twice-born protract the subsequent letter, then they likewise protract that letter situated at the beginning of a conjunct consonant. [The following verse is provided: “*na tv eva tu kvacid brūyād aham iti sva-nāma vai | abhivādye tu yaḥ kaścid vipro vidvān bhaved iha ||*” “But one should never, under any circumstances, say ‘I am’ using one’s own name here, even if some learned Brāhmaṇa is to be greeted. [The following verse is provided: “*nāma gotraṃ ca sahitaṃ gotrasyāntaṃ ca nāmataḥ | āmantrayeta yo vipro nānyathety abravīd yamaḥ ||*” “A Brāhmaṇa should address [another] by joining the name and the lineage, and the end of the lineage [with] the name; he should not do otherwise—so Yama has declared. [The following verse is provided: “*gotraṃ nāma ca sahitaṃ nāmno ‘nte ‘bhivādanaṃ | āyuṣmān bhava saumyeti vācyo vipro ‘bhivādane ||*” “The lineage and the name joined together, with the greeting at the end of the name: ‘May you be long-lived, O gentle one’—this is what the Brāhmaṇa is to be addressed with upon greeting. [The following verse is provided: “*nāmnāntyākṣaraṃ yac ca tat plaveta svare pare | vyañjanopadhave cāpi plāvayanty akṣaraṃ param ||*” “And whichever is the final syllable of the name, that should be protracted before a following vowel; and even when followed by a consonant, they protract the subsequent syllable. [The following verse is provided: “*nāmadheyasya yad antyam akṣaraṃ tat plaveta vai | svaravidhiḥ sa vijñeyo vyañjane parataḥ sadā ||*” “That which is the final syllable of the name should indeed be protracted; this is to be understood as the rule for vowels, always when followed by a consonant. [The following verse is provided: “*yo vāpy asya paro varṇas tam evāhur dvijottamāḥ | saṃyoge prathamaṃ varṇaṃ plavanta iti niścayaḥ ||*” “Or rather
"Regarding those ignorant persons who do not know the prolated vowel (*pluti*) at the end of their names when returning a greeting:
one may, at will, address them as 'this person' (*ayam*) after returning from a journey, just as one would address women."

Just as in the case of women, a salutation may be performed by means of any word whatsoever—even one not of the prescribed form, such as a local dialect—and likewise it occurs among them as well. The term "salutation" (*abhivādana*) is a general indicator, because it includes designations employed for women and others that are devoid of the formal modes. Regarding the specific mode of salutation, Āpastamba states: "A Brāhmaṇa should salute, extending his right arm level with his ear; a Rājanya, level with his chest; a Vaiśya, at the middle [of the body]; and a Śūdra, low [down], with palms joined. (ĀpDh 1.5.16) || 6.5 ||
Some say that there is no fixed rule regarding the salutation when a woman and a man meet. 6.6.1.208.

In the context of the union of a woman and a man—that is, in the meeting of wife and husband—the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). Although a rule for salutation has already been established, some authorities maintain that there is no fixed rule regarding the manner of such salutation. Even if the husband is capable of returning a greeting, they do not require a formal rule for the wife’s salutation to him. They do not accept a fixed sequence such as "I, so-and-so, salute you"; rather, they hold that a simple, general salutation is sufficient. Consequently, the wife must perform a daily prostration to her husband. Because of the word "some" (*eke*), however, according to the view of Gautama, the rule remains mandatory. (6.6)
One should not kiss women other than one's mother, paternal uncle's wife, or sister after returning from a journey abroad. 6.7.

This is an exception to the rule "every day" regarding social gatherings (*samavāya*). With the exception of one's mother, paternal uncle, wife, and sister, one should not perform the clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) or the formal salutation (*abhivādana*) for other women when not traveling abroad; rather, these acts should be performed only upon returning from a journey abroad. However, in the case of one's mother and the others, they should be performed every day even when not traveling abroad. Thus, another *Smṛti* states:
"A twice-born man should perform the clasping of the feet every day during a social gathering for his sister, his mother, and likewise for the wives of his paternal uncles. (6.7)
One should not practice sexual intercourse with the wives of one's brothers or with one's sisters. 6.8.

When one has returned from living abroad, he should not perform the formal clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) for these [female relatives], but salutation (*abhivādana*) is indeed still required. In that regard, for those who occupy the position of ultimate gurus, such as maternal uncles' wives and others, there is the clasping of the feet; for others, there is merely salutation. (6.8)
But one should rise to greet a younger officiating priest, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle after having first prostrated before them. 6.9.
One should perform the worship of officiating priests and others who are younger than oneself merely by rising from one's seat; however, they are not to be saluted with the formal greeting. 6.9.
Likewise, another who is an elder, even a Śūdra aged at least eighty, [is to be honored] as one's own son.

Just as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others are to be saluted by rising but not by bowing, so too is this person. He is "other than them" (*anyaḥ tebhyo 'nyaḥ*). "Earlier" (*pūrvaḥ*) means superior in age. "A townsman" (*pauraḥ*) means a resident of the city. Even though he is older in age, his inferiority due to being a townsman is stated. "Eighty" (*aśīti*) refers to the state of being eighty; one who is younger than that is an *aśītikāvaraḥ*, meaning one less than eighty years of age. Such a Śūdra, even if equal to one's own son, is to be saluted by rising but not by bowing. By the phrase "equal to one's own son," his relative youth is indicated. The mention of the Śūdra is an illustration for those of lower castes (*avaravarṇa*). Consequently, it is established that a Śūdra is [saluted] by all three castes, a Vaiśya by two, and a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa alone. (6.10)
Even a lower noble may [be honored] by a Śūdra. 6.11.

Even a Śūdra who is less than eighty years old must rise to meet a member of the three higher castes (traivarṇika), even if that person is of lower status or younger; however, he need not offer a formal salutation (abhivādana). Here, too, the mention of the "Śūdra" is intended as an illustration for those of lower caste. Consequently, it is established that the three castes must rise to meet a Śūdra, two must rise to meet a Vaiśya, and a Brāhmaṇa must rise to meet a Kṣatriya—provided they are of lower age—and yet they need not offer a formal salutation. (6.11)
One should avoid using his name. 6.12.

Regarding the phrase "of this one" (*asya*), there is an ellipsis of repetition (*vīpsā*); that is, one should not take the actual name of this person, who is superior to all others, but rather one should take a figurative name (*aupacārikam nāma*). (6.12)
And the messenger of a king is not subject to the ajapa fine. || 6.13 ||
One who does not recite [the Veda] is unlearned; one who performs menial service is a servant. Even a Brahmin of the highest caste should avoid pronouncing the name of an anointed king. 6.13.
"Bho bhavān" is used for a friend born on the same day. 6.14.

A *vayasya* is one who is equal in age. One born on the same day; here, the word "day" (*ahar*) signifies a year. One born in the same year may be addressed with either of these two terms: "bho" or "bhavan. (6.14)
A citizen ten years older [is fined] five *kalās*, a learned Brahmin three, and a bard two. (6.15)

A man who wears clean clothes but lacks qualities, one ten years older than oneself, and even among these, one who possesses some of the sixty-four arts and lives by any one of them becomes "venerable" (*vṛddha*) after five years. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda. A *cāraṇa* is a fellow student. All of these may be addressed with the word "Sir" (*bho bhavan*). However, Āpastamba desires that salutation (*abhivādana*) be performed in all such cases:
"Friendship based on city-dwelling lasts for ten years; that with a *cāraṇa*, five years;
and a *śrotriya* who is three years senior deserves salutation" (ĀpDh 1.14.13).
Those who perform the duties of Kshatriyas and Vaishyas are devoid of [sacred] knowledge. 6.16.

The word *karma* (action/occupation) is to be connected with each [term]: the occupation of a Kṣatriya and the occupation of a Vaiśya. Even a Brāhmaṇa, if he lives by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or the occupation of a Vaiśya, must be addressed as "Sir" (*bho bhavān*), even if he is extremely old. Furthermore, one who is devoid of learning, even if old, must be addressed in that same manner by one superior in learning. (6.16)
And one who has been initiated [remains so] until the purchase [of the Soma]. 6.17.

This refers to a friend. A consecrated friend (*dīkṣita*) may be addressed as "friend" prior to the purchase of the *soma*; thereafter, he is to be honored like an elder. Regarding those in the highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*), Uśanas states: "One who has studied the Vedas (*śrotriya*) becomes a teacher (*guru*) to all, even when eating. (6.17)
Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, learning, and age are grounds for respect,
yet each subsequent one is stronger than the preceding.

Since wealth and the like cannot be honored directly, those who possess them are indicated by these terms as being worthy of honor. One who possesses wealth is "wealthy" (*āḍhya*). One who possesses kin is "related," meaning endowed with distinguished siblings and others. One who possesses action is "one who performs the prescribed duties. One who possesses birth is "of noble lineage. One who possesses learning is "one who has studied the Vedas and the Shastras. One who possesses age is "advanced in years. Such persons are to be honored by those who do not possess these qualities. However, when they are encountered together, each subsequent one is stronger [in terms of claim to honor] and must be honored first. Honor consists of salutation and other forms of respect toward one who is worthy of honor. (6.18)
But learning is more important than all [these]. 6.19.

The thorough understanding of the meaning of the Vedas through the division into Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is more important, indeed much more important, than all [other things] such as wealth. This is stated in a separate sūtra to exclude the notion that what was previously mentioned—that "the subsequent is stronger"—might apply here. 6.19.
But from what [source] is it heard that [the Veda] is more venerable than all? To this he says:
"Because dharma and sacred learning (śruti) have that as their root" (6.20).

"Practice has its root in sacred learning (*śruta*); Dharma has its root in practice"—so says the Śruti. Furthermore, the root is the unbroken tradition (*sampradāya*). Therefore, sacred learning is of greater importance. The preeminence of sacred learning is established in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The Brāhmaṇa is called *Śaiśava*; indeed, Śiśu Āṅgirasa was a composer of mantras among the composers of mantras. Manu also says: "The wise Śiśu Āṅgirasa taught his ancestors; having encompassed them with knowledge, he said, 'O my sons! (MDh 2.151). || 6.20 ||
Way must be yielded to a wheel-turning monarch, one who stands at the tenth stage, a bridegroom, a bride, a student who has completed his studies, and a king. 6.21.

A *cakrin* is one who possesses a wheel, such as a cart and the like; one situated upon that is a *cakristha*. One situated in the tenth stage, the tenth decade of life, is a *daśamīstha*, meaning an elderly person. One worthy of favor is one afflicted by disease. A *vadhū* is a pregnant woman. A *snātaka* is one who has performed the ceremonial bath after completing his studies and vows. A king is one who has been consecrated. On the road, when meeting these [and others], the way must be yielded to them. (6.21)
In this regard, there is a distinction:
but the king [should give] to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya), indeed to a learned Brahmin. 6.22.
In an assembly of those learned in the Vedas, the king himself must yield the path. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the chapter. 6.22.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

It has been stated that sacred learning (*vidyā*) is the most important of all things, as it is weightier than everything else. That learning is to be acquired from a Brāhmaṇa; this is the primary rule (*kalpa*). In the absence of such a person, because learning must necessarily be acquired, he states the rule for times of distress (*āpad-kalpa*):
"The rule for times of distress for a Brāhmaṇa is the acquisition of learning from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. (7.1)
The Vedāṅgas, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.

"Utilization" (*upayoga*) means acquisition preceded by formal restriction. A non-Brāhmaṇa is a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must utilize knowledge [from them], and this constitutes the rule for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*). The statement "the rule for times of distress applies to the Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, it is established that a Kṣatriya may likewise utilize knowledge from a Vaiśya. This "rule for times of distress" remains in force until the end of the chapter. (7.1)
Following after and service. 7.2.
In that regard, service consists solely in following [the teacher] for as long as the period of study lasts, and not other things such as massaging his feet. (7.2)
When it is completed, the Brāhmaṇa is the teacher. || 7.3 ||
But when the study is completed, the teacher is indeed a Brāhmaṇa.
"Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts [are] for all.

(7.4) Sacrificing for others and the other [two] are the means of livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa; these are permitted for all [classes] in times of distress, and not for the Brāhmaṇa alone. Another [teacher] says: "In times of distress, one may sacrifice for all, teach all, and accept gifts from everyone; there is no fault in this reproach. And so Manu [says]:
"Not from teaching, nor from sacrificing, nor from accepting gifts that are reproachable..."
"For that fault of the Brahmins is indeed like fire and water. [MDh 10.103]. Thus ends section 7.4.
Each preceding one is more venerable than the following.

Among these—sacrificing for others and so forth—it should be understood that whichever one was mentioned earlier is more weighty than the subsequent one. In times of distress, he may live by accepting gifts; if that is impossible, by teaching; and if that is impossible, by sacrificing for others. (7.5)
In the absence of that, the occupation of a Kṣatriya [is permitted]. || 7.6 ||

This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa. If even the occupations of a Kṣatriya are unavailable due to the unacceptability of officiating at sacrifices for certain persons and so forth, he may adopt the livelihood of a Kṣatriya; that is, a Brāhmaṇa may live by service and the like. When the emergency has passed, Nārada says:

"Having crossed over the emergency, once his people have been supported by the Kṣatriya livelihood, the Brāhmaṇa should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation after performing purification for himself" (NSm 1.55). 7.6.
In the absence of that, he may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya. || 7.7 ||

Even when the occupation of a Kṣatriya is unavailable, a Brāhmaṇa may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya. The inclusion of the word "unavailability" is intended so that there may be no confusion between the prescribed occupations. That a Kṣatriya may subsist by the occupation of a Vaiśya is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (the principle of the implied). 7.7.
That is his merchandise. 7.8.

The items that must not be sold by that Brāhmaṇa who follows the occupation of a Vaiśya will now be stated. By the use of the word "his" (tasya), it is indicated that the items about to be mentioned do not constitute forbidden merchandise for a Kṣatriya who subsists on the occupation of a Vaiśya. (7.8)
Scented substances, liquids, prepared food, sesame, hemp, linen, and skins. || 7.9 ||

Fragrance refers to sandalwood and the like; flavor refers to oil, ghee, salt, molasses, and so forth; prepared food refers to sweetmeats, cakes, and the like; sesame seeds are well known; hemp refers to products derived from hemp such as sacks and the like; linen refers to a specific type of fine cloth produced from flax; and hide refers to skins such as those used for mats and the like. These are not to be sold. Since the prohibition regarding hemp and linen applies to their derivatives, there is no prohibition against the raw materials themselves. (7.9)
Two garments dyed red. || 7.10 ||
"Red" means dyed with lac and the like; "washed" means laundered by a washerman and so forth. Even such garments are not for sale. (7.10)
Milk with its by-products. 7.11.
Milk, together with its derivatives such as curd and the like, is not for sale. 7.11.
Roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and unwholesome things [are not to be accepted].

Roots are ginger, turmeric, and so forth; fruits are betel nut and so forth; flowers are *cambaka* and so forth; medicinal herbs are long pepper and so forth; honey is that produced by bees; meat, grass, and water are well known; and unwholesome things are poison and so forth—these are items not to be sold. Although liquids were already prohibited previously, the specific mention of honey here is for the purpose of prohibiting it even in cases where one is unable to subsist by any other means whatsoever. (7.12)
And animals [are the objects] when there is a connection with injury. 7.13.
Domestic animals such as goats and others must not be sold for the purpose of slaughter by butchers and the like when associated with an act of violence. (7.13)
And the meat of a man-servant, a maiden, and a cow-calf is always [forbidden]. 7.14.

"Men" refers to slaves and the like; "vaśā" is a barren cow; "kumārī" is a heifer; "vehad" is a cow that destroys the embryo. These are never to be sold. Because the word "always" (nityam) is used, there is a prohibition even in cases other than those involving injury. Another teacher says: because of the inclusion of the word "always" here, the prohibition regarding the previously mentioned items such as sesame seeds is not absolute. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "Or they may sell sesame seeds after having produced them themselves at will. (GDh 7.14)
According to some, [the term "wealth"] also includes land, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch cows, and oxen. 7.15.

Land is a dwelling place. Rice, barley, goats, sheep, and horses are well known. A bull is a cow capable of impregnation. A milch-cow is one that has calved once. An ox is a draft animal fit for pulling a cart. Some maintain that these also are not for sale; however, because of the word "one" (*eka*), we permit this. Even here, the mention of goats and sheep refers specifically to cases involving the act of slaughter. 7.15.
But there is a restriction: || 7.16 ||
"Restriction" (niyama) means exchange; however, by the word "but" (tu), restriction is authorized. Thus [ends] 7.16.
With the essences of the flavors. || 7.17 ||

An exchange should be made using only liquids such as oil, clarified butter, molasses, and so forth. For example: having given oil, clarified butter may be received. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "By means of liquids, it may be equal or less" (VaDh 2.37). || 7.17 ||
And [the same applies] to animals. 7.18.
An exchange of four-footed animals for other animals should be made. || 7.18 ||
Not [the word *lavaṇa*] with *anna*. (7.1.19)
The exchange of salt for cooked food is also forbidden. || 7.19 ||
And of sesame seeds. 7.20.

And an exchange of sesame seeds must not be made. The giving of salt, prepared food, or sesame seeds by accepting other goods in return is forbidden, because such an exchange is possible when the items involved are of equal value. (7.20)
But *samenāma* is used for the sense of "cooked" in the sense of "at present. || 7.21 ||

In the present context, a restriction regarding cooked food must be made with an equal measure—that is, with an equal quantity of uncooked rice—meaning for the purpose of its direct consumption. Manu, however, permits a restriction of sesame seeds by means of an equal amount of grain, stating: "Sesame seeds are equal to grain" (MDh 10.94). Because of the prohibition against selling [sesame], there would otherwise be no prohibition on buying them as long as they are required for use. By the word "restriction," even in the case of liquids and so forth, only their offering is intended; otherwise, since it would be impossible to substitute other substances for liquids and the like when they are unavailable, [the rule would be meaningless]. (7.21)
In every way, when unable [to follow his own rule], he may live according to the mode of life of one other than a Śūdra. 7.22.

Inability to maintain one’s family in the manner described constitutes "incapacity. When that exists, there is "subsistence in every way" (*sarvathā vṛtti*). The suffix *thāl* is used here in the sense of "manner"; thus, he may live by every possible means, even those that are prohibited. Even in that case, however, he must not live by the work of a Śūdra. (7.22)
Some say that even this [is permissible] when there is a danger to life. 7.23.
However, some teachers maintain that when there is a threat to life, even such work as that of a Śūdra is permitted. As Vyāsa says:
"Life is the foundation for the establishment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; by killing it, what is not killed? By protecting it, what is not protected? (7.23)
But there is a restriction regarding the mixing of castes and the consumption of forbidden food. 7.24.

“Restriction” means avoidance. Even for a Brāhmaṇa who subsists by the livelihood of a Śūdra, there is “intermixture” (saṃkara) such as sitting together on the same seat or physical contact with one of the Śūdra caste, as well as the consumption of forbidden food (abhakṣya) such as garlic and the like. Both of these must be avoided; one must not act according to whim, thinking, “I am following the livelihood of a Śūdra. (7.24)
Even a Brahmin may take up arms when his life is in danger. 7.25.

When there is a danger to life, even a Brāhmaṇa may take up a weapon for the sake of self-defense. Since taking up a weapon is already established by the rule that one may adopt the occupation of a Kṣatriya when such a weapon is unavailable, its restatement here is intended to show that there is no prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa’s own occupation [of self-protection]. By the use of the word "even" (api), it is implied: how much more so for a Vaiśya or a Śūdra! (7.25)
The duties of a Vaiśya belong to a Rājanya. || 7.26 ||
In a life-threatening crisis, a Kṣatriya may take up the occupation of a Vaiśya; by that means he should protect himself. (The repetition indicates the end of the chapter. 7.26
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
If one who has resorted to a livelihood in times of distress should find pleasure therein, by whom can he be restrained? To this he says:
"In this world, there are two who uphold their vows: the king and the Brahmin who is deeply learned. (8.1)

The world is the kingdom; here, the repetition [of the word] should be understood as being elided. In every world, there are two who uphold the vows—that is, the sustainers of the duties (vratas) and actions: the king and the highly learned Brāhmaṇa. These two are the warders-off of all calamities for everyone, by means of punishment and instruction respectively. 8.1.
The life of the fourfold species of humans—those with internal consciousness, those that move, those that fall, and those that crawl—is dependent upon these two. 8.2.

The intermediate origins of the fourfold human race—the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*)—such as those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and so forth, are not mentioned separately because they are rooted in those [four]. "Those with internal consciousness" refers to immobile beings such as trees, which possess growth and decay; they are so called because their consciousness is internal and not external. Thus Manu says:
"Driven by manifold darkness caused by karma, these become internally conscious and are endowed with equal pleasure and pain. (Manu Smṛti 1.49)

The moving are animals and the like; the flying are birds; the crawling are reptiles, such as serpents and the like. The livelihood of these—humans and others—is dependent upon those two, the king and the Brahmin; it is subject to them. The king, indeed, is the cause of their livelihood by means of suppressing adversaries and so forth. But how is the other (the Brahmin) "one who has heard much" (*bahuśruta*)? To this he says: "The oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born; from rain comes food; and from that, living beings. [MDh 3.76]
By such reasoning, this is the cause for living. 8.2.
Nor is it merely life itself that depends upon him; rather—procreation, protection, and non-confusion are his duty (dharma). 8.3.

"Procreation" means increase. Through punishment and instruction, increase occurs by way of causing people to act as prescribed, through rain and other such means, and by the pacification of afflictions such as disease. Protection also results from the suppression of thieves. Furthermore, the non-confusion—that is, the non-mixture—of the social classes (*varṇas*) occurs through the application of punishment and the prescription of penance. Righteousness (*dharma*) also arises through the instruction of what is enjoined and the imposition of punishment for the practice of what is prohibited. All of this depends upon those two [punishment and instruction]. (8.3)
He demonstrates what was stated as "one who is learned":
he is indeed such a one who is learned. 8.4.
"This very one" refers to the designation that is about to be stated. 8.4.
One who knows the worlds, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas. || 8.5 ||

By the word "world" (loka), the customs of regions and so forth established by worldly convention are meant. Of these, the Vedas are four: the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharvaṇa. The auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) are six: grammar, phonetics, prosody, astronomy, the ritual manuals (kalpasūtras), and etymology (nirukta). One who knows these both by recitation and by their meaning is [an expert]. (8.5)
He was skilled in dialogues, discourses, histories, and ancient lore.

Sentences consisting of arguments and counter-arguments useful for the Vedic scriptures; for example, in the *Mahābhārata*, such as "Who indeed wanders alone? The sun wanders alone," and so forth—this is *vākovākya*. The *itihāsa* consists of the *Mahābhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and other such works. The *purāṇa* is of eighteen kinds, such as the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and the *Śivapurāṇa*. One who is proficient in these is "skilled" (*kuśala*). (8.6)
Dependent on that, it functions therein. || 8.7 ||
"He looks toward" those things beginning with the worlds which have been mentioned; "his activity" is that of one who performs the rites prescribed therein. (8.7)
He was consecrated with forty purificatory rites. || 8.8 ||
The forty sacraments (saṃskāra), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and so forth, will be described; by these he is consecrated. 8.8.
Delighting in the three types of action. || 8.9 ||

Sacrifice, study, and giving are the three activities; he is devoted to them. He is one who performs them continuously. Although this is already established by the phrase "one whose livelihood is that," the repetition is for the sake of extreme firmness. (8.9)
Or in six [fingers]. 8.10.
Together with officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, there are six duties; he is devoted to these. By the word "or" (vā), there is a restriction to those previously mentioned.
He is thoroughly trained in the rules of customary conduct. || 8.11 ||

A convention is a human-established rule; the practices rooted in that are "conventional practices" (*samayācāra*). Those duties based on tradition (*smārta-dharma*) which exist within them are "pertaining to conventional practice" (*sāmayācārika*); he is "thoroughly disciplined" (*abhivinīta*) in these, having been properly instructed by his father and others. (8.11)
Such a Brahmin,
O King, is one who must be avoided by a king in six ways.
He is to be avoided by the king through the six methods about to be described, beginning with execution; "avoidance" (parihāra) means exclusion. 8.12.
He states those [prohibitions], beginning with non-killing:
"He is not to be killed, nor to be imprisoned, nor to be punished, nor to be banished, nor to be censured, nor to be avoided. (8.13)

Killing is beating; bondage is fettering; punishment is the confiscation of wealth; banishment is expulsion from the village and so forth; censure is the proclamation of faults; and exclusion is abandonment. These six—beginning with killing—are to be avoided by the king when committed unintentionally against a learned Brāhmaṇa, because there is no occasion for intentional [offenses]. The word *iti* indicates a manner; thus, whatever else is of this kind, such as improper conversation and the like, that too is to be avoided. (8.13)

It was stated that there are forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*); he now enumerates them: conception, the rite for a male child, parting the hair, birth rites, naming, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and initiation. 8.14.

This is a collective dvandva compound. *Garbhādhāna* (conception) refers to the *niṣeka* rite performed according to the injunctions stated by the authors of the Sūtras, involving rules regarding the proper time such as "one should approach [the wife] during her season" (GDh 5.1). The *saṃskāras* beginning with *garbhādhāna* are described in their respective Gṛhya-sūtras; however, in this context, only a mere indication of their essential nature is provided for the purpose of enumerating the *saṃskāras*. (8.14)
The four Vedic observances. 8.15.
These [rites] are prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras for each Veda and for each Śākhā. 8.15.
Bathing and union with the wife who shares the same dharma. || 8.16 ||
The ritual bath is the return home from studentship; marriage is the union with a partner for the practice of dharma together. 8.16.
The performance of the five sacrifices is for the sake of the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman. 8.17.

The sacrifices of the five classes of gods constitute their performance; this performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) must be carried out day by day. However, the accomplishment of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is not achieved by performing it only once. Because of the mention of "five," these five are distinct purificatory rites and do not constitute a single composite rite when combined. (8.17)
And of these [eighteen], || 8.18 ||
The performance of the pākayajñas, such as the aṣṭaka and others which will be described hereafter, constitutes a *saṃskāra*. (8.18)
He said to them:
"The Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī, the Caitrī, and the Āśvayujī—these are the seven forms of the Pākayajña sacrifices. (8.19)

The Chandogas maintain that there are three dark fortnights following the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, and in each of these there is one Ekāṣṭakā. Āśvalāyana states that there is an Aṣṭakā on the eighth day of each of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons. Āpastamba says: "That which occurs after the mid-winter full moon is the Madhyāṣṭakā; the eighth lunar day coinciding with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra is called the Ekāṣṭakā. Such is the Aṣṭakā. A *sthālīpāka* (cooked offering) performed on a *parvan* (festival day) is called *pārvaṇa*. The *māsi-śrāddha* is the monthly ancestral rite. The *Śrāvaṇī* is the *sarvabali* (universal offering). Regarding this, the Chandogas state: "On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, having brought forward the domestic fire," and so forth. Āpastamba says: "On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun has set, [one performs] the *sthālīpāka*. The *sarpabali* (serpent offering) and the *utsargahoma* (concluding oblation) are performed on the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, which falls in Mārgaśīrṣa. The rite known as *pratyavarohaṇa* (re-descending) during the winter is also designated by the term *āgrahāyaṇī*. The *śūlagava* (spit-ox sacrifice) takes place on the full moon of Caitra. Among the followers of Āpastamba, this is well known as the *Īśānabali*, and it occurs on the full moon of Caitra. However, Āśvalāyana states: "The *śūlagava* is in autumn and in spring. The Chandogas say: "For Rudra, on the full moon of Āśvayuja. Āśvalāyana prescribes the performance of that rite on the full moon of Āśvayuja: "Having adorned themselves, bathed, and put on clean clothes, they should offer a *sthālīpāka* to Paśupati and sacrifice it. The *āgrayaṇa* (first-fruits offering) for one who has not maintained the sacred fires also takes place at that same time. These two rites are intended here by the term *āśvayujī*. The name *pākayajña* belongs to the ritual procedures of Gārya. As Āpastamba says: "The word *pākayajña* applies to worldly [rites]. This means there are seven types of *pākayajña* according to their established forms. (8.19)

The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the fire-oblation (agnihotra), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), the first-fruits offering (āgrayaṇa), the four-monthly sacrifices (cāturmāsya), the independent animal sacrifice (nirūḍhapaśubandha), and the Sautrāmaṇī— these are the seven forms of the haviryajña. 8.20.

The rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) are enumerated among the purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāra*) as established by the Veda. Because of the mention of "seven," the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) constitute a single purificatory ceremony as a collective unit. They are called "sacrifices of cooked oblations" (*haviryajña*) because they lack a connection with the *soma* juice. (8.20)
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma—these are the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice. || 8.21 ||

The Agniṣṭoma belongs to a Kṣatriya. That sacrifice in which the Ṣoḍaśin cup is drawn is the Atirātra-Agniṣṭoma. One must consider how this [Atirātra] can be a purificatory rite for a Brāhmaṇa; the others are well-known. 8.21.
Thus, these are the forty formative factors (saṃskāra). || 8.22 ||

This concludes the summary. By the mention of the forty [sacrifices], there are exactly that many purificatory rites (saṃskāras). The others are the Smārta rituals, such as those performed for specific desires (kāmya) and so forth. 8.22.
Now, there are eight qualities of the self. 8.23.
The words "they will say" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. The word *atha* is used in the sense of possibility. 8.23.
Compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of weariness, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of possessiveness. || 8.24 ||
That which proceeds constantly with joy toward the welfare and auspiciousness of all beings as if toward oneself—this indeed is remembered as complete compassion. (1)
Whether reviled or even struck, one should neither revile nor strike in return;
being free from malice in speech, mind, and body—that is remembered as endurance and patience. (2)
The wise man who does not feel hatred toward one who attains virtue, wealth, pleasure, and even liberation— this is remembered by the learned as freedom from envy.
Purity of substance, purity of mind, as well as verbal and physical purity—thus has fourfold purity been proclaimed by the seers who perceive the truth. (4)
If at its commencement there should be constant and extreme suffering for oneself, one should avoid it even if it is righteous; that is proclaimed as "effortlessness" (anāyāsa).
The constant practice of what is praiseworthy and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—this indeed has been declared as auspiciousness by the sages who perceive reality. (6)
Even in the face of dire adversity, one should not become dejected toward anyone;
rather, one should take delight in sharing [one's resources]. This is called "freedom from wretchedness. (7)
A person should always avoid discontent regarding sense objects and the longing for the wealth of others; this is what is called "freedom from desire" by the wise. (8)
Thus, in the manner described, there are eight qualities of the self. 8.24.
He states their excellence:
"He who possesses these forty refinements but lacks the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with or residence in the same world as [Brahman]. (8.25)
*Sālokya* is the state of dwelling in the same world. It is *sālokya* due to conjunction with one part, while *sāyujya* is due to total conjunction. (8.25)
But indeed, he for whom even a single portion of these formative forces consists of the eight qualities of the self attains union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman. 8.26.

The word *tu* expresses a distinction. The word *khalu* indicates well-known fact. He for whom there exist the eight qualities of the self, even though he possesses only a few of the forty purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) rooted in the status of the twice-born—such a person surely attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman. The word *atha* is used for the purpose of specification. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 8.26.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having taken a wife, he who practices the duties of a householder as they have been described should observe these following vows. 9.1.

By the word "that" (tat), the king and the Brāhmaṇa mentioned in the preceding chapter are referred to. However, he will state a specific rule for the Vaiśya regarding the status of a Snātaka. Having performed the bath according to the prescribed rule—having brought the Vedic vows to completion, having performed the *samāvartana* ceremony, and having obtained a wife by performing the marriage rites—one should thereafter carry out these vows which are about to be described, while practicing the duties of a householder such as the honoring of guests as previously stated. One should cause them to reach oneself; that is, one should practice them. (9.1)
The Snātaka. || 9.2 ||
