The *calopa* is to be observed. A *snātaka* should likewise observe these vows of a householder. Because he has returned from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) and because there is no other stage of life apart from that of the householder, the preceding rule was begun with the words "after obtaining a wife. However, since it may be impossible for a *snātaka* to obtain a wife, another rule was begun stating that the duties of a householder must be performed for as long as one lives. Furthermore, this performance of the *snātaka* vows and the penance for their transgression are prescribed only for kings and Brahmins; as another *smṛti* states: "Only for kings and Brahmins, and not for others under any circumstances. (9.2)
What, then, are those vows?
One should be constantly pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing. 9.3.

He should always remain pure through acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) and the like; within his capacity, he should not remain impure even for a moment. He should be fragrant, having his limbs scented by being anointed with sandalwood and other perfumes; or alternatively, "fragrance" refers to good character, meaning he should possess excellent conduct (*suśīla*). He should be habituated to bathing, that is, he should bathe daily. Regarding this matter concerning the *snātaka*, Vasiṣṭha states:
"For *snātaka*s, there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper one, two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), a staff, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) containing water. (VaDh 12.14)
Manu says:
"He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot with water,
a sacred thread, a Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings" (MDh 4.36).
The Veda is a handful of dharma. 9.3.
If he possessed wealth, he would not be one whose clothes are like worn-out rags. || 9.4 ||
When another is available for his use, he should not wear a garment that is worn out, like a soiled cloth. || 9.4 ||
One should not wear clothing that is dyed red, gaudy, or worn by another. 9.5.

One should not wear garments such as these: those dyed with safflower and similar colors, those that are gaudy, those of great value, those previously worn by others—provided they were not worn by one's teacher—and likewise those already worn by others. The phrase "if one has the means" is understood to apply here. (9.5)
Nor a garland or sandals. 9.6.
One should not wear a garland or sandals that have been worn by another. || 9.6 ||
If he is unable [to perform the rite], it shall be washed. 9.7.

If nothing else is obtained, this constitutes a lack of means. In the event of such incapacity, he should wash and wear another person’s garment, garland, and sandals. In that regard, the washing of the garment should be performed by boiling it in alkaline water. 9.7.
One whose beard has grown should not do so suddenly. || 9.8 ||

The mention of "beard" (*śmaśru*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the nails and other parts of the body as well. One should not let the beard grow unless there is a specific reason; however, when a reason exists, one may let it grow. That reason is stated in another Smṛti:
"One should avoid the act of shaving in the sixth year, the sixteenth year, and likewise in the year of marriage, as well as while one's wife is pregnant."

Since shaving also has a prescribed time, as indicated by such rules as "in the Gaṅgā, in the field of the Sun" (*bhāskarakṣetra*), how then should it be performed? On this point, Manu says: "With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed" (*kḷptakeśanakhaśmaśruḥ*, MDh 4.35). *Kḷpti* (trimming) means making them even by cutting. And Yājñavalkya says:
"Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails short, and pure" (YDh 1.131). || 9.8 ||
One should not hold fire and water simultaneously. || 9.9 ||

One should not hold fire in one hand and water in the other simultaneously. Regarding this, Vyāghra states a specific rule: "A Snātaka, as well as his wife, should never hold water and fire together, nor water and food. (9.9)
One should not drink from one's cupped hands. 9.10.
Whatever drinkable liquid, such as milk or water, one should not drink with the cupped hands; the two hands joined together constitute the *añjali*. (9.10)
One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while standing with water drawn up [in a vessel]. 9.11.

One should not perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) while standing with water drawn up; one should perform it only while seated. Because of the expression "with water drawn up," the ritual sipping is not prohibited for one who is standing even in knee-deep water in places such as ponds, provided that the bank area is impure. Such is also the practice of the learned (śiṣṭas). 9.11.
Nor [should one eat] food offered by a Śūdra, nor that which is impure, nor that which is offered with only one hand. || 9.12 ||

One should not perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water that has been drawn out by a Śūdra—even if he is pure—or by a twice-born man defiled by contact with the untouchable, or with water drawn by only one hand. If it is argued that in the case of one’s own sipping, the state of being drawn by a single hand is the same [as the prohibited cases], we say no; for both hands are connected to the act of sipping, and such is observed in the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas). 9.12.
Nor should he discharge urine, feces, or impurities while facing the wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows. (9.13)

The *dvandva* compound ending with the word *ap* (water) does not take a *samāsānta* suffix because of its Vedic character (*ārṣatvāt*). According to the view of some, the application of *samāsānta* suffixes is not obligatory. "Deities" refers to images. The meaning is that one should not discharge urine and the like toward the wind and other such directions, whether intentionally looking at them or not intentionally looking. "Not [discharging] toward" implies avoidance by facing away. "Not while looking" means that even if one is facing that direction, one should not look at it due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*). Because urine and feces are mentioned separately, the term "impure substance" (*amedhya*) is intended to include spittle, food remnants, and so forth. If that were so, the term "impure substance" alone would suffice; however, the specific mention of urine and feces is for the purpose of emphasizing their particularly strict avoidance. (9.13)
One should not stretch out one's feet toward these deities. || 9.14 ||

One should not stretch out one's feet toward these deities, beginning with Vāyu. The mention of "feet" (pādau) is an elliptical expression; one should not stretch out even a single foot. The application of the term "deity" (devatā) to cows and Brahmins is likewise for the purpose of respectful metaphor. (9.14)
One should not remove urine or feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones. 9.15.
One should not perform the scraping or wiping away of urine and feces with leaves and such; however, one may do so with other materials. 9.15.
One should not step upon ashes, hair, nails, husks, potsherds, or heaps of grain.

One should not step upon ashes and the like. *Tuṣas* are the husks of rice and other grains; the others are well known. One should not stand upon them. By the word "stand upon" (*adhitiṣṭhet*), it is implied that there is no fault in a mere accidental touch. (9.16)
One should not converse with barbarians, impure persons, or those who are unrighteous. 9.17

Those who dwell in regions such as Siṃhaladvīpa that are devoid of the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma) are Mlecchas. Even those Āryas who are impure and do not perform prescribed acts such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana) are likewise designated [as Mlecchas]. Those who are unrighteous include the fallen (patita) and others. One should not converse with them. Although the meaning is already established by the use of the prefix *sam-* in "converse" (*saṃbhāṣeta*), the inclusion of the word *saha* ("with") is for the purpose of indicating that one should not converse even while engaged in a common task with them; therefore, there is no fault in [speaking] when asking the way and so forth. (9.17)
Having conversed with those who have performed meritorious deeds, one should meditate upon them in the mind.

If, due to necessity, one should converse with them, then one should mentally meditate upon meritorious beings such as Vasiṣṭha and others. The word "mentally" is a restatement of the nature of meditation. 9.18.
Or he may converse with a Brāhmaṇa. 9.19.
According to the context, even a Brāhmaṇa must be one who has performed meritorious deeds. 9.19.
One should say of a non-cow, "She is capable of being a cow. || 9.20 ||
A milch cow is a *dhenu*; a non-milch cow is the opposite of that. One should call even such a cow a "potential milch cow" (*dhenubhavyā*), but not a "non-milch cow" (*adhenu*). (9.20)
"An ill omen as a good omen. || 9.21 ||
One should speak even of an inauspicious thing as if it were auspicious. 9.21.
"The skull is the vulva. || 9.22 ||
When saying "skull," one should say "female organ. || 9.22 ||
"Maṇidhanus" refers to Indra’s bow (the rainbow). || 9.23 ||
Speaking of "Indra’s bow," one should call it "the jewel-bow. 9.23.
One should not point out to another a cow that is suckling her calf. || 9.24 ||

Regarding the root *dheṭ* [Dhātu Pāṭha 902]: this is an instance where, by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*), the agentive suffix is used in the sense of the object. One should not tell another person, the owner, that a cow is suckling her calf. However, in cases such as when calves have been separated for the sake of an oblation and might suckle [the cow], it must indeed be told; for there is a specific rule in the text of Āpastamba stating, "and [if she is] mixed with the calf" (ĀpDh 1.31.10). 9.24.
And one should not choose her as a bride. || 9.25 ||
And he should not restrain her himself either. || 9.25 ||
Having engaged in sexual union, he should not delay regarding purification. 9.26.

Having united with his wife, he should not delay regarding purification; he should perform it at that very moment. Regarding purification, Āpastamba has stated: "Either by touching water, or by washing off the stains and sipping water, there is the sprinkling of the limbs" (ĀpDh 2.12.3; 2.2.1). || 9.26 ||
And one should not recite the Veda while lying on that bed. 9.27.
In which sexual intercourse was practiced. || 9.27 ||
And having studied during the latter part of the night, one should not go back to sleep again. || 9.28 ||

He who, having slept during the first watch of the night, rises for the last watch and studies, should not sleep again. Since there is a long duration of time remaining, he should not sleep further but should remain awake for the rest of the night. Because of the inclusion of the word "again," there is no fault in sleeping if one had not already slept during the first watch of the night. (9.28)
One should not take pleasure in an unvirtuous woman. || 9.29 ||
He should not take pleasure in a woman who is unwell due to illness or other causes; he should not engage in sexual union with her. 9.29
Nor one who is menstruating. || 9.30 ||

One should not take pleasure even with a woman who is menstruating. Since the author will prescribe the penance for approaching a *udakyā* as "three nights" (GDh 23.33), this statement is made despite that rule being already established; its purpose is to prohibit intercourse even after three nights have passed, provided the menstrual flow has not yet ceased. (9.30)
And he should not embrace her, nor a maiden. 9.31.
One should not embrace or hug this girl while she is in her menses, even if she is unmarried. (9.31)

blowing on the fire with the mouth, engaging in contentious speech, wearing external perfumes and garlands, combing the hair, eating together with one's wife, applying collyrium, seeking alms, entering through a side door, washing the feet, and sitting on a wooden bench—
One should avoid overeating, crossing many rivers, and climbing up or down uneven trees, as well as excessive physical exertion that risks one's life. 9.32.

One should not blow upon a fire with the mouth, nor cause it to flare up. *Vigṛhyavādaḥ* is a verbal quarrel. *Gandhamālyayor bahirdhāraṇam* means wearing perfumes and garlands openly; Āpastamba states: "One should be without visible garlands or ointments" (ĀpDh 1.32.5). *Avalekhanam* by one who is inferior refers to scratching the head and other parts of the body with an impure object such as a piece of wood. The absence of the *luk*-elision in the third case (*pāpīyasāvalekhanam*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Eating together with a wife means eating from the same vessel as the wife. This prohibition applies even though such a practice might be established by custom in certain regions. Others, however, maintain that *sahabhojanam* (eating together) refers to eating at the same time. *Añjantyavekṣaṇam* means looking at a woman while she is applying ointment—either performing an oil massage or being adorned with collyrium and the like. Some say this refers specifically to one's own wife; others say it refers to women in general. *Kudvārapraveśanam* means entering temples, houses, and so forth through a place other than the door, or entering cities, villages, and so forth by an unestablished path. As Āpastamba says: "One should not enter a village by a shortcut; if one should enter, one should mutter this verse, 'Homage to Rudra, the lord of the dwelling,' or another verse addressed to Rudra" (ĀpDh 1.31.21). *Pādapādadhāvanam* is washing one foot with the other. *Āsandīsthabhojanam*: an *āsandī* is a small stool; eating food placed upon it is *āsandīsthabhojanam*. Alternatively, it refers to placing the food vessel on whatever seat one is sitting on and then eating. *Nadībāhutaraṇam* is crossing a river by swimming with the arms to reach the opposite bank. There is no fault in using a raft or similar means instead of swimming. The mention of "river" is illustrative of ponds and other bodies of water. *Vṛkṣaviṣamārohaṇāvarohaṇe* means climbing a tree and descending into a pit or other uneven ground. By the mention of "tree and uneven ground," very high places and deep depressions are indicated. *Prāṇavyāyacchanam* is exerting the vital breaths by jumping, or climbing onto water-machines and the like. One should avoid these acts, beginning with blowing on the fire with the mouth. (9.32)
One should not board a boat that is doubtful [of its safety]. 9.33.
One should not board a boat that is doubtful of its ability to reach the other shore or is incapable of doing so. 9.33.
Because it is impossible to recite every single word, he says in brief:
"One should protect oneself from everything. (9.34)
One should protect oneself from all means [of harm], according to such injunctions as: "One should not travel alone on a road" (MDh 4.60), and so forth. 9.34.
One should not wander about during the day with one's head covered. || 9.35 ||

There is a prohibition against walking about during the day while covering one's head; however, for one who is sitting, it is as he pleases. On a path, if there is distress from rain, heat, or other such factors, there is no fault in walking even with the head covered, because it has been stated: "One should protect oneself in every way" (GDh 9.34). 9.35.
Having wrapped [itself] at night. || 9.36 ||
But at night, one should wander about only with the head covered.
And [the same applies] to the voiding of urine and excrement. 9.37.

*Mūtraṇam* means urination and *uccāraḥ* means the act of defecation; this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). In that regard, the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "one should perform the action with the head covered, having wrapped the head. (9.37)
Not without having vanished from the ground. || 9.38 ||
One should perform the acts of voiding urine and excrement on the ground only after covering it with grass and the like; for another Smṛti states: "With sacrificially unfit grass" (VaDh 12.13). 9.38.
And from a human habitation. 9.39.
A dwelling is a house; one should not do [the aforementioned acts] near it. 9.39.
Nor [should one study] in places covered with ashes or cow-dung, in ploughed fields, or on paths frequented by travelers. 9.40.

*Karīṣa* is dried cow dung. A *chāyopajīvya* is a place where travelers and others seeking shade take refuge. A *kāmya* is a desirable or beautiful spot. One should not perform the acts of voiding urine or excrement in these places, such as those containing ashes and the like. (9.40)
But during the day, one should void both urine and feces while facing north.
If one voids urine or feces during the day, one should do so facing north. 9.41.
And during the two twilights. 9.42.
One should perform [the rite] facing north. || 9.42 ||
At night, facing south. || 9.43 ||
This is clear. 9.43
One should avoid a seat made of palāśa wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick [made of the same]. 9.44.
Based on the meaning of the particle *iti* and other such [implications], one should also avoid chariots and the like that are similarly constructed from *pālāśa* wood. Regarding this, they recite:
"One should avoid a seat, a bed, a vehicle, as well as household utensils; likewise, one should avoid sandals and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*. (9.44)
And one wearing shoes should avoid sitting on a seat, saluting, or bowing down. 9.45.

"Greeting" (abhivādana) has been explained previously; "salutation" (namaskāra) is prostration before a deity. One should not perform greetings and the like while wearing shoes. The mention of "shoes" (upānah) is an elliptical expression that includes sandals and similar footwear as well. (9.45)
One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly;
according to one's ability, one should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma. 9.46.

The fourth or fifth case endings are used in the sense of the third. One should not, according to one's ability, make the three parts of the day—beginning with the forenoon—fruitless by means of the three [activities] beginning with dharma. Rather, one should make them fruitful, corresponding respectively to each part. 9.46.
But among them, Dharma should be supreme. || 9.47 ||

The word "tu" (but) avoids the charge of infinite regress. Among those [three goals of life], dharma, artha, and kāma, one should have dharma as the highest; one should make dharma the primary concern. One should pursue artha and kāma only in a manner that does not conflict with dharma. And so Manu says: "One should abandon artha and kāma if they should be devoid of dharma. (MDh 4.176) || 9.47 ||
One should not look at another man's wife when she is naked. 9.48.

She is both "another" (parā) and a "woman" (yoṣit), hence "another's wife" (parayoṣit). Otherwise, widows, unmarried women, prostitutes, and so forth would not be included. One should not look at her while she is naked. 9.48.
One should not drag a seat with one's foot. 9.49.
One should not bring a seat near oneself with one's foot. 9.49.
One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, speech, or the eyes. || 9.50 ||

The term *cāpala* (restlessness) is connected with each [of the following]. Restlessness of the genitals is the desire for sexual intercourse at improper times. Restlessness of the stomach is the constant longing to eat. Restlessness of the hands is the desire to practice various crafts. Restlessness of the feet is wandering about. Restlessness of speech is engaging in worldly discourse by transgressing the rule: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly" (MDh 2.110). Restlessness of the eyes is the desire to watch dancing and the like. One should not perform these. (9.50)
One should not, without cause, perform cutting, splitting, scraping, crushing, or tearing apart. 9.51.

Cutting refers to [the cutting of] grass and the like; breaking refers to [the breaking of] jars and the like; scratching refers to scratching walls, the ground, and so forth with fingernails and the like; crushing refers to reducing clods of earth and the like to powder; snapping refers to stretching out the fingers with a sound. One should not perform these acts abruptly. However, there is no fault in snapping and the like when there is a specific reason; in the case of cutting and the other acts as well, one should seek [justification] according to what is appropriate. (9.51)
One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied. 9.52.
The "calf-tether" is the rope for binding a calf; one should not step over it. The word "calf" is an elliptical designation for the bovine species. (9.52)
He would not be one who goes from family to family. || 9.53 ||

One who goes from family to family (*kulam-kula*) is called *kulamkula*. The addition of the suffix *mum* is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Such a person [the practitioner] should not be like this: even when there is the opportunity for study and other gains by going elsewhere, he should not remain within his own family alone. Another says: one who goes from one family to another family—such as in the form of being given away in marriage and so forth—is a *kulamkula*; he should not be like that. He should not abandon his own *sūtra* and resort to another *sūtra*. Regarding this, there is another *Smṛti*:
"He who, having abandoned his own *sūtra*, practices another *sūtra*, should be known as a *śākhā-araṇḍa* (one who has strayed from the branch), excluded from all ritual acts. (9.53)
One who has not been invited should not go to a sacrifice. || 9.54 ||
One who has not been invited or formally requested should not go to a sacrifice. || 9.54 ||
But for the sake of seeing [him], indeed, [one may go]. 9.55.
Even if uninvited, he may go to see a sacrifice at his pleasure; however, not out of a desire for the office of officiating priest or similar roles. 9.55.
One should not eat foods from one's lap. 9.56.
One should not eat foods such as flattened rice (pṛthuka) and the like after placing them upon one's lap. 9.57.
Nor [should one eat] what has been brought by a servant at night. 9.57.
At night, one should not eat anything at all that has been brought by a servant or an attendant; it is not only food that is prohibited, as indicated by the use of the singular number. (9.57)
One should not eat foods whose potency has been removed, such as oil that has been extracted, boiled grains, oil-cakes, and buttermilk. 9.58.

One should not eat foods that have lost their vitality (*āttavīrya*) or whose essence has been extracted (*upāttasārāṃśa*). What, then, are these? Here is a detailed enumeration of examples: curd and milk from which the cream has been removed; butter that is merely the scum remaining after churning; the dregs of sesame seeds pressed in a mill, known as *piṇyāka*; and that which is churned but has had no contact with water—regarding this, the lexicographers say: "Buttermilk (*takra*) is indeed *udaśvit* when churned; it is *pādāmbu* [one-quarter water] when half-watered, and *nirjala* [waterless] when entirely without water."

And that [fresh butter] is of two kinds: fresh butter produced from milk (*āttanavanīta*) and other [kinds]. Of these, it is this [first kind] that is referred to here, for it serves as an illustration of [butter] produced from fresh curds. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), there is the inclusion of any other similar substance in the form of a paste (*kalka*). One must consider whether whey (*takra*) from which the butter has been extracted is fit to be drunk or not; however, according to established custom (*ācāra*), it is indeed fit to be consumed. Because it is mentioned here in the context of the transgression of the *snātaka* vows rather than in the section on forbidden foods (*abhakṣya*), the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) required for violating the *snātaka* vows applies to eating these substances, but not the expiation occasioned by consuming forbidden food. (9.58)
In the evening and in the morning, however, he should eat food that has been honored and is blameless, without finding fault with it. 9.59.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. One should eat at two specific times: evening, which is night, and morning, which is day. The phrase "not in between" serves as a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the meal that would otherwise be understood as permitted. In this context, there is an injunction regarding the quality of the food: "one should not disparage what is honored," meaning one should find it pleasing. "Without disparaging" means not reviling it due to defects such as being poor-quality food. Vasiṣṭha states: "One should honor the meals of morning and evening" (VaDh 3.69). 9.59.
One should never sleep naked at night. || 9.60 ||

"One may sleep at night, but one should not sleep naked. Thus, this is a prohibition against sleeping naked specifically at night; however, by implication, [it follows that] during the day one must never do so. Otherwise, it would have simply been stated: "One should not sleep naked at night. (9.60)
Or he may bathe. 9.61.
It is not simply by being naked [that one is forbidden]. Another Smṛti states: "One who is naked should not enter the water. (9.61)
Since it is impossible to recite every single practice due to their infinite variety, he says this in brief:
"Whatever those who possess self-control, the elders, the well-disciplined, those free from hypocrisy, greed, and delusion, and the knowers of the Veda declare—that one should perform. (9.62)

Those who possess self-control have conquered their senses; they are "elders" (*vṛddha*), meaning those whose age is mature, because in youth it is impossible to be free from subjection to the objects of the senses. They are "well-disciplined," having been properly instructed by their teachers. "Deceit" (*dambha*) is the cheating of the world under the pretext of righteousness; "greed" (*lobha*) is the desire for another's property through unjust means; and "delusion" (*moha*) is ignorance or knowledge contrary to worldly truth—they have abandoned these. They are "knowers of the Vedas" (*vedavidas*), being those who have mastered the Vedas both in recitation and in meaning. Here, "elders" is the substantive. What such elders as these declare must be done. Because of the use of the plural number, this applies when there is unanimity among many. (9.62)
One should approach the Lord for the sake of security and well-being. 9.63.

Yoga is the acquisition of what has not been obtained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been obtained. For that purpose, one should approach a lordly king. Because of the use of the prefix *adhi*—derived from the sense of "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*) in the rule *adhir aiśvarye*—one should approach him with independence and without servility.
Except for gods, teachers, and those who follow the Dharma. || 9.64 ||

The phrase "he shall not find anyone else" is a restatement meaning that he should not resort to anyone other than [the king], even if such a person were capable of providing security (*yogakṣema*). "Gods" refers to Indra and others; "elders" refers to fathers and others; "righteous persons" refers to those whose nature is to practice dharma. "Other than these" means that he must indeed resort to these alone.

One should strive to dwell in a residence that has an abundance of fuel, water, fodder, kusha grass, and garlands; where people go out for excursions; which is filled with noble persons; which is prosperous and free from laziness; and which is protected by righteous rulers. 9.65.

Fuel is wood; water is that suitable for bathing and drinking; fodder is grass for the sake of cattle; *kuśa* grasses are well known; garlands are flowers for the purpose of worshipping the gods and others; an exit is a place from which one goes out, namely an open space outside for the purpose of moving about and so forth. One should strive to dwell in a residence where such things are abundant. It is filled mostly with noble people—the three *varṇas*—who are the very inhabitants; it is enriched by those who are not indolent, being the opposite of those who are lazy and lacking effort in their duties; it is presided over by righteous ones whose nature is dharma. One should endeavor to inhabit a dwelling of this kind; one should live in such a place even with great effort. (9.65)
One should circumambulate from left to right any praiseworthy, auspicious shrine of a deity or crossroads. || 9.66 ||
In going out, entering, and so forth, one should act in such a way that they remain on one's right side. || 9.66 ||
Or, as an alternative in times of distress, he may observe that entire code of conduct mentally. 9.67.
But when it is possible, there should be direct performance alone. || 9.67 ||
One whose nature is truth.
Its intrinsic nature is truthful speech; it depends on the word "it may be" which is to be stated later. || 9.68 ||
One who follows the noble conduct. || 9.69 ||

He whose conduct was like that of the noble ones—such as being the first to speak and speaking kindly—and so forth; this is a compound where the middle term is elided, as in the word *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced"). 9.69.
A teacher of the refined [tradition]. || 9.70 ||
He is a teacher for the virtuous, but not for those who are unworthy. 9.70.
One who is disciplined in purity. || 9.71 ||

One who possesses the purity prescribed by the scriptures is "śiṣṭa-śauca-vān"; the inversion of the word order [from *śiṣṭa-śauca-vat*] is for the sake of the final member [of the compound]. He is one who possesses that [purity] through the purity ordained by the scriptures. The repeated mention of "purity" (śauca) is for the purpose of emphasizing the essential meaning. 9.71.
One should be devoted to sacred learning. 9.72.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas. || 9.72 ||
Always non-violent, gentle, firm in action, and characterized by self-restraint and generosity. || 9.73 ||

"Always," even when there is a cause [for violence], he is "non-violent," meaning his character is one of non-injury. "Gentle" means he is patient even when an offense has been committed against him. "Firm in action" means he is one who completes what has been begun, not one who merely initiates. "Self-control" is the restraint of the senses. "Generosity" is sharing; the phrase "he should have that as his character" is to be understood in connection with every preceding term. (9.73)
A Snātaka who conducts himself in this manner, seeking to liberate his parents and his ancestors and descendants from misfortunes, never falls from the worlds of Brahman; he never falls. 9.74.

One whose conduct is of the manner thus described is "of such conduct" (*evamācāra*). Being such, the *snātaka*—desiring to liberate his mother and father, his prior relations such as grandfathers and so forth, and his subsequent relations such as sons and so forth, from misfortunes and sins—that is, he liberates those who have already existed from hells and other realms of suffering, and he likewise desires to liberate those sons and others who are yet to be born. The meaning of the future tense (*mocayiṣyan*) is to be sought [in this sense]: he becomes one who will liberate. Such a *snātaka* never falls from the worlds of Brahmā for a long time. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the purpose of marking the end of the chapter. The mention of the *snātaka* again is for the sake of showing that this is the fruit of the duties of the *snātaka* alone, and not of those combined with the duties of a householder. (9.74)
Thus ends the ninth chapter and the first book in the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the second question; therein,
the first chapter.
The duties pertaining to the stages of life have been mostly stated. Now he declares the duties pertaining to the social classes:
for the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving. 10.1.

The correspondence of items here is not strictly numerical. Because more [categories] will be mentioned later, it will be explained in that very place. *Adhyayana* consists of the acquisition and practice of the Vedas; *ijyā* is sacrifice, the worship of gods and ancestors; *dāna* is the relinquishing of wealth to a worthy recipient (*pātra*). Because of the expression "of the twice-born" (*dvijātīnām*), these duties begin from the moment they have become twice-born, that is, when the initiation (*upanayana*) has been performed. Therefore, some maintain that those who are uninitiated have no entitlement even to giving. We, however, say "no. The term "twice-born" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those whose birth is from a twice-born [father]; thus, even for one who is uninitiated, there certainly is the duty of giving, provided he is capable and is prompted by well-wishers. (10.1)
For a Brāhmaṇa, there are the additional [duties] of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts. 10.2.

*Pravacana* is teaching; *yājana* is officiating as a priest; *pratigraha* (accepting gifts) is well known. These are the additional duties of a Brāhmaṇa over and above the previous ones, such as study and so forth. What is meant is that these [additional duties] and those [previous ones] are to be combined. Here too, accepting gifts is permitted even for one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), whereas officiating at sacrifices and teaching do not apply because they are impossible [for such a person]. Since the duties of a Brāhmaṇa—teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts—are already established, the inclusion of the word "additional" (*adhika*) is so that there should be no correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) with the preceding [verses]; thus, the former [duties] remain fixed first. 10.2.
But there is a restriction regarding the former [two]. || 10.3 ||

*niyama* means that which must necessarily be performed. Previous duties, such as study and the like, are mandatory; by not performing them one incurs sin (*pratyavaiti*), and by performing them one prospers (*abhyudeti*). However, activities such as teaching are for the sake of livelihood; therefore, there is no sin in their non-performance, nor is there spiritual prosperity in their performance. (10.3)

The gift of the Veda may be made to a teacher, a kinsman, a friend, a preceptor, one who has provided wealth, or one who has mastered the rules, except in the case of those previously mentioned [as unworthy]. 10.4.

*Brahma* is the Veda. *Saṃpradāna* is its correct bestowal. Beginning with the rule, “Having been permitted, he should sit down” (GDh 1.55), it has been stated that those who are desirous of learning are to be taught; such is the aforementioned regulation. Therefore, the phrase “even elsewhere than that” means that the *brahma* may be given even without [the formal initiation] to teachers and others. The teacher has already been defined. *Jñātis* are brothers, paternal uncles, and so forth. A *priya* is a dear friend. *Gurus* are maternal uncles and others. To these, the *brahma* should be correctly bestowed. Likewise, in the case of transactions involving wealth or knowledge (*dhanavidyāniyama*). The exchange of knowledge for wealth is a transaction of wealth; the exchange for another form of knowledge is a transaction of knowledge. To these as well, the *brahma* may be correctly bestowed. Furthermore, the transaction of wealth or knowledge applies only to qualified persons, because it has been stated that one is a teacher of the learned (GDh 9.70). Nor is this an exception to that [rule], for since study was prescribed according to the rules of proper reception, this is an exception specifically to that. (10.4)
Or agriculture and trade, provided they are not performed by oneself. || 10.5 ||

Agriculture is the production of crops by plowing; trade is the business of buying and selling. These two are permissible for a Brāhmaṇa provided they are not performed by himself, as they can be carried out through another person. (10.5)
And laziness. || 10.6 ||
Lending money for the purpose of accumulation is a form of indolence; yet that too is superior for a Brahmin, provided it is not done by himself. 10.6.
The king’s duty is the superior protection of all living beings. 10.7

For a consecrated king, the protection of all beings is his primary duty; this includes, by virtue of the term "all," the prevention of the cutting down even of stationary entities such as the *aśvattha* tree and others. (10.7)
The quality of administering just punishment. || 10.8 ||

That which does not deviate from justice is "just" (*nyāyya*); the state of possessing such punishment that is not contrary to the scriptures is "the quality of just punishment" (*nyāyyadaṇḍatva*). The reading *nyāyadaṇḍatva* has the same meaning. And this is the duty (*dharma*) of a king: that there should be no punishment that is either deficient or excessive due to passion, hatred, and so forth. (10.8)
He should support Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas. 10.9.
He should support those Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and have studied them by providing food and other necessities. 10.9.
And he [should avoid] Brahmins who lack enthusiasm. 10.10.

If [the king] is unable to provide encouragement for the sake of livelihood, he should support even those who are discouraged; how much more so, then, the Brāhmaṇas? According to the previous sūtra, having summoned equally even those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who are capable of performing [sacrificial] rites (*sarjana*), he should support them. || 10.10 ||
And the causes. || 10.11 ||

He should maintain as before those tax-exemptions granted by his predecessors to Brahmins and others, by removing any obstacles or other hindrances; furthermore, he himself shall not impose any new tax. (10.11)
And those who are students (upakurvāṇa). || 10.12 ||

He should support with gifts of food and other necessities those students who are engaged in Vedic study (*brahmacārin*) and those who are "dependent" (*upakurvāṇa*). If they are seekers, he should sustain them so that they may live independently, by turning them away from such occupations as forest-swallows and the like. Another says: "The *upakurvāṇa* are those who benefit the world, such as physicians and others. (10.12)
And yoga [is a cause] for victory. 10.13.
Yoga is the means and yoga is the domain of victory; this too is the king’s supreme duty. || 10.13 ||
Especially in times of fear. || 10.14 ||
One should apply oneself with particular effort toward the specific causes for overcoming others and so forth. 10.14.
And the practice is by means of the chariot and the bow. || 10.15 ||

*Carana* means movement. Moving in the outer area, he should move mounted on a chariot with a bow in his hand. The mention of the "chariot" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for elephants, horses, and so forth; the mention of the "bow" is an elliptical expression for swords and other weapons. (10.15)
In battle, his position is firm and he does not retreat. || 10.16 ||
Battle is combat; therein, "standing one's ground" means risking one's life. "Withdrawal" is flight; its absence is "non-withdrawal. These two are the preeminent duties of a king. 10.16.
For there is no fault in killing in battle. 10.17.

Where they call out to one another, that is a *āhava* (challenge). In such a battle, there is no fault even in the harming of enemies; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule that he is always non-violent (*ahiṃsra*). 10.17.
Except in the case of those who are without horses, charioteers, or weapons; those with joined palms; those with disheveled hair;
those who have turned their backs; those who are seated; those on dry land; those mounted on trees; messengers; cows; and Brahmins. || 10.18 ||

The word *vi-* is connected with three [terms]: *vyaśvaḥ*, *visārathiḥ*, and *vyāyudhaḥ*. He whose horse is killed is *vyaśvaḥ*; he whose charioteer is killed is *visārathiḥ*; he whose weapon is shattered or fallen is *vyāyudhaḥ*. With palms joined out of fear; with disheveled hair, being unable even to restrain his locks; turned away (*parāṅmukhaḥ*), having turned his back and fleeing out of fear; seated (*upaviṣṭaḥ*), sitting down because he is unable even to flee; mounted on a mound or a tree—*sthala* is an elevated place, and he has climbed upon that tree; or a messenger (*dūtaḥ*), one who carries news; those who say "I am a cow" or "I am a Brahmin" are called *gobrāhmaṇavādinaḥ*. Apart from these, there is no fault in causing injury in battle; but with regard to these [others], there is a fault. (10.18)
If another person should live by that [profession] of a Kṣatriya, he should do so according to his own livelihood.

If another person, being a kṣatriya, should subsist upon that king through such means as causing disturbances to the country and so forth, then he should live endowed with the same mode of livelihood and conduct as that king’s—namely, [the use of] chariots and bows and the like. For by this, he is regarded as equal to that king. || 10.19 ||
The victor shall obtain the wealth of the battlefield. || 10.20 ||
When a king’s servant or similar official, commissioned by the king, wins wealth after defeating enemies in battle, that conqueror alone shall receive it, not the king. (10.20)
But the vehicle belongs to the king. || 10.21 ||
Having conquered vehicles such as elephants and horses, they become the property of the king, not of the conqueror. || 10.21 ||
And there is extraction when there is no separate victory. 10.22.

If all the soldiers, having assembled together, should conquer and, having conquered, should obtain anything at all, then in that case where the victory is not individual, a special share (*uddhāra*) must be given to the king, chosen by himself. 10.22.
But the king shall distribute the remainder as is appropriate. || 10.23 ||

Whatever gems such as rubies he has chosen for himself, from those he should distribute the remainder as is appropriate—according to each person's respective function or according to their degree of valor—so that they may share in a manner consistent with that. He should cause it to be done in such a way that they receive what is fitting for them. (10.23)
The king’s tax shall be one-tenth, one-eighth, or one-sixth from the cultivators. 10.24.

The tenth, eighth, or sixth part of whatever is obtained by cultivators in the field must be given to the king as a tax in the form of a tribute (*bali*). This is the livelihood of this king, based on the protection [afforded] by the cultivators for what they have obtained in the field. This alternative arrangement is established according to the scope of excessive enjoyment, moderate enjoyment, or meager enjoyment of the cultivated land: in the case of excessive enjoyment, a tenth part; in the case of moderate enjoyment, an eighth part; and in the case of meager enjoyment, a sixth part. (10.24)
Some [teachers] maintain that for cattle and gold as well, the share is one-fiftieth.

Some maintain that those who live by means of livestock, or those who employ gold as usury, must give a fiftieth part to the king. For example: one who possesses fifty head of livestock should give one animal to the king every year; or, one who employs fifty *niṣkas* at interest should give one *niṣka* each year to the king as a tribute. (10.25)
The toll on merchandise shall be one-twentieth. 10.26.

That which is sold by merchants is called *paṇya* (merchandise). A twentieth part of that must be given to the king; this very thing being given is designated as *śulka* (toll/tax). The locations for the collection of tolls include *pratibhāvya*, *vaṇik-śulka*, and so forth. (10.26)
The sixth [category] consists of roots, fruits, flowers, herbs, honey, meat, grass, and fuel. || 10.27 ||

Roots include turmeric and the like; fruits include mangoes and the like; flowers include blue lotuses and the like; medicinal herbs include *bilva* and the like; the remaining items are well known. From these commodities, a sixtieth part must be given to the king by the seller. (10.27)
But why should it be given to the king in this way? To this he says: "Because it is his duty to protect it. (10.28)
Because he possesses the duty (*dharma*) consisting of protecting those who pay taxes, it is with the thought that "he is their protector" [that they honor him]. (10.28)
But one should be constantly devoted to them. || 10.29 ||

Regarding those [subjects] such as farmers and others, he should be constantly diligent; he should always be attentive in their protection. Another says: regarding those [revenues] such as taxes and so forth, he should be constantly diligent; he should collect the toll with focused intent, thinking, "This is indeed his wealth. (10.29)
Livelihood by means of what is superior. 10.30.

Regarding what was stated—that the king’s protection is paramount—the wealth that comes in through that means shall be used for his own maintenance, for his dependents, and for the upkeep of elephants, horses, and so forth; however, he should not live off that which was previously accumulated and stored as a treasury. Yet, in times of distress, he may live even by that. As Vyāghra says:
"He should constantly provide for the maintenance of his family and maintain a treasury; except in times of distress, he should never draw upon the treasury. (10.30)
Artisans shall perform one day's work each month.
One task is to be accomplished in one day. Artisans, such as smiths and others, must also perform one day’s work for the king every month; this is their tax. (10.31)
By this, those who live off their own selves are explained. 10.32.

Those who subsist on themselves by means of physical labor, such as wood-carriers and the like, as well as these artisans already mentioned, should each perform one day’s work every month; this same principle applies to dancers and others as well. (10.32)
And they have no wheels for their boats. 10.33.

*Naucakrāḥ* means those who possess both boats (*nau*) and wheels (*cakra*). By the word *cakra*, a cart is likewise indicated. Those who possess these are *naucakrīvantaḥ*. The formation of the word is somehow established by the rule beginning with *āsandīvad-aṣṭhīvad-ādi*. Those possessing boats are boat-livelihoods; those possessing carts are cart-livelihoods. They too shall perform that work for the king for one day. (10.33)
One should give food to them. 10.34.
The king shall provide food—namely, cooked rice for the daytime meal—to those artisans who have been enumerated starting from the phrase "month by month," provided they perform their work. 10.34.
Merchandise must be paid back by merchants with interest. 10.35.

The phrase "one for each month" is understood to follow here. It has been stated that the toll (*śulka*) on merchandise is one-twentieth part; beyond that toll, these merchants shall pay to the king one [part] every month, having calculated a slight reduction in the price obtained through the depreciation of value. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Then they shall pay the toll, and likewise one [part] of the merchandise every month;
those merchants shall pay individually a price reduced by half. (10.35)
Having found lost property that has no owner, they shall announce it to the king.

"Lost" means fallen away from its owner; "ownerless" means one whose owner is unknown. Having found it—that is, having discovered it fallen on the ground—those appointed to protect the countryside should report it to the king. Or others who have seen it may also speak of it. (10.36)
What, then, should be done by the king? Having made a proclamation for one year, he must protect [the child]. (10.37)

Having made a proclamation by beat of drum throughout the city—“This object of such a kind has been found and is being guarded; let him to whom it belongs come forward”—it shall be kept for one year. If the owner arrives before the end of the year, then, having questioned him regarding its characteristics, if they match, it must be returned to him. If they do not match, he shall be punished. And so says Yājñavalkya:
“Property lost and found shall be delivered by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by marks, he deserves a fine equal to the value of that property.”
Those who, having understood this, do not declare it, shall be punished. 10.37.
Now, he states what is to be done after one year has passed:
"After [the year], the remainder belongs to the king for the student. (10.38)
To him by whom [the truth] has been realized and proclaimed, the king, having given a fourth part, shall take the remainder. || 10.38 ||
The owner [is established] in the cases of inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding.

Inheritance (*riktha*) is that which is obtained upon the absence of the father and other [heirs]. Purchase (*kraya*) is acquisition by means of a price. Partition (*saṃvibhāga*) is the mutual division of common property among brothers and others. Appropriation (*parigraha*) is the initial taking possession of wild things, such as trees, that have no owner. Discovery (*adhigama*) is the acquisition of lost items, such as treasure-troves, whose owners are unknown. Through these causes, the person who takes possession of the object becomes its owner. Thus, in the case of a lost item that has been discovered, it is logical that ownership belongs both to the king and to the discoverer; this is the connection with the context. Crops and other produce grown in fields belong to the owner of the field, just like the field itself. By this, the case of salt and other products produced in mines is explained. These are the grounds for ownership common to all social classes (*varṇa*).
What is obtained in excess belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. || 10.40 ||
Whatever has been obtained in the form of a gift, that is the basis for the Brāhmaṇa’s superior ownership. || 10.40 ||
The domain of the Kṣatriya. 10.41.
What is obtained by a Kṣatriya through victory is his own additional property. || 10.41 ||
It has indeed been entered [into the text] for the Vaiśyas and Śūdras. || 10.42 ||

"Consumed" means acquired through labor; for a Vaiśya, this is by means of agriculture and so forth, and for a Śūdra, by means of service and so forth. That [wealth] is in excess for these two. 10.42.
Now he states an exception to the rule that "the fourth [part] belongs to the finder of lost property": "The discovery of a hidden treasure is the king's wealth. (10.43)
If a treasure-trove has been discovered, it belongs solely to the king; however, something should be given to the finder as a reward appropriate to his discovery. 10.43.
Of a handsome Brahmin. 10.44.

He was handsome and devoted to the six duties. If that brahmin were to discover a hidden treasure, it would not be the king's property; rather, it would belong to the brahmin who discovered it. (10.44)
Some say that even one who is not a Brahmin may obtain the sixth [share] as an expounder. 10.45.

Some traditionalists maintain that even a non-Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure, if he reports it—saying, "This has been found in such a manner"—shall receive a sixth part of that treasure; this [share] is to be assigned to a Brāhmaṇa who is not worthy [of the full reward]. (10.45)
Having recovered what has been stolen by thieves, he shall restore it to its proper place.

Property stolen by thieves, having recovered it from them, he should restore it to its proper place; he should give it back to the owner alone, while the victor receives some small reward for his victory. (10.46)
Or he may give from the treasury. || 10.47 ||

If, even after searching, the thieves are not found, or if they have departed after defeating [the guards], then the king shall take from his own treasury and give that amount of wealth to the owner which was stolen by the thieves. || 10.47 ||
The property of a minor must be protected until he reaches legal majority. 10.48.

A child is one who has not yet reached his sixteenth year. If he has no well-wishers or guardians such as his father and so forth, or if those who exist are foolish and unrighteous, then his property must be protected by the king. Until when? Until he reaches legal majority, that is, until he becomes sixteen years old. (10.48)
Or until the completion of his studies. || 10.49 ||
The prefix *āṅ* is understood [from the previous rule]. *Samāvṛtti* is the return from the teacher’s house by one who has studied the Vedas; or rather, it refers to that [period] until then. 10.49.

Thus the king’s primary basis for ownership has been stated; now he speaks of that of the Vaiśya: "For the Vaiśya, agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending are the primary [bases of ownership]. (10.50)

Agriculture is well known. "Vaṇij" refers to trade (*vāṇijya*). The work of cattle-herding is *pāśupālya*. Lending money for the sake of interest is *kusīda*. Whatever is acquired through agriculture and the other [occupations] is the additional property belonging to the Vaiśya. (10.50)
The Śūdra is the fourth caste; he has a single birth. || 10.51 ||

Regarding the phrase "the fourth caste": although it shares the commonality of being a *varṇa*, the specific mention of the "fourth" is intended to establish that the three preceding castes—the Brāhmaṇa and the others—are distinct *varṇas* from it. Since the members of the three [higher] castes are already established [as having the rites], they possess one birth, namely initiation (*upanayana*), which constitutes their second birth; this [second birth] does not exist for him (the Śūdra). Because initiation is prohibited for him, the study of the Vedas—which is preceded by that initiation—does not take place either. Regarding this matter, the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra* says: "For the Śūdra as well, the rites of impregnation (*niṣeka*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the tonsure (*caula*) are prescribed to be performed at the proper times, though without mantras. His marriage also takes place without mantras, according to local custom. (10.51)
For him also, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity [are required]. 10.52.

Lest there be a lack of conduct even in the absence of initiation (*upanayana*) and Vedic study, duties such as truthfulness and the like belong to that Śūdra as well. Truthfulness is speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived. Absence of anger is the disposition not to harbor malice toward others. Purity consists of the previously mentioned purity of substances, purity of mind, and so forth. Vasiṣṭha, however, states: "For all [castes], truthfulness, absence of anger, charity, non-violence, and procreation" (VaDh 4.4). 10.52.
Some [teachers] say that for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana), one should simply wash the hands and feet. 10.53.

Regarding the matter where sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed for the preceding castes, some hold the view that for a Śūdra there is only the washing of hands and feet, and no other ritual for sipping water. Manu, however, prescribes drinking water once: "But a woman and a Śūdra [should sip] once each" (MDh 5.139). Regarding the subject of daily bathing, Uśanas states: "A virtuous Śūdra should bathe; an unvirtuous Śūdra should wash his hands and feet. (10.53)
The rite for the ancestors (śrāddhakarma). || 10.54 ||
“Beginning with the words ‘on the new moon day’ (GDh 16.35), whatever Śrāddha rite is about to be described, that too must be performed by a Śūdra, excluding the mantras. (10.54)
The maintenance of dependents. 10.55.

A servant is one who must be supported, belonging to the class of those to be nourished; and his maintenance must be performed by him [the master]. Therefore, he [the master] must also acquire wealth in accordance with that [requirement]. || 10.55 ||
One should confine one's conduct to one's own wife. || 10.56 ||

His conduct is restricted to his own wives alone; he is subject to punishment if he indulges even with the wives of others who are of the same caste, or with prostitutes. Another teacher says: his conduct remains restricted solely to his own wife, and there is no attainment of another stage of life (āśrama) for him. 10.56.
And service toward those who are superior. 10.57.
The service and attendance upon the three higher castes [is the duty] of those in the remaining [caste]. 10.57.
"This very [activity] is for the sake of livelihood," he says:
"From them, one should seek a livelihood. (10.58)
From those who have been served, he should seek his livelihood. || 10.58 ||
In that regard, one should attend upon each preceding one in order.

And so says Āpastamba: “In each preceding caste, the highest good is greater” (ĀpDh 1.1.8). Thus, just as among the acts of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, receiving gifts is the primary livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa, so too is service the primary livelihood for a Śūdra; and in that regard also, it is said, “in each preceding caste. 10.59.
Worn-out sandals, umbrellas, garments, brooms, and so forth. || 10.60 ||

*Kūrca* refers to grass and the like; the rest is well known. Worn-out items such as sandals and so forth, having been used, should be given to the Śūdra who serves him. However, this rule pertains to the Śūdra whose livelihood is service (*śuśrūṣā*), not to one whose livelihood is that of a householder (*gṛhastha*). For the latter, however, there is a distinction based on the specific requirements of his own livelihood, though in a general sense it applies. (10.60)
He returns once more to the subject at hand: eating the remnants of food. 10.61.

That which remains after he has eaten in his food vessel is his meal. As for the rule, "One should not give the leavings to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa" (ĀpDh 1.31.22), that refers to a slave; others hold it refers to a Śūdra householder. And so Vyāghra says:
"Food that is leavings should be given to a Śūdra who is not a householder;
but to a householder, food that is not leavings should be given day by day. (10.61)
And the livelihood of an artisan. || 10.62 ||
The crafts are painting and so forth; he may also subsist by these. In this regard, there is a specific rule for a Mānava:
"But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having reached a state where his wife and children are in distress, may live by the work of artisans" (MDh 10.99). || 10.62 ||
And whoever he may rely upon for support must be maintained by him, even if he himself is impoverished.

If a Śūdra who lives by service becomes exhausted and is unable to perform his work, nevertheless, he must still be supported by the one whom he previously relied upon and for whom he performed services, out of consideration for what was done before. (10.63)
And by that, the subsequent [is established]. 10.64.

And that Śūdra must support his superior when the latter’s means of livelihood are exhausted, by means of crafts and the like, having regard only for what was previously done [for him]. On this point Jātūkarṇya says: "If a noble man should take refuge with a low-born person, he should always show himself as such;
even the low-born person should behave toward him as if making himself a slave."
A poor Brāhmaṇa who is self-controlled and has mastered the Vedas must always be supported even by a Śūdra, even if he is not seeking support.
"A wise man should always support a Brāhmaṇa with every effort;
out of compassion, even a Śūdra who possesses wealth should do so for others as well. (10.64)
His accumulation of wealth would be for that purpose alone. || 10.65 ||
The accumulation of this Śūdra—the collection of wealth—should be for that purpose; it should be for the sake of supporting that latter [person]. This is the reason for the preceding sūtra. 10.65.
The mantra for his salutation is authorized. || 10.66 ||

For this Śūdra, in the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, the wise in Dharma have authorized a mantra consisting of the form "namo namaḥ," while mentally meditating upon the specific deity-passage ending in the dative case for each respective deity. Another says:
"To the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis;
to Svadhā and to Svāhā—eternal salutation, salutation!"

Thus, this mantra is intended by the word "salutation" (*namaskāra*). It occurs in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*). Regarding this, the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra* says: "Having seated the Brahmins, one should mutter the mantra beginning with the deities. (10.66)
Some say that he should himself perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices. 10.67.

The term *pākayajña* is well known to apply to domestic rites (*gārhya-karman*) characterized by cooked offerings as well as those characterized by uncooked offerings. As Āpastamba says: "The term *pākayajña* refers to worldly [rites]. (10.67)
And all should serve one another in successive order. || 10.68 ||

Indeed, all those beginning with the Vaiśya should serve each successive higher caste, not only the Śūdra; for the Brāhmaṇa, however, there is no one higher. Between them stand the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. Nevertheless, the plural number in the word "all" (sarve) is intended to include those born of intermediate castes. Another [teacher] says: even within the same caste, whoever is superior by virtue of qualities, him a lower person, being lower himself, should serve; such is the meaning. 10.68.
In the case of the interchange between the noble and the ignoble, there is equality of action;
it is equality. 10.69.

The noble one is one of the three [upper] castes; the non-noble one is a Śūdra. When there is an inversion or reversal of their respective duties and conduct, equality alone exists between them, and the relationship of server and served no longer persists. Even a Brāhmaṇa or others, if they perform the work of a non-noble, should not be served by a Śūdra. Likewise, even a Śūdra, if he performs the work of a noble, should not be despised by others of non-noble conduct on account of his low birth. By this, the cases of the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya, as well as the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, are explained. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 10.69.
Thus ends the first chapter in the second book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The king is the restrainer in cases of conflict between the noble and the ignoble; therefore, he states his duties: "The king has authority over all, with the exception of the Brāhmaṇas. (11.1)

A consecrated king exercises authority over all the people residing in his own realm regarding matters such as punishment and favor. Is this without exception? No, he says: "excluding Brāhmaṇas," that is, setting aside the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, even when they deviate from their own duty (*svadharma*), they should be established in it through conciliation. This statement is intended to demonstrate their independence in their own religious practices. As Nārada says: "All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent. (NSm 1.29) || 11.1 ||
He states that his independence applies only to matters not contradicted by the scriptures: "One who acts rightly and speaks rightly. (11.2)

One who acts rightly is one whose character is to conduct himself in accordance with the scriptures. One who speaks rightly is one who, at the time of legal proceedings, speaks impartially regarding both his own side and the opposing side. 11.2.
He should be well-trained in either the triple Veda or in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī). || 11.3 ||

The three Vedas consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* constitute the *Trayī*. The *Atharva* Veda is included within them; for even there, the mantras are either *ṛc*s or *yajus*s, though the distinction between them is based on the manner of recitation (*pravacana*), or else it is based on the difference in the subject matter (*prameya*), such as rites for pacification (*śāntika*) or prosperity (*pauṣṭika*). *Ānvīkṣikī* is the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*). He was "thoroughly trained" (*abhivinīta*) in those two by his gurus, meaning he was properly instructed by them. Manu, however, states: "From those learned in the three Vedas, he [the king] should learn the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), the eternal science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*), and the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*); and the undertaking of economic pursuits (*vārtā*) from the people. (MDh 7.43) || 11.3 ||
Pure, with senses conquered, and endowed with virtuous companions and skillful means. || 11.4 ||

Pure means being free from longing for the property of others and the like internally, while externally being devoted to bathing and other such rites. Having conquered the senses means being devoid of vices such as women, dice, hunting, and drinking. Virtues refer to tranquility and the like. "Endowed with companions" means being joined by those possessing such qualities, such as the three types of conciliation (sāma) and so forth; and "endowed with means" refers to one who employs them—conciliation and the rest—in accordance with the place, time, and circumstances. The phrase "he should be [thus] in all respects" is to be understood as required from what follows. (11.4)
He should be impartial toward all subjects. || 11.5 ||
At the time of worldly interaction, he should remain impartial toward both the hateful and the beloved. || 11.5 ||
One should do what is beneficial for them. 11.6.
He should be intent upon the welfare and security of these subjects. || 11.6 ||
While he was seated above, others besides the Brahmins should sit below him. 11.7.

They should sit on the ground below that king—who possesses such qualities—while he is seated high upon the lion-throne or similar seat. Is this without distinction? No; "others" refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas. Since it is already established that they should sit below, the phrase "seated above" is a restatement of the natural state [of the king], indicating that he is always seated above and not even on the ground when in private.
They too would think thus of him. || 11.8 ||
Those brahmins too would regard him as a king and honor him with blessings and other marks of respect. || 11.8 ||
He shall protect the social classes and the stages of life according to the law. || 11.9 ||

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and the others; the *āśramas* are the student (*brahmacarya*) and the others. He should protect these according to justice—that is, in accordance with the scriptures—by accepting for himself a sixth part of their produce and so forth, protecting them on all sides. This means that through the performance of the duties of the *varṇas* and *āśramas*, they may become free from danger. Alternatively, "according to justice" means he should protect them in such a way that there is no violation of the local customs and other such laws. The intermediate castes (*avāntaraprabhava*), such as those born of *anuloma* unions, are included within these very categories. While the protection of all beings from thieves and the like has been mentioned previously, this present statement is intended to ensure that there be no confusion regarding the duties of the *varṇas* and *āśramas*. (11.9)
And he should establish those who have strayed in their own duty. || 11.10 ||
If they should deviate from their own duty due to laziness or other such causes, then as they deviate, he himself must restrain them by means of that very same duty and establish them in it.
But why does he act in this way? He says: "For he becomes a sharer in a portion of the Dharma. (11.11)

For it is known that a share of *dharma* accrues to the king who protects; this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that even for one who does not protect, a share of *adharma* accrues. On this point, Manu says: "A sixth part of all *dharma* accrues to the king from his protection;
indeed, a sixth part of *adharma* also accrues to him if he fails to protect" (MDh 8.304). 11.11.
And he should appoint as his domestic priest a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, noble lineage, eloquence, beauty, youth, and good character, who is of righteous conduct and ascetic. 11.12.

“‘He is one who has heard much’ (GDh 8.4) — thus begins the description of learning (*vidyā*). Noble birth in a distinguished family is lineage (*abhijana*). Speech is refined *bhāratī*. Form is captivating. Age is middle-aged, neither too young nor too old. Character (*śīla*) is purity of the internal organ or external conduct. Endowed with these qualities—learning and the rest—and prosperous; one whose conduct is righteous, following a way of life not opposed to the world; and ascetic, being devoted to austerity rather than worldly enjoyment—one should place such a Brāhmaṇa at the front, that is, appoint him as the domestic priest (*purohita*). (11.12)
He is called the *purohita* because he is placed at the front (*puras*) in all ritual acts; this is what [the text] shows.
One should perform the rites impelled by him. 11.13.

Impelled by that domestic priest—authorized and instructed as to how this or that must be performed—he should carry out the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, those belonging to the Purāṇas, the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika), the propitiatory (śāntika), the nourishing (pauṣṭika), and the malevolent (ābhicārika). By the phrase "impelled by him," the author cites the Brāhmaṇa as the source for this statement. (11.13)
For it is known from scripture: "The Kṣatriya born from the Brāhmaṇa prospers and does not suffer. (11.14)

The Brahman was born from the Brāhmaṇa, and the Kṣatra was indeed authorized by him; thus the Kṣatriya [the Kṣatriya caste] prospers—that is, it becomes successful—and does not falter, nor does it fear anything from any quarter. The meaning is that it shall be free from harm. It is understood in this manner through tradition; it is seen thus in succession. 11.14
And whatever those who contemplate divine portents might declare, he should take that into account. || 11.15 ||

Astrologers are those who contemplate fate; augurs are those who know omens. They understand beforehand the results of portents. Whatever they might declare—such as, "This is a disturbance caused by another planet," "This is an ill omen today," "This is a portent today," and "This is the remedy for these"—he should respect all of that and not neglect it. || 11.15 ||
For what purpose? For some indeed maintain that even the acquisition and preservation of property (yogakṣema) depends upon him. || 11.16 ||

It is not only the performance of prescribed duties such as protection; rather, even that which is declared by those who contemplate divine portents and the like as something to be done when there is an anomaly of the planets and so forth—that too depends upon Him. *Yoga* is the acquisition of what has not been obtained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been obtained. This is a collective dvandva compound of the two. In expressions such as “may he obtain *āyoga* and *prajā*” and “may *yogakṣema* be ordained for us” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.5.18.1), the gender follows the final member of the compound, just as in the case of *ekaviṃśati* and other such terms. For example: *eka* and *viṃśati* together form *ekaviṃśati*. Thus, some teachers maintain that this *yogakṣema* [depends on Him]. 11.16.

One should perform in the domestic fire (śālāgni) rites associated with peace, auspicious days, prosperity, longevity, and blessings— those pertaining to worldly success— as well as those involving incantations for causing enmity, subjugation, malevolent magic, and the ruin of enemies. 11.17.

In this regard, Āpastamba, having introduced the topic with, “But we shall state the specific rules for the king” (ĀpDh 2.25.1), and referring to the three locations—the palace (*veśman*), the residence (*āvasatha*), and the assembly hall (*sabhā*)—says: “In all of these, the sacred fires (*agnayaḥ*) should be perpetual, and the worship of the fires should be constant, just as in the domestic sacrifice” (ĀpDh 2.25.6–7). Among these, the fire here is the *śālāgni* (the hall-fire), neither the *aupāsana* nor the *tretāgni*, because those two are restricted to domestic and *śrauta* rites respectively. [The following types of rites are performed in the *śālāgni*: 1. Those connected with pacification (*śānti*), such as the *grahaśānti* and *mahāśānti*, which are performed to avert the decline indicated by divine portents. 2. Those connected with auspicious days (*puṇyāha*), such as those performed at weddings and other ceremonies to destroy daily defects. 3. Those connected with benediction (*svastyayana*), such as those performed at the start of a journey. 4. Those connected with longevity (*āyuṣmat*), such as those performed on birth-stars and the like for the increase of life-span. 5. Those connected with auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), such as the *dūrvā-homa* and *vāstu-homa*, performed at the entry into a new house and similar occasions. These are *ābhyudayika* (prosperity-related) rites, performed on account of prosperity. 6. Those connected with inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), by which one’s enemy becomes hated by his own subjects. 7. Those connected with subjugation (*saṃvanana*), by which one’s enemies become submissive and prostrate. 8. Those connected with malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), by which one’s enemies die. 9. Those connected with misfortune (*vyṛddhi*), which is the absence of prosperity; specifically, the misfortune of enemies (*dviṣad-vyṛddhi*), by which one’s enemies are deprived of their power. 10. Those connected with eradication (*uccāṭana*), etc. All these should be performed in the *śālāgni*. Who performs them? The king. And his agency here consists precisely in this: his role as the organizer through the provision of funds and other means. As the saying goes: even one who sits silently in a secluded place but provides the food, seed, and oxen is said to be "plowing with five plows. Another says: the domestic priest (*purohita*) should perform the *ābhyudayika* rites himself, while he should have the others performed. Furthermore, one does not perform the non-prosperity rites in the same fire where the *ābhyudayika* rites are performed; rather, they are performed in another fire, distinct from those previously mentioned. (11.17)
As it has been said: "The officiating priests [perform] the others. (11.18)

As for other domestic (*gārhya*) and scriptural (*śrauta*) rites, those officiants who have been prescribed for whichever rite should perform that many duties as stated therein. For example: in the *aupāsana* and *agnihotra*, there is one *adhvaryu*; in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, four; in the *cāturmāsya*, five; in the *paśubandha*, six; and in the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others, sixteen. Regarding this, Manu says:
"He should choose a domestic priest (*purohita*), and he should certainly choose officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). (MDh 7.78).
In those cases where there is an officiating priest, some maintain that the *purohita* is the *adhvaryu* and the *brahmā*. (11.18)
And its conventional expression consists of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences, the Upavedas, and the Purāṇa. 11.19.

That by which people conduct their affairs is "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*). For that king who is authorized to protect his subjects, the Vedas and other such sources are the means for conducting legal procedure. He should conduct legal procedure exactly as it is set forth in the Vedas and other authorities. Legal procedure is the establishment of the boundaries of worldly conduct. (11.19)
The laws of regions, castes, and families are authoritative when they are not in conflict with the traditional scriptures. 11.20.

Regarding local customs (*deśadharma*) and caste customs (*jātidharma*), even if their foundational source such as the Vedas is not perceived while they are being observed as specifically determined, nevertheless, provided there is no conflict with the Vedas and so forth, they are to be maintained in that very way; they must not be violated on the grounds of a lack of a [Vedic] foundation. In this regard, *deśadharma*s: When the sun is situated in Aries (*meṣa*), in the region of Caula, young girls draw the sun together with his retinue upon the ground using powders of various colors and worship him morning and evening. On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, adorned, they wander through the village and offer whatever they have obtained to the deity. When the sun is in Cancer (*karkaṭa*), on the two *Phalgunī* constellations, having worshipped the goddess Umā according to their means, they give sprouted barley and salt to beggars. When the sun is in Pisces (*mīna*), on the two *Phalgunī* constellations, householders worship the goddess Śrī. As for *jātidharma*s: At a wedding, Śūdras drive a pillar into the ground, place a thousand wicks in a single vessel, light a lamp for each wick, take the bride by the hand, and circumambulate [the pillar]. Other similar practices are to be understood in this manner. *Kuladharma*s (family customs): Some have the topknot in the middle; some have the topknot at the back. However, those who engage in sacred study and the like have the topknot on both sides depending on the time. And their kinship relations are with their respective groups. But those local customs which contradict the traditional scriptures (*āmnāya*), such as marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle, or exerting effort in other pursuits without having studied the Vedas, are not authoritative here.
Farmers, merchants, cattle-herders, usurers, and artisans [should be assigned] to their respective classes. 11.21.

Farmers are those who live by agriculture; merchants are those devoted to the business of buying and selling; cattle-herders are cowherds; usurers are moneylenders; and artisans are carpenters, washermen, and so forth. These are authoritative within their own respective classes regarding matters known among their own class. (11.21)
And therefore, when there is a deviation from the Dharma among farmers and others,
the settlement of the Dharma occurs by withdrawing their wealth according to their respective entitlements. 11.22.

From those respective groups, having brought back and ascertained the matters—that is, the various modes of conduct—from those who are authorized as the administrators within each group according to their specific jurisdiction, the establishment of the dharma should be carried out. When they have declared, "In this manner our own custom is established," it should be settled exactly so. (11.22)
If they were to speak falsely out of partiality, then how is the truth to be known? Reasoning is the means for attaining right understanding. (11.23)

In the comprehension and ascertainment of a matter established by logic (*nyāya*), reasoning (*tarka*) is the means of inference (*anumāna*). The prefix *abhi-* follows the sense of the verbal root. Regarding this, Manu says:
"By outward forms, by gestures, by gait, by movement, by joyfulness, and by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived" (MDh 8.26). 11.23.
And therefore: having inferred that, he should cause it to go to its proper place. || 11.24 ||
Having inferred by means of that reasoning and having determined that "this matter must be thus," one should lead it to its proper place—that is, to whichever side the matter belongs. || 11.24 ||
