Now, since the self is difficult to comprehend even by reasoning when one is alone,
one should resolve any conflicting views by consulting those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas,
and thereby attain certainty.

When there is disagreement and the matter is difficult to ascertain, he should assemble those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas; having deliberated with them on the true nature of the matter and having received their instruction, he should reach a definitive conclusion. He should lead [the king] to that position in which the matter has been settled. || 11.25 ||
What comes to one who acts in this way?
For in this manner, his supreme good (niḥśreyasa) is attained. 11.26 ||

For one who makes such a determination, there arises the highest good in both worlds: here, through the affection of the people, and in the hereafter, through the attainment of dharma; for this reason. (11.26)
Success belongs not to the king alone; rather, it is shown that it belongs also to the Brahmin judges. To demonstrate this, he cites a Vedic text:
"It is known that Brahman, when joined with Kṣatra, sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings. (11.27)

It is established by the Śruti that Brahman, characterized by the three Vedas, when joined with Kṣatra—that is, together with the king—discriminates the Dharma and sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings. When this determination has been made, men perform the prescribed actions; and by the principle that "the gods subsist upon that righteous action and the ancestors do not perish," the sustenance of all is secured. || 11.27 ||
If, however, one does not approve of the established rule regarding immorality, they say: "Punishment is for the sake of subduing"; therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued.

Those who know the Dharma say that the word *daṇḍa* possesses the nature of *daṇḍa* because of its connection with the act of subduing (*damanayoga*). Therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued and bring them under control. Although the meaning "one should subdue the unsubdued by means of *daṇḍa*" is already established, [the specific types of punishment are:

"First, one should apply the punishment of reproach (*dhig-daṇḍa*); after that, the punishment of verbal censure (*vāk-daṇḍa*); thirdly, the punishment of fines (*dhana-daṇḍa*); and after that, the punishment of corporal death (*vadha-daṇḍa*). (MDh 8.129)
"Even the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when they are oppressed by the rod alone. (MDh 7.23) || 11.28 ||

Now, one might ask: how is the perfection of the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*) achieved when they are established in their respective duties by the king through the authority of the scriptures? To this, he says:

"The classes and stages of life, being devoted to their own respective duties, after death experience the fruit of their actions; then, by the remainder [of that karma], they attain distinguished place of birth, caste, family, form, lifespan, learning..."
They attain birth endowed with good conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence. || 11.29 ||

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; the *āśramas* are the student (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. Those who were devoted to their own duties performed the duties pertaining to the *varṇas*, those pertaining to the *āśramas*, and those pertaining to both. Having died and gone to another world, they experienced the fruits of those respective actions, such as heaven and the like. Thereafter, by means of the "remainder"—the karma left over after what has been enjoyed—they experience specific places and other conditions, and then obtain birth. In this context, the word "specific" (*viśiṣṭa*) is connected with all the following: place and so forth. A "specific place" is Āryāvarta and the like. A "specific caste" is the Brāhmaṇa caste. A "specific family" is one endowed with Vedic study and other virtues. "Specific form" means possessing beauty. "Specific lifespan" is one hundred and sixteen years, based on the observation that "he lived for one hundred and sixteen years. Freedom from disease is also a particularity of lifespan. "Specific learning" has been explained in the passage: "And a Brāhmaṇa who is well-learned" (GDh 8.1). "Specific conduct" is character free from defects. "Specific wealth" is that acquired through righteous means and employed for righteous purposes. "Happiness" is the enjoyment of permitted pleasures by abiding in a secure state. "Specific intelligence" is the capacity to grasp the meaning of texts; the fact that the word *medhā* ends in *s* is an archaic (Vedic) usage, as seen in examples such as *sumedhas* and *durmedhas*. Thus, the meritorious and non-meritorious actions being experienced are experienced only with a remainder, because even the bodily existence in this life is caused by merit and demerit. (11.29)
Moving in opposite directions, they perish. || 11.30 ||

Those belonging to the various castes and stages of life who do not perform their own duties according to rule become perverted and distracted; wandering into various wombs, they perish, experiencing a succession of misfortunes. || 11.30 ||
The instruction of the teacher and punishment protect them. || 11.31 ||

The instruction of the teacher protects those castes and stages of life as long as they do not act contrary to what has been prescribed; even there, for one who does not abide [in that teaching], the king's punishment [is applied]. 11.31.
Since this is so, therefore the king and the teacher are beyond reproach; they are beyond reproach. 11.32.

For that reason, the king and the teacher are to be honored and beyond reproach. Even though they may act as leaders during times of restraint out of a desire for one's welfare, nevertheless, no criticism of them should be made. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 11.32.
Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
It has been stated that "one should subdue the unsubdued by means of punishment. To address the question of what specific punishment should be meted out for what specific offense, he says:
"A Śūdra who, having maliciously intended against twice-born men, strikes them with verbal or physical abuse, shall have that limb cut off by which he has caused them injury. (12.1)

The Śūdra is the fourth caste. If he, having intended to insult—that is, having overcome—the three twice-born castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa by means of verbal abuse, and having struck them with physical violence—that is, having intentionally and premeditatively beaten them—the term "staff" (daṇḍa) is an illustration that includes the hand and other limbs as well. Acting in this manner, he is to be deprived of a limb; he is to be separated from that specific limb by which he might have harmed or committed the offense. If he strikes with the hand, his hand is to be cut off; if he strikes with the foot, his foot is to be cut off; if he does so with speech, his tongue is to be cut off. On this point, Manu says:
"Whatever limb of a Brāhmaṇa a person of lower caste might offend with, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu. (MDh 8.279).
Because of the inclusion of the term "harshness," this does not apply to speaking unpleasant words in jest, nor to striking [another] in jest or similar circumstances. 12.1.
For violating an Arya woman, there shall be the excision of the organ and the confiscation of one's property. 12.2.

The word "Śūdra" refers back to the subject under discussion in the genitive case. "Āryas" refers to those of the three [higher] castes. If a Śūdra should have sexual intercourse with the wife of any of them, his punishment shall be the excision of his organ—that is, its removal—and the confiscation of whatever property he possesses. Although the phrase "intercourse with an Ārya woman" would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "woman" (strī) is intended to indicate that this applies even when the Ārya women are married to other Śūdras. In such cases, if she is a Vaiśya woman, there is confiscation of his property; if she is a Kṣatriya woman, there is excision of the organ; and if she is a Brāhmaṇa woman, both punishments apply. (12.2)
If he is the protector, the punishment shall be more severe than death. || 12.3 ||
If he is a Śūdra who acts as their protector, then he must be put to death; because of the mention of "excessive," both of the previously mentioned punishments also apply. || 12.3 ||

Now, for one who eavesdrops upon his Veda, there shall be the filling of the ears with molten tin and lac; for reciting it, the cutting off of the tongue; and for memorizing it, the destruction of the body. 12.4.

Now, *atha* is used here as a particle of emphasis (*vākyālaṃkāre*). *Upaśrutya* means the deliberate grasping of syllables through the intellect; that is, "overhearing. For this Śūdra who overhears the Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac (*trapu-jatubhyām*). By the word *upaśravaṇa*, there is no fault in merely hearing the sound by chance. If he should utter or pronounce the syllables of the Veda together with the twice-born, his tongue is to be cut off. Once he has mastered them, such that even when gone elsewhere he is able to recite them himself, then his body is to be pierced with an axe or similar weapon. (12.4)
One who seeks to obtain another's seat, bed, or path [by force] shall be fined. 12.5.

If a Śūdra seeks equality with the twice-born in matters such as sitting and so forth—that is, if he desires a status equal to theirs—he should be punished for that. And the punishment has been shown by Āpastamba: “In the case of speech, the path, the bed, and the seat, they become equal; [the penalty is] flogging with a rod” (ĀpDh 2.27.15). This means he is to be struck with a rod. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from Manu: “An inferior person who seeks to sit together with a superior should be branded on the hip and banished, or else his buttocks should be cut off” (MDh 8.281). 12.5.
A Kṣatriya [shall pay] one hundred for insulting a Brāhmaṇa. || 12.6 ||

If a Kṣatriya should revile a Brāhmaṇa with harsh speech or insult him, he shall be fined one hundred. In all matters concerning fines, the traditional legal practice (*smārta vyavahāra*) is that the term refers to copper *kārṣāpaṇas*. Thus, he is to be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. In cases of physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), the fine is double. Now Bṛhaspati says:
"Whatever fine is prescribed for someone when verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) is committed, one should cause that very person to pay double that fine, except in the case of death. (12.6)
A Vaiśya [should give] one and a half. || 12.7 ||
But a Vaiśya, upon reviling a Brāhmaṇa, shall be fined one hundred and fifty; that is, he shall be fined one hundred and fifty, which is fifty more than one hundred. || 12.7 ||
But a Brāhmaṇa [should pay] fifty [paṇas] for a Kṣatriya. 12.8.
But a Brāhmaṇa, when reviling a Kṣatriya, shall be fined fifty paṇas. || 12.8 ||
Half of that [is the fine] for a Vaiśya. || 12.9 ||
For insulting a Vaiśya, he shall be fined half of that, namely twenty-five paṇas. || 12.9 ||
Nothing at all [is prescribed] for a Śūdra. || 12.10 ||

When a Śūdra is reviled, however, a Brāhmaṇa should not be fined any substance at all. This [omission] should not be stated [as a general rule], for the absence of punishment would be established simply by the fact of its non-mention; rather, it was stated for the purpose of prescribing a fine when a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya reviles a Śūdra. Thus it has been said by Uśanas: "Having reviled a Śūdra, a Kṣatriya shall be subject to a fine of twenty-four paṇas, and a Vaiśya thirty-six. (12.10)
The Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya are like the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya.

Whatever punishment is prescribed for mutual verbal abuse between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, the same applies to mutual verbal abuse between a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya. Accordingly, the Sūtra should be adapted as follows: "A Vaiśya [should pay] one hundred for abusing a Kṣatriya; but a Kṣatriya [should pay] fifty for abusing a Vaiśya. This should be understood to apply to those born of intermediate castes as well. On this point, Jamadagni says: "For those born in the natural order (anuloma), the status is equal to that of the mother; for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), it is equal to that of the father. (12.11)
The punishment for violence has been stated. He now states the punishment for theft:
"The guilt of theft for a Śūdra is eightfold. (12.12)

*Steya* means theft. Property acquired through theft is called *kilbiṣa* because it is the cause of sin. A Śūdra must restore eightfold the property acquired by theft; this genitive case (*steyakilbiṣasya*) refers to the agent. The meaning is that the Śūdra shall pay eightfold for the stolen property as a fine to the king. Of that, one part is to be given to the owner, and the remainder to the king. And it has been stated: "Having recovered what was stolen by a thief," and so forth (GDh 10.46). 12.12.
For the other castes, the [distances] increase twofold for each successive class.

For the others—the Vaiśyas and so forth—the sins of theft must be increased twofold for each successive caste: sixteenfold for a Vaiśya, thirty-twofold for a Kṣatriya, and sixty-fourfold for a Brāhmaṇa. (12.13)
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "In the case of a transgression by one who knows, the punishment is more severe. (12.14)

Just as the excellence of knowledge increases with the excellence of caste, so too does the severity of the punishment increase upon the transgression of what is prescribed. For one who acts even after knowing the fault inherent in the prohibition, there is an excess of guilt; however, for one who acts without knowing, there is leniency, like that afforded to one falling into a blind well. This is an exception to the rule concerning the "eightfold fine" (aṣṭāpādya) and so forth. [12.14]
In the case of taking fruits, green vegetables, or grain, [the fine] is five *kṛṣṇalas* for a small amount.

Fruit refers to mangoes and the like; green grain refers to rice and other crops while still standing on the stalk; and vegetables refer to vāstūka and similar greens. For the theft or taking of these, the fine is five *kṛṣṇalas*. A *kṛṣṇala* is the size of a *guñjā* seed. Regarding the weights:
"A *māṣa* should be known as the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kṛṣṇala* is proclaimed to be a fourth part of a *māṣa*. Thus it is said.

A collection of five *kṛṣṇalas* is called a *pañcakṛṣṇala*. If that is small—meaning if it consists of fruits and the like sufficient merely to fill the stomach—then [the fine is] as stated; however, if it is more than that, it is indeed an *aṣṭāpādya* [fine]. 12.15.
When cattle are harmed, the fault lies with the owner. 12.16.
When crops and other plants are damaged by cattle, the fault lies with the owner of the cattle; the measure of the fine will be stated later. (12.16)
But when that [body] is joined with a protector (pāla), || 12.17 ||

If that animal has been entrusted to the herdsman by its owner, then the fault lies with that herdsman. "Herdsman" (pāla) means one who protects; it refers to the cowherd. This applies when the act was committed through negligence; however, if it was done intentionally, the fine is double, as is seen in another Smṛti text. 12.17.
On a path or in an uncultivated field, [the responsibility for damage falls] upon both the herdsman and the owner of the field. || 12.18 ||

The owner of the field has other fields, but his field is open along the path; when cattle cause damage there, the punishment for both the keeper and the owner of the field shall be equal halves, because of the keeper’s lack of vigilance and the owner’s failure to provide an enclosure.
For it is seen in the *Mānava* (Manu Smṛti): "And one should construct an enclosure there such that even a camel cannot look over it" (MDh 8.239). || 12.18 ||
He states the measure of the fine:
"Five *māṣas* for a cow. (12.19)
Uśanas has set forth the *māṣa*:
"A *māṣa* should be known as the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākiṇī*, however, is declared to be a fourth part of a *māṣa*. Thus it is said.
The fine for destroying crops and the like when they have been damaged by cows is five māṣas. || 12.19 ||
Six [mātrās] for a camel or a donkey. || 12.20 ||
The compound is treated as a singular collective (dvandvaikavadbhāva). However, if a camel or a donkey causes injury, the fine shall be six māṣas for each animal. 12.20.
For a horse and a buffalo, ten [days]. 12.21.
The gender is not intended to be significant. For a horse and for a buffalo, the fine is ten māṣas each. (12.21)
Among goats and sheep, there are two each.
For those who seize goats and sheep, two māṣas each; the plural number is used because they act together. For each goat and for each sheep, the fine is two [māṣas] each. (12.22)
There is sorrow at the destruction of everything. 12.23.

Furthermore, so that there may be no further growth [of the crop], the penalty for total destruction is *śada*. *Śada* is a term denoting a portion. Whatever portion would have arisen there, that much must be paid to the owner; and a corresponding fine must be paid to the king. (12.23)
In the case of failing to perform prescribed duties and engaging in prohibited acts, there shall always be the forfeiture of one's own property, starting from the clothing and the alms-bowl.

The prescribed [duty] has been stated. Regarding the constant non-performance of what is prescribed and the constant practice of what is forbidden, one must effect the seizure of whatever property he possesses beyond the clothing and the food—where "clothing" means a garment and "food" means a morsel—and that by which those two are satisfied; anything more than that must be taken. Having set aside whatever is necessary for clothing and seating, the remainder of his property is to be seized; thus [the rule applies] until he desists from those acts. (12.24)

Regarding the prohibition against taking what is not given, he states an exception: "One may take grass, firewood, and the flowers of creepers and trees for the sake of cows or for the sake of the sacred fire, as if they were one's own; and likewise the fruits of those that are not enclosed. (12.15)

The fire referred to is that for *śrauta* and *smārta* rites, not the common (worldly) fire. Grass is for the sake of cattle; fuel—consisting of shrubs (*vīrud*), trees (*vanaspati*), creepers (*latā*), and plants—is for the sake of the fire. The flowers of trees are for the purpose of worshipping deities, not for personal enjoyment. Because they are mentioned in conjunction with cattle and fire, it is understood that they are for the sake of the deities. One may take these grasses and other items even if they have not been given by their owners, treating them as one's own. Just as an owner takes them without hesitation, so may one take them. If those shrubs and trees are unenclosed, one may take their fruits as well as one’s own, without regard for the owner. This state of being unenclosed applies to the fruits and not to the grasses and other items, because they constitute separate statements.
Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five māṣas per month for every twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]. || 12.26 ||

The term *kusīda* refers to wealth lent for the purpose of interest. Uśanas has stated: “A *māṣa* is the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. Where five *māṣas* are given as interest on twenty [coins], that is called *pañcamāṣikī*. In the sense of “that in which this is given as interest, profit, toll, or tax,” the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.47 (*prāgvahateṣṭhak*). Although the elision (*luk*) would have been required by Pāṇini 5.1.28 (*adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug asaṃjñāyām*), it was not applied by the Sage out of his own discretion. Thus, when twenty *kārṣāpaṇas* yield five *māṣas* per month, such an arrangement does not deviate from the legal rules regarding interest on loans (*kusīdavṛddhi*).
