[text omitted] ...[Manu 8.262]... [text omitted] ...[Manu 8.
"One should employ the interest ordained by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
a moneylender may take one-eightieth part from a hundred per month.

[MDh 8.140] Here too, this very same rate of interest is stated. How so? A *māṣa* is the twentieth part of a *paṇa*. Twenty *paṇas* amount to four hundred *māṣas*. Of those four hundred, five *māṣas* constitute the interest, which is one-eighthieth; thus it becomes five hundred [from four hundred]. As for Yājñavalkya, however:

"The interest shall be one-eightieth part every month when there is a pledge; otherwise, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per hundred, according to the order of the castes. (YDh 2.37) That which is deposited for the sake of confidence, such as gold and so forth, is called a *bandhaka* (pledge). When such a loan of wealth is mentioned, the principal becomes increased by two, three, and so on, respectively, according to the sequence of the castes among the debtors, such as Brāhmaṇas and others. 12.26.
Some say that it should not exceed one year. 12.27.

Regarding this lawful interest characterized by an eightieth part: some maintain that one should not take it if it exceeds the annual rate—that is, once a year has passed; rather, only an eightieth part should be taken each month within a single year, and nothing at all beyond that, for this is lawful. The grammatical derivation of the term *atisāṃvatsarīm* is to be considered. 12.27.
He states his own view:
"In the case of long-term storage, there is a doubling of the loan. (12.28)

For as long as it takes for the lent capital to become double, for that much time alone it increases by lawful interest, and not beyond that. This refers specifically to items such as gold. On this point, Vasiṣṭha states: "Gold becomes double; grain becomes triple. By grain, liquids are explained. Tree roots and fruits, as well as things weighed on a scale, become eightfold" (VaDh 2.44–47). Because of the mention of "long duration," even after a thousand years, it does not increase beyond the state of doubling. 12.28.
A pledge that has been used does not increase [in value]. || 12.29 ||

That which is deposited for the sake of trust, such as a bronze ornament and so forth, is a pledge (*ādhi*). If it is used [by the creditor], the principal amount does not increase; in that case, the very use constitutes the interest. (12.29)
And for one who intends to give, and for one who is obstructed [from giving]. || 12.30 ||

The wealth of a debtor who wishes to pay a creditor does not increase. If the creditor, out of greed for interest, does not accept it under some pretext, then on that very day it must be deposited in the hands of a third party; from that point on, the interest ceases to grow. Likewise, the property of a debtor who intends to give but is detained by the king or others, and is thus unable to pay, also ceases to increase from that time forward. (12.30)
Now, he states other types of interest for times of distress:
compound interest and periodical interest. 12.31.

The term *vṛddhi* (interest) is connected with each preceding word. *Cakravṛddhi* is interest on the principal—that is, the interest itself becomes the principal, and interest is again charged upon that amount for the duration of time during which such interest accrues. As Nārada says:
"Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*" (NSm 1.89).
*Kālavṛddhi* is that interest which is agreed upon by contract according to the rule: "for this period of time, there shall be this much interest. (12.31)
And [the fruits] consisting of activity, body, crest-lock, and enjoyment. 12.32.

The word "for increase" (*vṛddhaye*) is the remainder [of the sentence]. Interest that is either abundant or small, determined by the practitioner and the receiver according to the requirements of place, time, purpose, and circumstances, is called *kāritā* (contracted interest). *Kāyikā* (corporeal interest) is that which is to be cleared through bodily labor. Thus Bṛhaspati says: "Corporeal interest is connected with labor. Vyāsa, however, states:
"Corporeal interest is declared to be that which is joined with the work of milking or carrying.
Kātyāyana speaks of *śikhāvṛddhi* (interest on interest):
That interest which is collected daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi*;
it increases perpetually through the *śikhā* (the principal), but ceases upon the cutting off of the head (the principal).
"When the root is given, this [series] is likewise known as 'the increase of the crest' (śikhāvṛddhi). Thus it is said.

An example: "A handful of rice is taken daily from a measure (*prastha*) of rice. *Ādhibhoga* is the enjoyment or experience of the field that has been pledged. In this case, the experience itself constitutes the interest. And that [interest] does not cease even after a hundred years; furthermore, the field does not revert to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). It belongs to the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) whenever the principal is repaid. Others say it is *ādhibhoga*. It exists with reference to enjoyment (*bhoga*), hence it is *ādhibhogavṛddhi*. In this case as well, the meaning is the same. In these types of interest, such as *cakravṛddhi* and others, because the interest doubles, it indeed continues to accrue even beyond that limit. (12.32)
One may accept from a lazy person [gifts] such as cattle, wool, fields, grain, and vehicles, provided they do not exceed five times [the value of the service]. || 12.33 ||

*Paśūpaja* (animal-products) refers to ghee, milk, and the like produced by livestock. *Lomakṣetra-śadaḥ* (wool-field-rent) refers to wool, blankets, chowries (*cāmara*), tail-fans (*vālavyajana*), and so forth. *Vāhya* (draught animals) refers to oxen and the like. Most read it as *bāhya* (external), but even there the meaning is the same. When these—animal-products and the rest—are employed [as loans], that usury increases until it becomes fivefold; it does not exceed the state of being fivefold. Another says: regarding animal-products, when the principal substance is lent and not returned at that time, it increases until it becomes fivefold, and through lawful interest, it does not exceed the state of being fivefold. (12.33)
Property belonging to minors or those not yet of age, if enjoyed by others for ten years in the presence of the owner, belongs to the enjoyer. || 12.34 ||

One who is an idiot, one who is insane, or a minor whose legal capacity has not yet manifested—if the property of one who is neither an idiot nor a minor is enjoyed by others in his very presence for ten years, then it is determined that the property belongs to the enjoyer alone. That very enjoyment indicates that the property has departed from the owner’s possession through acts such as gifting and so forth. Otherwise, how could he remain silent regarding such a matter in the world of the living for so long? Regarding this matter of land, Yājñavalkya says:
"For one who sees but does not speak, there is loss of land after twenty years;
for wealth being enjoyed by another, the loss occurs after ten years. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.24)
He who, while witnessing another giving away land, does not prevent it,
is not entitled to receive that land, even if he possesses a written title.
Thus says Bṛhaspati. On this point, Manu states:
"Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence while remaining silent, he does not deserve to recover it. (MDh 8.147)
"But he who enjoys [wealth] that has not come [to him]," and so forth, refers either to cases of non-proximity or to cases involving the dull-witted and the like. || 12.34 ||
The exception to this is:
"Not [with] a Vedic scholar, a renunciant, or a royal official. (12.35)

When property is being used by a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) or others, it does not become theirs merely through that use, because it is logically possible for them to be indifferent to it. Indifference on the part of the learned scholar and the renunciant (*pravrajita*) arises from a thirst for dharma; on the part of the king’s servant, however, it arises from fear. The mention of the king’s servant is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those who possess power. By this, violent offenders (*sāhasika*) are also explained. Furthermore, even for a renunciant who possesses no property, the enjoyment of an ownerless thing—such as an empty house—is possible. (12.35)
For women who are like cattle, there is no excessive enjoyment [of sexual intercourse]. || 12.36 ||

Livestock are four-footed animals; land consists of fields, groves, and so forth; women are female attendants and slave-girls. Regarding livestock and the other items, excessive enjoyment is not required; even with a small amount of enjoyment, they become the property of the enjoyer. How could one neglect a cow seen in the house next door while personally purchasing and consuming buttermilk and the like? Or how could one neglect a grove yielding abundant fruit? Or how could one neglect a young female slave who serves as an attendant every day? (12.36)
The heirs of the inheritance shall discharge the debt.
Those who are the heirs of one's estate shall repay that debt. However, even in the absence of an heir, it must be paid by sons and grandsons. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"A son must pay his father’s proven debt as if it were his own;
a grandfather’s debt is to be paid equally [by the grandson], but that [debt] is not to be paid by the grandson’s son."
Nārada says: Grandsons shall pay that debt of their grandfather which was contracted in due order and discharged by their fathers; it ceases with the fourth generation. [NSm 1.4]
Yājñavalkya says:
"Even when the father is abroad, deceased, or overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons and grandsons; if it is denied, it is established by witnesses. (YDh 2.50) || 12.37 ||
Sureties for a guarantee, merchants' duties, liquor, gambling, and fines shall not descend upon their sons. (12.38)
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"For the purpose of attendance, for the purpose of payment, and likewise for the purpose of assurance—
the wise have observed three kinds of sureties in these very three matters" (NSm 1.104).
"When his surety has died, he should cause even the heirs to pay," so says [Manu].
Viṣṇu and Yājñavalkya state: "Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment."
"But if the first [surety] is proven false, they shall be made to pay, as shall the sons of the other.
[Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.53; Viṣṇu Dharmaśāstra 6.41] Therefore, this rule also should be understood as referring to cases other than those involving a surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*).

"I will show him this person"—having given such a guarantee (*prātibhāvya*) and then, upon the death of the father, that person is not to be shown by the son. Or, as for wealth acquired by a merchant for the sake of trade, that too does not devolve upon his sons. When someone, having promised "I will return the principal with profit," takes wealth from another and goes abroad for trade, and then dies, it is not to be repaid by his son. Likewise, having promised a bride-price (*śulka*) and performed the marriage, if he dies, that bride-price does not devolve upon his son. Similarly, if one drinks much liquor and dies after promising "I will pay the principal," it need not be paid by his son. Likewise, if one loses at gambling and dies without paying the stakes, his son is not required to pay them. Just as one defeated in a legal dispute who dies without paying the fine to the king—that fine likewise does not devolve upon his sons. (12.38)
Deposits, pledges, borrowed goods, purchased items, and trusts that have been lost through no fault of the person involved shall be made good by all those who are blameless. || 12.39 ||
A *nidhi* is a deposit (*nikṣepa*). It is that in which one’s own property is deposited out of trust and without hesitation;
that is a deposit. An *anvādhi* is an open deposit (*upanidhi*); it is well known as *aupanidhika* in another legal treatise (*smṛti*). Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

"If one should hand over an object by placing it in the hand without describing what is contained in the vessel, that is a *upanidhi* deposit; it must be returned in exactly the same manner. [YDh 2.65]

"Yācita" refers to ornaments and the like borrowed for festivals and such occasions. "Avakrīta" means that which has not been paid for, or for which only half the price has been paid. "Ādhi" refers to a pledge (specifically a *gopyādhi*, or a pledge for custody). If these items—treasure-trove (*nidhi*) and the rest—are lost without any fault on the part of the person, such as being stolen by thieves or the like, they declare all of them to be "anindita," meaning blameless or without fault. Not only do they not have to pay for the sons, but they also do not have to compensate those from whose possession the treasure-trove and other items were received. Regarding the term "anindita": if they had previously been seen to be guilty of faults, then this [exemption] applies only to the current instance. As for "fault on the part of the person" (*puruṣāparādha*), it occurs if the holders fail to protect the items as they would their own property; for example, if in the event of a fire or similar danger, they take their own goods and neglect the treasure-trove and so forth, or if they deposit their own goods in a secure place and leave the treasure-trove outside. When such a fault on the part of the person exists, they must indeed pay. (12.39)
A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a club, shall go before the king, proclaiming his deed.
A thief is one who commits the theft of gold.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, shall proclaim his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me. [MDh 11.99]

Thus says the *Mānava*. "With disheveled hair" means with loose, untied hair. "An iron or khadira-wood pestle"—this is from another *Smṛti*. "Possessing that," as Āpastamba says: "Having placed the pestle on his shoulder" (ĀpDh 1.25.4). He should go before the king proclaiming his deed, saying: "I am one who has committed such an act; punish me. (12.40)
He is purified by both execution and release. || 12.41 ||

"Killing" (*vadha*) means a beating that ends in death. Āpastamba states: "He should strike him with that very [weapon]" (ĀpDh 1.25.4). The beating is to be done only once, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "Having seized the club, the king himself should strike him once" (MDh 11.100). "Release" (*mokṣa*) means setting free, saying: "Do not do such a thing again; go. By these two—killing and release—the thief becomes purified. For it is said: "Even when killed he is purified; even when released he is purified. (12.41)
If he does not slay [the offender], the king becomes a sinner. || 12.42 ||
If the king does not slay him out of compassion or other such motives, he himself becomes guilty; whatever guilt belongs to the thief, that becomes his. (12.42)
But this [rule] regarding punishment shows that it excludes the Brāhmaṇa;
corporal punishment is not a punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. (12.43)
Even for a Brāhmaṇa who has arrived of his own accord, corporal punishment must not be inflicted; rather, there must be release alone. And so says Manu:
"A thief is purified by execution, and a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone" (MDh 11.100).

Here, by the force of the word "alone" (*eva*), the meaning is that even for such a Brāhmaṇa, at that time, there is release through austerity; under no circumstance whatsoever, even for any cause, should [punishment] such as the cutting off of the hand be carried out. And so says Manu:
"These [penances] shall apply to the three [lower] castes; an unharmed Brāhmaṇa may depart. [MDh 8.124] This refers to the case of an ascetic Brāhmaṇa. 12.43.
But for others, he prescribes punishment according to the offense: disqualification from office, public proclamation of the crime, banishment, and branding. 12.44.

Furthermore, the non-performance of that action in such a way that it is not repeated constitutes the separation from the act. This includes the confiscation of all property, taking a surety, and so forth. Public proclamation (*vikhyāpana*) is the announcement throughout villages, cities, and other areas by means of the mark of a thief. Banishment (*vivāsana*) is expulsion; [this may be] from a village, a city, or a kingdom, according to the offense. Branding (*aṅkakaraṇa*) is the making of a mark. Regarding this, Manu says:
"In the case of violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag."
"But for theft, the mark of a dog's foot should be made; for killing a Brahmin, the mark of a headless man" (MDh 9.237).

Regarding these punishments—such as the removal of specific limbs—the arrangement must correspond to the nature of the offense according to the principle that "for heavy sins, the penalties are heavy; for light sins, they are light. This refers specifically to the category of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). However, the branding of the body applies even to a Brahmin who has performed penance. 12.44.
If he does not engage in it, he must perform an expiation. || 12.45 ||

But that king who does not exercise such punishment within his own territories becomes personally liable for penance when it is not so applied. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "Upon the release of one deserving of punishment, the king shall fast for one night and the domestic priest for three nights; upon the punishing of one undeserving of punishment, the domestic priest shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance and the king for one night or three nights" (VaDh 40–43). 12.45.
A minister who acts with deliberate intent is equal to a thief. 12.46.

"Assistance" refers to providing support such as shelter, food, and so forth. If that assistance is intentional—that is, if one provides it even after knowing, "This person is a thief"—then he is equal to a thief and must be punished like a thief. However, in the case of ignorance, ignorance itself is the defense. (12.46)
The recipient as well [is not purified] when [the gift] is joined with unrighteousness. || 12.47 ||

Because of the word "api" (also), the phrase "intentionally" (*matipūrva*) is understood to carry over. He who, knowing that another has stolen a substance, accepts it from that person, is equal to a thief in that unrighteous acceptance (*adharmasaṃyukta-pratigraha*). Although this is established by the context alone, the explicit mention of "unrighteous" is for the purpose of making known that in other sinful matters as well, the specific sin accrues to the recipient. (12.47)
The application of punishment follows from the knowledge of the continuity of the offender's personal capacity and transgression. || 12.48 ||

"Person" refers to the caste of the individual, such as a Brahmin and so forth. "Capacity" concerns whether the punishment for the offense involves much wealth or little wealth; regarding corporal punishment, it concerns whether the person is weak or strong. "Offense" refers to whether the agency was direct or that of an accomplice. "Consequence" refers to repetition. Having ascertained these factors—person and the rest—a corresponding punishment must be applied. (12.48)
Or rather, there is permission [to study other texts] because of the statement of a gathering of Veda-knowers; because of the statement of a gathering of Veda-knowers. 12.49.
A *saṃgha* is an assembly of three or four who are knowers of the Vedas. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Whether they be four or even three, that which those who have mastered the Vedas declare should be known as *dharma*; not that of thousands of others."

One must either grant permission at the request of that Saṃgha, or speak according to the rule of non-obstruction. If they should say this, then one should say: "I grant you permission; go as you wish. [The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the chapter. 12.49
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta;
now begins the thirteenth chapter.
In the event of a dispute, the determination of truth is based on witnesses. 13.1.
In the event of a disagreement, witnesses are to be questioned; the truth must be established exactly as stated by them. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the treatises by the wise;
among them, five are said to be appointed (kṛta) and six are unappointed (akṛta)."
The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness,
the secret witness, and the corroborating witness— thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds.
Furthermore, other witnesses have been declared who are not specifically designated:
the village community, the presiding judge, and the king for those engaged in legal proceedings.

"One who is an insider in the affairs, one who has been sent by the plaintiff, and those involved in disputes between kinsmen and non-kinsmen—they too may be witnesses. (NSm 1.129–132) Thus ends [verse] 13.1.

Furthermore, as to what they are like and how many there are, he says: "They should be many, blameless in their own duties, trustworthy to kings, and free from both affection and resentment toward either side. (13.2)

One's own duties—those pertaining to caste, those pertaining to the stages of life (āśrama), and those pertaining to both, whether based on the Śruti or the Smṛti—must be performed blamelessly; for by their non-performance or by performing them otherwise, one incurs fault. Now, Yājñavalkya says:
"Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti. (YDh 2.69)

*Pratyaya* means trust; those who act with that are *prātyayikas*. Such persons are trustworthy to kings because they are free from the fault of partiality. They are those who have no affection for, nor attachment to, nor hatred toward either the plaintiff or the defendant. There should be many witnesses of this kind. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"Even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is agreed upon by both parties" (YDh 2.72).
However, in the case of a deposit, even a single internal witness is declared sufficient.
A witness sent by a plaintiff becomes competent even if he is alone, provided he has been formally requested.
Thus says Kātyāyana:
"Even a single person may be authoritative, especially in cases of violence.
Thus says Vyāsa. (13.2)
Even Śūdras [may do so]. 13.3.

"If even Śūdras of such a kind may be witnesses, how much more so the twice-born? Thus it should be understood that in the absence of virtuous twice-born men, even Śūdras who possess these qualities may serve as witnesses. (13.3)
But a Brahmin who speaks like a non-Brahmin is not to be detained, provided he is not bound [by other obligations]. 13.4.

"A Brahmin here is not a learned *śrotriya*. When it is stated by a non-Brahmin that "this Brahmin is a witness to this matter," he should not be constrained as a witness nor compelled by insistence, provided he is unrecorded—that is, if he has not been entered in writing. However, one who is recorded in writing is certainly a witness. There is no reason for this other than the statement itself being the authority. On this point, Nārada says:
"Even those who are not witnesses have been seen by the wise in the scriptures to be of five kinds:
by virtue of their speech, their defect, their division, their self-statement, and a different opinion."

Where there is a conflict among witnesses in a legal dispute— arising from the testimony of one learned in the Vedas, from the observation of faults in a thief, or from their internal divisions— that constitutes a contradiction.

"One who speaks of his own accord, unpointed out, having come himself; one who speaks after another has died while the claimant is still alive; or one who is about to die—[these are excluded], except for those who have been formally informed.

[NSm 1.137–139] Regarding this, Nārada’s position is that a *śrotriya* (a learned Vedic scholar) never serves as a witness in any case. However, because it was stated here that [the rule applies to] "non-Brāhmaṇas," a *śrotriya* who is a Brāhmaṇa certainly may serve as a witness when so designated. (13.4)
Those who are not members of the assembly and have not been questioned shall not speak. || 13.5 ||
Those who are not assembled together, nor gathered, nor questioned by the king or the judge shall not speak; however, those who are assembled and questioned shall declare [the truth]. 13.5.
They would be at fault both for not speaking and for speaking otherwise. || 13.6 ||

If those who have become such as these should know [the truth] yet not speak it, or should speak otherwise, then they would be guilty and wicked; they would be punished by the king in this world, and in the next world they would be denizens of hell. 13.6.
Heaven results from truthful speech; in its opposite, hell.
If those who speak indeed speak the truth, then there is heaven; in the opposite case, by speaking untruth, there is hell. || 13.7 ||
It should also be stated even by those who are not bound [to the teaching]. 13.8.

Those who are "appointed" (nibaddha) are those specifically designated as witnesses here. Those who are the opposite, the "unappointed" (anibaddha), must also give testimony; they are to be understood from Nārada’s statement beginning with, "Others, moreover, are unappointed. (13.8)
There is no binding [of the mind] for the sake of causing pain. 13.9.

"Causing pain" means inflicting injury. "Connection" (*nibandha*) refers to a relationship with the subject matter and so forth. Regarding the infliction of pain—that is, in matters of violence—the connection of witnesses need not be investigated; no defect whatsoever arises from their relationship with the subject matter and the like. Vyāghra says:

"In cases of theft, violence, association [with outcasts], and likewise in the case of women, as well as in the employment of poisons and the like, no fault is recorded regarding the witnesses. (13.9)
And [the same applies] to what is spoken by one who is intoxicated. 13.10.

Negligence is a lack of attention. Even regarding that which was spoken by a witness incidentally in the final or subsequent statement, there is no formal recording; thus, there is no defect such as a lack of connection to the subject matter. || 13.10 ||
In the opposite case, hell is declared. That [punishment] applies not only to the witness alone;
rather, when there is an injury to the system of dharma, the fault lies with the witnesses, the members of the court, the king, and the judge.

*Tantra* refers to worldly legal procedure. When there is an injury to either the Dharma or the *tantra*, guilt falls upon all parties: the witnesses, the members of the court (*sabhyas*), the king, and the perpetrator. The mention of the "perpetrator" is for the sake of illustration; it implies that as much guilt as attaches to the perpetrator likewise attaches to the witnesses and the others. Although the guilt of witnesses was mentioned previously, their inclusion here is intended to include the members of the court and others even in cases where witnesses are present. Otherwise, it would have been stated that in a lawsuit without witnesses, the guilt lies with the members of the court and others, whereas in a lawsuit with witnesses, the guilt lies with the witnesses alone. (13.11)
Some perform the act of truth by means of an oath. 13.12.
Where there is no such confidence in the witnesses, some maintain that the matter should be settled by means of an oath; having caused the oath to be taken, the truth must be declared. 13.12.
That [gift] should be given to non-Brahmins in an assembly of Brahmins who are kings of gods. || 13.13 ||

That act of swearing occurs in an assembly of gods, in the presence of formidable deities, or in an assembly or council of Brahmins. For Kṣatriyas and others, there is an option depending on the gravity or lightness of the matter at hand: in a major matter, it takes place in the presence of deities; in a minor one, elsewhere. Because of the expression "of non-Brahmins," the act of swearing does not apply to Brahmins. On this point, Viṣṇu states: "The king should question the Brāhmaṇa, saying 'Speak'; the Kṣatriya, saying 'Speak the truth'; the Vaiśya, with [threats regarding] cattle, seed, and gold; and the Śūdra, with all sins. Thus the king should question witnesses according to the order of the castes" (ViDh 8.20–23, 38). Manu, however, says:

"One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by cattle, seed, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all [the aforementioned] sins" (MDh 8.113). Thus [it is said]. 13.13.
By stating that "in the opposite case, one goes to hell," the fault of the witness has been stated in general terms. Now, he describes the specific fault in a particular type of legal proceeding:
"In the case of falsehood regarding small cattle, the witness destroys ten. (13.14)

Small animals are goats, sheep, and so forth. Regarding them, a witness who speaks falsely kills ten; he incurs as much guilt as would result from the slaughter of those ten. Both the punishment and the penance should be understood to correspond accordingly. (13.14)
In the case of cows, horses, humans, and land, [the fines] increase tenfold at each subsequent stage.

The answer to those [questions] stated above is as follows: regarding the subject matter of cattle and so forth, a witness who speaks falsely incurs a fault ten times greater than that previously mentioned for each successive category. This is what is meant: for a false statement concerning cattle, the witness incurs the same fault as killing a hundred cows; for a horse, the fault of killing a thousand horses; for a human being, the fault of killing ten thousand men; and for land, the fault of killing a hundred thousand of the inhabitants of that land. "He kills five by lying about small livestock, he kills ten by lying about cattle."

"One kills a hundred horses by a lie regarding [the sale of] cattle, and a thousand men by a lie regarding [the sale of] humans" (MDh 8.98)—this [rule], however, refers to the case of extremely insignificant animals and the like. 13.15.
Or everything on the ground. || 13.16 ||
Or, if one speaks falsely regarding land, it destroys the entire human race; there is an alternative view that it refers to large tracts of land such as villages and districts. (13.16)
In taking [it] away, there is hell. || 13.17 ||

This is incidental. The word "bhūmeḥ" (of land) is connected by way of transposition [to the verb]. By seizing land, one falls into hell. The limit of the duration of time is to be understood from other scriptures. 13.17.
He states the subject at hand: "As on the earth, so in water. (13.18)

In the case of falsehood regarding water, the fault is equal to that of killing a hundred men for land, and for its theft, it is equal to hell; by the word "water," reservoirs such as wells and ponds are indicated. (13.18)
And in the case of sexual union. 13.19.
In such cases as "he goes to another's wife through a lie connected with sexual intercourse," it is understood from the word "and" (ca) that [the offense is] like that of the soil. 13.19.
As in the case of animals, so it is with honey and clarified butter. || 13.20 ||
In the case of honey or clarified butter, there is a fault equal to that of [lying for] small livestock when one speaks untruth. (13.20)
As in the case of a cow, so it is with clothing, gold, grain, and the property of a Brahmin. || 13.21 ||

"Brahman" refers to the Veda. Regarding matters such as clothing and the like, speaking untruthfully incurs a fault equal to that of killing a cow. To say "I have not studied this" after having actually studied it, and so forth, constitutes falsehood regarding the Veda (brahmānṛta). (13.21)
Like a horse in vehicles. || 13.22 ||

Vehicles such as elephants, carts, and palanquins: regarding these, there is a fault in speaking untruth, just as in the case of horses. Others, however, beginning with the phrase "in the case of untruth concerning small cattle," apply this to the instruction of witnesses (*sākṣiśrāvaṇa*). In the case of untruth concerning small cattle, the witness incurs the fault of killing ten animals; therefore, the witness must be instructed: "Therefore, you must speak only the truth. This applies everywhere, including what follows. (13.22)
Having thus stated the fault regarding matters that are not perceived, he now declares the punishment for witnesses in matters that are perceived:
"A witness who speaks falsely shall be censured and punished. (13.23)

When a witness is seen to speak falsely, he is to be censured and reproached by all as one with whom no legal transaction may be conducted, and he is to be punished by the king. Regarding this, Manu says:
"On account of greed, he should be fined one thousand [paṇas]; on account of delusion, the first amercement;
on account of fear, two middle amercements; and on account of friendship, four times the first amercement."
For perjury out of desire, the fine is ten times the amount previously mentioned; for perjury out of anger, it is twice that;

for perjury out of ignorance, it is two full hundred; but for perjury out of childishness, it is exactly one hundred. Furthermore, a righteous king should punish the three social classes who give false testimony as follows: [MDh 8.120–121]

“Having fined him, one should banish [the offender]; however, a Brāhmaṇa one should exile. [MDh 8.123]. Viṣṇu states: “For false witnesses and for those who live by bribery, there shall be confiscation of all property. [ViDh 5.180–181]. 13.23.
There is no fault in speaking untruth if one's livelihood depends upon it. 13.24.

When, by speaking the truth, there would be mutual slaughter, whereas by speaking a falsehood the life of another—who is dependent on that lie—is preserved rather than his being killed, then in that instance of lying there is no fault as previously described. On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "In a case where the death of those belonging to the [four] castes would otherwise occur, one should speak a falsehood as a witness. To purify oneself from that [sin], the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī. (YDh 2.83). 13.24.
But not the life of an evil person. 13.25
But if by speaking an untruth the life of one who is more wicked—more sinful and devoted to harming others—is preserved, then it is certainly not a fault; rather, it is indeed a virtue. || 13.25 ||
Now, as to by whom the witnesses are to be questioned, he says:
"The king, the judge, or a Brahmin learned in the scriptures. (13.26)

One who asks is a *prāṭ*. One who speaks after having investigated is a *vivāka*. Due to the observation [of these forms] in the *nyaṅku* group, there is the substitution of *vṛddhi* and the change to *k* [for *p*]. Thus, a king may be a *prāḍvivāka*. But when he is occupied with other matters, a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures appointed by him [should preside]. On this point, Manu says:
"Or, if the king himself does not perform the decision of legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to decide the case" (MDh 8.9). 13.26.
He should approach the judge. 13.27.

*Adhi* means "being above" or "sovereignty"; *āṅ* has the sense of "coming. One who has a legal matter (*kāryārthin*) should come for a long time, either as a subordinate or from below, to this aforementioned judge (*prāḍvivāka*) who is seated above; however, the judge himself must not initiate the case or summon anyone. Thus says Manu: "Neither the king nor his official shall himself initiate a legal case" (MDh 8.43). 13.27.
In the case of non-appearance [of the defendant], he shall wait for one year.

When a defendant, a plaintiff, or a witness lacks presence of mind (*apratibhā*), such that they say, "It does not occur to me," either because they are personally afflicted by dullness and the like, or because the matter is difficult to determine due to having occurred long ago, then one should wait for a year. After this much time, one should grant them the period [to deliberate], saying, "Deliberate and then speak. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
"For those who are dependent, the dull-witted, the insane, children, those initiated for sacrifice, and the sick, the period may be less than a year, according to their own desire."

Nārada says: "Because of the complexity of legal disputes and because even the memory [of the facts] may fail, one may take as much time as desired regarding debts and other matters, out of a desire to ascertain the truth. [NSm Mā. 1.38]
Prajāpati [is the witness] for one day, or two, or three, or five, or seven; however,
in matters such as debt, when the case is complex, the time limit is recorded as being up to even three fortnights.
And in the case of one who has sexual intercourse with a cow, a bull, or a woman’s generative organ, [the penance must be performed] quickly.

The word "connected" (*saṃyukta*) is to be construed with each [term]. In a dispute concerning what is connected to a cow and so forth, one should settle the dispute quickly. "Procreation" refers to marriage, because it is the cause of that; "woman" refers to a female slave and the like. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and likewise procreation, as well as in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and similarly in sale and purchase."
"In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, violence, deposits, fraud, and false testimony, one should institute a lawsuit immediately. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.29)
And in cases of emergency. 13.30.
Where dignity departs, and where destruction and abandonment occur—that is not the time to act; for that matter is indeed urgent.
Thus says Kātyāyana: "In such urgent matters as these, one should litigate immediately and must not grant time. Yājñavalkya says:

"In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations, and urgent matters concerning women, one should litigate at once; in other cases, time is prescribed according to one's wish" (YDh 2.12). || 13.30 ||
Truthfulness in speech is weightier than all other things; truthfulness in speech, indeed, [is weightier]. 13.31.

This is more important than all the duties enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti: that one should speak the truth when questioned by the judge. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the end of the chapter. 13.31.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the Mitākṣarā, the commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now follows the determination of impurity (āśauca).
Impurity due to death (śāva) lasts for ten nights for the sapinda relatives, except for those who are officiating priests, those initiated for sacrifice, and celibate students. 14.1.

*Śāva* refers to that which pertains to a corpse (*śava*). *Āśauca* is the state of impurity. For ten nights—that is, ten days and nights—there is impurity for those who are *sapiṇḍas*, with the exception of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and others. An *ṛtvij* is one who performs sacrifices; one who is *dīkṣita* is one who has performed the initiatory rite (*dīkṣaṇīya*) and is engaged in the ritual. A *brahmacārī* (celibate student) is well known. The term *āvabhṛtham* applies to the two preceding cases [the *ṛtvij* and the *dīkṣita*]; [for the *brahmacārī*, it extends] up to the end of his studentship (*brahmacarya*). What, then, is the definition of this impurity? It is non-qualification for ritual acts, the state of having food unfit for consumption, untouchability, and non-qualification for giving gifts and so forth. On this point, Manu says:
In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, sacrifice, and Vedic study are suspended.
"And those who are not nearby shall not touch the near relatives of the deceased," so it is said. And Aṅgiras states:
"But when a Brahmin, especially one who is a religious student (brahmacārī), is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka)..."
One might drink water, eat food, or touch [something] out of ignorance.
"One should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while drinking water;
for eating [contaminated food], it is prescribed for three nights; and having touched [it], bathing is ordained. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
"One should bathe if touched by those who are menstruating or impure; if touched by them, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet). [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.30] Saṃvarta says:
"After the collection of the bones, touching the limbs is prescribed."
"A tiger! For one whose union with the sacred fires is not to be performed through death alone, cremation must indeed be performed;
for one whose ritual procedure is that of the three sacred fires, it must be carried out through burning alone. Thus [it is said].
Śaṅkha says:
"In the fourth [generation], it shall be ten nights; in the fifth, six nights for a male;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days."
All of this refers to those who are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). Regarding those who possess qualities (*guṇavat*), Parāśara states:
"A Brahmin who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days, while one devoid of qualities is purified in ten days."
Bṛhaspati says: "A Brahmin who maintains the Veda and the sacred fires is purified in three nights;
one who lacks the sacred fires is purified in five days; but one who merely bears the name of a Brahmin is purified in ten days."
Here, the mention of the *brahmacārin* (celibate student) is intended as an illustration for the other stages of life (*āśrama*) besides that of the householder. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:

"For those who are lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*), those established in vows, ascetics (*yati*), and celibate students, no impurity is declared on account of birth (*sūtaka*) or likewise on account of death (*śāva*)."
The mention of "one who has been initiated" (*dīkṣita*) is intended as an illustration for those engaged in vows such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:

"There is no fault for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor likewise for those performing sacrificial sessions (*satrin*); for they always occupy the station of Indra and are never impure. (VaDh 19.48) [14.1]
For a Kṣatriya, it is eleven nights. || 14.2 ||

For a Kṣatriya other than one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) or is a student (*brahmacārin*), the period of impurity upon the death of a relative is eleven nights. Yājñavalkya says, "By twelve nights" (YDh 3.22); Vasiṣṭha says, "By fifteen nights" (VaDh 4.28); Parāśara says, "By ten nights"; and Paiṭhīnasi says, "Sixteen days. Among these, there is an option depending on whether the sacred fires and Vedic study have been maintained in their entirety or partially.
For a Vaiśya, it is twelve nights; some say half a month.
“Eleven nights,” says Parāśara; “twenty nights,” say Vasiṣṭha and Paiṭhīnasi. As before, there is an option. 14.3.
For a Śūdra, [the penance lasts] one month. || 14.4 ||

"‘For virtuous Śūdras, [the impurity lasts] for half a month,’ says Uśanas. Those who serve members of the three higher castes and seek their livelihood from them are ‘virtuous Śūdras’; for we have stated that this is their highest form of livelihood. Regarding slaves, Bṛhaspati says:
‘Slaves, apprentices, laborers, and students living together are purified by the same degree of purity as their master in cases of death or birth.’"
Regarding this, Baudhāyana states concerning marriage in successive order:
"If there are kinsmen of a Brāhmaṇa who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes,
it is prescribed that the Brāhmaṇa's purification from their impurity occurs after ten days."
"Even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, when [dealing with] kinsmen of lower castes,
should undoubtedly observe their own period of impurity for the sake of purification.
Thus says Bṛhaspati.
"A Brahmin is purified in ten days from birth or death among those of his own caste;
however, among those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, he is purified in seven, five, and three nights respectively.

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "For a Brāhmaṇa, purification occurs in six nights, three nights, and one night among Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; for a Kṣatriya, it is by six nights and three nights among Vaiśyas and Śūdras; and for a Vaiśya, purification from a Śūdra is after six nights. This is the context. The application of these rules is determined by considerations such as conduct (*vṛtta*) and so forth. Regarding the case of a higher caste, Manu says:

"All [members] of the higher castes, however, should respectfully observe impurity for [the death of] those [of their own caste], according to the rules prescribed for that caste; but for those of their own birth, they should observe their own impurity based on their own lineage.

Thus, it is stated that the impurity resulting from the death of those of the higher castes should be observed by others in the manner prescribed for that specific caste, whereas for those of one's own birth (svayoni), one should observe one's own impurity caused by one's own caste. From this very point, it is understood that the duties of those born in the direct order (anuloma) are conjoined with the caste of the mother. (14.4)
If that [period] should recur within it, they shall be purified by the remainder [of the first period]. || 14.5 ||

When there is a requirement for a correlate regarding an interrupted period of impurity, the phrase "impurity due to death is ten nights" is connected to the context of the ten-night period and so forth that was previously introduced. If, while one such impurity of ten nights or similar duration is still ongoing, another impurity due to death—occurring at the same time or for a shorter duration—should again fall upon or arrive, then they shall be purified by the remainder alone; that is, by those very days remaining from the ten-night period or other duration that was first occurring. It does not mean, however, that one must wait for the completion of the newly arrived period. Here, because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule "the same applies to birth," if during the midst of a full period of impurity due to birth, another period of impurity due to birth should arrive at the same time or for a shorter duration, they shall be purified by the remainder. In a case where a full-duration impurity should fall during the midst of a shorter-duration impurity, one proceeds by means of that [full duration] itself. On this point, Manu says:
"If death and birth should both occur within ten days, a Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period has not yet reached its ten-day conclusion. Thus says Devala. (MDh 5.79)

"But when the initial [periods] coincide, the purification should be known as the more weighty. Thus says Aṅgiras: "If the father dies while the mother has already died [and her period of impurity has passed], [the purification follows the father's]."

"Purification from the father's [impurity] occurs through the remainder [of the period]; however, one should observe a *pakṣiṇī* [period] for the mother. And: "Impurity due to death (*śāva*) is double that of birth (*sūtaka*); impurity due to menstruation (*ārtava*) is double that of death; impurity due to birth is double that of menstruation; and for one who burns a corpse, it is even greater than that."

Vṛddhātri states: "By this specific prior impurity of the cremator and the woman who has given birth, there is purification from the subsequent [impurity]. On this point, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* says: "When birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs while corpse-impurity (*śāva*) has already arisen, the birth-impurity is purified by the corpse-impurity; birth-impurity does not purify corpse-impurity. (14.5)
During the remainder of the night, [he should recite] with two [stanzas]. 14.6.
If, while the preceding period of impurity still has one night remaining, another [period of impurity] should occur, then they shall become pure after two days. (14.6)
At dawn, with three [verses]. || 14.7 ||
Now, if ten days or more have elapsed, and on the following morning at the *saṅgava* period another death occurs, they shall be purified in three nights. Regarding this, Manu says:
"But he who hears that one who was abroad has died before the ten-day period has passed, shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten days. (MDh 5.75) || 14.7 ||
For those killed by cows or Brahmins, [the purification occurs] immediately.

For those who are *sapiṇḍas* of persons killed for the sake of cows or for the sake of Brahmins, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts as long as the corpse is visible. "As long as it is visible" (*anvakṣam*) means as long as the corpse is directly perceived; at the conclusion of the funeral rites, having bathed, they become pure. Regarding this matter of immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*), Manu says:
"In the case of [death] for the sake of cows or Brahmins, and also for one whom the king desires [to be pure immediately].

[MDh 5.95] The meaning is that for the kinsmen of those killed by a cow or by a Brahmin, the impurity lasts as long as the corpse is visible. Likewise, Uśanas states: "There is immediate purity for those killed by cows and for those killed by Brahmins. (14.8)
And because of the king’s anger. 14.9.

The word "of those killed" (*hatānām*) is to be understood as connected [to the preceding]. For the kinsmen of those who have been killed due to the king's wrath, there is also immediate impurity (*anvakṣam āśaucam*).
In battle. || 14.10 ||

The word *ca* (and) is carried over [from the previous rule]. Furthermore, for those killed in battle, impurity lasts until the sight [of the event]. On this point, Manu says: "And for those killed in a riot, in battle, by lightning, or by the king" [MDh 5.95]. *Ḍimba* means a crowd or tumult. Immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) is the subject under discussion. However, we do not favor the alternative reading. Or rather, let that very reading stand; the word division would be *ā-yuddha*. *Āyuddha* means a place of combat (*āyodhana*), that is to say, a battle. In any case, a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is not favored. 14.10.
And for those who desire [death] by means of fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice]. || 14.11 ||

"Prāya" generally refers to the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*). Since this may occur even against one's will due to fear of the king and other such causes, the phrase "of those who desire it" is stated [to specify those who act voluntarily]. In the same way, for the subsequent cases as well, desire and lack of desire should be understood according to the circumstances. *Aśana* means eating; from the root *aś*, *āśa* means food. That itself is *āśaka*; its opposite is *anāśaka*. This refers to the cessation of eating out of anger or other motives while edible substances are actually present. Weapons, fire, poison, water, and hanging are well known. *Prapatana* is falling from a tree or a mountain. Through these methods beginning with *prāya*, and by others of a similar kind indicated by the word "and" (*ca*), there is immediate impurity (*anvakṣam āśauca*) upon self-destruction. On this point, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
Out of anger, those lowest of men who resort to fasting, poison, fire, weapons, hanging, water, or falling from mountains and trees;
Those who have been struck down by the Brahma-staff, those who have been slain by Brahmins,
and those who are great sinners— these are proclaimed to be the fallen (patita).
"For those who have fallen [from their caste], there shall be no cremation, nor shall there be a collection of bones;
there shall be no shedding of tears, nor the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), nor should the performance of the Śrāddha rite be undertaken. On this point, Aṅgiras says:
"If someone should die through negligence by means of fire, water, or other such causes, impurity must be observed for him and the water-libation rite must be performed. (14.11)
It has been stated, "of the sapindas. Who are those sapindas? He says:
"The cessation of the rice-balls occurs at the seventh or the fifth [generation]. (14.12)

Sapiṇḍya extends from the *kūṭastha* (the common ancestor) down to the sixth degree; at the seventh, however, it ceases. At the seventh degree alone, there remains the status of being a *sodaka* (sapinda by water-offering), because it has been stated: "But it ceases at the seventh" (MDh 5.60). Beyond that, there is only the status of being a *sagotra* (same lineage). As for what was said regarding the fifth degree, that refers to cases other than the *aurasa* (legitimate son born of wedlock); even in those cases, it should be understood according to the circumstances. The meaning is thus: one should offer the *piṇḍa* to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and beyond them to two more—thus, including oneself, up to the sixth degree one should give the *piṇḍa*. But at the seventh, there is cessation. The rule "or at the fifth" refers specifically to the case of the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*). On this point, Baudhāyana says: "How, then, is the *piṇḍa*-offering for the son of an appointed daughter? [He offers: 'This is for you, O father of such-and-such a woman; O my grandfather, and those who follow you... This is for you, O grandfather of such-and-such a woman; O my great-grandfather, and those who follow you... This is for you, O great-grandfather of such-and-such a woman; O my great-grandfather, and those who follow you. For him offering the *piṇḍa* in this manner, when the fifth degree is reached, the offering of the *piṇḍa* ceases. [Thus it is stated] in the Mātsya Purāṇa.

"Those beginning with the fourth [descendant] are sharers of the lepa (the smearings); those beginning with the father are sharers of the piṇḍas; the seventh among them is the giver of the piṇḍa; such is the sapindya relationship extending over seven generations. (14.12)
The same applies to birth as well. || 14.13 ||

The extension [of the rule] applies from the passage beginning with "impurity due to death lasts ten nights" up to the end of "at dawn, with three [verses]. It should be understood that just as it is with impurity due to death, so it is also with birth. || 14.13 ||
Or from the mother and father, or from the mother alone. || 14.14 ||

"The impurity resulting from that [birth] belongs to both parents, or to the mother alone; because of the mother's primacy, it pertains to the father even more so. Regarding kinsmen in that case, Vyāghra says:
'But birth-impurity (sūtaka) belongs to the sapindas, or to the parents, or to the mother alone.
It is said, 'or to the parents, because they are the cause of it. But Manu says:"
"Even in the case of birth, for those who desire precise purity,
the impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) applies to all, but the impurity due to birth (sūtaka) applies only to the mother and the father. [Manu Dharma Śāstra 5.61–62] — thus says Yājñavalkya.

“Impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) is prescribed for three nights or ten nights; however, in the case of a child less than two years old, the impurity (sūtaka) belongs to both parents, yet it belongs to the mother alone. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.18] Baudhāyana states: “Regarding birth, there is ten days of impurity for both the mother and the father. Some say it belongs to the mother alone because she carries the child; others say it belongs to the father because of the predominance of the seed (*śukra*). For it is heard in scripture that there are even sons not born from a womb (*ayonija*). Yet, it belongs to both the mother and the father because of the commonality of their physical contact. [Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra 1.11.19–23] Aṅgiras says:
No impurity is declared for the sapindas in any way during a birth;
however, there shall be impurity for the mother and father, and the birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone.
"The impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) applies to all, but the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) applies to the mother and father;
or rather, the birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone, for the father becomes pure by touching water.
Thus [says the text]. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The same applies to birth. In that case, both the mother and father are impure; according to some, however, it is only the mother. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"At birth, the sapindas are pure, but there is impurity for the mother and father;
the impurity (sūtaka) belongs to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution. Thus it is said.

In this context, the ten-day period depends on the specific circumstances; there is no optionality regarding these [periods]. Others say that impurity characterized by loss of eligibility applies to all, because of the observation in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not eaten. However, impurity characterized by untouchability applies only to the mother and father. And it is said that for the father who lives in another house and does not come into contact with them, it does not apply; they also recite: "During a birth-impurity, contact is not forbidden, except with those who are themselves under birth-impurity. (14.14)
In the case of the miscarriage of the fetus, [the penance lasts for] as many nights as there were months of gestation. (14.15)

"Up to the fourth month there may be a flow; in the fifth and sixth months, it is a miscarriage (pāta). Beyond that, for women, the flow is called a birth. Thus, there are three types of fetal misfortunes, all of which are designated by the term *sraṃsana* (miscarriage). For whichever month the miscarriage occurs, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for as many nights as there are months. The accusative case is used here to denote duration. From the second month onwards, the number of days corresponds to the number of months. (MDh 5.67)
Or for three days. 14.16.
In the second month as well, it occurs for three days; however, the maximum duration is four months.
And having heard [of it], for ten days or for three nights thereafter. || 14.17 ||

The mention of the “tenth day” (*daśamī*) is an elliptical expression for the full period of impurity (*āśauca*) beginning with the ten days. A *pakṣiṇī* is a night situated between two days, or a day situated between two nights. As before, the application of the second [period] follows from the context of calamity (*vipatti*). If, after the ten-day period of impurity caused by a death has elapsed, one hears of the death of a relative, then there is impurity for a *pakṣiṇī*. If the news is heard during the day, it consists of that intervening day, the following nights, and the day on the next morning; if heard at night, it consists of that night and the day and night of the following day. On this point, Manu says: [Manu 5.75–76] If, after the ten days have passed, one hears of the death of a relative, one shall remain impure for a *pakṣiṇī*; likewise if one hears of a birth. If the news of a birth or death is heard within ten days, one becomes pure immediately; but if it is heard after the ten days have passed, one is purified by a *pakṣiṇī*. If the news is heard during the day, the impurity lasts for that day, the intervening nights, and the day on the next morning; if heard at night, it lasts for that night and the day and night of the following day. Thus says Manu.
"But when ten days have passed, one shall be impure for three nights" (MDh 5.76).
Likewise, Jābāli says:
"When the period of birth-impurity has elapsed, one shall be impure for three nights according to each respective [period]."

In this context, the word *sūtaka* is a synonym for *āśauca* (impurity). Viṣṇu, however, states: “But when more than a year has passed, [the impurity lasts] for one night” [ViDh 22.40]. This regulation is determined in consideration of the place, time, and specific dharma. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: “For three months, it is three nights; for six months, it should be a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night);
and all of this applies prior to one year. On this point, Manu says:
"But when a year has passed, one is purified simply by touching water. [MDh 5.76] Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"If both parents should die, even a son who is far away..."
"Having heard [of the death], from that day onward one shall be in a state of impurity for ten days. Thus [it is said]. In another Smṛti:
"When the wife of one's father has passed away, the best of the twice-born [shall observe impurity] with the exception of his mother."
When a year has elapsed, one shall remain impure for three nights.
Having heard that his kinsmen had died ten days ago and that a son had been born.
But this refers to the case of those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas up to the seventh degree). || 14.17 ||
To one who is not a sapinda, to a relative by birth, and to a fellow student. || 14.18 ||

One whose *sapiṇḍa*-relationship has ceased is an *asapiṇḍa*, who is a *samānodaka* (a distant relative). A blood relation (*yonisaṃbandha*) includes the maternal grandfather, the mother’s sister, her sons, and so forth; for married women, it includes their father and others, as well as their sisters and so forth. A fellow student (*sahādhyāyī*) is one who has studied the entire Veda under the same preceptor. By the word “and” (*ca*), those mentioned in other Smṛtis—such as the father’s sister, her offspring, and others—are also included. When these persons die, there is a period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasting for a "winged day" (*pakṣiṇī*) among themselves. However, once that period of the winged day has passed, there is merely a bath. Manu, however, prescribes three nights of impurity for a *samānodaka*.

"Those who touch a corpse are purified in one night and day, or indeed by three triple-nights; but those who offer water [for the deceased] are purified after three days" (MDh 5.64). The application of these two rules is to be determined as before. Both of these refer to the death of one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). Prior to that [initiation], there is only bathing. Regarding birth as well, a period of three days for *samānodaka* relatives has been shown by Manu.
"But for those who provide food and water at a birth, purification is held to occur here after three days" (MDh 5.71). || 14.18 ||
For one day for fellow celibates. 14.19.
A fellow student of sacred knowledge, a companion in the life of celibacy, and a friend—when such a person has died, there is impurity for one day and night. || 14.19 ||
And also when a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) has arrived as a guest. || 14.20 ||

A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda. "Dependent" (*upasaṃpanna*) means one who relies [on him] through living in his house and so forth. Upon his death, there is impurity for one day. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the phrase "for one day" is understood to carry over. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says: "If anyone dies in someone's house, that person's *sapiṇḍas* should likewise be known to have impurity for three nights; there is no doubt about this."

Manu says: "But upon the death of a learned *śrotriya*, one shall remain impure for three nights" (MDh 5.81). The statement of Aṅgiras as well refers to the case of a *śrotriya*. On this point, Viṣṇu also states: "Marriage is the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for women; among women who have undergone that rite, there is no impurity on the paternal side. However, if their birth or death occurs in the father's house, then there shall be one night and three nights [respectively]" (ViDh 22.32–34). This is a fixed alternative: one night for a birth and three nights for a death. 14.20.
Upon touching a deceased person, there is impurity for ten nights if it was done intentionally.

In this context, by the word *upasparśa*, mere touching is not intended; for regarding that [act], bathing with one's clothes on will be prescribed later in the passage beginning with "a fallen man (*patita*) or a *caṇḍāla*. What, then, is *upasparśana*? It is the carrying out of a corpse (*pretanirharaṇa*). In that case, there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten nights. If that carrying out is done with the intention of receiving wages or some other motive, and not for the sake of dharma—even though the general heading of impurity is already present—the repetition of the term "impurity" is for the purpose of making known its distinction from the preceding [types of] impurity. Consequently, the rules to be stated later, such as sleeping and sitting on the ground, do not apply in this instance; it is characterized solely by the heading concerning untouchability (*aspṛśyatā*). (14.21)
The [rules] for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra have been stated. || 14.22 ||

With reference to this matter of touching a *preta* and so forth, the previously mentioned period of impurity for Vaiśyas and Śūdras—twelve nights or half a month—is not explicitly stated here. (14.22)
Or [the verses] relating to the menstrual period. 14.23.
Or the period of impurity lasts for as many nights as there are seasons; there are six seasons, or five by combining the cold season (hemanta) and the dewy season (śiśira). 14.23.
And in the case of the two preceding [rules]. 14.24.

The period of impurity (*āśauca*) has been stated for the two preceding castes, the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, as well as the impurity consisting of the nights of menstruation (*ārtavī rātrīḥ*). The repetition of the phrase "of the Brāhmaṇa" after "of the two preceding [castes]" is for the purpose of establishing the alternative (*vikalpa*) regarding the nights of menstruation. As before, this alternative depends upon the place, time, circumstances, and so forth. Regarding the carrying out of a corpse without wages, Manu says: "A Brāhmaṇa, having carried out a deceased person who is not a *sapiṇḍa* like a kinsman, becomes pure after three nights; likewise, having carried out maternal relatives."

"He who eats their food becomes pure after ten days; he who does not eat their food becomes pure in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house" (MDh 5.101–102). "Like a kinsman" means out of affection or similar ties. Regarding those carrying [the corpse] while dwelling outside the village, the purification lasts as long as the light [of the sun or stars]: as Hārīta says, "Those who have touched the deceased shall not enter the village until the appearance of the stars at night, or until the appearance of the sun by day; thereafter there is purity. But regarding entry into the village, the one-day period from the *Mānava* text applies—"he who does not eat their food becomes pure in a single day. Regarding the case of one who is destitute (*anātha*), Parāśara [states]:
Those twice-born who carry the deceased Brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in due succession.
"A Brahmin is not defiled by contact with or the funeral rites for a *preta*;
both the carrier of the body and the giver of the fire are purified immediately by bathing. (14.24)
Or for three days. || 14.25 ||
Starting from the rule "upon touching a preta" (GDh 14.21), for all castes there is a period of three days; this refers to the case of an extremely superior person. 14.25.
The same applies toward the teacher, his son, a wife, one for whom he performs sacrifices, and a pupil. (14.26)

"The teacher (ācārya) is one who has initiated a pupil," as defined by the verse beginning "But he who, having initiated a pupil... (MDh 2.140). His son is the "teacher's son. The "teacher's wife" is his spouse. The "sacrificer" (yājya) is one for whom a sacrifice is to be performed; in relation to the officiating priest (ṛtvij), this refers to the patron of the sacrifice (yajamāna). The "pupil" (śiṣya) is well known. When these have died, the impurity lasts for three days in this manner. || 14.26 ||
He states the subject regarding the removal of impurity caused by a different caste:

"If a person of lower caste should touch one of higher caste, or if one of higher caste should touch one of lower caste, in that case the period of impurity is declared to be the same as that for a corpse. (14.27)

The "lower" is the inferior caste, such as a Kṣatriya and so forth, in relation to a Brāhmaṇa; the "higher" is the superior caste, such as a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, in relation to a Kṣatriya and so forth. When these two carry out each other's corpses, the impurity (āśauca) prescribed for that particular caste of corpse-bearer applies. For instance, when a Kṣatriya carries out the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa, his impurity lasts ten nights; when a Brāhmaṇa carries out the corpse of a Kṣatriya, his impurity lasts eleven nights, and so on. Regarding this very matter, Vyāghra states concerning service: "If an inferior carries out a superior caste, or if a superior carries out an inferior, one must observe the impurity pertaining to that corpse; however, if it is for a visible purpose [such as gain], the impurity shall be double. (14.27)
He states the purification for the mere intentional touch of a corpse, along with incidental cases:

"Upon touching an outcaste (patita), a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth (sūtikā), a menstruating woman (udakyā), or a corpse, or upon touching one who has touched them, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on. (14.28)

An outcast is one who has killed a Brahmin and so forth. A Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and a corpse are well known. Upon touching these, or touching those who have touched them, or touching those who have touched those [who touched them]—that is, upon touching those who have touched [the primary polluter]—one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on (*sacaila*) after that touching. Since purity is achieved through bathing while wearing one's clothes, the reading [of the term *sacaila*] as an adverbial modifier is incorrect. In the case of unintentional contact, the rule of Manu applies: "A Divākīrti, a menstruating woman, an outcast, and likewise a woman who has recently given birth..."
"Having touched a corpse or one who has touched it, one becomes pure by bathing. [MDh 5.85] Thus [ends the verse]. 14.28.
And likewise when following a corpse. 14.29.
"Even if one follows this relative or even a stranger out of one's own desire, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. [MDh 5.103]

Some authorities desire that bathing should take place even after the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*); the source for this must be sought. Yājñavalkya also says only this much: "Having touched fire, one who has consumed clarified butter becomes pure" (YDh 3.26). This refers to cases involving those of the same caste. Regarding a Brāhmaṇa following a Kṣatriya, Vasiṣṭha states: "Having touched a human bone, there is impurity for three nights; but if the bone-breaker [is the one who touched it], it is for a day and night; and the same applies to following a corpse" (VaDh 23.24–26). The phrase "and the same applies" extends the rules of three nights and one day [to these cases]. Here, the settled rule is that following a Kṣatriya results in one night, while following a Vaiśya results in three nights. However, regarding following a Śūdra, Aṅgiras says:
But a Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse as it is being carried away, shall remain impure for three nights.

"But when three nights have passed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean, one becomes pure by performing a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and consuming clarified butter. For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya following a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the rule should be applied as for a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya following a Śūdra, there is one night [of fasting] and a hundred breath-restraints. Thus says Manu.
"Having touched a human bone that is still moist with fat, one should enter the water wearing one's clothes;

however, if it is not moist with fat, one should merely perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) and then touch a cow or look at the sun. [MDh 5.87] This refers to a case where the act was unintentional. Vṛddha-Manu says:
One who has entered the womb [of another] should not perform either the cremation or the carrying away of another deceased person;
however, he should always perform both for his own father.
"Or [the impurity lasts for one day] for an elder brother who is childless, or for the son of a maternal uncle.
In this context, "of the father" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the mother as well. Regarding weeping during a time of affliction, Pāraskara states:
"If one weeps before the collection of the bones, one should perform a bath."
"Within ten days of the death of a Brāhmaṇa, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed for those who weep after that period.

This rule applies equally to all castes who weep when a Brāhmaṇa has died within the ten-day period. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "For every deceased person, after shedding tears with the relatives, purification is attained by bathing; if the collection of bones has not yet been performed, one must bathe with one's clothes on" [ViDh 22.61–62]. From the context, it is understood that this refers to "purification. This applies to weeping for the death of a Kṣatriya or others by those of equal or lower status, with the exception of Śūdras. They cite the *Brahmapurāṇa* regarding weeping for the sick among the three higher castes: [The text continues with the citation from the Brahmapurāṇa.]
If a Brahmin cries over a heap of bones belonging to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya,
he becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on on the second day.

"But when the collection [of bones] has been performed, the Brahmin becomes pure by means of bathing alone. This same [rule] should be inferred for a Kṣatriya even when there is the manifestation of illness in a Vaiśya. Regarding the manifestation of illness in a Śūdra, Pāraskara says:
"If a Brahmin should shed tears before the collection of the bones..."
If a Śūdra has died, having gone to his house, one becomes pure after three nights.
After the collection of the bones, for up to one month,
the twice-born are purified by a single day and night, as well as by the washing of their clothes.
Thus, enough of this digression following upon a digression. || 14.29 ||
And [the same applies] to dogs. || 14.30 ||

Even when combined, it requires [the same purification]. Upon touching a dog, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on; the separate mention is for the purpose of precluding the application of the rule regarding those who have touched such a person. 14.30.
Some say that one should destroy it. 14.31.

Some, however, maintain that one should wash only that limb which a dog might defile. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from Āpastamba: "One who has been defiled by a dog should immerse himself with his clothes on; or, having washed that spot and touched it with fire, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure" [ĀpDh 1.15.16–17]. Jātūkarṇya states the following distinction: "If a donkey touches a part of the body above the navel—excluding the hands—one must bathe; for parts below, washing is required. If it touches the body above the navel, excluding the hands, one should bathe. If it touches a part below the navel, one should wash that spot. If it touches the hands, one should wash them and sip water. If it touches the mouth, one should bathe. If it touches the eyes or the ears, one should touch clarified butter. If it touches the nose, one should sip water. If it touches the teeth, one should rinse the mouth. If it touches the hair, one should bathe.
