"In that case, bathing must be performed; otherwise, one becomes pure by washing [the hands]. (14.31)
The offering of water for one whose tonsure ceremony has been performed is to be done by the sapindas.

For that deceased person whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has been performed, the offering of water (*udakadāna*) must be made by his *sapiṇḍas* for as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts; not before then. The cremation rite (*agnisaṃskāra*) belongs to him as well. As Laugākṣi says:
"One should offer water silently and likewise fire silently;
for all those who have had their tonsure performed, both [rites] may also be done according to one's wish even otherwise."

And thus, for one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed, the rites of cremation (*agni-saṃskāra*) and the offering of water (*udaka-dāna*) are mandatory; however, for one whose *cūḍā* has not been performed, they are not mandatory, and there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in their omission. By the mention of the *cūḍākaraṇa*, the third year is indicated, as that is how it is seen in many *smṛtis*. Manu also says: "The water-rite should not be performed by Brahmins for a child less than three years old; or rather, it may be performed once teeth have appeared, or when the naming ceremony (*nāman*) has been done" (MDh 5.70).
The mention of "taking fire and water" is an elliptical expression for the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*). Regarding this, Devala states a specific rule:
"If the death of a child (*paugaṇḍa*) occurs before the twelfth year, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite shall not be performed; one should instead perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites. (14.32)
And that [is the rule] for women as well. 14.33.
That offering of water should be performed for women who have undergone the tonsure ceremony.
Some [say it belongs] to those who have been given away. 14.34.

Some maintain that the offering of water is for women who have been given away in marriage, but not at all for those who have not; and for those who have been given away, it should be offered by the members of the husband's family. 14.34.
Now, during the period of impurity, how should the relatives conduct themselves?
All of them shall sleep and sit on the ground and observe celibacy.

They should sit on the ground itself for their bodies, and not on mats, seats, or the like; they should also avoid sexual intercourse. The mention of "all" is intended to include those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas beyond the seventh degree). 14.35.
They should not wipe [the body]. || 14.36 ||
Washing is the removal of bodily impurities; and they should not perform that. 14.36.
They shall not eat meat until the offering has been made. 14.37.
A *śrāddha* is a ritual offering. They should not eat meat until that [offering] has been completed. 14.37.
The water-rites are performed on the first, third, seventh, and ninth days.

On the first and subsequent days, water mixed with sesame seeds must be offered by the sapinda relatives to the deceased, saying: "To the deceased of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, I give this water with sesame. On the first day, three [handfuls] are given; on the third, nine; on the seventh, thirty; and on the ninth, thirty-three. Thus, seventy-five handfuls of water are to be offered. However, according to custom, three are given on the first day, and from the second day onward, one more is added each time.
And there is the abandonment of clothes. 14.39.
The garments worn at the time of the water-offering should be discarded on the first, third, fifth, and ninth days; other garments should be put on in their proper order. 14.39.
But for those of the lowest [caste], it is with those of the lowest [caste]. || 14.40 ||
Among the castes, for those of the lowest caste, the Śūdras, the discarding of clothes occurs on the ninth day after their death.
The birth of teeth and so forth [are determined] by the mother and father. || 14.41 ||
From the time of the eruption of the teeth, the mother and father should offer water for their son; the mother alone does so silently. 14.41.
There is immediate purification for children, those living in a foreign land, renunciants, and those who are not sapinda relations. (14.42)

A "child" (*bāla*) is one whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed. One who is "separated by region" (*deśāntarita*) is one who is obstructed by distance and resides in another country. "Renunciants" (*pravrajitāḥ*) are those who have taken lifelong vows (*naiṣṭhika*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*). Those who are "not *sapiṇḍas*" are those who are merely "water-kin" (*samānodaka*). Upon their death, there is immediate purification for the relatives; purity is attained through bathing alone. Regarding the case of a child, Yājñavalkya states: "One should bury a deceased child less than two years of age, but no water libation (*udaka*) should be offered thereafter. Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony, it is prescribed to last one night. [YDh 3.1–2]
"For three nights until the instruction of the vows, and ten nights thereafter. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 3.23]. Āṅgiras says:
"Even if he has not had the tonsure ceremony performed, if he has teethed and then passes away..."
"Even after cremating him in this manner, one should observe impurity for three days. But Manu says:
"Relatives should place a deceased child who is less than two years old outside [the village]."
Having adorned [the body], one should place it on pure ground, except for the collection of bones.
"No fire-rite (agnisaṃskāra) should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation (udakakriyā) be performed;
having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, one should pass only three days [in mourning]. [MDh 5.68–69]

Āśvalāyana states: "For one who has not yet cut teeth, or for one recently born, [the impurity lasts] one day. Āpastamba, however, says: "In the case of those related to the mother by blood-connection or to the father up to the seventh person, or as far as the relationship is known—if they die, there is the touching of water (purification) for them, excluding fetuses less than a year old; among these, only the mother and father [are affected], as are those who carry [the corpse]. The application of these rules is determined in relation to the customs of the region and the family. Regarding this matter of unmarried girls, Āpastamba says: "But in the case of an immature girl, immediate purification is ordained."

"Aprauḍhā" means one whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed. [Yājñavalkya says]: "But for unmarried girls and young boys, purification occurs on the same day" (YDh 3.24). This refers to the period after the *caula* ceremony. Vyāghra says:
"When an infant dies, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is prescribed for the sapindas;
[however, it lasts] for ten days in the case of a husband and wife, and likewise for uterine brothers.
This, however, refers to the impurity (sūtaka) resulting from death occurring within the ten-day period. And so it is said:

If the *niṣkramaṇa* (first outing) of a newborn infant occurs within ten days, Śātātapa declared that the purification for the parents shall be by means of the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) itself. 14.42.
And because it would conflict with the duties of kings. (14.43)

And for the king, there is immediate purification because of the conflict with his duties; "duty" refers to the protection of the subjects and so forth. Because of the use of the plural number, this applies also to others such as ministers who have similar duties. As Manu says: "And he whom the king desires [to be pure]" (MDh 5.95). 14.43.
And for the sake of the Brahmin’s cessation of Vedic study, for the sake of the cessation of Vedic study. 14.44.

Furthermore, this is stated so that for a Brahmin who has many disciples and is engaged in teaching, there may be no interruption of his Vedic study, even though he is subject to immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. Thus ends the section on impurity. 14.44.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now, the ancestral offering (śrāddha). 15.1.

The word *atha* (now/then) indicates the commencement of a topic (*adhikāra*). The ritual known as *śrāddha* is now introduced. That in which faith (*śraddhā*) is present is called *śrāddha*. It is of five kinds:
the obligatory (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and furthermore, the *pārvaṇa*; thus should the fivefold *śrāddha* be understood by the wise.
Regarding this, Manu has said: "One should offer the *śrāddha* daily with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors."
"One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the *pāñcayājñika* rite;
however, one should not feed anyone at all there for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*.

[MDh 3.82–83] That which is performed on occasions such as the lunar eclipses (*grahaṇa*) is the occasional (*naimittika*) rite. Its performance is like that of the *pārvaṇa* rite. The *ekoddiṣṭa*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the *aṣṭakā*—these too are indeed occasional rites. Among them, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is of sixteen kinds.

"However, on the day of death, it should be performed every month for a year, and likewise annually; the first [rite] is on the eleventh day," so says Yājñavalkya. "The Ekoddiṣṭa should be performed," thus says Laugākṣi in the first quarter [of the verse]. Vyāghra [says]:
"On the eleventh day it should be performed, and likewise on the half-month [the twenty-first day];
thereafter, one should diligently perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite at the end of six months.
Then, when the year is complete, or likewise on the half-month [the twenty-first month], it should be done in the same manner.
"One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* either before [the end of the year] or upon the occurrence of a *vṛddhi* (prosperity) ceremony. Thus says Jātūkarṇya:
"In the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh [month]."
Whatever food is given to a living being is called a *navaśrāddha*.

And thus they recite: these four [rites] are established according to the sequence of the [lunar] days. That very *śrāddha* performed on the eleventh day is the primary one. The mention of the "eleventh day" is an indication for the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*). And in that [period], at the same time each month, is the monthly (*māsika*) rite. At the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, there is an *ekoddiṣṭa* for the deceased and a *pārvaṇa* for the ancestors and so forth. There too, at the same time each month, is that very monthly rite. In between, there are ten monthly rites; including those at the three-fortnightly and six-monthly marks, and another at the anniversary of death each year as the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rite—these are the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭas*. And they recite:
Through sixteen śrāddha rites— performed at nine fortnights, three fortnights, six months, one year, and monthly intervals— the deceased is released from the state of being a piśāca.
"For him for whom these sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites are not performed, the state of being a *piśāca* remains fixed, even by hundreds of *śrāddhas* performed. Thus it is said.

On the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, or on one of them, the Aṣṭakā rites are performed. When performed on the first day with a specific desire—such as the wish that a daughter be born—it is called *kāmya* (optional). That too is exactly like the *pārvaṇa* rite. On the day before marriages and other *vṛddhi* ceremonies, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is to be performed. The Brāhmaṇa text states: "Therefore, it is performed for the ancestors on the preceding day. In that case, an even number of Brāhmaṇas are invited, and barley is used instead of sesame seeds. Everything else is like the *pārvaṇa*. The *pārvaṇa*, however, will be described later. (15.1)
On the new moon day, one should give to the ancestors.

The day on which the sun and moon dwell together is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Because of the plural form "to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*), one should offer [the oblation] to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. The procedure for the offering is stated in the *Gṛhyasūtras*: "The fire-oblation, the feeding of Brahmins, and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). However, in this context, there is a specific rule regarding the feeding of Brahmins. (15.2)
Or [the rites may be performed] during the latter fortnight, beginning from the fifth day. 15.3.
The "other fortnight" is the dark fortnight; one should give [the gift] starting from its fifth day. 15.3.
According to one's faith, or in its entirety. || 15.4 ||
Or one may give on every day of the dark fortnight, according to one's faith, as much faith as one possesses. || 15.4 ||
Or, when there is an abundance of wealth, location, and Brahmins present, there is no restriction regarding time. 15.5.

Beginning with the words "sesame and mung beans" (GDh 15.15), each specific substance that is about to be described is considered praiseworthy. A sacred place (*deśa*) refers to Gayā, Puṣkara, and so forth:
"At Puṣkara, the Śrāddha is inexhaustible, and likewise at Kurukṣetra;
one should also offer it at the great ocean, in a lake, in a cow-pen, and likewise on a mountain."

Thus says Vyāsa. "Whatever one residing at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity," so says Yājñavalkya (YDh 1.261). The *brāhmaṇas* who purify the company (*paṅktipāvanas*) are those to be described hereafter, such as those learned in the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅgavid*) and others. Regarding these [requirements], such as the presence of materials and so forth, when they are brought together in combination, there is a rule of time: "presence itself is the time. The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative.
According to one's ability, one should increase the excellence of the food through the application of qualities and refinements. 15.6.

Regarding food, there are rules for its qualities, such as being milk-rice (*pāyasa*), pure, or well-prepared; and there are rules for its preparation, such as roasting it or making it fragrant with black pepper, cumin, salt, and so forth. One should, according to one’s ability, bring these to excellence—that is, make them superior. (15.6)
One should feed an odd number of guests, with nine as the minimum.

Those for whom nine is the maximum number are "nine-attendants" (*navāvara*); he should feed that many Brahmins. "Odd" (*ayuja*) means an odd number. In the case of nine, there are three for the father, three for the grandfather, and three for the great-grandfather. Because of the inclusion of the term "maximum," fifteen, twenty-one, and so forth are also permitted. By the statement "odd," the exclusion of twelve and other even numbers is intended. (15.7)
Or according to one's enthusiasm. || 15.8 ||

According to one's capacity, one may feed even fewer than nine; because of the continued application of the rule "an odd number," one may feed exactly three. Thus says Āpastamba: "An odd number, at least three. In other scriptures, the feeding of Brahmins for the Viśvedevas and for the maternal grandfathers is prescribed. As Yājñavalkya says: "Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one for each;
likewise for the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common procedure. (YDh 1.228)

For the rite for the gods (*daiva*), two Brahmins should be seated facing east; for the purpose of the ancestors (*pitrya*), they should face north. Or else, there may be only one for each. That is to say, one for the gods and one for the three beginning with the father. The same applies to the maternal grandfathers as in the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors. Alternatively, there may be two for the gods and three for the sake of the maternal grandfather and others; or the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Vaiśvadeva may be common to both the *śrāddha* for the father and the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather. (15.8)
What kind of people should one feed? Regarding this, he says:
"Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) who are endowed with eloquence, beauty, age, and virtuous character" (15.9).

One should feed those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), who have studied the Vedas; who are endowed with excellence of speech—that is, whose speech is well-trained through the use of Sanskrit and the like; who are endowed with beauty, meaning they have a pleasing appearance, neither deficient nor redundant in their limbs, and are not marred by skin diseases such as leucoderma; who are endowed with youth, meaning they are not too young; and who are endowed with character, that is, purity of the internal organ. One should feed those possessing such qualities. (15.9)
The gift for the young is first. || 15.10 ||
The primary rule for the offering of a *śrāddha* is that it should be given to young men endowed with such qualities.
Some [behave] like fathers. 15.11.

Some believe that a gift should be given according to the [status of] the ancestors, as with one's father and so forth; for example—youths to the father, the elderly to the grandfather, and those even more aged to the great-grandfather. 15.11.
And one should not perform the work of a friend with that [wealth]. || 15.12 ||

And one should not perform a friendly service for that faithful person; one should not feed someone with whom friendship ought to be cultivated while having regard for material gain. The meaning is that one should not feed them for the sake of creating a sense of obligation in a friend. Āpastamba, however, states specifically: "One should feed them without regard for material gain. (15.12)
In the absence of a son, the sapindas, the mother's sapindas, and the disciples shall offer [the funeral cakes]. || 15.13 ||

"Sons shall give"—this is the primary rule. In their absence, the *sapiṇḍas*, such as brothers and their sons; in their absence, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, such as the mother’s brothers and their sons; in their absence, the disciple. (15.13)
In their absence, the officiating priest and the teacher [shall perform the duties]. 15.14.
In the absence of a disciple, the officiating priest; in his absence, the teacher shall also give [the gift]. || 15.14 ||

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, one who has fallen from his caste, an atheist, one who lives by such [atheistic] means, a killer of a hero, one who marries before his elder brother, one who officiates at sacrifices for women, a village priest, a goat-herd, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, a drinker of intoxicants, a rogue, a false witness, or a juggler. (15.15)

A thief is one who steals gold. A eunuch (*klība*) is one whose virility is fruitless, not a third gender (*tṛtīyā-prakṛti*). One who has fallen [from his caste] due to lack of Vedic learning is a killer of a Brahmin and so forth. An atheist (*nāstika*) is one who denies the existence of life after death. One who follows that way is one who lives as an atheist. Even having accepted the existence of life after death, he does not act accordingly due to the influence of association. A destroyer of the sacrificial fire (*vīra-hā*) is one who intentionally extinguishes the sacred fires despite having the means to maintain them; for it is heard in scripture: "He who extinguishes the fire is a destroyer of the heroes of the gods. Some read the term *agredidhiṣū* with a long final vowel; the word "husband" (*pati*) is to be connected with each [term]: the husband of an *agredidhiṣū*, and the husband of a *didhiṣū*.

"If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried, she is to be known as *agredidhiṣū*, while the elder is remembered as *didhiṣū*. The husbands of these two are [the respective types of *didhiṣūpati*]. However, the Naighaṇṭukas state:
"A *punarbhū* is a woman remarried; her husband is called a *didhiṣū*. But that twice-born man whose wife she becomes is an *agredidhiṣū*. Thus it is said.

A female priest is one who instructs women in religious observances and causes them to perform them. A village priest is one who performs sacrifices for many people. A goat-herder is one who lives by the protection of goats. One who has abandoned the sacred fires is one whose fires have been extinguished due to impurity or negligence. A liquor-drinker is one who drinks intoxicating substances other than *surā* (grain-liquor); however, one who drinks *surā* is declared to be an outcast (*patita*). A person of evil conduct is one whose behavior is contemptible. A false witness is one who speaks untruthfully when giving testimony. A doorkeeper is one whose livelihood consists of guarding a gate. One should not feed these. This prohibition applies even to those such as the outcasts whose sight or touch is otherwise forbidden, in order to ensure their exclusion even after they have performed penance. (15.15)
The paramour. || 15.16 ||
An upapati is a paramour. || 15.16 ||
And he belongs to whomsoever it may be. || 15.17 ||
That man is her paramour, and he is her actual husband; both of them are not to be fed. || 15.17 ||
One who eats from a common vessel, a seller of Soma, an arsonist, a poisoner,

one who has violated his vow of chastity, a servant of a guild, one who approaches a woman who should not be approached, a violent person, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, a younger brother who marries before his elder brother, one who causes a marriage to be performed for another, one who officiates at such a marriage for another, one who abandons himself, one with deformed nails, one with a black toenail, and one with black teeth or leprosy.

[One should avoid] those who have remarried, gamblers, those defeated at dice, messengers, impostors, the sons of Śūdra women, those who have renounced their vows, those afflicted with chronic illness, usurers, merchants, those who live by manual crafts,
and those whose habitual practices consist of gambling, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, and singing. || 15.18 ||
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa is one born while the husband is alive; the Golaka is one born when the husband is dead. [MDh 3.174]

Thus says Manu. One who eats the food from that *kuṇḍa* (vessel) is called a *kuṇḍāśin*. The mention of the *kuṇḍa* is also an elliptical designation for the *golaka* (the son of an adulteress). The prohibition against those such as the *kuṇḍa* is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*). Another [commentator] says: A *kuṇḍa* is a cooking vessel; in a certain region, they eat directly from it and do not discard it, and thus they are called *kuṇḍāśins*. A *somavikrayin* is one who sells the *soma* plant at a sacrifice. An *agāradāhin* is a burner of houses. A *garada* is a giver of poison. An *avakīrṇin* is one who has fallen from his vow; or alternatively, one who, being a religious student (*brahmacārī*), approaches a woman. A *gaṇapreṣya* is one who performs errands for groups. An *agamyāgāmī* is one who approaches a woman of the same *pravara* lineage. A *hiṃsra* is one who delights in the killing of living beings.
A younger brother who takes a wife while his elder brother remains unmarried is called a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.

Thus ends the *Nighaṇṭu*. Regarding the eldest who has not performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) while the youngest has performed it: the younger is the *paryādhātṛ* (the one who causes the consecration), and the elder is the *paryāhita* (the one for whom it is caused). [As stated by] Vasiṣṭha:
"One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, an outcast, a eunuch, or likewise afflicted with consumption—such a person should not be abandoned after examination."
Śātātapa says:

"In the case of one who is impotent, one who has perished in a foreign land, one who is an outcast, one who has renounced the world, or one who is devoted to the Yoga-śāstra, there is no fault in superseding him. Thus it is said.

One who has abandoned his life is a reckless person who engages in such acts as hanging himself. *Durvāla* means one who is bald; others say it means one whose penis is covered with hair. A *kunakhī* is one whose nails are discolored without cause; others say it means one whose nails are deformed. A *śyāvadant* is one whose teeth are naturally black. A *śvitrī* is one afflicted with white leprosy (*śvitra*). A *paunarbhava* is the son of a *punarbhū*, that is, a woman who has married a second time. A *kitava* is a gambler—one who deals in *kita* (dice) or one who lives by means of stakes. An *ajapa* is one who does not perform the prescribed recitation (*japa*) of the *Sāvitrī* and other mantras. A *rājapreṣya* is a servant of the king, such as a messenger and so forth. A *prātirūpika* is one who practices fraud with false weights, measures, and the like. A *śūdrāpati* is one for whom a Śūdra woman alone is his wife. A *nirākṛti* is one who neglects his Vedic study. Although the term "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*) has already been mentioned, because of this further prohibition, even if they possess learning, speech, appearance, age, and good character, they are still excluded from the list. *Kilāsa* is a skin disease known among the Dravidians as *balalī*. The suffix here denotes abundance. A *kusīdī* is a usurer who lives on interest. A *vaṇik* is one who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, namely trade; [the text refers to] one who lives off a merchant. A *śilpopajīvī* is one who lives by crafts such as painting and the like. The word *śīla* (habit/occupation) is connected individually with each of the following terms: *jyāśīla* is one who lives by the science of archery; *vāditraśīla* is one whose livelihood is beating drums such as the *bherī*; *tālaśīla* is one whose livelihood is keeping time (*tāla*); and those whose habits are dancing and singing. Thus, one should not feed these people. (15.18)
Those who have been divided by their father against his will. || 15.19 ||
And those who have been divided from their father against his will, one should not feed them. || 15.19 ||
And some [teach] their disciples and those of the same lineage. 15.20.

Some teachers state that disciples and those of the same lineage (sagotra) are persons with whom one should not eat; however, our own view is that they are permitted to eat together because they belong to a single *grāmaṇa* (village/lineage). In this regard, it means that when qualified persons are unavailable, these may be accepted provided they possess the necessary qualities. Thus says Āpastamba: "Even a uterine brother who has attained learning (*samudeta*) should be fed" (ĀpDh 2.17.5). 15.20.
One should feed more than three [guests]. 15.21.

By the phrase "according to one's enthusiasm," there is the possibility that even a single person might be intended for all purposes; therefore, to exclude that, [the text specifies] "he should feed at least three," based on the observation in the *Āpastamba* [Dharmasūtra] that "at least three" is required. 15.21.
One who possesses virtues. || 15.22 ||

By employing the singular number, one may feed even a single person if he is virtuous; as Vasiṣṭha also says: "Or else, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, who is endowed with good character, conduct, and virtues, and who is free from inauspicious marks. [VaDh 11.29]

Manu also says: "One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors; one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras" (MDh 3.129). 15.22.
One who performs a Śrāddha immediately after having sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman causes his ancestors to dwell in her excrement for a month.

He who has eaten at a *śrāddha* is called a *śrāddhin* for that day and night; [the suffix] *-in* or *-tha* is applied because "he has eaten a *śrāddha*. If he should approach the bed of a *śūdra* on that same day—where the mention of "bed" (*talpa*) signifies a wife—even if she is a married *śūdra* woman, he leads the ancestors into her excrement for a month immediately. (15.23)
This rule is to be applied to other wives. Therefore, he says:
"On that day, he should remain a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī). 15.24.
A rule is also stated for the giver among men:
"A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedic hymns, and that [rite] shall be his śrāddha" (MDh 3.188). || 15.14 ||
It is defiled by looking at a dog, a caṇḍāla, or one who has fallen from his caste. 15.25.

Food looked upon by dogs and other such creatures becomes defiled and unfit for consumption; likewise, a Śrāddha ceremony that has been looked upon becomes defiled and as if it were never performed. || 15.25 ||
Since this is so, therefore one should give [the gift] in an enclosed space. 15.26.
"Seclusion" (pariśrayaṇa) means separation by means of a curtain or similar object. || 15.26 ||
In the event of inability to do that, one should scatter sesame seeds instead. 15.27.
On this point, Bhṛgu says:
"Even water, when given to a twice-born man mixed with sesame seeds, becomes a cow of plenty for the ancestors; therefore, this is a secret of the ancestors. (15.27)
Or one who purifies the assembly may pacify it. || 15.28 ||
He by whom a row [of diners] is purified is a "purifier of the row"; he shall neutralize that defect which arises from the sight of a dog or similar impurity. (15.28)
Who, then, is that person? He says:

one who purifies the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*), one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅgavid*), one who studies the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who has performed the three *Nāciketa* fire-altars, one who knows the three *Madhu* verses, one who knows the three *Suparṇa* verses, one who maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*), and one who is a *snātaka*.
One who knows the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, who understands the Dharma, and who belongs to a lineage of those given in marriage to Brahmins. || 15.29 ||

The six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual manuals (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), astronomy (*jyotiṣa*), etymology (*nirukta*), and metrics (*chanda-viciti*). One who knows these both by recitation and by meaning is a "knower of the six auxiliaries" (*ṣaḍaṅgavid*). A "knower of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*" (*jyeṣṭhasāmika*): among the Talavakāras, one who sings the two [hymns] beginning with "ud u tyam" and "citram" is a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*; among the Chandogas, however, the *Jyeṣṭhasāman* consists of the triplet beginning with "tad id āsīt" and "tad yogayā"; one who knows that is a knower of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*. One who has performed the *Nāciketa* fire-altar three times (*triṇāciketa*): the *Nāciketa* rite is prescribed in many branches—namely in the Taittirīya, the Kaṭhavallī, and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. He who knows that together with a Brāhmaṇa priest is a *triṇāciketa*. The verse "madhu vātā ṛtāyate" is the "Threefold Honey" (*trimadhu*); in it, there are three occurrences of the word "madhu" in each verse. Āśvalāyana also says: "Having known them to be satisfied, he should cause the 'Honeyed' verses to be heard. Here, however, a person who studies that [text] is called "Threefold Honey" (*trimadhu*). The "Three Suparṇas" (*trisuparṇa*): in the Ṛgveda, it is the triplet beginning with "ekaḥ suparṇaḥ sa samudram āviveśa"; in the Taittirīyaka, it refers to the three sections (*anuvākas*) beginning with "brahmam etu mām". For it is heard there: "Whoever should give this *Trisuparṇa* unasked to a Brāhmaṇa... As before, the term applies to the person. "One who maintains the five fires" (*pañcāgni*): one who studies five sections including those for the *sabhyā* and *āvasathya* fires. An "initiated student" (*snātaka*): one who has completed both his studies and his vows. "A knower of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas" (*mantrabrāhmaṇavin*): one who knows the meaning of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. "A knower of Dharma" (*dharmajña*): one who knows the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras. "One whose lineage is descended from a Brāhmaṇa gift" (*brahmadeyānusantāna*): one whose lineage descends from a woman married according to the Brāhma rite. By the use of the particle "iti," anyone else who is similarly endowed is included. Those who are so on both the mother's and father's side, who have practiced for ten years in learning and austerity, and whose lineages on both sides are not non-Brāhmaṇical; those characterized as "on the father's side" and so forth—all such persons are "purifiers of the assembly" (*paṅktipāvana*).
And likewise with the sacrificial oblations. 15.30.

By the word "oblation" (havis), both divine and human rites are meant. Thus, even those who are senior [in age] should be fed if they are Brahmins possessing the aforementioned characteristics; however, those who are prohibited—such as thieves and the like—are not to be fed. (15.30)
Some say that one should offer [the food] to Durvāsas and others at the śrāddha ceremony itself.

Some, however, hold that those who were enumerated beginning with the Durvālas should be fed only at a *śrāddha* rite, and not at rites for the gods or for humans; but in our own view, they are not to be fed even in those cases. (15.31)
And likewise in the case of a *śrāddha* where cooked food has not been prepared, it is thus and thus. || 15.32 ||
The repetition is as before. 15.32.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Having performed the upākaraṇa ceremony on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or that of Proṣṭhapada, he shall study the Vedas during the rainy season.

The full moon day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa is called *śravaṇā*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] when time is conjoined with an asterism," the elision (*lup*) occurs according to the rule "there is elision of *aṇ* when no specific distinction is intended. However, the treatment of the compound as being like its first member (*yuktavad-bhāva*) does not apply here, because of the specific grammatical instruction: "optionally so for *phālgunī* and *śravaṇā*. Thus, the form *śrāvaṇī* also occurs. For in the case of the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the elision does not occur, as evidenced by the specific mention of *phālgunī*, *kārtikī*, and *caitrī*. But in the word *śravaṇa*, both cases apply. It is traditionally taught: "Whichever new moon (*darśa*) occurs while the sun is situated in Aries and the subsequent signs, the twelve lunar months ending with those [new moons] are known as Caitra and the others."
Among those, whichever day is the full moon is traditionally designated as Caitrī and so forth;
this is the established conclusion regarding the lunar mansion, based on its occasional conjunction with that constellation.

Thus, when the sun is situated in Leo (Siṃha), the new moon occurs; at the end of that lunar month, the full moon is called Śrāvaṇī because it is associated with the asterism Śravaṇā, whether such a conjunction actually takes place or not. By this, the Proṣṭhapadī is also explained. In the term *proṣṭhapadīm*, the accusative case is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), or perhaps to denote continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoge*). Having performed the rite known as the *upākarma* according to the rules of one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* on either the full moon of Śravaṇā or Proṣṭhapadī, one should then study the Vedas characterized by the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. The teacher should teach the pupils, and the pupils should study. This study is called "the annual" (*vārṣika*), meaning it occurs during the rainy season or every year. Teaching is also considered "study" from the teacher’s own perspective—just like the recitation of a whole text (*pārāyaṇa*) and so forth—whereas from the perspective of the pupils, it is "teaching. 16.1.
For how long should he study?
For four and a half months, or for five months, or during the southern course of the sun. 16.2.
"Those for whom the fifth is half" means four months and a half, or five full months, or as long as the sun's southern course (dakṣiṇāyana); studying in this manner. 16.2.
A student of sacred knowledge who has shaved his body hair shall not eat meat. || 16.3 ||

He should be a *brahmacārī* (celibate student); he should avoid sexual union with women. He should have his hair removed, but not his beard grown. Regarding the word "suddenly" (*akasmāt*) used here, it refers to the removal of body hair; he by whom that has been removed is one whose hair is "removed. Being such, he should not eat meat. This is an instruction for the teacher, since there is no possibility of a *brahmacārī* [being the subject here]. Āpastamba also says: "One intent on teaching should avoid sexual intercourse during the rains and autumn" [ĀpDh 1.32.1]. And as for one who, having completed the mere observances (*vratas*), takes a wife and afterwards studies—the same applies to him here in order to include him as well. Āśvalāyana also says: "Having returned [from his teacher], [he should live] according to the rule of the *brahmacārī*. In that case, however, approaching [one's wife] during her season (*ṛtu*) is accepted as optional. Thus it is said: "Some say one may approach [the wife]; that is the *prājāpatya* [form of marriage]. (16.3)
Or the observance may last for two months. || 16.4 ||

The term *dvimāsya* refers to one who has been, or will be, for two months. According to the rule *māsād vayasi yat-khañau*, the suffixes *yat* and *khañ* are applied after the word *māsa* when denoting age; furthermore, they are also employed after a *dvigu* compound. Thus, *dvaimāsya* means the same. This observance of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth lasts for two months; the option depends upon one's capacity. (16.4)
Now, the occasions when study is forbidden are being stated:
one should not study during the day when the wind carries away dust.

"Carrying away dust" means one that sweeps up dust. When the wind blows during the day carrying away dust, one should not study; when it does not carry away dust, there is no fault. Even when it carries away dust at night, there is no fault. || 16.5 ||
At night, [one should recite it] so that it is heard by the ear. || 16.6 ||

This is an instance of the agentive suffix being used in the sense of the object through grammatical inversion (*vyatyaya*). That which is heard by the ears is "heard-by-the-ears" (*karṇaśrāvī*). When such a great noise prevails as the wind blows, one should not study at night. 16.6.
In the sounds of arrows, kettledrums, clay drums, and the cries of distress. || 16.7 ||

The *vāṇa* is a specific kind of lute, as seen in the *Mahāvrata* ritual where it is said, "the *vāṇa* has a hundred strings. The *bherī* and *mṛdaṅga* drums are well known. The *garta* is a chariot, as seen in such passages as "O Varuṇa and Mitra, ascend the chariot" (*ārohataṃ varuṇa mitra gartam*) and "Praise the famous one who sits in the chariot" (*stuhi śrutaṃ gartasadam*). An *ārta* is one distressed by the death of a kinsman or similar causes. When the sound of these is heard, one should not study for that duration of time. (16.7)
In the clamor of dogs, jackals, and donkeys. || 16.8 ||

*Saṃhrādaḥ* means making noise together. One should not study during the simultaneous barking of dogs, jackals, and donkeys; however, by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), the prohibition for these three when they make noise together is already established. (16.8)
In the red clouds, rainbows, and mists. || 16.9 ||
When the sky is red, when Indra’s bow (the rainbow) is seen, and during mist or heavy frost—for that duration of time, one should not study. 16.9.
And when clouds appear outside the rainy season. 16.10.
The period from the end of the hot season until the rainy season is the *apartu*. During that time, one should not study upon seeing a cloud accompanied by water. 16.10.
The words *mūtrita* and *uccārita* [mean] having urinated and having defecated. || 16.11 ||

If one has urinated when there was only a small amount of urine, or likewise if one has defecated, even Śreyas should not study there. For it will be stated later that after voiding, one is impure even in mind. (16.11)
At night, in the waters of the twilight [ablutions]. || 16.12 ||
The middle portion of the night is *niśā*; during that time, at twilight, and while standing in water, one should not study. || 16.12 ||
And it rains. || 16.13 ||
Furthermore, one should not study while it is raining; only the general meaning of the verbal root is intended here, not a specific measure [of rain]. (16.13)
Some [have] a continuity of ribs. || 16.14 ||

Some think that *valīka-saṃtāna* means the *valīka*, which is the *nīdhra*, the edge of the house roof; when rain falls so that a stream of water flows along there, one should not study while it rains. 16.14.
When serving food to the teacher. || 16.15 ||

The two teachers are Jupiter and Venus; one should not study while they are eclipsed. Another says: "Eclipsing" (pariveṣaṇa) means the serving up of food, such as hard and soft foods, as seen in passages like "having served the Brahmins with food. Thus, one should not study while the teacher is being served [food]. 16.15.
And [the same applies] to the two luminaries. 16.16.

The sun and the moon are the well-known luminaries. One should not study while they are eclipsed. In the second alternative of the preceding sūtra, one must accept a difference in the meaning of the word *pariveṣaṇa*, which was previously understood as "serving food. (16.16)
One who is afraid, one standing in a vehicle, one lying down, or one with feet raised [should not recite]. || 16.17 ||

One who is afraid, one who is currently in fear; one standing in a vehicle, i.e., mounted on a horse or the like; one lying down, i.e., reclining upon a bed; one with legs outstretched, i.e., placing one foot upon the other, or having his feet placed upon a stool, seat, or similar object—in such a state, one should not study. || 16.17 ||
In cremation grounds, at the edge of a village, on great roads, and in places of impurity. || 16.18 ||

A cremation ground is a place where corpses are burned. The edge of a village is its boundary. A highway is well known. Impurity is the absence of purification; one should not study in these places. Alternatively, impurity refers to that characterized by untouchability caused by birth or death; one should also not study during that state. (16.18)
In the presence of a Śūdra, one should avoid foul odors, internal corpses, and those of ill repute.

“Foul-smelling” refers to a stench in the air. “Divākīrtya” means a *caṇḍāla*. The word “inside” (*antaḥ*) is connected with both: “in a village that has a corpse inside” and “in a village that has a *divākīrtya* inside. One should not study in the presence of a *śūdra*. This is a dual compound treated as a singular. Āpastamba also says: “In a village that has a corpse inside, and in one that has a *caṇḍāla* inside” (ĀpDh 1.16.20). 16.19.
And [one should not recite] when there is an eructation after eating. || 16.20 ||
One should not study when one has eaten sour food, nor when there is a sour eructation occurring. 16.20.
And the word "Sāman" refers to as much as the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda. || 16.21 ||

The *ṛc* and the *yajus* together constitute the *ṛgyajuṣa*; this is a *nipāta* (irregular formation) according to the rule beginning with "acatura. As long as the word *sāman* is heard [in the vicinity], one should not study the *Ṛgveda* or the *Yajurveda*. However, the reading with the genitive case-ending does not appeal to us. 16.21.
Thunderbolts, earthquakes, the appearance of Rāhu, and meteors are not immediate [in their results]. || 16.22 ||

A thunderclap is the falling of lightning; an earthquake is the shaking of the earth; the appearance of Rāhu is an eclipse; a meteor is the falling of a firebrand. From the context, it is understood that these are the causes of *anadhyāya* (cessation of study) that are "immediate" (*ākālika*). The time during which these occur, extending until the following day, is called "immediate" (*ākāla*); that which is connected to this is "immediate" (*ākālika*). 16.22.
And when the thunder, rain, and lightning appear while the sacrificial fires have been kindled. || 16.23 ||

"Stanayitnu" means the sound of thunder; the rest is well known. When the fires have been kindled at the time for the Agnihotra oblation, if thunder and the other phenomena occur during the twilight, each one constitutes a cause for the suspension of study until the same time the following day. This applies when it is not the rainy season. 16.23.
He says "ṛtau" at the beginning of the day; "ahar ṛtau" [is said] at the end of the day. 16.24.

If these [clouds] should appear during the twilight of the rainy season, then there is no study for the duration of the day if it is morning; however, if it is evening, there is no study during the night—this being established by the sense of the matter, it was not explicitly stated. 16.24.
And in the case of lightning, [the impurity lasts] for the night until the end of the second watch.

If lightning is seen at night but not during the twilight, then from the latter part of the night—that is, the third part of the night known as *apararātra*—there is no study until that time has passed; after that, one may study. However, regarding lightning during the morning twilight, Jābāla says: "When there is lightning in the morning, the day is unfit for study. (16.25)
When [the moon] has advanced by one-third [of its diameter] and so forth, all [the previously mentioned effects occur]. 16.26.
If lightning strikes beginning from the third part of the day, neither during the twilight alone nor at night, then there is a suspension of study for the entire night. || 16.26 ||
According to some, meteors and lightning are included [among these]. 16.27.

A meteor is equal to lightning. Just as there is a suspension of study during lightning and at night from the latter part of the night onwards, so too, according to the opinion of some, is there a suspension during the fall of a meteor. 16.27.
The thundering occurs in the afternoon. || 16.28 ||
If thunder occurs in the afternoon, but not at twilight, then it is equal to lightning; it causes a suspension of study until the latter part of the night. || 16.28 ||
Even at nightfall. || 16.29 ||
Even at dusk, thunder and lightning are equal [in their effect]; until the end of the night, they are a cause for the suspension of study.
Everything [is considered] night until midnight. 16.30.
Thunder that begins from the first part of the night until midnight is a cause for the suspension of Vedic study for the entire night. (16.30)
If it is by day, he should do so while there is still light. || 16.31 ||
If there is thunder during the day before the afternoon, then there is a suspension of study as long as the light lasts; that is to say, for the entire day. || 16.31 ||
And when the king residing in his realm has died. || 16.32 ||

When the king who is the sovereign of the region where one himself resides has died, there is a suspension of study for as long as the light lasts; others say it is until the same time [the next day]. 16.32.
And having lived abroad, they shall reunite with one another. || 16.33 ||

When fellow students dwell apart from one another, yet some remain together with their teacher, then there is a suspension of study for as long as the light lasts. According to some, this lasts until they have reunited; according to others, it lasts for the duration of that day and night. (16.33)

In the case of eating at a *śrāddha* for humans or at sacrifices (*yajña*), following the completion of the Veda-study of those who have gathered in a crowd, there is an impurity lasting for one day and night.

A "disturbance" (*saṃkula*) refers to an affliction of a village or similar place caused by thieves and the like. An "affliction" (*upāhita*) refers to a fire conflagration. The "completion of the Veda" (*vedasamāpti*) means the completion of a recensional branch (*śākhā*). "Vomiting" (*chardana*) refers to the regurgitation of what has been eaten. A "śrāddha" refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other such rites. A "human sacrifice" (*manuṣyayajña*) refers to spring festivals and the like. The word "eating" (*bhojana*) is connected with both; thus, there is "eating at a śrāddha" and "eating at a human sacrifice. On these occasions, there is no study for a day and a night. Others maintain that a "human sacrifice" is a sacrifice to deities who have humans as their primary form. As Āpastamba says: "Some say that one should not eat after a sacrifice to deities who have humans as their primary form" [ĀpDh 1.11.3]. Those who, having been humans, became gods through eminent austerity—their sacrifice consists of feeding Brāhmaṇas for the sake of pleasing them. (16.34)
And on the new moon day. || 16.35 ||
On the new moon day, there is a suspension of study for a full day and night.
Or for two days. 16.36.

On that day and on the preceding day, there is a two-day suspension of study. Regarding the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, however, another basis for the suspension of study must be sought. The same applies to the first days (pratipad) of the lunar fortnights. 16.36.
The full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha. || 16.37 ||

The three full-moon days beginning with Kārttikī are causes for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) for a day and a night; regarding the suspension of study on other full-moon days, the source must be sought.
The three Aṣṭakās last for three nights each. || 16.38 ||

After the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, during the three dark fortnights, there are three Aṣṭakā festivals; these, along with the day itself, the preceding day, and the following day, are causes for a three-night suspension of Vedic study. 16.38.
Some [teachers] say that the last [verse] [is the one to be recited]. 16.39.
Some consider the final Ekāṣṭakā to be a cause for the suspension of Vedic study.
On both sides of the rainy season. || 16.40 ||

Regarding what was stated—that the period beginning with the *śravaṇā* [constitutes] the annual [period of suspension]—some teachers maintain that there should be a three-day suspension from study on both sides (before and after) of those two rites, namely the *upākaraṇa* and the *utsarjana*, even when they have been performed. Thus says Manu:
"At the *upākarma* and at the *utsarga*, a three-night cessation is prescribed" (MDh 4.119).
Uśanas states: "At the *upākarma* and at the *utsarga*, there is a three-day suspension from study. (16.40)
All [these occur] during the convergence of rain, lightning, and thunder. || 16.41 ||
All teachers agree that when the three [periods], beginning with the rainy season, coincide simultaneously, there shall be a suspension of study for three nights. 16.41.
In that which is flowing. 16.42.
*Prasyanda* refers to heavy rain and the time during which it falls; as long as that flow continues, there is no study for two days, three days, or four days. (16.42)
After a meal, [one should not study] during a festival. || 16.43 ||
On festive occasions such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), there is no study on that day after the meal has been taken. (16.43)
And for one who has studied [the Veda], [it is forbidden] during the four muhūrtas of the night. || 16.44 ||

Having performed the *upākaraṇa* rite, one who has begun to study is called *prādhīta*. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*) and refers to the agent. For him, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for four *muhūrtas*—that is, eight *nāḍikās*—during the night. This is identical in meaning to the rule of Āpastamba: “Having performed the *upākaraṇa* on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the first month at twilight” (ĀpDh 1.9.1). By the use of the word “and” (*ca*), the prohibition for four *muhūrtas* during the night is shown to apply even to the twilight of the thirteenth lunar day. (16.44)
Some [say] it is permanent in the city. || 16.45 ||
Some teachers maintain that one should never study in the city; the inclusion of the word "always" (nityam) is for the purpose of excluding the specific rule regarding the night.
Even the mental [action] is impure. || 16.46 ||
Being unpurified, one should not perform even mental study. Likewise, among other causes for the suspension of study (anadhyāya), mental recitation is not prohibited. 16.46.
For those who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha), [the impurity lasts] until the same time [day]. || 16.47 ||

One who possesses *śrāddha* is called *śrāddhī*, meaning one who performs a *śrāddha* sacrifice; this is according to the rule *ata iniṭhanau*. It does not mean "one by whom *śrāddha* has been eaten," because eating [at a *śrāddha*] was already prohibited for such a person previously. For those givers of *śrāddha*, there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) lasting until the same time the next day. Another says: the previous prohibition of a full day and night applies to those who have merely eaten at a *śrāddha* and were not invited as vessels for the sake of the ancestors and so forth; however, this present prohibition until the same time applies to those who have eaten as vessels for the sake of the ancestors and so forth. (16.47)
Also when there is contact with one who has performed a śrāddha for which no food was prepared. || 16.48 ||

When food is unavailable, if uncooked food is given to the ancestors, that is an *akṛtānna-śrāddha*. Even upon contact with that, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for the duration of the day; it is not only for one who has eaten. Regarding this, Manu says: "Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever constitutes a Śrāddha offering—upon touching even that, there is a suspension of study; such Brahmins are declared to be 'pure-mouthed' (*pāṅktya*). [MDh 4.117]
This indeed is the characteristic mark of the *āmaśrāddha*.
And whatever vehicles they remember for each penetration. || 16.49 ||

Regarding each specific science and each treatise on dharma, one should not study during those periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*) that the traditionalists (*smartāraḥ*) prescribe; one should also refrain from studying for those reasons mentioned therein. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says: "In the event of a conflagration, a mountain collapse, or a fall of stones, blood, or dust, the suspension lasts until the same time the next day" (VaDh 13.35). Furthermore: "One should never study beneath a *śleṣmātaka*, a *śālmali*, or a *madhūka* tree, nor under a *kovidāra* or a *kapittha* tree."
The same should be understood elsewhere as well. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 16.49
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
It has been stated that even the mind is impure; since that impurity can also be produced by food, the section concerning what may and may not be eaten is now commenced.
A Brāhmaṇa should eat from those twice-born men who are praiseworthy in their respective duties. (17.1)

A Brahmin should eat in the house of those twice-born men who are praised for their own duties—whether those duties pertain to their caste (*varṇa*), their stage of life (*āśrama*), or both—thinking, "Ah, this man performs his own duty. The purpose of engaging in eating is to alleviate hunger; and it is possible for anyone to alleviate hunger by eating in the house of just anyone. In this regard, the author specifies: "A Brahmin should eat only in the houses of these [twice-born], and not in the houses of others. (17.1)
And he should accept it. 17.2.
The acceptance of gifts from these alone, and not from others, is likewise [prescribed]. || 17.2 ||
The exception to this is as follows: firewood, water, grass, roots, fruits, honey, [protection from] fear,
a bed, a seat, a dwelling, a vehicle, milk, curd, a vessel, a sapharī fish, and priyaṅgu [are not subject to the same restrictions].
Roads, paths, and vegetables are not to be refused by anyone. || 17.3 ||

*Edhas* is firewood. *Udaka* is water, even that contained in jars and the like. *Yavasa* is grass and such. *Mūla* is ginger and the like. *Phala* is mangoes and the like. *Madhu* is honey. *Abhaya* is protection. *Abhyudyata* is that which has been brought by the giver himself, saying "Take this," even without being asked. *Śayyā* is a mat and the like. *Āsana* is a stool and the like. *Āvasatha* is a shelter. *Yāna* is a cart and the like. *Dadhi* and *payas* are well known. *Dhānā* are parched barley grains. *Śapharī* is a species of fish. [Some read *priyaṅgu* for *rājikā*. *Sraj* is a garland. *Mārga* is venison, or *mārga* means a path. *Śāka* is *vāstūka* and the like. These items, beginning with firewood, are not to be refused; they are to be accepted from everyone, even if one must ask for them. *Abhyudyata* cooked food and the like are not to be refused; it is a fault to reject them. One should accept it, provided it is not meat or the like. But meat, honey, salt, and food prepared for a specific person (*uddiṣṭa*) should be avoided. [The English translation follows: tathā ca manuḥ | "Food brought by someone who has risen [to give], even if it is impure, should not be rejected. One should accept it, provided it is not meat or the like. But meat, honey, salt, and food prepared for a specific person (*uddiṣṭa*) should be avoided. [The Sanskrit text follows: abhyudyatam annam apūtam api pratigrāhyam | na tu māṃsādi | māṃsaṃ madhu lavaṇam uddiṣṭaṃ ca varjayet || iti | [The English translation follows: abhyudyatam annam apūtam api pratigrāhyam | na tu māṃsādi | māṃsaṃ madhu lavaṇam uddiṣṭaṃ ca varjayet || iti | [The Sanskrit text follows: tathā ca manuḥ | "Food brought by someone who has risen [to give], even if it is impure, should not be rejected. One should accept it, provided it is not meat or the like. But meat, honey, salt, and food prepared for a specific person (*uddiṣṭa*) should be avoided. [The English translation follows: tathā ca manuḥ | "Food
Prajāpati considered alms that are being offered, brought forward, and not previously announced as fit to be eaten even from one who has committed evil deeds.
"The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who treats her with contempt. [ĀpDh 1.19.13] This is the exception to that rule.
"The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, an unchaste woman, and a eunuch—these are not to be eaten. [ĀpDh 1.19.14] Thus [it is said]. 17.3.
There is also another [type of giving] for the sake of supporting one's father, gods, teachers, and servants. 17.4.

The support of one’s ancestors consists in performing the *śrāddha* rites without interruption; the support of the gods consists in the *agnihotra* and other such sacrifices. The "elders" (*guru*) are the father and others; the "dependents" (*bhṛtya*) are the sons, slaves, and so forth. Their support consists in the giving of food and other necessities. On these occasions, even things other than those already mentioned should not be refused. And Manu says: "One who intends to rescue his elders and dependents, or to honor the gods and guests, may accept gifts from anyone; yet he himself should not find satisfaction therein. (MDh 4.251) || 17.4 ||
If there is no means of livelihood [otherwise], it may be obtained from a Śūdra. || 17.5 ||
If one's livelihood—that is, one's subsistence—cannot be maintained without accepting gifts from a Śūdra, then one may accept them even from a Śūdra. 17.5.
Cowherds, field-ploughers, family associates, those who cause work to be done, and attendants are those whose food may be eaten. 17.6.

He who tends another’s cattle and cultivates his field; he who has been associated with one’s family through tradition, having come as a friend; and he who is one’s servant or slave—these are those whose food may be eaten. They may eat even cooked food from them. A *kāru* is a craftsman. For it is observed [in the texts] that "the barber (*nāpita*) shaves the beard upwards. And he who is born to a Brahmin from an unmarried Vaiśya woman is also one whose food may be eaten. Regarding this, Manu says: "The owner of the field, the family friend, the cowherd, the slave, and the barber..."
"These are those among Śūdras whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (MDh 4.253). And this refers to a situation of extreme distress. 17.6.
And a merchant who is not an artisan. 17.7.
And a merchant whose food may be eaten, provided that he is not a craftsman such as a potter or the like. 17.7.
Now he speaks of what is unfit to be eaten:
"That which is always unfit to be eaten. (17.8)

One should never eat in another's house. This prohibition applies to the householder, as seen in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "Those foolish householders who subsist on the cooked food of others... (MDh 3.104). Whatever is given to others every day is always unfit to be eaten. 17.8.
[Food] into which hair or insects have fallen. || 17.9 ||

Furthermore, food that is contaminated by hair or insects is also unfit for consumption. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "One may, at will, remove the hair and insects, sprinkle it with water, scatter ashes over it, and then consume it if it has been commended by word" (VaDh 14.23). Manu, however, says:
"Food pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or spat upon, as well as that defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth" (MDh 5.125).

Thus, their rule is established according to preference. Another says: regarding food that has begun to cook but is contaminated by hair or insects, the rule of Gautama applies; however, for what is cooked further, the rule of Vasiṣṭha and Mānava applies. 17.9.
It was defiled by the footprints of a menstruating woman and a black bird.

The "black bird" is the crow. The mention of the "foot" is an elliptical expression intended to include other parts such as the beak and so forth. Food that has been defiled—that is, touched—by a menstruating woman or by the term "black bird" (i.e., by a crow) is unfit for consumption. However, regarding a large quantity of food, Parāśara states: "Food exceeding one *droṇa* in measure, even if defiled by dogs or crows, need not be discarded; for the sake of its purification, one should present it to Brāhmaṇas."

"Food that has been sprinkled with water purified by the *gāyatrī* mantra recited eight thousand times, and over which the fire has been carried by Brahmins, is [fit for consumption]. This should be done after removing the defiled portion. (17.10)
[Food] looked upon by a killer of an embryo. 17.11.

A *bhrūṇahan* is a slayer of a Brahmin. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "By killing a Brahmin, one becomes a *bhrūṇahan*" (VaDh 20.23). Therefore, even food looked upon by such a person is unfit to be eaten. 17.11.
Defiled by intention. || 17.12 ||
That which is given by a giver out of contempt, or which causes impurity of mind to the eater, is defiled in its essence (bhāvaduṣṭa); that too is unfit to be eaten.
Smelled by a cow. || 17.13 ||
And that which has been smelled by a cow near it is unfit for consumption. 17.13.
Sour gruel alone, without curd. 17.14.

That which has become sour by the power of time is called *śukta* (fermented liquid) alone; that is unfit for consumption. Because of the use of the word "alone" (*kevala*), even a sour substance mixed with milk, water, and so forth is fit for consumption. Curd (*dadhi*), however, is fit for consumption even when it is not sour. Since buttermilk (*takra*) and sour gruel (*kāñjika*) are not [sour] through the process of ripening, this prohibition does not apply to them. Furthermore, the practice regarding buttermilk is undisputed, whereas there is some dispute regarding sour gruel. (17.14)
Again, it is established. 17.15.

If the same kind of cooking is performed again on what has already been once cooked—such as that which was previously cooked with sour gruel—that is "re-cooked" (*punaḥsiddha*). That is unfit for consumption. However, there is no fault in another cooking, such as frying, of something that was cooked in a different manner. || 17.15 ||
One should avoid stale food, vegetables, cooked grains, oils, meat, and honey. || 17.16 ||

That which has remained overnight (*paryuṣita*) is that which has passed through the interval between sunrise and sunset. Food cooked by day is called "cooked by day," and that cooked at night is "cooked by night"; such food is unfit for consumption even if it is not fermented. However, vegetables and the like, though they have remained overnight, are fit for consumption. Vegetables have already been mentioned. Edibles (*bhakṣa*) include flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), cakes (*apūpa*), and so forth. Fats (*sneha*) include ghee, oil, and the like. Meat is well known. Honey as well—these, when they have remained overnight, are unfit for consumption. Since fats, honey, and the like do not become "overnight" simply because they are uncooked, their specific mention here is for the purpose of excluding those items that have remained overnight *only* when mixed with other substances. Therefore, food mixed with them may be consumed even if it has remained overnight, provided it is not otherwise censured.
"That which has stood overnight may be eaten, as may whatever remains of an oblation.

[The same applies] for those who have abandoned their wives, prostitutes, those accused of crimes, those of unknown origin, staff-bearers, carpenters, misers, prison guards, physicians, hunters, those who live by arrows, those who eat the leavings of others, and those who hate their own groups. (17.17)
"Utsṛṣṭaḥ" means abandoned by his parents;
the abandonment of those born upon a wen (gaṇḍa) is prescribed.

For these reasons—such as being unable to provide protection during a famine, or due to hostility—a *puṃścalī* is a woman who is unfaithful to men, whether she be an adulteress or a courtesan. An *abhiśasta* is one notorious for a fault, whether real or unreal. An *anapadeśya* is one unworthy of designation, such that one cannot say, "This person is such-and-such. According to others, a third gender (*tṛtīyā prakṛti*) is that which cannot be designated as either female or male. A *daṇḍika* is one appointed by the king to the office of administering punishment. A *takṣā* (carpenter) is born from a *śūdra* father and a *vaiśyā* mother through inverse order (*prātilomya*). A *māhiṣya* is born from a *vaiśya* father and a *kṣatriyā* mother. A *karaṇī* is born from a *vaiśya* father and a married *śūdrā* mother; a *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) is born from a *māhiṣya* father and a *karaṇī* mother. According to others, he is a *takṣā*. A *kadarya* is a miser, concerning whom Manu has said: [Manu 4.226]... [text continues].
"Of a learned Vedic scholar who is miserly, and of a usurer who is generous. [MDh 4.224]

A *bandhanika* is a guard of a prison. A *cikitsika* is a physician or a surgeon. One who is a hunter but does not go about with arrows, but rather goes about with snares, is a hunter who does not use arrows—a trapper (*vāgurika*). An eater of leavings is self-explanatory. A *gaṇa* is a multitude of people. An enemy is one who bears malice. The food of these—beginning with the aforementioned—is unfit to be eaten. The mention here of those who are not among the praiseworthy twice-born is for the purpose of prohibiting what has already been mentioned. Thus says Āpastamba: "Of a physician and of a hunter," and so forth. Others hold that this is for the purpose of prohibition even in times of distress (*āpad*). (17.17)
Those unworthy of the company [at a meal] are mentioned prior to Durvāla.
Furthermore, the food of those previously designated as unfit for company (apaṅktya), beginning with the thief and ending with the self-seller, is also not to be eaten [cf.
[These acts] are rendered in vain if performed while eating food, while rinsing the mouth, or while standing up. || 17.19 ||

That which is cooked for one's own sake and not for the sake of guests and others is "vain food" (*vṛthānna*). For it is heard in scripture: "The thoughtless man obtains food in vain," and so forth. When, during the course of a meal, one sips water again or rises due to anger and the like, that is called *vyapeta*—meaning "departed" from the company—as opposed to *apeta*. These two cases involve food that is separated by the acts of sipping water or rising. These, including "vain food" and the rest, are unfit to be eaten. Regarding this, Uśanas says: "By those who are not elders, there is [the fault of] sipping water or rising. When many are eating in a single row, if even one person other than an elder performs the act of sipping water or rising, the food of the others also becomes unfit to be eaten; however, if it is done by elders, there is no fault.
From worship [offered] with equal or unequal [means], there arise unequal or equal [results]. || 17.20 ||

One who is equal in terms of family, conduct, and so forth, is "equal" (*sama*); one who is the opposite is "unequal" (*asama*). The words *viṣama* and *sama* refer to the states [of being unequal and equal]. *Viṣamasama* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). Regarding honor—consisting of such things as providing a seat and attending upon—the food is unfit to be eaten when equality is practiced toward an equal in honor while inequality is practiced toward an unequal. (17.20)
And [the same applies to] that which is not honored. || 17.21 ||
That which is given without honor, such as saying, "O son of a widow, eat!", is also unfit to be eaten. This is the same regarding the act of receiving a gift as well. As Manu said:
"He who receives a gift with honor, and he who gives it with honor—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell. [MDh 4.235]
"One should honor the meals in the evening and in the morning," says Vasiṣṭha (VaDh 3.69). Others hold that eating without performing this [act of honoring] is "unhonored" (anarcita). 17.21.
And the milk of a cow that has recently calved is forbidden during the period of birth-impurity. 17.22.
*Sūtaka* means birth. The milk of a cow that has recently calved and whose ten-day period has not yet elapsed is unfit for consumption. (17.22)
And [the same applies] to goats and buffaloes. 17.23.
The milk of a goat or a buffalo during their period of birth-impurity, before ten days have passed, must not be drunk. 17.23.
The milk of sheep, camels, and one-hoofed animals is always unfit for drinking. (17.24)

Because of the inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*), it is not only the milk of those within ten days of calving that is forbidden. A ewe is a female sheep; a camel is well known; "single-hoofed" (*ekaśapha*) refers to those with one hoof, such as horses and the like. The milk belonging to ewes and the others is always unfit to be drunk. However, Manu says:
"But among all wild animals, except for the buffalo, the milk of females must be avoided, as indeed must all sour substances" (MDh 5.9). 17.24.
And [the milk] of cows that are flowing, those whose calves have died, and those that are in heat. 17.25.

That cow from whose udders milk flows spontaneously is called *syandinī*. A cow that gives birth to twins is a *yamasū*. A pregnant cow that yields milk is a *saṃdhinī*; others say it is one whose milk is drawn at the same time [as her calf]. The milk of such cows and other animals is unfit for drinking. (17.25)
And [the same applies] to one who has no offspring. 17.26.

One that is separated from its calf is "without a calf. And the milk of such a cow or similar animal is unfit to be drunk. In this context, some authorities maintain that even curds and other products derived from prohibited milk are likewise forbidden. However, the traditional practice regarding a cow within the ten-day period of impurity is as stated, while elsewhere it is not fixed. (17.26)
Now he states those things which are inedible by their very nature:
"And five-clawed animals, except for the śalyaka, the hare, the porcupine, the iguana, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise. (17.27)

He will state later that these are not to be eaten. Those five-nailed animals whose nails on their hands and feet number five—such as monkeys and the like—are not to be eaten, with the exception of the *śalyaka* and others. The *śalyaka* is a particular kind of wild boar whose hair is shaped like iron arrows (*nārāca*). The hare (*śaśa*) is well known. The *śvāvit* is a porcupine, whose skin is used to make armor. The *godhā* is large-bodied and resembles a chameleon. The *khaḍga* is a specific type of deer (or a distinct species of animal) that dies by its own horn. The tortoise (*kacchapa*) is well known. Regarding this, they recite:
"The urine of animals whose flesh is not to be eaten, as well as their excrement, is likewise declared to be unfit for consumption; and their feces especially must be avoided with great care. (17.27)

Animals with teeth in both jaws, those with hair on their bodies, those without hair, those with solid hooves, and the kalaviṅka, plava, cakravāka, baka, and haṃsa birds [are not to be eaten]. || 17.28 ||

Horses and the like have teeth in both jaws; the substitution for *danta* [with *dat*] is a Vedic archaism. Keśins are animals such as the *camari* yak, which possess an abundance of hair. Those without hair include snakes and the like. One-hoofed animals are those with a single hoof. This [list] is intended to exclude those that do not have teeth in both jaws. The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow. The *plava* is the bird known as the *śakaṭabila*. The *haṃsa* and *cakravāka* are well-known. These are also inedible. (17.28)
Crows, herons, vultures, hawks, water-birds with red feet and beaks, domestic cocks, and pigs. || 17.29 ||

Crows and the like are well known. Water-birds are also indeed birds because they are mentioned in proximity to crows and the others; their qualification is "red-footed and red-beaked. That which exists in a village is "village-born" (*grāmya*). This is a qualification for the latter two [categories], as in "village cock" and "village pig. There is no prohibition regarding wild [cocks and pigs]. (17.29)
And [the same applies] to the words *dhenu* and *anaḍuh*. || 17.30 ||

A *dhenu* is a milch cow; an *anaḍvān* is a bull fit for drawing a cart. Regarding the form *dhenvanaḍvāhau*, it might be argued that it is not obtained because of the rule prescribing the specific compound-ending (*samāsānta*) nipātana for dual *dvandva*s beginning with *acatura-*; however, that has been disregarded, or it is a corrupt reading. Furthermore, both the *dhenu* and the *anaḍvān* are inedible. But in the *Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra*, after stating that meat from cows and bulls is edible, it says: "But according to the Vājasaneyaka, the meat of the *dhenu* and the *anaḍvān* is edible, and the *ānaḍuha* [bull's meat] is pure" (ĀpDh 1.17.30–31). The meaning is that the *ānaḍuha* is not only edible but also pure. It is heard in the *Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇas*: "Just as when a king of men arrives, or someone else worthy of the *Ṛk* verses, they slaughter a bull or a barren cow. In that context, it is edible for the guest but inedible for others. Indeed, even slaughter was permitted there: "The *dāśa* and the *goghn* at the time of giving"; the one for whom the cow is slaughtered is the *goghn*, namely the guest. Such, indeed, was the former custom; nowadays, even the smell [of such meat is avoided]. (17.30)
Meat from animals that have not been slaughtered for sacrifice, meat from animals that have died naturally, and meat obtained for no purpose. || 17.31 ||

The *apannada* is one whose teeth have not fallen out; even though it is not explicitly forbidden, it is not to be eaten. For the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa* states: "When the teeth of an animal fall out, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. And Āpastamba says: "It is known that what has not lost its teeth is the impurity of animals. *Avasanna* means diseased. *Vṛthāmāṃsa* (meat not consecrated by ritual) is explained by the rules regarding *vṛthānna* (food not consecrated by ritual). The repeated prohibition of meat is intended to impose a greater penance for its consumption. (17.31)
The exudations from the shoots of the śuna trees were agitated by young sprouts.

*Kisalaya* is a sprout, a new shoot at the tip; *kyāku* is a mushroom; *laśuna* is well known [as garlic]; *niryāsa* is the resinous exudation from tree bark that has become solidified, such as asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and the like. Sprouts and the others mentioned are also unfit for consumption. (17.32)
The red ones are the felling tools. 17.33.

The exudations (*niryāsa*) that arise from the incised parts of trees and the like are called *vañcana*; if they are red, they are not to be eaten. Exudations that flow spontaneously (*svayaṃsūna*), whether red or non-red, are not to be eaten; however, those produced by incision (*vraścanaprabhava*) are [forbidden] only if they are red. Manu states: "Likewise, red exudations of trees produced by incision... (MDh 5.6).

Some, however, include the word *lohita* (red) among items such as young shoots and the like. As for asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), it must be considered whether it is a resinous exudate or not produced from incision; in any case, even the learned consume it. Camphor, however, is neither a resinous exudate nor produced from incision, nor is it red; therefore, it is certainly fit to be eaten. (17.33)
The *nicu*, woodpecker, crane, *balākā*, *śuka*, water-fowl, *tiṭṭibha*, *māsthāla*, and nocturnal prowlers are not to be eaten. || 17.34 ||

The *nicudāru* is the woodpecker; the *madgura* is the water-crow; the *māsthāla* is the "speech-maker" (a type of crane); the *naktaṃcaras* are the owls and so forth; the others are well known. The phrase "not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyāḥ*) is connected starting from the word "five-toed animals" (*pañcanakhāḥ*). (17.34)
Those that peck with their beaks, those that scratch with their claws, and web-footed birds may be eaten. || 17.35 ||

Those that eat by pecking repeatedly with their beaks are *pratuda*s. Those such as peacocks that eat by scattering [food] with their feet are *viṣkira*s. Those whose feet have a web-like structure are *jālapāda*s. These are edible. Although it is understood from the mention of non-edible animals that others are edible, the explicit inclusion of the term "edible" is so that eating may occur only in times of distress (*āpad*), and not in times of no distress. (17.35)
And the cognitions are unmodified. || 17.36 ||
Those with deformed human heads and so forth are "altered" (vikṛta), while those opposite to them are "unaltered" (avikṛta) and thus fit for consumption. || 17.36 ||
And those who deserve execution may be spared for the sake of dharma. || 17.37 ||

Those animals which are declared to be edible are not only to be eaten when they have died naturally or been killed by another, but may also be slain for the sake of dharma, such as in the honoring of guests and similar rites.
