[PārSm 12.65–69] Regarding this, Sumantu says: "A killer of a Brāhmaṇa shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, announcing his deed, subsisting on alms, and dwelling among the sandy banks of celestial rivers, confluences, hermitages, cow-pens, mountains, springs, groves of asceticism, and sacred forests; he shall not sit in the *vīrāsana* posture. When the year is complete, he shall give gold, gems, cows, grain, sesame seeds, land, and clarified butter to Brāhmaṇas; thus he becomes purified. Regarding specific castes and specific stages of life (*āśrama*) in this context, Aṅgiras says:
The assembly for Brahmins is considered to be [one person]; that for kings is held to be double;
for Vaiśyas it is declared to be triple. And the penance is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly.

"If those belonging to the other stages of life commit the same sins as householders, they should perform purification twice as much as the householder, until the realization of Brahman. This is the purification for householders; it is double for students.
"It should be triple for those dwelling in the forest and quadruple for ascetics. On this point, Bhārgava says:
"He who is eighty years of age, or a child less than sixteen,"
"Women or those who are ill deserve [the rites] for the purpose of expiation. Thus says Hārīta:
"But if one who has set out for expiation should die in the midst of it..."
"On that very day, he becomes pure both in this world and in the next. Thus it is said. (22.13)
The penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa has been stated. Now, regarding the killing of a Rājanya:
for killing a Rājanya, one shall observe the standard student-discipline (brahmacarya) for six years and give away a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh. 22.14.

When the killing of a Kṣatriya has been committed, that same vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) which was prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa must be performed for six years. That too means one should perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa for six years in its natural form, without the use of a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and other such items. One should give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh—that is, one thousand cows plus one bull. On this point, Uśanas says: "For the killing of a Kṣatriya, there is a six-year vow of Brahman-conduct, and at its conclusion, the gift of a thousand cows with a bull. This applies to the intentional killing of a consecrated (*abhiṣikta*) Śrotriya who observes vows. For the killing of that same person if he is not a Śrotriya or is devoid of vows, there is only the gift of cows. For the killing of one who is devoid of both [Śrotriya-hood and vows] and is unconsecrated, there is only the six-year penance. However, for the killing of one who is unconsecrated but possesses both [qualities], the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "A Brāhmaṇa, having killed a Kṣatriya, shall observe the vow for eight years. For these same cases, if the act is unintentional, half of the penance should be prescribed. Regarding the killing of one who is a Kṣatriya by caste alone:
"Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya, as well as atheism (nāstikya), are minor offenses (upapātaka).
Having stated this, he says:
"Twice-born men who have committed such minor offenses shall perform this very same vow."

"Or else, for the sake of purification, one may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, with the exception of the Avakīrṇin rite"—this which was stated by Manu is to be understood here. For the killing of one who possesses some merit, there is the standard (prākṛta) one-year vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) which will be mentioned later in the verse: "And likewise for those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who are excluded from society (*nirākṛti*), and those who commit minor offenses (*upapātaka*). This same principle is to be understood in subsequent cases as well. In all instances, if the act is unintentional, the penance is half; if intentional, it is full. 22.14.
Now, regarding the killing of a Vaiśya:
for a Vaiśya, however, one should perform a three-year penance and give away cows together with a bull as the hundred-and-first.
This [penalty] applies to the intentional killing of one who possesses supreme virtues; by this, the case of others is explained. || 22.15 ||
For killing a Śūdra, one shall give a cow for each year of his life and eleven bulls.

This [penance] also applies to the case of one who possesses extreme virtues. Regarding the killing of a *śūdra* who is utterly devoid of merit, the *Auśanasa* states: "Having killed a *śūdra*, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra*. Now, regarding the case of those born in the direct order (*anuloma*), Vyāghra says: "In the case of all those born in the direct order, whatever [penance] is prescribed for the killing of their respective mothers, the learned should prescribe that very same [penance]; and for women, half of that [should be prescribed]."
"Regarding the killing of an Ātreyī woman, one should state that which is prescribed for the [killing of] a husband;
likewise when the fetus is known to be present, it is according to the word of Vyāghra. Thus says Laugākṣi concerning the killing of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
How should it be for the killing of those born of Śūdras who are of inverse (pratiloma) caste?
If done intentionally, it shall be a Parāka penance; if unintentionally, an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa) is prescribed by tradition.
"For the others, a fourth part is prescribed for the father by the wise. (22.16)
And the same applies to the case of an Anātreyya woman. 22.17.

And likewise for the killing of a woman other than an *ātreyī*, a Śūdra shall perform penance for one year and give ten cows with a bull as the eleventh. This refers to the intentional killing of a virtuous Brāhmaṇī who is a housewife. And Yājñavalkya says:

"Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should observe the vow prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra. (YDh 3.269) "A killer of a Śūdra shall also observe this for six months, or else give ten cows. (YDh 3.267)
"Having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly, one should give, respectively, for purification, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep.

As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "In the case of a Kṣatriya, the standard period of celibacy is six years; three years for a Vaiśya; one and a half years for a Śūdra; as for a Brāhmaṇa, it is like that for a Kṣatriya; for a Kṣatriya woman, like that for a Vaiśya; for a Vaiśya woman, like that for a Śūdra; having killed a Śūdra woman, nine months"—that refers to the case of an exceptionally eminent teacher or similar person. (22.17)
And [the penance for killing] a cow is like that for a Vaiśya. || 22.18 ||

Having killed a cow, one should perform that penance prescribed for the killing of a Vaiśya: "In the case of killing a Vaiśya, one should give three years' worth of food and one hundred and one bulls along with cows" (GDh 22.15). This applies to the intentional killing of a cow that is young, productive, and yields much milk, belonging to a man of good conduct and Vedic study who is impoverished and has a large family. For the killing of such a cow that is pregnant, yielding a single fruit, or used as an auxiliary to a ritual, the penance is that of Yama: "One who has well-performed his vows should give a thousand or even a hundred cows;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas. (MDh 11.134)
A two-month vow is the subject under discussion here. In this very context, however, for an intentional act, there is the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana, which excludes the gift of a cow.
Furthermore, the killer of a cow shall dwell in a cow-pen, clothed in its hide;
he shall constantly follow the cows, wearing a girdle of muñja grass, rags, an antelope skin, and so forth.

"Afflicted by the fear of rain, cold, heat, suffering, fire, mud, and [other dangers], one who is thus distressed shall be liberated through every possible effort; he is purified in three years. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "If one should kill a cow, he shall remain for six months wrapped in her raw hide, performing either the *kṛcchra* or the *taptakṛcchra* penance, and he shall give away a bull and a barren cow (*vehad*). A *vehad* is a cow that has been harmed by a bull. In the phrase "he shall give," the agentive suffix is used in the sense of the object. Yājñavalkya says:
A cow-killer, drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), shall remain self-restrained for one month;
sleeping in a cow-pen and following the cows, he is purified by the gift of a cow.
"Or, being composed in mind, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, one should give eleven cows along with a bull. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 3.263–264]. Jābāla says:
"If one has killed a cow unintentionally, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for a month;
he should follow the cows for their benefit and is purified by the gift of a cow," so says Viṣṇu.
"For one who has killed a cow, there shall be three *pala* of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) daily for one month, or else a *parāka* penance, or even a *cāndrāyaṇa*."

Kāśyapa says: “Having killed a cow, one should be clothed in its hide, sleep in a cow-pen for a month, bathe at the three periods of the day, and constantly subsist on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Śātātapa says: “One should subsist on the five products of the cow for a month. Śaṅkha and Pracetas say: “The killer of a cow shall subsist on the five products of the cow; he should fast for twenty-five nights, shave his head including the top-knot, be clothed in a cow-hide, follow the cows, sleep in a cow-pen, and give a cow as a gift. Paiṭhīnasi says: “The killer of a cow becomes pure by eating for a month gruel made from a handful of rice, while doing what is pleasing to the cows. Manu [says]:
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall subsist on barley gruel;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a wet hide.
"Having restrained his senses, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at the fourth mealtime,
and perform his bath with cow urine for two months.
Beginning thus [from MDh 11.108–109], and so forth...
But he who, following this rule, attends upon cows,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
"One who has successfully observed the vow should give eleven cows along with a bull. Thus [Manu Smṛti 11.115–116].

Sumantu says: "For the killer of a cow, there is the gift of a cow, sleeping in a cow-pen for twelve nights, consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and following after the cows. Saṃvarta says:
"One should subsist on barley meal, barley gruel, alms-food, milk, curd, clarified butter, and cow dung."
One should eat these in succession for half a month, being well-composed in mind.
"Having fed the Brahmins, one should give a cow for the sake of one's own purification.

Bṛhaspati states: "For twelve nights, one should subsist on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). The appropriate distribution of these penances among the various subjects, such as Brahmins and others, should be inferred according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional. There is a specific rule in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "When [the sin] has just arisen, it is one quarter; when it has become firm, it is two quarters."
Having killed an insentient fetus, a vow one-quarter less than the full penance is prescribed.
When the fetus is complete with all its major and minor limbs and endowed with consciousness, one should perform a double cow-vow; this is the atonement for a killer of a cow.
Bṛhatpracetā states:
"When a calf one year old is killed, a quarter-penance (kṛcchrapāda) is prescribed;
if it was unintentional, it shall apply to a man; however, for a two-year-old calf, it shall be half a penance."
"In the case of a three-year-old cow, it shall be three-quarters of a *prājāpatya*;
beyond that, [the penance is] according to another *smṛti*:
'An excessively old, excessively emaciated, excessively young, or diseased [cow...']"
Having killed [a bird], a twice-born man should observe the half-vow according to the previously prescribed rule.
"One should feed Brahmins according to one's ability and likewise give gold and sesame seeds.
Thus say Saṃvarta and Āpastamba.
"If a single woman is somehow killed by several people through some accident," [the rule applies].
But for each foot of the offense of killing, they shall perform penance separately.
"But if many [cows] have perished due to confinement or even bondage, and if a physician has administered a wrong treatment, one should perform the *govrata* twice.

Thus, even in the case of the killing of many [cows], it is precisely double [the penance] by virtue of the force of the scriptural statement; it is not a repetition for each individual cause (*pratinimittam*).
Vyāsa says: Medicine, salt, and even food for the sake of merit—these should not be given in excess; one should cause only a small amount to be given at the proper time.
"If there is injury when the excess is greater than that, a *kṛcchra* penance for one quarter is prescribed.
Thus says Āpastamba. [He continues:
"Whether by means of stones, clubs, weapons, or anything else, through force..."
Those who cause cattle to perish therein must indeed perform that vow.
"One quarter [of the penance] should be performed for obstructing [a path], two quarters for binding,
one minus a quarter for yoking, and one should perform the whole for causing a fall. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.

"Cows should not be tied with coconut fibers, nor with hemp, nor even with muñja grass, nor with leather thongs or chains. Having tied them, one should stand guard over them, holding an axe. Thus [it is said]. 22.18.
And [the same penance applies] for the killing of frogs, mongooses, crows, porcupines, iguanas, mice, and dogs. || 22.19 ||

The *bimba* is a lizard capable of changing its form at will; the *dahara* is a small-bodied mouse—some say it is a muskrat (*chucchundarī*), while others are well-known by their common names. For the killing of these animals when committed together, the penance is that prescribed for a Vaiśya. This refers to cases of intentional and habitual practice. In other instances, the rule of Āpastamba applies: "For the killing of a crow, a crane, a water-fowl, a peacock, a ruddy goose, a swan, a vulture, a frog, a mongoose, a *sairika*, or a horse, the penance is that prescribed for a Śūdra" (ĀpDh 1.25.13). Manu also says: "Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog..."
"And having killed a dog, a monitor lizard, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance for killing a Śūdra. [MDh 11.131] But in the case of intentional killing of each of these—
cats, monitor lizards, mongooses, frogs, dogs, and birds— [the following applies]:
"One should drink milk for three days, or perform a quarter *kṛcchra* penance"—this statement by Yājñavalkya should be observed. For an intentional act, the rule of Manu applies:
"One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana* on foot" (MDh 11.132). || 22.19 ||
Then, having slain a thousand of those [enemies], he proceeded. || 22.20 ||
Having killed a thousand vertebrate creatures such as lizards and the like, the penance is the same as that for a Vaiśya.
And [the same applies] to boneless animals and to the carrying of a load by an ox. || 22.21 ||

For those creatures such as gadflies and mosquitoes that are boneless, having killed as many as one is able to carry on a bullock, the penance is the same as for a Vaiśya. Both of these cases refer to instances of repeated practice; otherwise, that which was stated by Yājñavalkya applies:
"But for those with bones, a thousand; likewise for those without bones, a cart. [YDh 3.269]
"The penance for killing a Śūdra is the six-month rite prescribed [for killing a Vaiśya], or he should give ten cows. (22.21)
Or rather, one may give something to each of those who possess cattle. || 22.22 ||

The word *api vā* indicates an alternative. One should count however many bone-possessing creatures have been killed—whether a thousand or more or less—and give something small to each one. This expiation for those with bones may be performed either as described here or according to the previous rule.
A small amount (*kiṃcit*) is eight handfuls (*muṣṭi*); eight of these make a *puṣkala*;
four *puṣkala*s are proclaimed to be an *āḍhaka*.
Four āḍhakas constitute a droṇa; such is the definition of measurement.
Thus says the Smṛti. For boneless creatures, however, there are that many breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). And so Manu says:
"In the case of killing a creature with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin;
for in the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-restraint" (MDh 11.141). || 22.22 ||
For a eunuch, a load of straw and a māṣa of lead. || 22.23 ||
Regarding this, Devala said:
"He who is a eunuch (ṣaṇḍha) and possesses deficient sexual organs is not at all worthy of the sacraments."

Thus, when he has been killed, if the act was intentional, both a load of straw and a *māṣa* of lead—these two combined—must be given as a fine; in other cases, however, only one of the two. Lead (*sīsa*) is a specific type of metal resembling silver that melts instantly. The measure of a *māṣa* has already been explained previously. Furthermore, no distinction regarding the species is heard of anywhere in the *Smṛti*; only this much is mentioned: "the *ṣaṇḍha*, the *ṣaṇḍhaka*. In that regard, just as a sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa or others does not apply even when there is a commonality of species, so too the penance occasioned by killing him does not apply; rather, only what is specifically stated takes effect. Others, however, consider this to refer to wild animals and birds—that is, when those among wild animals and birds who are *ṣaṇḍhas* are killed. (22.23)
In the case of a boar, there is a jar of ghee. || 22.24 ||
When a boar has been killed, a jar filled with clarified butter should be given.
An iron staff against a snake. || 22.25 ||

When a snake has been killed, an iron rod (*lohadaṇḍa*) should be given as penance. By the word "iron" (*loha*), black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*) is meant, as seen in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an adze made of black iron" (MDh 11.133). The statement from the *Auśanasa* [Dharmaśāstra], "Having killed a snake, one should give a *māṣa*," refers to an intentional act.
In the case of a woman who is a mere nominal Brahmin (brahmabandhū) and is fickle, [the son born to her] is Nīla. || 22.26 ||

A woman who is a Brāhmaṇī by birth alone is a *brahmabandhū*. A *calanā* is an unchaste woman. When she has been killed, a blue bull is to be given; "blue" refers to a blue bull. Manu, however, states the sequence according to the castes: "For the purification of all four castes, one should give separately a blue bull, a bow, a goat, and a sheep, respectively, after having killed women who have strayed from their conduct. (MDh 11.138) || 22.26 ||
Something [is achieved] by means of the erotic arts. 22.27.
That woman who goes about in secret with many men should be known as an adulteress, and she is openly a courtesan.

Thus says Prajāpati: When a woman of the priestly class who lives by the profession of a courtesan (vaiśikena veśyākarmaṇā) is killed, something must be given; "something" is defined as eight handfuls [of grain]. 22.27.
For [the theft of] a bed, food, or wealth, the years [of penance] are distinct. || 22.28 ||

By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated. *Anna* means prepared food; *dhana* refers to gold and the like. Regarding the "obstruction of their acquisition"—that is, one who prevents them from being obtained by raising objections on account of some fault—he shall perform the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year, separately for each individual cause. The rule of Auśanasa, stating that "in the case of an obstruction to a maiden, food, or wealth, a *Prājāpatya* [penance is required]," refers to cases where the act is intentional. This present rule, however, concerns the obstruction of the acquisition of a Brāhmaṇa. For Kṣatriyas and others, the penance is reduced by half for each successive class. (22.28)
There are two [types of] adultery. || 22.29 ||

For approaching another's wife, there is a period of two years of ordinary celibacy (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*); this applies when the act is intentional and during her fertile season. However, for one who is without desire, this same penance is to be applied by reducing it by half. (22.29)
Three [days] for one learned in the Veda (śrotriya). 22.30.

In the very same case mentioned above, for one who approaches the wife of a *brāhmaṇa* learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), there is a period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for three years; here too, if it was unintentional, it is half [of that]. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says: "One who has spilled his seed upon a Vaiśya woman shall observe celibacy for one year and perform the three daily ablutions (*triṣavaṇa*). For a Kṣatriya woman, two years; for a Brāhmaṇa woman, three years. And for a Śūdra woman married to a Brāhmaṇa, it is the same as for a Vaiśya. Saṃvarta says:
"A Brāhmaṇa, having approached a Śūdra woman, [shall observe penance] for a month or even half a month."

"One who subsists on cow urine and barley gruel shall remain [in that state] until liberated from that sin. Thus, there is a fixed option: for intentional [intercourse], one month; for unintentional, half a month. However, in the case of twice-born women such as Brahmin women during a period other than their fertile season (*anṛtu*), the penances prescribed by Manu—lasting three months, two months, or a *cāndrāyaṇa*—apply. For Kṣatriyas and others, when approaching Kṣatriya women and so forth, the penance is the same as for a Brahmin. Regarding this, Uśanas says:
"But whatever vow there may be for sexual intercourse, one should perform double that [penance] in the case of pregnancy. (22.30)
And upon obtaining wealth, there shall be its renunciation. 22.31.
And if any property whatsoever has been obtained from another's wife, its relinquishment—that is, its renunciation—must be performed. 22.31.
Or he may cause him to go until his bath. || 22.32 ||
Or he may cause that which was obtained at the bathing place to be conveyed there. || 22.32 ||
If one who has performed the Sahasravāka rite engages in the recitation of forbidden mantras. 22.33.

Regarding those who are prohibited from the practice of mantras (mantrayoga), such as outcasts and the like—if one engages with them in the practice of mantras characterized by studying, teaching, sacrificing for oneself, or officiating at sacrifices for others—for one year, one must observe the standard vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). This applies if that practice of mantras consists of a "thousand utterances" (*sahasravāka*). A "vāka" is a word or phrase; thus, if it consists of a thousand words, this penance is required. This refers to an act committed unintentionally; however, in the case of intentional action, the status of an outcast (*patita*) would ensue. Regarding minor offenses (*upapātaka*), the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti states: "Upon hearing of an outcast, a Caṇḍāla, a corpse, or a birth-impurity, they shall remain silent for three nights; it is known from tradition that by reciting [the Veda] at least a thousand times, they become purified. By this same rule, teachers of censured subjects and officiating priests are explained. It is also known from tradition that they become purified by the renunciation of their sacrificial fees. Others, however, explain *mantrayoga* as joint study and joint sacrifice. (22.33)
And the same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who have been excluded from society, and those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka). || 22.34 ||

One whose nature it is to extinguish the sacred fires is called an *agnyutsādī*, meaning one who intentionally extinguishes them. A *nirākṛti* is one who, despite having the capacity, does not study the Vedas. Regarding minor offenses (*upapātakas*), those such as killing a cow or committing Brahman-murder—which precede the list beginning with Durvāsas—are explained among those unworthy of sitting in the company of others (*apaṅktyas*) [GDh 21.11]. For these very cases, starting with the extinguisher of the fires, the rule is that one must observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year. This refers to one who, out of atheism or due to the calamities of the country and so forth, abandons the fires and does not re-establish them for a long time even after they have been pacified. In that same context, regarding a shorter period, the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti states: "He who abandons the fires, having performed a *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall re-establish them" [VaDh 21.27]. For one who abandons them out of laziness, the rule of Manu applies.

"A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that is equal to the killing of a hero. (MDh 11.41). The grammatical connection is "shall neglect [the fires] for one month."
"If an Agnihotrin intentionally abandons the sacred fires for more than a month, he should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances without hesitation.
Regarding this, some authorities maintain that the Cāndrāyaṇa is required even for abandonment occurring within a month; however, this applies to the Smārta fire.

"A twice-born man who abandons the sacred fire out of atheism should perform the Prājāpatya penance; otherwise, there shall be a re-consecration of the fire, as well as the giving of gifts. Thus says Manu.

"Eating only at the sixth meal-time for a month, the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*, and daily burnt offerings with *Śākala* wood—this is the purification for those unworthy of the company. [MDh 11.200] || 22.34 ||
A woman who is unfaithful, even if she is guarded, shall nevertheless receive her maintenance.

A woman who transgresses against her husband, commits adultery, or has sexual intercourse with another man, shall perform this same penance: celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year. And as long as she completes that penance, remaining protected, she receives only a morsel of food (*piṇḍa*). This applies to intentional intercourse on a single occasion. In other cases, "one should cause her to observe that same vow which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others" (MDh 11.176).

This refers to cases involving those of the same class (*sajātīya*). Regarding a Brāhmaṇa woman in relation to a Kṣatriya, Vasiṣṭha states: "In the event of sexual intercourse, she should wear a garment smeared with ghee for one year; she should eat while sitting on a bed of cow-dung mud or *kuśa* grass and sleep on the ground. After half a year, she should offer oblations of her head with eight thousand repetitions of the *Sāvitrī* mantra while submerged in water" (VaDh 21.8). Regarding a Vaiśya, however, Auśanasa states: "An unfaithful woman shall perform the *Kṛcchra* penance for one year. On this point, Bṛhat-Pracetas says:
"Brāhmaṇa women who have had contact with a Śūdra, but have not borne a child from him..."
The expiation prescribed for her is the Kṛcchra penance and three Cāndrāyaṇas.
For a Brahmin woman’s sexual union with a Vaiśya, two Cāndrāyaṇas and one Kṛcchra are prescribed;
for her union with a Kṣatriya, there should be one Kṛcchra and one Cāndrāyaṇa.
A Kṣatriya woman, through contact with a Śūdra, shall perform the Kṛcchra penance and two Cāndrāyaṇas;
one who has united with a Vaiśya shall perform a Cāndrāyaṇa and a Kṛcchra.

"Having approached a Śūdra, a Vaiśya woman shall perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa; she who acts in the direct order [of castes] shall perform the Kṛcchra reduced by one-quarter. Regarding a Brāhmaṇa woman who has given birth, there is a specific rule in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
If a Brahmin embryo is miscarried, the penance shall be a Parāka; likewise for a Kṣatriya, it is an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa).
For a Vaiśya, if the act was unintentional, the penance is both an Aindava and a Parāka.
"If there is an abortion in the womb of a Śūdra, one becomes a Caṇḍāla;
therefore, in the case of a miscarriage due to defects of the bodily constituents (dhātudoṣa), one should perform three Cāndrāyaṇas.
However, in the case of intentional action (kāmakāra), one should perform double the Parāka and other penances. Vasiṣṭha, however, says:

The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not. However, for one who has already conceived after having been wedded, if she subsequently has intercourse with a Śūdra or the like...
But a woman who is pregnant, having been approached by a lustful man,
shall not perform penance until the fetus has emerged.
Once the child is born, one should subsequently observe the vow of subsisting on barley-gruel for one month;
there is no defect regarding the pregnancy in that case, and the child should be consecrated according to the prescribed rite.
Thus, what is stated in another Smṛti should be understood. However, when one does not perform penance due to misconduct, then the following applies:
"In the case of inverse intercourse, there shall be death for men, and for women, the cutting off of the nose and so forth" (YDh 2.286).
"She who has been enjoyed by one of inferior caste shall be branded or even put to death," so says Parāśara. Branding consists of marking with the male organ. (22.35)
In the case of non-human females—with the exception of cows—for the sake of sexual intercourse, there shall be an oblation of ghee with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras; [an oblation of ghee]. || 22.36 ||

When sexual intercourse is practiced for the sake of a woman with non-human females such as female buffaloes and the like—excluding cows—an oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛta-homa*) must be performed with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras. The explicit mention of "excluding cows" is for the sake of clarity; for the author will state later: "And [intercourse] with a cow is equal to violating the Guru’s bed" (GDh 23.12). Consequently, that same penance will apply to the case of approaching a cow. This [penance] applies to a single act of intercourse; in the case of repetition, that which was stated by Śaṅkha applies: "In approaching animals or a prostitute, the *Prājāpatya* penance [is required]. On this point, Kaṇva says: "He who has procreated upon a prostitute, being self-controlled and subsisting on alms..."
"By practicing the Sāvitrī one hundred thousand times, one attains purity. Thus the repetition has been stated. (22.36)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
He now states the penance for drinking liquor, which follows in due order:
"In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor, they should pour hot liquor into his mouth; he becomes pure upon death. (23.1)
There are three kinds of *surā*. As Manu has said:
"The *gauḍī*, the *mādhvī*, and the *paiṣṭī* are to be known as the three kinds of *surā*;
just as one [type] is not to be drunk, so all are [forbidden] by the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.94).
The term *dvijottama* refers to Brāhmaṇas. For Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, however, it is only the *paiṣṭī* (grain-based liquor). As he himself has stated:
"Liquor is indeed the dregs of food, and evil is called a dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor" (MDh 11.93).

The impurity of foods is *paiṣṭī* liquor (liquor made from flour). Here, the mention of a "Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the twice-born (*dvijāti*) in general. A "liquor-drinker" (*surāpa*) is one who drinks that specific liquor which has been forbidden to him. Into the mouth of such a twice-born person, they should pour that very same liquor while it is hot. This act of pouring is directed at the instructors; for they indeed pour the liquor into his mouth themselves. They instruct, saying, "This is the expiation for that liquor-drinker by whom the liquor must be drunk while extremely hot. However, the one who performs the pouring is the offender himself. And so says Āpastamba: "A liquor-drinker shall drink liquor heated by fire" [ĀpDh 1.25.3]. The plural number in "they should pour" (*āsiñceyuḥ*) indicates the plurality of the instructors. Manu also says:
"Those who know the Vedas shall declare the expiation for their sins;

for that is their means of purification, since the speech of the learned is indeed purifying. [MDh 11.85] Because of the statement "the deceased shall be purified," liquor must be heated in such a way that death occurs for the drinker. Paiṭhīnasi says, "He shall drink while wearing wet clothes," and the *Pracetas* state, "In a vessel made of iron or copper. Now, Yājñavalkya:
Having drunk any one of these— liquor, water, ghee, cow urine, or milk— that resembles fire in appearance,
the drinker of liquor attains purification through death.

"Clad in hair-cloth or with matted locks, he should perform the vow for the murder of a Brahmin; or he should eat oil-cake or grain-husks at night for a year. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 4.253–254). Among these, the penance ending in death applies to the case of intentional and repeated practice. In that same context, the twelve-year vow for the murder of a Brahmin applies to the case of drinking [Soma] once. Regarding women in this matter, Śaṅkha says: "One should avoid non-edible things such as spirituous liquor, garlic, onions, leeks, meat, and so forth; for this body consists of food. Vasiṣṭha also says:

"Half of the body of that man whose wife drinks *surā* falls [with her]; for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation (*nikṛti*) is prescribed. (VaDh 21.15) In this regard, *surā* is forbidden for women as well, and an expiation must be performed. It was stated previously that in such cases, the expiation for women is half. Since it is impossible to determine half of a penance ending in death, in the case of intentional, single consumption, the twelve-year penance is halved. In the case of repetition, there is a repetition of that very same penance. (23.1)
If he drinks milk, ghee, water, or air for three days each, that is the *taptakṛcchra*; thereafter, his consecration (*saṃskāra*) takes place. || 23.2 ||

But he who drinks *surā* unintentionally—that is, without prior conscious intent—mistaking it for *yavāgū* or the like, shall drink four substances—milk and the rest—hot and heated. Because of the use of the accusative case, it is understood that he "shall drink. For three days each: on the first three days milk, on the second ghee, on the third water, and on the fourth air. The heat of the air is obtained by staying in a place exposed to the sun. This *kṛcchra* penance, being of such a nature, is the *taptakṛcchra* expiation for him. After that *kṛcchra*, a re-consecration—that is, a second initiation (*punar-upanayana*)—must be performed for him. In this regard, there is a specific rule from the *Mānava*.
"Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
these are indeed omitted in the rite of re-initiation. (MDh 11.151) This refers to the case of slight repetition [of the offense].
"Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the purificatory rite alone" (MDh 11.146)—this statement of Manu refers to the case of drinking once. As for that which says:
"Or one should eat oil-cake or even grain-particles at night for a year" (YDh 3.254).

This is the statement of Yājñavalkya. As for the rule of Āpastamba, beginning with “Having committed theft or having drunk *surā*... [ĀpDh 1.25.10], both of these refer only to repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). [Furthermore: “To remove the sin of drinking *surā*, one should eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year, wearing hair-cloth, with matted hair, and carrying a banner. [MDh 11.92]
These and other rules from the *Manava* and other legal codes are to be established as applying specifically to cases where the act was unintentional, depending on the degree of repetition. 23.2.
And [the same penance applies] upon consuming urine, feces, or semen. || 23.3 ||

And for consuming urine and the like, the penance is a *punaḥsaṃskāra* (re-initiation) accompanied by the *taptakṛcchra*. This refers to cases where the act is intentional. Regarding unintentional consumption, [Manu Smṛti 4.222 states]: "Having eaten the food of any one of these [outcastes] unintentionally, one should fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, as well as semen, feces, or urine, one should perform a *kṛcchra*."
Thus:
"Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or even that which is mixed with *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite again" (MDh 11.150).
And thus it is said; and Kaṇva has also stated clearly:
"In the intentional consumption of semen, urine, or feces..."
"And if he eats intentionally, the twice-born man shall not eat for three days and shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (23.3)
And [the same applies] to the limbs of beasts of prey, camels, and donkeys. 23.4.

Tigers and other forest-dwelling beasts of prey; camels and donkeys are well known. Their "limbs" refer to their flesh, hide, and so forth. For consuming these, there is the *taptakṛcchra* penance and a rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). When there is intentional and habitual practice, both [penances] are combined. In the case of a single intentional act or habitual unintentional practice, there is the *taptakṛcchra*. In the case of a single intentional act, there is only the rite of re-consecration. (23.4)
And [the same applies] to the village cock and the pig. 23.4.
And for consuming the flesh of a village cock or a pig, this same penance applies; and the determination of the specific case is as before. 23.5.
If one who has drunk liquor smells a fragrance [of it], he must perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consume clarified butter (ghṛta).

But as for one who drinks *surā*, if he smells the odor of that *surā*—yet not the odor of the body, nor the odor of the substance remaining in the vessel—the penance for him consists of three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). This applies collectively to a Brāhmaṇa; for a Kṣatriya, it is breath-restraints alone; for a Vaiśya, it is the consumption of clarified butter. A specific rule regarding a Soma-drinker is shown by Manu:

"A Soma-drinker, having smelled the odor of a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk *surā*, becomes purified by sipping water three times with his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and consuming clarified butter" (MDh 11.149).
Thus:

"For a Brāhmaṇa, causing pain, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with men are recorded as causes for loss of caste (jāti-saṃkara). [MDh 11.67]
Thus:
"Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; if unintentionally, the *prājāpatya*. (MDh 11.124)
Thus [is the rule] regarding the smelling of the scent of liquor from a vessel belonging to a Mānava. 23.6.
And [the same applies] to one who has been bitten by [a snake] previously. || 23.7 ||

For one bitten by the aforementioned beasts of prey and the like, the expiation consists of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). Manu, however, states:
"One bitten by dogs, jackals, donkeys, or by domestic carnivorous animals, as well as by humans, horses, camels, and pigs, is purified by breath control" (MDh 11.199).
Regarding the case of a Brāhmaṇa, there is a specific rule by Vasiṣṭha:

"But a Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog becomes pure by going to a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and consuming clarified butter. [VaDh 23.31]
Jātūkarṇya says: "A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā who has been bitten by a dog or even by wild beasts is purified by bathing with her clothes on; of this there is no doubt. (23.7)
One who has violated the teacher's bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed.

In this context, "guru" refers to the father: "That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the rules, and who nurtures [the child] by other means, is called a *guru*. (MDh 2.142)

Thus says Manu. The mention of the "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is indicative of all social classes (*varṇa*). By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated; therein, both the mother and her co-wife are included. One who approaches them is a violator of the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpaga*). He should lie upon a heated iron bed made of black iron in such a way that death surely occurs. (23.8)
Or he should embrace a glowing iron image. || 23.9 ||
A woman made of iron is a *sūrmī*; one should embrace it while it is blazing, glowing like fire, and heated, until the separation of life. 23.9.
Or, having cut off his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands,
he should walk straight toward the southwest until he collapses from exhaustion.

Having uprooted the *liṅga* with its seed by cutting it off with a razor or similar instrument, and having placed it in his joined palms, he should walk straight toward the southwest direction until his body collapses. Vasiṣṭha says: "Avoiding wells and such, he should remain right where he is struck down until the dissolution of the world" (VaDh 20.13). 23.10.
One who has died shall become pure. || 23.11 ||

This is the general rule: among the modes previously mentioned, the violator of the Guru’s bed is purified only by death in one of those ways, and not otherwise. All three of these [penances] apply to approaching one’s own mother with the notion that she is one’s wife and so forth, when it is unintentional, as well as to approaching her co-wife; and also to the intentional approach of a woman of the same caste. But he who, having recognized his father’s wife to be of the same caste, approaches her, or approaches his own mother without recognizing her, does not become pure unless he dies.

Thus it is seen in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*. Regarding intentional intercourse with one’s mother, the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* states: “Having been shaved clean and anointed with ghee, he should burn himself with a fire of cow-dung, starting from his feet” (*VaDh* 20.42). The same applies even to repeated unintentional practice. However, regarding the repeated unintentional approach to a mother’s co-wife who is of the same caste or of a higher caste, that which was declared by Śaṅkha applies:
“Sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, and eating only once a day—for twelve years having passed... (*Śaṅkha-smṛti*).

"The stealer of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru's bed—these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow. Thus [it is said].
In the case of a single act of intercourse where both parties have acted out of mutual desire, the rule of Manu applies.
"Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with his mother-in-law, in a lonely forest, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind. [MDh 11.105]

When she has been incited by him, or when he has been incited by her, two penances prescribed by Uśanas are to be observed in sequence: "One who violates the bed of his guru shall observe the vow of a student for one year, or perform the *taptakṛcchra* for six months. In this same manner, regarding the subsequent penances as well, it should be understood that the heavier penance applies when he has incited her himself, while the lighter applies when she has incited him; however, if both have acted by mutual desire, the intermediate penance applies. On this point, Vyāghra says: "The *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and likewise the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*..."

"A Brahmin who has approached the wife of his Guru [shall observe] three months of penance for approaching a Kṣatriya woman. This refers to an intentional act performed once; for repeated intentional practice, it is one year.
Having intentionally gone again to the wife of his Guru, a twice-born man [who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya]...
"Having cut off the penis, excluding the testicles, he becomes pure upon death. Thus says Kaṇva:
"The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra."
"Having once gone to the wife of his guru who is a Kṣatriya woman out of ignorance, a twice-born man [must perform penance]," so says Jātūkarṇya:
"Having again gone to the wife of his guru who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya, unintentionally..."
"Having cut off only the testicles, he is purified, whether living or dead. Thus says Kaṇva:
"For [killing] a Guru, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra, the Parāka, and likewise the Sāntapana."
"Having approached a Vaiśya wife once, a twice-born man should perform penance for one month with full awareness. Thus says Laugākṣi:
"Having approached a Guru’s Vaiśya wife—whether once or repeatedly—"
"Having cut off the tip of the *liṅga*, he shall then be purified from that sin. Thus says Prajāpati:
"He shall not eat for five nights, or likewise for seven or eight."
"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, has once approached his guru’s Vaiśya wife... — thus [says the law]. Hārīta says:
"A Brahmin, deluded by ignorance, having repeatedly practiced [sexual intercourse] with the guru’s Vaiśya wife..."
"He should practice celibacy with its six limbs for as long as he lives. Thus says Jābāli.
Likewise, [he may perform] the Atikṛcchra, the Taptakṛcchra, and the Parāka.
"Having approached the Śūdra wife of his guru even once intentionally, a Brāhmaṇa should perform [penance] from that point. Thus says Upamanyu:
"If a Brāhmaṇa, being composed, should again intentionally approach the Śūdra wife of his guru..."
"One of uncorrupted soul should practice celibacy for twelve years"—
thus says Dīrghatapas.
[The penances are] the Prājāpatya, the Sāntapana, and fasting for seven nights.
"Having approached the Śūdra wife of his guru even once, a person should perform [penance] out of ignorance.
In that same context, regarding repeated practice, the rule of Manu is to be observed:
"Or, with his senses restrained, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months."
"Or with sacrificial food (haviṣya) or with barley-gruel (yavāgū), for the removal of the sin of violating the Guru’s bed. [MDh 11.106].
On this point, Vyāghra says:
"Adultery with another's wife as prescribed by caste, and likewise the act of violating the Guru’s bed..."
"And for a woman who is common property, there is no such thing as defiling a maiden. (23.11)
Sexual intercourse with a female friend, a woman born of the same womb, a woman of the same lineage, the wife of a pupil, a daughter-in-law, or a cow is equal to violating the Guru’s bed. || 23.12 ||

A *sakhī* is a female friend; a *sayoni* is a sister; a *sagotrā* is one of the same lineage; a *snuṣā* is a daughter-in-law, that is, the wife of one’s son. Regarding these, as well as a female disciple and a cow, in the act of sexual intercourse, the fault is equal to that of violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). Yājñavalkya states:

"Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one’s own womb, women of the lowest castes (*antyajā*), women of the same lineage, and the wives of sons is declared to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed."
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife,
the daughter-in-law, the mother’s co-wife, the sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter—

"But one who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru's bed; having had his penis cut off, he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing. Thus says Nārada (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.231–233).
A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal aunt,
the wife of a paternal uncle or a friend, a female disciple, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law;
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
"Approaching any one of these women is called violating the Guru's bed;
in that case, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained. Thus says Kātyāyana (NSm 12.72–74).
One should know that approaching one's mother, sister, daughter,
or daughter-in-law constitutes an extreme sin.
But those who have committed heinous crimes should enter the fire.
Bṛhadyama states: "Having discharged semen into virgins, women of one's own kin, women of the lowest castes,
female sapindas, or the wives of others, the abandonment of life is prescribed."
He himself [should approach]: a Cāṇḍālī, a Pulkasī, a Mlecchī, a daughter-in-law, a sister, a female friend,
the sister of his mother or father, one who has been entrusted to him, and one who has come for refuge.

"Having approached a maternal aunt, a female ascetic, a woman of the same lineage, the wife of a king, the wife of a disciple, or the wife of a teacher, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus [it is said]. 23.12.
"Some say it is on a heap of refuse. 23.13.

Some maintain that the fault in approaching a female friend or others is "emission" (*avakīrṇa*), and that in this case the penance is the vow of the *avakīrṇin*, not the vow for violating the Guru’s bed. Among those penances enumerated for approaching a female friend and so forth, those ending in death apply to cases of intentional, continuous, and excessive repetition. Those which are extremely light, however, apply to cases where one has acted with the notion that she is one's own wife, but having realized the truth midway, desists before the emission of semen. For intermediate cases, intermediate penances should be prescribed.

"One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in all manner of sins"—this statement from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], however, refers to cases other than those involving great crimes (*mahāpātaka*) that merit the penalty of death. (23.13)

In this regard, he states the punishment for women who do not perform penance when they have had intercourse with a man of lower caste: "The king shall have the woman publicly devoured by dogs. (23.14)

If she practices sexual intercourse with one of inferior caste, the king, standing in the midst of the assembly while all look on, shall have her devoured by dogs; he shall have her eaten. On this point, Manu says:
"But that woman of low birth who, proud of her caste and virtues, violates her husband—the king, standing in the assembly surrounded by many, shall have her devoured by dogs" (MDh 8.371).
Vasiṣṭha, however, states a distinction based on the specific nature of the caste:

If a Śūdra should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a donkey, one should cause her to be paraded along the high road; it is declared that she thus becomes purified. If a Vaiśya should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red Darbha grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a donkey, one should cause her to be paraded along the high road; it is declared that she thus becomes purified. If a Kṣatriya should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a donkey, one should cause her to be paraded along the high road; it is declared that she thus becomes purified. In the same manner, a Vaiśya [is punished] for [intercourse with] a Kṣatriya woman, and a Śūdra for [intercourse with] a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman. [VaDh 21.1–5]
As they were proceeding in reverse order from the anulomas, the tiger said:
"When there is an intermixture of the anuloma castes with one another in a contrary sequence, then the king shall have that woman devoured by monkeys."
"If a man deserves death for intentionally killing jackals, then this same [penalty] applies to those of lower castes for transgressing against their own kind. Thus [it is said]. 23.14.
One should cause a man to be executed. || 23.15 ||
In the matter just mentioned, the man who has committed the act shall be executed by the king; and the manner of execution has been shown immediately following by the words of Vasiṣṭha. (23.15)
Or as it has been stated: 23.16.

The removal of the [sexual] organ and so forth, or the infliction of punishment as previously described, should be carried out; this alternative depends on whether there was conscious intent or not, and whether the act was habitual or not. || 23.16 ||
One who has committed the avakīrṇin offense should sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a donkey.

"An *avakīrṇin* is one who, being a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), has gone to a woman," so says Yājñavalkya. He shall sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a donkey as the victim. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from the *Mānava*:
"But an *avakīrṇin* [shall sacrifice] at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey."
"According to the procedure for the *pākayajña* sacrifices, one should offer sacrifice to Nirṛti in that direction.

[MDh 11.118] Vasiṣṭha, however, states: "If a student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣas at a common fire in a forest or at a crossroads; or he should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) to Nirṛti. He should offer oblations from it, saying: 'To Kāma, svāhā! To Kāmakāma, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities who are the Rakṣases, svāhā! [VaDh 23.1–3]. || 23.17 ||
Having put on its skin with the hair facing upwards, wearing red garments, he should go for alms to seven houses while proclaiming his deed.

Having thus sacrificed with a donkey, he shall put on the skin of that very donkey with its hair standing erect, carry a red vessel—a red earthen pot—in his hand, announce his deed, and beg for alms, saying, "Give alms to one who has broken his vow of chastity. He shall wander for alms at seven houses; in those seven houses, he shall eat only as much as is obtained. If nothing is obtained, he shall fast.
He shall be purified after one year. || 23.19 ||
One should observe this vow for one year; then one becomes pure. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Subsisting on alms obtained from them, eating only once a day, and bathing at the three periods of the day, one becomes purified in one year" (MDh 11.123).

And this one-year penance is to be understood as applying to a learned Brāhmaṇa who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of a Vaiśya. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One who has spilled his seed in a guarded Vaiśya woman shall perform the three-sessions rite for one year; for a Kṣatriya woman, two years; for a Brāhmaṇa woman, three years. Here, “guarded” means protected by qualities such as being the wife of a learned Brāhmaṇa. Aṅgiras says:
“On account of the offense of an *avakīrṇin*, however, he should perform the vow prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa;
wearing clothes of bark for six months, he is thus released from the sin.”
That [penance] prescribed by Gautama applies when it is unintentional and concerns a woman who is a lustful object. Furthermore, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"One who has discharged semen in a wanton *vṛṣalī* shall bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. In the case of a Vaiśya woman, he shall eat only at every fourth meal-time, feed Brāhmaṇas, and give a load of barley to cows. In the case of a Kṣatriya woman, having fasted for three nights, he shall give a vessel of clarified butter. In the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman, having fasted for six nights, he shall give a cow. One who has discharged semen in cows shall perform the *Prājāpatya* penance. One who has discharged semen in a eunuch shall give a load of straw and a *māṣaka* of lead. Thus it is said.
And this expiation for the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) is common to all students of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). Thus says Śāṇḍilya:

"A twice-born man, a king, or even a Vaiśya who has become an *avakīrṇin* becomes pure after one year, provided he remains concentrated, subsists constantly on alms, and performs the sacrifice with a donkey. (23.19)
In the event of the emission of semen, fear, illness, or dreaming,
one should perform the kindling of fire, gathering fuel, and begging for alms for seven nights;
failing to do so, one should offer oblations of clarified butter or fuel-sticks with the two *retasyā* verses.

If the semen of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) should be discharged due to fear, disease, or in a dream, then an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) must be performed with the two *retasyā* verses, or else fuel-sticks (*samidh*) [should be offered]. The word "oblation" (*homa*) is understood as being connected to all these cases. However, this rule regarding fear, disease, and so forth applies even to those other than the celibate student. Likewise, if one fails for seven nights to tend the fire, to offer fuel-sticks, or to go begging for alms, an oblation must be performed as before. The two *retasyā* verses are: “May my virility return to me,” and “May my mind return, may my self return to me,” according to some; however, Āśvalāyana prescribes “May my virility return to me” and “These which are the supports for Agni.”

"In the event of fear, illness, or a dream, having involuntarily emitted semen, one should worship the Sun and then mutter the *ṛc* beginning with 'punar mām'. Thus, the *prājāpatya* penance applies to a single instance of emission; the rule of Gautama applies to repeated instances. Hārīta says:

"Whether intentionally or unintentionally, he who commits [an offense] while still a student (upakurvāṇa) must perform that very same penance doubled; however, a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika brahmacārī) must do so [four times].

On this point, Vasiṣṭha states: "This same [penance applies] to the intentional emission of semen during the day or in a dream, and likewise during other observances. The context here is: "One should sacrifice an ass as an animal offering, or one should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) dedicated to Nirṛti."
If a forest-dweller or an ascetic intentionally breaks his vow,
he shall perform the penance of an Avakīrṇin, conjoined with three Parāka fasts.
Thus says Śāṇḍilya:
Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man, or having made an effort to discharge semen,
a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should bathe according to his practice and then perform a sacrifice with an oblation (havis).
Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man, a forest-dweller or an ascetic becomes pure from that sin by performing the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Thus says Kaṇva:
Having emitted semen in a dream, a householder should perform three prostrations to the Sun;
likewise, an ascetic and a forest-dweller should each perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite three times.
Thus says Kāśyapa:
"But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman, or likewise on a bullock-cart, in water, during the daytime, or while sleeping, one should perform a bath. [MDh 11.174]
Thus says Manu. Regarding the householder:
"It is traditionally taught that for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse during the fertile period, bathing is prescribed because of the suspicion of pregnancy;
but when he approaches his wife outside the fertile period, purification is as required after voiding urine or feces."

Thus says Aṅgiras. And Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: "But he who should have sexual intercourse with her after she has been taken by the hand (i.e., married), his semen shall cause his ancestors to lie [in hell] for that month. (23.20)
A student who has risen with the sun shall remain standing for the day without eating,
and one who has set with the sun shall remain sitting through the night, reciting the Sāvitrī.

But the student who falls asleep while the sun is rising is one "overcome by the rising sun" (*sūryābhyudita*); he should remain standing for the entire day without eating. And he should remain seated for the entire night if he falls asleep after the sun has set, because of the rule regarding the *kṛcchra* penance: "He should stand during the day and sit during the night" (GDh 26.6). The injunction "reciting the Sāvitrī" applies equally in both cases. Because of the specific mention of the "student," there is a different penance for householders and others. Regarding the householder, Āpastamba states: "Some say he should restrain his breath until he faints" (ĀpDh 2.12.15). Vasiṣṭha says:

"If a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) and an ascetic (*yati*) are risen upon by the sun [while still impure], they shall subsist on *brahmakūrca* and recite the *drupadā* verse for a day. This same rule applies even to those [who were already impure] when the sun set. So says Prajāpati.
Having taken either a leaf of the palāśa tree, a lotus leaf, copper, or even gold,
and having set it down, one should then begin with the kūrca grass.
Taking cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."
With the mantra "śukram api jyotir asi," one takes clarified butter; with "devasya tvā," the water from kuśa grass.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, one should then perform the rite on the full moon day.
One should give urine twice the amount of cow dung, ghee four times the amount,
milk eight times the amount, and curd five times the amount.
Then, having placed [the food] upon *darbha* grass with *pālāśa* leaves,
one should lift it up and offer it to the deities in the proper sequence.
Having offered oblations to Agni, Soma, and Savitṛ with their respective mantras, as well as with the Praṇava, one should likewise perform the Sviṣṭakṛt offering with the Praṇava.
This is the *kūrca* fashioned by Brahmā, and likewise the *pavitra*;
having offered these in this manner, one should then, with a concentrated mind, meditate upon the remaining sin.
Having stirred it with the *praṇava* alone, having churned it with the *praṇava*,
and having drawn it up with the *praṇava* alone, one should drink it with the *praṇava*.
A twice-born man should perform this *kūrca* rite, established by Brahmā, month after month;
with his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the heavenly world.

"Whatever sin resides in the bodies of embodied beings, reaching even to the skin and bones, the *brahmakūrca* shall consume it all, just as a blazing fire consumes fuel. This [rule] applies equally to both intentional and unintentional acts; and thus says Manu:

"If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition, or should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting [the sacred texts]. (MDh 2.220). The word "day" is an elliptical indication; in the case of the sun setting, one should fast for the night. According to the statement of Jābāli, "of one who is free from fear and disease," there is no expiation in cases of fear or illness. 23.21.
Having seen something impure, one should look at the sun after performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).

An impure person refers to a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste. Upon seeing such a person, one should perform a single breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and look at the sun; this applies to a religious student (*brahmacārin*) during the time of recitation and other observances.
Having sipped water and become pure, he should always recite, upon seeing something impure, the solar mantras according to his energy and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability. (MDh 5.86)

Thus, the rule from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] applies to lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*) and others. The statement in the *Jābāli-gṛhya-sūtra*, "Upon seeing something impure, a twice-born man (*dvija*) should mutter the *praṇava*," concerns the householder. The rule of *Auśanasa*, which states that upon seeing something impure one may look at the sun, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, or fire, applies except during the time of fixed observances (*niyamakāla*). Because the term "twice-born" is used in the *Jābāli-gṛhya*, there is neither a mandatory injunction nor a prohibition for a Śūdra.
In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten, or consuming impure substances, purification is achieved by becoming free of excrement.

Beginning with the rule, “That which is constantly unfit for consumption is that into which hair or insects have fallen” (GDh 17.8–9), various things unfit for consumption have been described. These are of many kinds: those corrupted by their very nature (*jāti-duṣṭa*), such as garlic and the like; those corrupted by time (*kāla-duṣṭa*), such as food that has stood overnight; those corrupted by ownership (*parigraha-duṣṭa*), such as the food of those who have renounced worldly ties and so forth; those corrupted by contact (*saṃsarga-duṣṭa*), such as food defiled by hair, insects, and the like; and those corrupted by ritual action (*kriyā-duṣṭa*), such as food served after one has performed ritual sipping (*ācamana*) or risen from one’s seat. Regarding the eating of these unfit foods, and regarding the consumption of impure (*amedhya*) and unclean substances—impurity being caused by the place, the vessel, the cooking, the touch, the giver, and so forth—one must effect a state of being free from fecal matter (*niṣpurīṣībhāva*). One should act in such a way that the stomach becomes void of waste. 23.23.
How is that so?
By fasting for at least three nights. 23.24.

For three nights, one should eat nothing, chew nothing, and drink nothing. In this way, the state of being free from feces (*niṣpurīṣībhāva*) is attained. Because of the mention of "at least" (*avara*), there is also the possibility (attainment) of four nights and so forth. At most, it is seven nights. And thus says Āpastamba: "Having eaten what is unfit to be eaten, that state of being free from feces is attained in seven nights" [ĀpDh 1.27.3–4]. 23.24.
Or, for seven nights, he may subsist on fruits that have fallen of their own accord, without overstepping this limit.

The word "is purified" is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. Alternatively, he need not fast; rather, by eating fruits that have withered or fallen of their own accord, without overstepping [the rule], and without going out to seek other sweet fruits when encountering unsweet ones—by acting in this manner for seven nights, he is purified. 23.25.
Before the five-clawed animals [are eaten], there shall be emetics and the consumption of ghee.

In that very section on forbidden food (*abhojya-prakaraṇa*), among those foods declared inedible by the eight sūtras beginning with "and five-toed animals such as the porcupine" (*pañcanakhāś ca śalyakety-ādi*), there are certain foods declared inedible prior to those by the nineteen sūtras beginning with "always inedible" (*nityam abhojyam*, GDh 17.8). Having consumed these, one becomes pure by vomiting and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Thus, the two preceding penances apply specifically to naturally defiled items such as five-toed animals. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "Upon consuming any of the impurities or intoxicants, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance; and upon eating garlic, onion, leek, the meat of village pigs, village cocks, or human flesh—one should undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*) as the penance for all these for the twice-born. Bṛhaspati says:
For consuming things that should not be licked, drunk, or eaten,
as well as semen, urine, and feces, purification is declared to be the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Aṅgiras:
For consuming things that should not be licked, drunk, or eaten—
including semen, urine, and feces— the Ṛṣikṛcchra penance is the means of purification.
Having drunk water from these— lotus, udumbara, bilva, kuśa, and palāśa— one is purified by that very same [act] even if it be hot.

Kāśyapa: In the case of eating garlic, onions, *gṛñjana*, or chicken; drinking fat or semen; officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed (*ayājya*); eating what should not be eaten (*abhojya*); eating what is unfit to be eaten (*abhakṣya*); and likewise having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached (*agamyā*), one should inform the Brāhmaṇas and, having fasted for six nights, go toward the eastern or northern direction to a place where the sound of domestic animals is not heard. There, having kindled a fire and spread out a seat for the Brahman (*brahmāsana*), he deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again according to the procedure prescribed therein. Sumantu:

In the case of eating garlic, onion, or leeks; at a *vīra-śrāddha*; or eating food from a woman who has recently given birth, honey, meat, urine, semen, or other impure, forbidden foods—one should pour water-oblations (*saṃpāta*) over one's head eight thousand times while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra. These same acts are not prohibited for a sick person when performed as part of medical treatment. There is likewise no fault regarding other similar cases. Having unknowingly eaten these four—onion, garlic, leeks, and mushrooms—a twice-born man should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
But Manu says:
"Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, onions, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]."
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; regarding the remaining [forbidden] items, one should fast for a day.

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance during the course of a year for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, for food known [to be impure], the penance must be specifically greater.

Śātātapa states: "For eating garlic, onions, leeks, safflower, mushrooms, and impure substances, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. Viṣṇu states: "For eating eggplants and mushrooms, the *sāntapana* penance is required" (ViDh 51.34). Paiṭhīnasi states: "For eating garlic, onions, and leeks, the *prājāpatya* penance is required. Devala states: "For eating what is not to be eaten, the *kṛcchra* penance is required. Paiṭhīnasi states: "For eating what is not to be eaten, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is required. Saṃvarta states:
"Having consumed food that should not be eaten, a group consisting of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas becomes pure after seven nights by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*)."
Bṛhaspati says:
Having drunk white decoctions and having eaten forbidden food, a Brahmin becomes impure; his ritual action shall lead to a downward rebirth.
Viṣṇu: "In this case, one should fast after consuming all white substances except for curd. This is the context. Śaṅkha:

"Having eaten red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by cutting, and having eaten what is cooked in a frying pan (*ṛbīsa*), one who observes the vow shall remain under penance for three nights."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of consuming the milk of all [female animals] that have two teats, this same [penance applies], excluding the goat; in this instance, there is fasting for six nights and a *cāndrāyaṇa*," as is the established rule. Upon consuming the milk of a cow within ten days of calving (*anirdaśā*), one must fast for that day and perform a bath with one's clothes on. Śātātapa says: "Having consumed camel’s milk, sheep’s milk, food during a period of death or birth-impurity, the food of a thief, or food at a *navasrāddha*, one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*."

Paiṭhīnasi states: "Upon consuming the milk of a sheep, a camel, or a human, there must be a second initiation and a Prājāpatya penance. Baudhāyana says: "For drinking the milk of a sheep, there is a Kṛcchra penance, except in the case of a cow; for a cow's milk, there is a fast for three nights" (BDh 1.12.12–13). Śaṅkha states:
"Having drunk the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, or the milk of a goat or a buffalo, or the milk of a cow whose calf has died, one should observe a vow for a fortnight."
A wise person who eats the products of those milks that are unfit for consumption should perform the vow prescribed for this case for seven nights.

Sumantu states: "Upon consuming the milk of a one-hoofed animal, a camel, or a female ass; or upon consuming the milk of cows, buffaloes, or goats within ten days of calving, one must subsist on barley-gruel for three nights and bathe at the three periods of the day. Viṣṇu says: "With the exception of the milk of cows, goats, sheep, and buffaloes, one should fast after consuming the milk of all other animals, as well as the milk of those within ten days of calving, of a cow that is 'syandinī' (exuding milk from her udder), of a cow in heat (*sandhinī*), or of one whose calf has died, and the milk of animals that eat impure things" [ViDh 51.38–41]. This is the established rule. Hārīta states: "For eating animals not specifically mentioned, one should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance; for domestic animals, a *cāndrāyaṇa*. Yama [says]:
So too are the boar, one-hoofed animals, the crow, and the cock;
as well as all carnivorous creatures and those that have been declared unfit for consumption.
Having consumed meat, urine, or feces, as well as beef,
or the flesh of dogs, jackals, and monkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
Or, having fasted for twelve days, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.

Vasiṣṭha: “Upon eating the flesh of a dog, a cock, a village pig, a crow, a vulture, a jackal, a crow, a pigeon, a human, a raven, or an owl, one must fast for seven nights, become free of feces, consume clarified butter, and undergo the purificatory rite again.
[VaDh 23.30] “Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a mouse, or the leavings of a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*. [MDh 11.159]
Food contaminated by hair or insects, as well as that tasted by women,
or touched by a dog or a menstruating woman, is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Yama states:
Having eaten honey, molasses, vegetables, milk products, salt, or ghee when these are offered directly by hand, one should perform the Sāntapana penance.
Śaṅkha:
"He who gives unequally to those seated in a single row,
and he who eats [the food so given]— all such persons must perform the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin."
Yama says: For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras eating together,
the penances are respectively the Prājāpatya, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra.
The expiation known as Cāndrāyaṇa is thus declared in its proper sequence.
Śātātapa says: "He who considers himself a householder without having taken the marriage fire—
his food must not be eaten, for he is declared to be one who cooks in vain."
Having eaten the food of one who cooks in vain, a twice-born man should perform an expiation;
by practicing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consuming clarified butter, he becomes purified.
Aṅgiras says: For those who maintain the sacred fires (agnihotrin), there is no fault in eating the food of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas during the period of impurity caused by birth or death,
provided it is after the collection of the bones.
The Cāṇḍāla, the Śvapaca, the Kṣattṛ, the Sūta, the Vaidehaka,
as well as the Māgadha and the Āyogava— these seven are the Antyāvasāyins.
He who, out of desire, eats the food of those who dwell at the very end [of the social order],
shall perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or the Taptakṛcchra.

Yama says: A Śūdra who gives food to Brāhmaṇas, and a Brāhmaṇa who gives food to Śūdras—both of these have food that is unfit to be eaten; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (23.26)
In cases of verbal abuse, falsehood, or violence, the highest penance lasts for three nights.

Except in cases involving major or minor sins (*mahāpātaka* or *upapātaka*), when there is verbal abuse—whether true or false—when there is excessive speech due to some fault, and when there is falsehood regarding matters other than witness testimony (since such falsehood has already been addressed therein); likewise, except for violence toward living beings (since that has been addressed in the context of living beings)—under these circumstances, "supreme austerity" (*paramaṃ tapaḥ*) must be performed, which consists of fasting for three nights and observing celibacy. By the inclusion of the word "supreme," even one night and so forth may be understood. In that regard, the rule is as follows: for verbal abuse against a Brāhmaṇa, three nights; for a Kṣatriya, two nights; for a Vaiśya, one night; and for a Śūdra, one day.

The same applies even in the case of falsehood. Likewise, when there is injury—even if unintentional—to trees and such things belonging to Brāhmaṇas and others, with regard to their fruit-bearing or non-fruit-bearing status, the same rule holds. On this point, Prajāpati says: "For a Soma-drinker who has spoken falsely, one should perform the supreme penance for three nights, or one should offer a full oblation with the verse, 'Seven are thy [fires], O Agni'."
Thus it is said:
"Upon speaking a falsehood, upon spitting, upon touching the teeth,
and upon conversing with those who have fallen [from their caste], one should touch the right ear."

This refers to falsehoods uttered for the purpose of jesting and the like. Hārīta states: "If one should speak a falsehood after having made a formal promise, whether it be a lie or even a truth, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow accompanied by the Taptakṛcchra penance."
Prajāpati says:
Having eaten meat, a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) must undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) again;
in case of repetition, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, and one who has taken a lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika) must perform it twice as much.

"One who dwells in the forest should perform it threefold, and an ascetic (yati) should perform it fourfold, in the case of eating meat, speaking untruth, and likewise in carrying out a corpse. (23.27)
Regarding verbal abuse, there is a specific rule: for truthful speech, one should perform an oblation with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses. 23.28.

When verbal abuse occurs, or when a true statement [is made that causes offense], an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) should be performed with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses. The maximum duration is three nights. The Vāruṇī verses are: “*yat kiṃcedam*,” “*imaṃ me varuṇa*,” “*tat tvā yāmi*,” and “*avate heḍa*.
