The Mānavī verses are the fifty-nine ṛks beginning with “*agnir ukthe purohita*” and continuing until the end of the chapter; these were seen by Manu. Among them, the last four—beginning with “*makṣū devavata*”—are prescribed in the *Taittirīyaka* as *dhāyyā* verses for the *Saumāraudra* sacrifice, stating: “One should use two Mānavī verses as *dhāyyās* in the anuvāka beginning with ‘*asāv āditya*’. The author of the Sūtras also says: “One should use two of these as *dhāyyās*, namely the Mānavī verses beginning with ‘*makṣū devavata*’. Regarding this, some maintain that the oblation should be performed with these last four verses, while others hold that it should be performed with all the verses recited in the Ṛgveda. (23.28)
Some say there is no fault in speaking untruth in connection with marriage, sexual intercourse, jesting, or when one's life is at stake. 23.29.

At the time of marriage, there is no fault in speaking of qualities that do not exist, or in promising "I will give this to you" and then failing to give it; likewise, in the context of sexual union, having said "I will give this to you," there is no fault even if it is not given once the sexual act has been performed. In jest—that is, in the context of humorous banter—there is no fault in speaking untruths. For example, when a brother-in-law or similar guest comes to the house desiring food, one might say to him: "Come, my friend, you shall eat rice; it has already been eaten by the guests. Such cases are of this nature. In the context of distress, there is no fault in speaking an untruth for the sake of pacifying the suffering of one who is afflicted. Therefore, there is no penance for speaking untruths under these specific circumstances. (23.29)
But indeed not for the sake of one's teachers. 23.30.
Even for the sake of a guru's purposes, such as marriage and the like, one must not speak untruth. || 23.30 ||
Why? Because:
"Even by speaking a falsehood to his teacher for the sake of trifling matters, though only in his mind, he slays seven generations before and after him. (23.31)

The word "hither" (itaḥ) refers to oneself. Starting from oneself, one strikes—that is, afflicts and joins with evil—seven generations of descendants, such as sons and grandsons, and seven generations of ancestors, such as fathers and grandfathers. If one commits a falsehood against a guru even by thinking of it in the mind for the sake of minor purposes, how much more so when speaking it aloud, especially for great purposes? (23.31)
For sexual intercourse with an Antyāvasāyinī woman, there shall be a year-long Kṛcchra penance.

For approaching women of the lowest castes (antyāvasāyinī) and engaging in sexual intercourse with them, the penance is a year-long Kṛcchra, consisting of remaining for one year according to the Prājāpatya rule; this applies when the act is intentional. 23.32.
For ministers, the penance lasts twelve nights. || 23.33 ||
When *kṛcchra* is the subject under discussion, the mention of "twelve nights" is for the purpose of including the *parāka* penance; and thus it is said:
"In the case of approaching outcastes (*antyaja*), eating [their food], or killing them, one becomes purified by the *parāka*—so said the venerable Aṅgiras."

This also applies to one who has desisted before the emission of semen. But for cases occurring thereafter, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "He shall subsist on water for twelve nights, fast for twelve nights, or go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. By this, intercourse with a *caṇḍālī* woman is explained" (VaDh 23.38, 40–41). || 23.33 ||
In approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night penance.

When one has sexual intercourse with a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), the penance must be observed for three nights by means of celibacy and fasting. This applies to a single instance of intentional intercourse; in the case of repetition, the rule of Manu applies:

"Having discharged semen into non-human females—with the exception of cows—into a woman in her courses, into non-vaginal orifices, or even into water, one should perform the *Sāntapana Kṛcchra*. (Manu Dharmaśāstra 11.173)

Regarding unintentional, single instances of approaching [a woman during her menses], Śātātapa states: “In the case of voiding urine or excrement without water, upon being touched by a crow, and likewise upon approaching a woman in her menses, one should bathe with one’s clothes on and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the Mahāvyāhṛtis. Regarding repeated practice, Vasiṣṭha says: “Upon approaching a woman in her menses, one should give a white bull with reddish-brown spots. [The repetition [of the rule] serves to state the aforementioned meaning. 23.33.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
The secret expiation shall now be declared:
secret expiation is for a fault that has not become publicly known. 24.1.

For that sin whose fault is not made known by others, the expiation is secret; that is to say, it must be performed in such a way that it is not known by others. What is prohibited here is its being known by anyone other than those without whom that particular transgression could not have been committed. Therefore, even if adultery or cohabitation with an outcast is known by others, the expiation to be described below still applies. (24.1)
One who desires to accept something that should not be accepted, or who has already accepted it, should mutter over water the four verses beginning with *taratsamandī*. (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 24.2)

The black antelope skin and other such items belonging to a person who is defiled by birth or defiled by his actions are inherently impure and must not be accepted. Desiring to accept them—that is, wishing to take them—one should mutter the hymn consisting of four verses beginning with *taratsamandī dhāvati* while standing in water reaching up to the navel, according to some; others say while submerged. One may mutter it either after having accepted the gift or after the act of acceptance; thus there is an equal option. Others maintain that if it is known to be unacceptable before the acceptance, the muttering occurs beforehand; if it is known afterwards, the muttering occurs afterwards. On this point, Manu says:
"Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is released from [the sin] after three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn. Thus [says] Prajāpati (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 11.253).
"The best of the twice-born, having become known for his faults, should perform the fulfillment of his recitations (*japa*) and so forth;
likewise, he should practice that very same [remedy] for a fault committed in secret.
This refers to the subject of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). 24.2.
Desiring to eat what is unfit for consumption, one might as well sow it upon the earth. || 24.3 ||

It has been stated: “That which is constantly contaminated by hair or insects is unfit for consumption” (GDh 17.8–9). If, due to the absence of any other alternative, one wishes to eat that very food, then one should scatter it upon the earth—that is, throw dirt over it—and thereafter eat. || 24.3 ||
Some say that for one who has sexual intercourse during another season, purity is attained by touching water. 24.4.

Some say that if one has sexual intercourse during the menstrual period or approaches a woman in her courses, purification occurs through bathing with one's clothes on after touching water. The rule, "In approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night penance" (GDh 23.33), refers to cases where the act is public. The inclusion of the word "some" (eke) is connected to the subsequent rules as well. 24.4.
Regarding women: 24.5.

Some consider that touching water [is sufficient] for one's own wives, while others maintain that it is three nights elsewhere. Another says: regarding women—even those such as mares—with the exception of cows, some consider that purification comes from touching water when sexual intercourse has been practiced. 24.5.

Now, the secret expiation for killing a Brahmin: for ten nights he shall subsist on milk; for a second [period] on clarified butter; for a third, on water. Eating only once during the day and night, with his clothes wetted by water, he performs oblations of hair, nails, skin, flesh, blood, sinew, bone, and marrow, ending each with the formula: "I offer myself into the mouth of Death. This is the expiation for all [offenses], even for the murder of an embryo. (24.6)

Feticide and the killing of a Brāhmaṇa—this expiation for that is now stated. For the first ten nights, one should observe the milk-vow, subsisting on milk alone. For the second ten nights, one should live on clarified butter. For the third, on water; or, according to the word "or" (*vā*), one may eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) instead. The option depends on one's capacity. During these days, eating only once a day, one should consume only one of the aforementioned items—milk and so forth—at a time. When? At the morning hours and so on, but not in the evening nor at midday. During these days, one should wear wet clothes, remaining clothed in moisture. Likewise, eight oblations (*homāḥ*) must be performed daily with clarified butter. The mantras therein are: "hair, nails, skin, flesh, blood, sinew, bone, marrow"—at the end of each, one should append: "all these of my own self I sacrifice into the mouth of Death, Svāhā! This is because the injunction for the *juhoti* rite specifies the offering with the utterance of *svāhā*. Thus: "Hair of my own self I sacrifice into the mouth of Death, Svāhā! Nails of my own self I sacrifice into the mouth of Death, Svāhā!"—such are the oblations. (24.6)
Now, another expiation for the killing of an embryo is stated.
The rule has been explained. (24.7)
The phrase beginning with “or one who observes the milk-vow” (GDh 24.6) should be understood as applying even to what will be stated hereafter. || 24.7 ||
One should offer oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis beginning with "O Agni, do thou protect us," and with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, using clarified butter.

With the verse “O Agni, do thou ferry us across” (RV 1.189.2), with the Great Utterances beginning with *bhūḥ*, with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, and with those beginning “Whatever offense against the gods, O gods” (VS 20.14), he should offer clarified butter once each in sequence. || 24.8 ||

Or, remaining under that very vow, one who is exhausted by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while muttering the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn for the [sins of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the Guru’s bed, attains equality with the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse-sacrifice; and this is also an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). (24.9)

Or else, observing that very vow—endowed with the vow prescribed by him [Gautama Dharmasūtra 24.6] beginning with "or one who subsists on milk"—he should perform the penance for the four sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. Exhausted by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* with as many breath-restraints as are required until he becomes exhausted. The *aghamarṣaṇa* is the hymn seen by the seer Aghamarṣaṇa, beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*). And that is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice. By the use of the present participle "reciting," it is indicated that he should observe the vow every day for thirty nights. On this point, Manu says:
Just as the horse-sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the destroyer of all sins, so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the destroyer of all sins. [MDh 11.260] || 24.9 ||
Or, by repeating the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, he indeed purifies his own self. || 24.10 ||

The phrase "only that vow" (*tadvrata eva*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], as is the phrase "exhausted by breath-restraints" (*prāṇāyāmais tāntaḥ*). The only difference is that one must repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times; everything else remains the same. By acting thus, he purifies himself—that is, he cleanses himself from the four [great sins] beginning with the killing of a Brahmin. The word *ha* indicates well-known fact, and *eva* serves for emphasis. Consequently, the practice of the *Sāvitrī* is also a cause of purification for other sins. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"The divine [verse] which has a maximum of one thousand [repetitions], a middle of one hundred, and a minimum of ten..."
"One who desires purification should employ [this], even while remaining amidst all sins. Thus [says Vasiṣṭha 26.15]. Vyāghra also said:
"There is no recitation equal to the Sāvitrī; there is no oblation equal to the Vyāhṛtis."
"There is no gift equal to food and water, and no austerity equal to non-violence. (24.10)
He states another expiation:
"Or, by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sins. (24.11)

Remaining under that very vow, submerged within water, one who practices the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times for thirty nights is liberated from all sin, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally; and the repetition [of the rule] has already been explained. 24.11.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.

The secret penances for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) have been declared. Now, about to declare the penances for the minor sins (*upapātaka*), he first cites a Vedic text to demonstrate the extreme deprecation of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy), in order to state his penance:
"Regarding this they say: 'In how many ways does the *avakīrṇin* enter [the earth]? " (25.1).
The word "tat" (that) introduces the statement. The exponents of Brahman ask: in how many ways does the *avakīrṇin* enter [into various states], and what does he enter in each manner? || 25.1 ||
To this, the following reply is given:
The Maruts [consecrated him] with breath, Indra with power, Bṛhaspati with sacred splendor, and Agni with all other [powers]. || 25.2 ||

Through the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), he enters the Maruts, the winds; through strength, he enters Indra; through the perfection of his conduct and Vedic study, he enters Bṛhaspati; and through all other faculties, such as sight and the rest, he enters Agni alone. Thus, being short-lived, lacking energy, devoid of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and deficient in sight and the other senses, he becomes an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of chastity). Therefore, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. 25.2.
Then he says:
On the night of the new moon, having kindled the fire, he offers oblations of clarified butter as expiations. 25.3.

Having thus committed the violation, on the night of the new moon at midnight, he establishes the fire according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, kindles it, and at the conclusion of the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he offers oblations of clarified butter as expiations. 25.3.
In this regard, there are two mantras:

"I am besprinkled by desire, I am besprinkled, O desire; svāhā to desire! and "I am oppressed by desire, I am oppressed, O desire; svāhā to desire! Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire with these, having sprinkled water around it, and having performed the rite for the sacrificial site, he should rise and worship [the fire] three times with the verse, "May he pour together. 25.4.

At the end of the *homa*, having silently placed one fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire, he sprinkles water around the fire while reciting the formulas beginning with "O Aditi, you have assented" (*adite 'nvamaṃsthāḥ*). Then he performs the ritual for the sacrificial site (*yajñavāstu*). Regarding this, in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of the Chandogas, it is stated after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "Having placed a fuel-stick, and having thrice dipped blades of *darbha* grass and the sacrificial oblations into the clarified butter—[dipping them] at their tips, middles, and bases—and having sprinkled them with the verse, 'Licking what is anointed, let the birds fly apart' (*aktaṃ rihāṇā vi yantu vayaḥ*), he should cast them into the fire with the formula: 'May Rudra, the lord of beings, who wanders along the threads and is the bull, not harm our cattle; may this be an offering for you, Svāhā! One should perform this ritual for the sacrificial site everywhere. Having performed this ritual for the sacrificial site, he should rise, stand near the fire, and worship the fire three times with the verse, "May he sprinkle together" (*samāsiñcatu*). 25.4.
This is an explanatory praise of the threefold stationing:
"These are the three worlds; for the sake of conquering and mastering these worlds. (25.5)

For there are three worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar. Their conquest (*abhijiti*) is the bringing about of their fitness for enjoyment. Their mastery (*abhikrānti*) is the remaining state of presiding over them with sovereignty. The connection is that it must be done in this manner for that very purpose. (25.5)

Regarding this very matter, some maintain that for one who might be as if impure, he should offer the oblation in this manner and recite the mantra in this manner, with a boon as the sacrificial fee; for there is no specific distinction made regarding the expiation. 25.6.

One who is as if impure, or even another who considers himself as if impure—not only one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin)—should, with reference to this very rite, offer oblations in this manner and recite the consecratory formulas (anumantrayeta) in this manner; he should thus perform the oblation and the ritual attendance (upasthāna). A boon (vara) is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); indeed, a cow is the boon. Because it is performed by oneself, and because of the specific scriptural statement that "it is to be given to the Brahman priest," [the cow is the fee]. According to the opinion of some, this penance applies without distinction to all those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin). 25.6.

Having committed acts of dishonesty, calumny, or forbidden conduct; having consumed forbidden food; having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening; or having performed a blameworthy act intentionally—even in these cases—one should touch water while reciting the *ābliṅga* verses, the *vāruṇī* verses, or other purificatory mantras. 25.7.

Crookedness is deceit. Backbiting is the pointing out of another’s faults. Prohibited conduct is the performance of forbidden acts. Eating what is not to be eaten (anādya) is the consumption of forbidden food. In these cases—having emitted semen in a Śūdra woman, or having emitted semen in a non-vaginal opening such as the mouth and so forth; or having performed a faulty action consisting of causing pain to others or theft, whether premeditated and intentional, or by implication, unintentional—one should touch water with the *ṛk* verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" (RV 10.9.1), the three verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" (TS 5.6.1.1), the Vāruṇī verses beginning with "yat kiṃcedam," "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tat tvā yāmi," and "ava te heḍaḥ" (RV 7.89.5, 1.24.11, 1.24.14), or with other purificatory (*pavitra*) hymns such as "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ. Having first bathed, one should afterwards pour water from the joined palms onto the head with these mantras. Although eating what is not to be eaten is also a form of prohibited conduct, because it is mentioned separately, it should be understood that among those [other acts], purification is performed with many [verses], whereas in the case of eating what is not to be eaten, it is according to the circumstances. (25.7)
In the event of a transgression of speech or mind regarding that which is forbidden, the five *vyāhṛtis* ending with *satya* [are to be recited]. 25.8.

Regarding that misconduct of speech and mind—that is, reprehensible activity—concerning prohibited objects, the five *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *satyam*, which were mentioned in the first chapter, are to be recited there. The reading *vāṅmanasoḥ* does not appeal to us, because it would entail the application of the rule for forming compound endings such as *acatura-* (Pāṇini 5.4.77), and because the inclusion of the term *pratiṣiddha-“prohibited” would be difficult to construe [with the rest of the compound]. (25.8)
In all [waters] he should sip water with the formula: "May the Day and the Sun purify me," in the morning; and "May the Night and Varuṇa purify me," in the evening. (25.9)

For all evil deeds, such as dishonesty and the like, one should sip water after consecrating it with these two mantras; one should drink in the morning with the words "And the day," and drink in the evening with the words "And the night. (25.9)
Or he should offer eight fuel sticks; by offering with the verse "devakṛtasya," he is released from every sin. || 25.10 ||

Alternatively, one should offer eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) by means of the mantras beginning with "devakṛtasya" (VS 8.13). By offering [these], one is released from all sin—not only from dishonesty and the like, but even from the sin of officiating at sacrifices for those who should not be officiated for. The particle *eva* ("only") is used to demonstrate the preeminence of this oblation; that is, "only after having offered, and not having performed anything else. Therefore, when possible, this alone is superior. The eight mantras are: "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods, svāhā," and so forth. (The repetition [of the verse number] indicates the end of the stated topic. 25.10
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third book of the *Mitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Śrīgautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
The Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and Cāndrāyaṇa have been mentioned. Regarding these, he now states the nature of the Kṛcchra and the others in their proper order:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the Kṛcchras. (26.1)

The word *atha* (now) signifies the commencement of a topic; the word *ataḥ* (hence) signifies a reason. Since these [rites] that have been mentioned cannot be performed [by everyone], we shall therefore explain the *kṛcchra* penances. 26.1.
Having eaten sacrificial food for breakfast, he shall not eat for three nights. || 26.2 ||

Having eaten the morning meals—prepared with sacrificial grains other than *varaka* and the like, mixed with clarified butter and such, and devoid of alkaline substances and salt—the morsels (*āśā*) being those things to be eaten; that is, having consumed the mouthfuls fit for daytime eating, one should fast for three nights. Since it will be stated later, "Then for another three days" (GDh 26.3), it is understood here as well that this refers to three days. The prohibition against eating at night during those three days is formulated in accordance with the Vedic text: "He should not eat for three nights. This must be further explained: "Twice-born men have their eating prescribed by the Śruti for both evening and morning."

Thus, because of this restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*), eating is established as occurring only twice. In that context, when it is said "having eaten the morning meal," the cessation of eating at night is established by virtue of that restriction, just as the cessation of eating during the day is established later on. (26.2)
Then, for another three days, he should eat only at night.
Having thus spent three days eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day, he should thereafter eat only at night for three days; [the food must be] sacrificial food indeed. 26.3.
Then, for another three days, he should not beg from anyone at all. || 26.4 ||

Now, after the three days of eating only at night, for the next three days he should not ask for anything from even a relative; this is a prohibition against begging. However, there is no prohibition regarding his own property or what is obtained unasked. If this were stated [without qualification], the restriction to sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) would not apply, and because no specific time is mentioned, eating twice a day would also follow. In the phrase "he should not ask," the term "sacrificial foods" (*haviṣyān*) likewise carries over. Even in the case of what is obtained unasked, the meal is accomplished only once. Why? Because the expression "then another [period]" implies a meaning similar to the preceding one. That [eating] may be either by day or by night as he wishes. Others, however, citing the rule of Āpastamba, "For three days he observes the vow of not begging" (ĀpDh 1.27.7), explain that for those three days his subsistence must be solely through what is obtained unasked, neither through his own property nor through what is obtained by begging. The practice is indeed in this manner. 26.4.
Then he should fast for another three days. 26.5.
This is clear. Thus, this is the *kṛcchra* penance to be accomplished in twelve days. Vasiṣṭha has also shown another method:
"One day in the morning, one day at night, one day with food not requested, and one day he should fast;
thus [he performs] two further sets of four days."

"For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma, has indeed declared the *śiśukṛcchra* for children, the elderly, and the sick. Thus [says VaDh 23.43]. Bharadvāja says:

"If a Brahmin performing the *prājāpatya* penance is unable [to do so] day by day, he should properly feed five pure Brahmins at a minimum, having honored them well. This applies only on the day he is unable; on other days, it is as before. If he is unable even then, or if he is unable on the days of fasting, he should provide a meal for Brahmins and then eat *haviṣya* food himself properly. (26.5)
Now follows the rule for the qualities of the *kṛcchra*:
one who desires speed should stand during the day and sit during the night. (26.6)

He who desires, "May I be purified quickly," should pass the day standing; he may sit during the night provided it does not conflict with eating and other necessary activities. Even his sleep shall be while remaining seated. Vasiṣṭha, however, states another method for one desiring speed: "If he hastens to perform [the penance], he should subsist on air during the day and remain standing in water at night; that is equal to the Prājāpatya."
Having performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times when the sun has risen, one is liberated from all sins, provided one is not a killer of an embryo. (VaDh 27.17–18) 26.6.
One should speak the truth. 26.7.
Truth is that which is seen as it really is; even in matters such as marriage and the like, one should speak only the truth. (26.7)
One should not converse with those who are ignoble. || 26.8 ||
Since gender is not intended to be significant for those other than the twice-born, he should not converse even with their women. 26.8.
One should constantly employ the Raurava and Yaudhājaya [Sāmans]. || 26.9 ||

The *raurava* and *yaudhājaya* *sāmans* are those sung upon this *ṛc*: “O Soma, being purified, flow with thy stream” (*punānaḥ soma dhāraya*, RV 9.63.28). One should employ them daily—that is, one should sing them every day. Another says: “One should employ them again daily. (26.9)

At each pressing, he should touch water and perform the ritual purification with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which contain the word *pavitra*, and with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ. (26.10)

Sprinkling with water (*udakopasparśana*) constitutes bathing; this should be performed during the three daily libations (*savana*). Immediately thereafter follows the ritual purification (*mārjana*) with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. Those verses in the section [of the *Ṛgveda*] beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ" are called *pavitravatyaḥ* (purifying verses) because of the presence of their characteristic marks (*liṅga*). In the fifth book, sixth chapter of the *Taittirīya*, the verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" are recited; these number ten. Among them, one uses eight. However, if in another recension (*śākhā*) only eight are recited, then those alone should be taken. (26.10)
Now follows the libation of water. 26.11.
Now, immediately after the purification, the libation with water (tarpaṇa) should be performed. 26.11.
In that regard, the mantras are as follows:

Homage to the one who removes delusion, the one who dispels confusion, the one who shakes off ignorance, the ascetic, the Punarvasu; homage! Homage to the one girt with a girdle of muñja grass, to the one who dwells on the earth, to the finder of wealth, to the finder of all things; homage! Homage to the one who has gone to the further shore, to the one who has well crossed over, to the one who has reached the great further shore, to the one who causes others to cross; homage! Homage to Rudra, the Lord of Creatures, the Great God, the Three-Eyed One, the Solitary Wanderer, the Sovereign, Hara, Śarva, Īśāna, Ugra, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, the Compassionate One, the one with matted hair; homage! Homage to Sūrya, to Āditya; homage! Homage to the Blue-Throated One, to the White-Necked One; homage! Homage to the Black One, to the Tawny One; homage! Homage to the Eldest, to the Best, to the Ancient, to Indra, to the Golden-Haired One, to the one whose vital seed is drawn upward; homage! Homage to the True One, to the Purifier, to the One of Purifying Color, to Desire, to the One who takes any form at will; homage! Homage to the Radiant One, to the One of Radiant Form; homage! Homage to the Sharp One, to the One of Sharp Form; homage! Homage to the Auspicious One, to the Supreme Person, to the Great Person, to the Middle Person, to the Highest Person, to the Vow-Observer; homage! Homage to the One with the Moon upon his forehead, to the One clothed in a skin; homage! (26.12)

This is not a single mantra, because of the use of the plural number in the phrase "these oblations of clarified butter" (*etāś cājyāhutayaḥ*). What then? These are thirteen mantras. All of them begin with a salutation (*namaskāra*) and end with a salutation. Among them, in the first [mantra], there are six names of the God ending in the dative case; in the second, four; likewise in the third. In the fourth, there are thirteen. In the fifth [mantra], the term *mahādeva* alone is stated in its expanded form as *mahate devāya*. In each of the three beginning with the fifth, there are two [names]. In the eighth, there are six. In the ninth, five. In the tenth, two; likewise in the eleventh. In the twelfth, there are six. Thus, there are fifty-six names of the God. With these mantras, one performs the libation (*tarpaṇa*) at each pressing of the Soma. (26.12)
This indeed is the worship of the sun. 26.13.

That by which the Āditya is worshipped is the "worship of the Āditya. This means that the Āditya is to be worshipped with this entire mantra. This too is to be performed at each pressing (anusavana) every day. Others say it is to be done once [daily], because of the separate formulation of the rule; otherwise, he would have composed a single rule as follows: "the libation of water (udakatarpaṇa) and the worship of the Āditya. (26.13)
These indeed are the offerings of clarified butter. 26.14.

The word *etāḥ* (these) also refers to the mantra; its feminine gender is due to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the oblation (*āhuti*). It is thereby stated that the clarified butter (*ājya*) must also be offered with these very thirteen mantras. In that regard, since "an injunction to offer (*juhoti-codanā*) involves the utterance of *svāhā*," the oblation (*homa*) should be performed daily once with those [mantras] accompanied by the *svāhā* formula. 26.14.
At the end of the twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial oblation (caru), he should offer it to these deities.

Having spent twelve nights in the manner thus described, on the thirteenth day, at its conclusion, he should cook a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* and offer it to the deities who are about to be mentioned.
She said: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! To Agni and Soma! To Indra and Agni! To the Viśvedevas! To Brahmā! To Prajāpati! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! || 26.16 ||

There are nine oblations together with the *sviṣṭakṛt*. The twofold recitation of the word *svāhā* is for the purpose of showing the manner of the *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation); that is to say, all [the mantras] end with *svāhā*. || 26.16 ||
Then follows the gratification of the Brahmins. || 26.17 ||

Then, immediately after the fire-oblation, the Brahmins should be gratified with food and other offerings. Āpastamba states: "In all ritual acts, one should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras" (ĀpDh 2.15.11). 26.17.
By this very [rule], the *atikṛcchra* is explained. || 26.18 ||
This is clear. || 26.18 ||
But he states its specific distinction:
"He should eat only as much as he would take up [in a single mouthful]. (26.19)

One should eat only as much as can be taken up in a single handful with one hand. The specific rules—that the food must be sacrificial (haviṣya), that it may be eaten during the day or at night, and that it must be unasked for—remain in force. Regarding this, Manu says: "One should eat a single morsel for three periods of three days each, as before; and one should fast for the final three days. This is called the Kṛcchra. (MDh 11.213) 26.19.
Subsisting on water for the third [day] is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. || 26.20 ||

During the very same meal-times mentioned previously, one should drink water alone; this is to be known as the third penance, called the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. On the days of fasting here, even the drinking of water does not take place, with the exception of sipping water (*ācamana*). These three *kṛcchras* have thus been described. (26.20)
Having practiced among them first, one becomes pure, purified, and fit for action. 26.21.

Having first performed the *prājāpatya* penance, he becomes pure. One who neglects the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts; thus, he is free from the defect caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties. Being "purified" (*pūta*), he is devoid of the unrighteousness (*adharma*) produced by the practice of forbidden acts. He becomes "fit for action" (*karmaṇya*), that is, capable of performing rituals. By the use of the term "fit for action," it is made known that even one whose fault is unknown becomes fit for desired rites through the performance of the *kṛcchra* penance. (26.21)
Having performed it a second time, one is liberated from whatever other sin one commits that is other than the great mortal sins (mahāpātaka). || 26.22 ||
Having performed the second *atikṛcchra* penance, one is liberated from sins other than the *mahāpātaka*s. || 26.22 ||
Having performed it for a third time, one is released from all sin. || 26.23 ||
Having performed the third penance, the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra, one is released from all sin, even from the great crimes (mahāpātaka), provided they were committed unintentionally. || 26.23 ||
Having thus stated the fruit of these [penances] performed individually, he now speaks of them collectively:
"Now, having performed these three *kṛcchra* penances, one becomes as if bathed in all the Vedas;
one becomes known by all the gods. (26.24)

He who performs these three *kṛcchra* penances without interruption obtains a fruit equal to that of one who has studied all the Vedas and performed the ritual bath (*snāna*); by him, the worlds of all the gods have been conquered. (26.24)
Now, the praise of the wise one:
"And he who knows thus, and he who knows thus. 26.25.

And he who understands these [sacrifices] by way of their essential nature, their procedure, and their fruit—he too has bathed in all the Vedas; he is known by all the gods. The meaning is that what is thus understood is praiseworthy. [The repetition of the sense already stated serves to conclude the section. 26.25.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, follows the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. 27.1.
This is to be explained as before. *Cāndrāyaṇa* is the ritual action that serves as the cause for attaining the moon; thus, he will state at the end: "One attains the same world as the moon. (27.1)
The rule for that has been stated in the section on the Kṛcchra penance.
The rule beginning with "He should remain standing during the day" (GDh 26.6), which describes the *kṛcchra* penance, should also be understood to apply to the *cāndrāyaṇa*. 27.2.
But as for the specific rule, it is stated: he should perform the shaving and observe the vow. 27.3.
He states that *vrata* refers to expiation:
"By these vows, the twice-born who have manifested their sins are to be purified" (MDh 11.226).

This is seen from such passages as these. If the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is performed for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then shaving (*vapana*) must also be performed; and even though no distinction is made, it applies only to men. Regarding women, there is the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Baudhāyana: "That same [penance] applies to a woman, with the exception of shaving the hair" (BDh 2.2.45). Since shaving is prescribed specifically for the Cāndrāyaṇa, it does not take place even in the *kṛcchra* penance when performed for expiation. Because of the injunction "one should observe the vow," there is no shaving in the Cāndrāyaṇa when it is performed for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or for the purpose of making oneself fit for ritual action. (27.3)
On the day after the full moon has occurred, he should observe the fast.
Having understood that "the full moon will occur tomorrow," one should fast on the preceding day, the fourteenth. Fasting is the abstention from eating.

The satiation, the oblation of clarified butter, the consecration of the sacrificial food, and the worship of the moon are performed with these [verses]: "Swell up," "May thy milks," and "New, new. (27.5)

The four rites beginning with the libation (*tarpaṇa*) are to be performed with the mantras beginning with "āpyāyasva" and so forth. Due to the disparity in number, they do not correspond respectively. In this regard, the libation and the fire-oblation (*homa*) are performed with each individual mantra; the recitation following the act (*anumantraṇa*) and the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) are to be combined. Some maintain that because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules for the *kṛcchra* penance, those acts such as the water-libation which are obtained through the *raudra* [rite] are also to be combined. Others hold that the prescribed [acts] supersede those obtained by extension. (27.5)
One should offer oblations with the four verses beginning, "O gods, whatever offense against the gods... (yad devā devaheḍanam). || 27.6 ||

One should offer clarified butter with the first four verses of the section beginning with “yad devā devaheḍanam” [VS 20.14], since no specific instruction is given; thus, there are seven oblations of clarified butter, including the three preceding ones. || 27.6 ||
And at the end [of the rite], with fuel-sticks, [he offers] with the verse beginning "devakṛtasya. || 27.7 ||

At the conclusion of the *ājya* oblations, an oblation with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) must be performed using the eight previously mentioned mantras beginning with "devakṛtasya" (VS 8.13). Although this is established by the very order of instruction, the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is a restatement of what has already been reached. Others, however, explain that it ends with the *cāndrāyaṇa*; for them, the word "and" (*ca*) would not be appropriate. (27.7)

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tapas, satyam, yaśas, śrīs, ūrj, iḍ, ojas, tejas, varcas, puruṣa, dharma, śiva"—with these [mantras], one should mentally perform the consecration of each morsel with every mantra. 27.8.

There are fifteen mantras beginning with the *praṇava*; one should perform the mental consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of each morsel (*grāsa*) with each individual mantra. Eating is to be done according to the sequence of these consecrations. However, when there are fewer morsels, then as many mantras as there are morsels should be taken from the beginning; those at the end are omitted. Because of the statement "consecration of the morsels," these are not mantras for the act of eating itself. Consequently, the mantras for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings are not suspended. When there are four morsels, then two [mantras] are used first; when three, the first two are used by two [mantras] each; when two, the first is used by two [mantras] and the latter by three; when there is only one, it is done with all [the mantras]. Regarding the previously mentioned "consecration of the sacrificial oblation" (*haviṣaḥ*), here it is the "consecration of the morsels" that applies, and thus the *prāṇāhuti* mantras remain in force. The practical application (*prayoga*) therein is as follows: having placed all the food to be eaten in a vessel and consecrated it with the mantras beginning with *āpyāyasva*, one should divide it into morsels, consecrate them in order with the mantras beginning with the *praṇava*, perform the *prāṇāhuti* offerings, and then eat.
Or he may offer to all [the ancestors] with "namaḥ" and "svāhā. 27.9.

Alternatively, one should consecrate every morsel with the formula "namaḥ svāhā. There is an option between these two: "namaḥ" and "svāhā. Others maintain that the mantra consists of both together. 27.9.
The measure of a mouthful is that which can be taken without distorting the mouth. 27.10.
The measure of a morsel is such that when it is being swallowed, the mouth remains undistorted. 27.10.
Caru, alms-food, barley-meal, grains, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, and water—these sacrificial offerings are increasingly praised in the following order. || 27.11 ||

The *caru* is rice-gruel prepared with sacrificial ingredients (*haviṣya*), freshly boiled, clear, and well-cooked. Alms-food (*bhaikṣa*) is that which has been personally brought by a student (*brahmacārin*) or a disciple and the like, since for a householder the practice of wandering for alms is prohibited. *Lāja* refers to parched grain reduced to powder; *saktu* is flour. *Kaṇa* refers to the husks of grain. *Yāvaka* has been mentioned previously. The others are well known. These are the twelve sacrificial offerings (*havir*). Among them, each subsequent one is more excellent than the preceding one. In that regard, the liquid substances are to be formed into mouthfuls using leaf-cups or similar vessels. And the penances (*tapas*) should be heavy when the sins (*enas*) are heavy, and light when they are light. (27.11)
Having eaten fifteen morsels on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight by decreasing [the number] by one each day. || 27.12 ||

Having thus fasted on the fourteenth day, one should eat fifteen morsels on the following day, the fifteenth. Thereafter, by decreasing by one [morsel] at each repetition, the meaning becomes clear: that there is a reduction of one morsel every day. One should eat in this manner throughout the entire dark fortnight (*apara-pakṣa*). When a decrease in lunar days (*tithi-hrāsa*) occurs such that the meal on the ninth day is reached, if the ninth day lasts for five *nāḍīs* in the morning and the tenth day does not exist on the following day, then having eaten nine morsels on the ninth day that arrived on the previous day, one should eat eleven morsels on the following day when the eleventh day arrives. This results in the omission of the ten morsels that would have been eaten on the tenth day. Similarly, when an increase in lunar days (*tithi-vṛddhi*) occurs such that the meal on the eleventh day is reached, if the tenth day lasts twenty-six *nāḍikās* during the day and the eleventh day lasts four [during the day], and the eleventh day also exists for some time during the night on the following day, then having eaten eleven morsels on the eleventh day that has commenced on the previous day, one should eat those same eleven on the following day as well. On that following day, the practice is to eat twelve.

"In whatever manner one may eat three hundred and eighty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) with a concentrated mind for a month, he attains the same world as the Moon"—thus another *cāndrāyaṇa* is prescribed in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]. However, this is not a restriction on the number of morsels within the two previously mentioned forms of *cāndrāyaṇa* consisting of increase and decrease (*upacaya-apacaya*). And so it has been clearly stated by Yājñavalkya:
"In whatever manner one might consume two hundred and forty morsels in a single month, that is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa," thus [it is said in Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.324]. 27.12.
Having fasted on the new moon day, he should spend the waxing fortnight by increasing the number [of morsels] by one each day.

Thus, as he consumes [the food] by decreasing it by one [mouthful] each day, on the fourteenth day there is one mouthful. On the new moon day (amāvāsya), there is a fast. Having fasted on the new moon day, on the first day of the waxing fortnight (pūrvapakṣa-pratipad), having eaten one mouthful, he should eat throughout the entire waxing fortnight by increasing the food by one mouthful at a time. On the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), there are fifteen [mouthfuls]. This is the "ant-waisted" (pipīlikā-madhya) Cāndrāyaṇa, because of its thin middle. 27.13.
For some, it is the reverse. || 27.14 ||

According to the opinion of certain teachers, this very procedure is reversed: having fasted on the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the portion by one each day, and then, beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight, one should eat during the dark fortnight by decreasing the portion by one each day, so that there is one morsel on the fourteenth day. There is a fast on the new moon day. Because it is thick in the middle, this is the barley-middled (*yavamadhyam*) *cāndrāyaṇa*. (27.14)
In this manner, the month of Cāndrāyaṇa is completed. || 27.15 ||

Thus, the *cāndrāyaṇa* is accomplished in a month; by association with that [practice], this month is called *cāndrāyaṇa*. Even though, according to the method described, there are thirty-two days in the "ant-waisted" (*pipīlikāmadhya*) version and thirty-one in the "barley-waisted" (*yavamadhya*) version, it is nevertheless referred to as "this month" according to the maxim: "not even by a single syllable [is a rule set aside]. (27.15)
Having attained this, one who is free from evil and free from sin destroys all transgression. || 27.16 ||

In this very manner, having completed such a Cāndrāyaṇa for a month—having performed this vow that is accomplished in a month—one becomes free from sin, devoid of the impurity born from the non-performance of prescribed duties. Being "free from sin" (vipāpmā), one is also devoid of the impurity arising from the performance of prohibited acts. One destroys every transgression, including even those other subtle sins accumulated in previous births; indeed, one destroys them all. (27.16)
Having attained the second [birth], he purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first, as well as his line of kin. || 27.17 ||

Although one should have said "having attained two," the expression "the second" is used for the sake of continuity, meaning "having attained the second month continuously. But how is such continuity possible? For it has been stated that one should fast on the full moon day of the following day (*śvobhūtā*) after having eaten fifteen morsels on the full moon; likewise, having fasted on the new moon, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the morsels by one each day. Thus, that performance ends within the second full moon. Immediately thereafter, at the commencement of the second [Cāndrāyaṇa], there would be a fast on the fourteenth day, and fifteen morsels on the fifteenth day—which is not tenable. Therefore, this must be explained here as follows: there is no injunction for two separate Cāndrāyaṇas here. What then? There is one Cāndrāyaṇa to be accomplished over two months. This is its rule for the fruit. At its beginning, there is a fast on the fourteenth day, and the performance ends on the third full moon. In the middle, it is as previously described. And the second full moon serves both as the end of the first and the beginning of the second through a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Similarly, in the "barley-shaped" (*yavamadhya*) version, the second new moon is the end of the first and the beginning of the second. By this, the phrase "or having attained a year" is also explained. (27.17)
Having attained this for a year, one becomes equal to the moon and attains the same world;
one attains the same world. || 27.18 ||

He who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow without interruption for one year attains the same world as the Moon (sālokya). The repetition [of the term] has already been explained. Regarding this, Manu says: "Restraining his self, he who performs the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food when the sun has reached the meridian."

“A twice-born man, being composed, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set while performing the *śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa*. And: “In whatever manner [he obtains] the morsels,” so it is said. (MDh 11.218–219; 11.220) 27.18.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Now, the division of inheritance: after the father's death, the sons shall divide the estate. 28.1.

After the father has died, upon the death of the father, his heirs—his wealth consisting of house, field, slaves, cattle, horses, gold, and so forth—the sons shall divide; the sons are the sharers therein. This means that the ownership of that property belongs to the sons. Because of the statement "after the father," while he is alive, the sons have no ownership over it. And thus says Manu:

"After both the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having come together, shall divide the paternal inheritance; for they have no power over it while the two are living" (MDh 9.104).

Since the word *pitṛ* (father) is inherently a relative term, the inclusion of the word *putra* (son) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, a collection of statements such as "when dividing after the father's death, the mother shall also take an equal share" is not the intention of the Teacher [Baudhāyana]. He considers that the sons alone, having taken all the wealth and so forth, should protect the mother properly. And it is heard in scripture: "Therefore, women are powerless and have no inheritance. Manu also says: "The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth."
"But sons [are responsible] in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. (MDh 9.3) || 28.1 ||
When the mother's menstrual flow has ceased, provided she is alive and desires it. || 28.2 ||

Alternatively, even while the father is alive, the sons may divide the inheritance if he so desires; that is to say, with his permission. The time for this is: "when the mother's menses have ceased. This means when she has ceased to menstruate and her capacity for procreation has ended. (28.2)
Or the eldest may support all the others like a father. (28.3)
The eldest alone, having taken possession of all the wealth and having received it, should support the other younger brothers; they too should live with him as sons. 28.3.
But upon partition, there is an increase in merit. 28.4.

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that the eldest alone should maintain [the family]; rather, as has been stated, partition itself is superior because therein there is an increase in dharma. As Bṛhaspati said:

"For those living together under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one; for those who are divided, that same worship must be performed in every individual household. (28.4)

Now he describes the method of partition when the father has passed away, and while he is still living: "The twentieth part belongs to the eldest; [he shall also receive] a pair [of animals], a chariot yoked with animals on both sides, and a bull. (28.5)

From the entire paternal estate, the twentieth part [is the preferential share]; "pair" refers to a pair of male and female animals such as cows; "with teeth in both rows" refers to horses, mules, and donkeys—a chariot yoked with either of these, or a bull, that is, a prime ox. This is the preferential portion for the eldest son. (28.5)
There were many kinds of people there: the one-eyed, the lame, the humpbacked, and the blind. || 28.6 ||

"One-eyed" (*kāṇa*) means having one eye; that is to say, having a defective limb. "Khora" means old. If the reading is *khoṭa*, it means having defective feet. "Kūṭa" means hornless. "Vaṇeṭa" means having a defective tail. Among cows, horses, and so forth, whatever is of such a form is the share for the middle-ranking [son]. And that [share] belongs to the one-eyed and others, provided they are more than one. For there is also a scriptural injunction regarding the others as well. (28.6)
A ram, a house made of iron, a cart yoked with oxen, and one of each kind of quadruped for the youngest brother. || 28.7 ||

*Aviḥ* means woolly sheep; the singular is used because the term refers to the species. Since it is already established that "as many as there are sheep" applies to one [of the brothers] and one each for the quadrupeds, another says: "Even though there is only one sheep for the father, nevertheless it belongs to the youngest; whereas the rule 'one each for the quadrupeds' refers to a large number [of animals]. *Dhānya* refers to rice and other grains. *Aya* refers to iron, such as a sickle and so forth. *Dhānyāyasī* (the dual) means grain and iron. Whatever of these two is in the house—where one resides—is included. *Anaḥ* means a cart yoked with two oxen. And among the quadrupeds, such as cows and others, he should take one preferred animal. This is the preferential share (*uddhāra*) for the youngest. And this applies to the absolute youngest. For the others, the preferential share is that which belongs to the middlemost. (28.7)
And everything else is to be understood in the same way. || 28.8 ||

All others should take the remaining extracted portion equally; "equally" is the meaning. The suffix *dhā* is employed as seen in such expressions as *dvidhā* (twofold) and *bahudhā* (manifold). || 28.8 ||
Or, each person obtains one desirable form of wealth, with each preceding one receiving more than the next. || 28.9 ||

In many other [types of] divisions, they should take one item each from among the fields and so forth in the order of seniority as the special portion (*uddhāra*). Alternatively, whatever is desired by whomsoever, that he may take. Among all [possessions], what is desired by the eldest is his special portion; in the absence of such desired items, what is desired by the next [in seniority] is his. This is the special portion for all. (28.9)
In this very context, there is a distinction regarding the sacrificial animals: ten animals. 28.10.
That which has ten parts is a "tenfold" (*daśaka*). Among cattle such as cows and the like, he receives ten at a time, each time, rather than just one. || 28.10 ||
The exception to this is:
not [the meat] of single-hoofed animals or those with two feet. 28.11.

They should not take a tenth part from single-hoofed animals such as horses, nor from bipeds such as female slaves; rather, they should take only one share each as previously stated. In the reading "dvipādānām" (of bipeds), the word *pada* has the same meaning as the word *pāda*. Thus, the division with the preferential share (*uddhāra*) for those born of the same mother has been described. (28.11)
Now he speaks of those who have more than one mother: "The *ṛṣabha* [tone] is additional for the eldest. (28.12)

Because of the statement "of the son of the eldest wife" (*jyaiṣṭhineyasya*) in the subsequent sūtra, this [son] is the eldest, even if he is the son of the youngest wife. If he is the son of the youngest wife, then his special share (*uddhāra*) is a bull; the rest is equal. 28.12.
The sixteen-year-old bull belongs to the son of the eldest wife. || 28.13 ||

The term "of the eldest" carries over from the previous context. And the son who belongs to the eldest [wife] is the one who belongs to the eldest [husband]; for him, fifteen cows and one bull constitute the preferential share (*uddhāra*). The rest is to be divided equally. 28.13.

Now, the rule that "the bull is the additional share for the eldest" is an exception [to the general rule]; however, among younger brothers, the additional share is equal with the son of the wife of the eldest brother.

The word "jyeṣṭhasya" (of the eldest) is supplied [from the preceding rule]. And because it stands in grammatical apposition with the term "ajyaiṣṭhineyena" (by one who is not the son of the eldest), it becomes a word ending in the third case. By means of the *ajyaiṣṭhineya*—that is, by an eldest son born of a younger wife—the division of the shares among the younger *jyaiṣṭhineya* brothers shall be equal. For while the seniority of one is based on birth (*janmataḥ*), that of the others is based on their mother (*mātṛtaḥ*). 28.14.
Or, according to each mother, there is a specific share for each respective group. 28.15.

The specific allotment of shares that was stated—beginning with "one-twentieth for the eldest," and so forth—should be applied according to each mother within their respective groups. This is what is meant: when the wealth is divided among as many mothers as have sons, one should combine the shares belonging to however many sons belong to a single mother; then, within each such group, the specific allotment of shares beginning with "one-twentieth for the eldest" applies to whichever son is the eldest. Thus has the division for those who have sons been explained. (28.15)

Now, regarding one who has no son, it is said: a father may designate an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), having sacrificed to Agni and Prajāpati, after having made an agreement that "this offspring is for our sake. (28.16)

The father should release her—that is, he should give her away. This is an indication by means of a future designation, as in the expression "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*). Being childless—meaning having no son—the father, having sacrificed to Agni and Prajāpati in the *aupāsana* fire with clarified butter immediately after the *ājyabhāga* offerings, saying "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Prajāpati!", and having made an agreement that "the offspring shall be for our sake," and having caused an agreement to be made with the one to whom he gives her; in this regard, the procedure has been shown by Vasiṣṭha: "I shall give to you an unbrothered maiden, adorned."

"In her a son shall be born; may he be my son. When she is given away in this manner, she is a *putrikā* (appointed daughter); a son born of her belongs to the maternal grandfather alone, and not to the biological progenitor. Therefore, Manu says:
"The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*) should first offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to his mother."

"The second [son] belongs to her father, but the third belongs to her father's father. (MDh 9.140) Thus, all such offspring—even this daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*)—is a substitute for a son of the father. [The suffix] *kan* is applied here in the sense of "likeness" (*iva*) when forming a name, according to Pāṇini 5.3.96. She alone is the heir to the inheritance. And so Manu says:
"But if, after a daughter has been appointed as a son, a son is subsequently born..."
"In that case, there shall be an equal division, for there is no seniority for a woman.

(MDh 9.134) Her lineage (*gotra*) is also that of her father alone; however, with respect to religious duties, she is merely a companion to her husband, and her fruit is sexual pleasure. For the sake of obtaining a son, however, another marriage must be performed for the purpose of continuing one's own family line; otherwise, there is fault. (28.16)
According to some, [the status of] a "daughter" arises merely from the intention [of the parents]. 28.17.

Some maintain that at the time of giving her away, if the father has the intention, "This girl of mine shall be a *putrikā*," she becomes a *putrikā* by that alone, without depending on the fire-oblation (*homa*), the formal agreement (*saṃvādana*), or other such rites. (28.17)
And therefore:
"One should not marry a woman who has no brother, because of the doubt concerning her [legitimacy]. (28.18)
This is due to doubt regarding him, doubt regarding the intention, or doubt regarding her being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). Manu also said:
"A wise man should not marry a girl whose brother does not exist or whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). (MDh 3.11) || 28.18 ||
Those related by funeral offerings, lineage, or ancestral sages shall divide the inheritance; or, in the case of one who has no offspring, the wife shall take it.

He who has no offspring, not even a daughter, is childless (*anapatya*). His inheritance shall be divided among those related by the *piṇḍa* (ancestral offerings) and so forth, or by the wife. Those related by the *piṇḍa* are the *sapiṇḍas*; those related by *gotra* (lineage) are the *sagotras*, as in the case of "Hārīta’s [descendant] is Hārīta. Those related by the sages (*ṛṣi*) are those with the same *pravara* (ancestral lineage), such as Harita, Kutsa, Piśaṅga, Śaṅkha, Darbha, and Haimagava, who are mutually related in this way. In other cases as well, the *sapiṇḍas* and others shall take the property according to the order of proximity. Thus says Āpastamba: "In the absence of a son, whoever is the nearest *sapiṇḍa*" [ĀpDh 2.14.2]. For example: the father, the mother, their uterine sons, the brothers born of different wombs, their sons, the paternal uncle, and so forth. In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, the *sagotras* [take it]; in their absence, those with the same *pravara*. The wife, however, is included together with all these, beginning with the *sagotra*. When the *sapiṇḍas* and others take the inheritance, the wife shall also receive one share along with them. Thus:

"When dividing after the father's death, the mother shall also take an equal share. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.123) For this very reason, the woman is mentioned separately from the *sapiṇḍas* and others who share equally. However, according to the view of the Teacher, the wife does not receive an inheritance. Manu also says:
"Women are devoid of sensory power and are perpetual non-inheritors; such is the settled rule. (Manu Smṛti 9.18)
In this regard, regarding the absence of sapindas and others, Bṛhaspati states:
"Except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, however, the king devoted to righteousness shall provide a livelihood for those women; this is declared to be the rule for inheritance."
For the sake of food, one *prastha* of rice with fuel should be given in the afternoon;
and one garment purchased for three *paṇas* should be given once every three months.
"Only this much is enjoined by the rule for virtuous women: the destruction of [their] prescribed duties.

Thus, Manu and Bṛhaspati have stated that there is an absolute absence of a wife's inheritance. However, Yājñavalkya has stated that wife's inheritance in the passage beginning with "The wife and the daughters... (YDh 2.135). On this point, Vyāsa says:
"A share of two thousand paṇas of wealth should be given to the wife."
"And whatever wealth has been given by her husband, she shall receive that according to her desire.

However, the Teacher (Ācārya) has stated that the *sapiṇḍas* and others should take equal shares. In that regard, the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*) is that the *sapiṇḍas* and others, having taken all the wealth, should protect the women for as long as they live. In the absence of that possibility, they should set aside a portion of wealth, fields, and so forth sufficient for food and clothing as their share, and take the remainder. And likewise, Bṛhaspati, after prohibiting the wife’s inheritance, stated at the end: "Of clothing, of food, and likewise of silver..."
Having set aside these three, one should assign what remains to the heirs.
"Previously, they calculated their companions, the substances that end in smoke, as well as their food and clothing; thus they perished in wealth. (28.19)
Or he may seek to obtain seeds. 28.20.

Or rather, it may be that a woman should seek seed from her sapinda relatives and others; the meaning is that she should procreate offspring. Under this view, however, the sapindas and others shall not take the property, but shall preserve it for the sake of the offspring. (28.20)
In this case, there is a distinction:
that which is born of another [man] in Devaravatī is without a share. || 28.21 ||

If, while a brother-in-law (devara) is present, she should seek offspring from another, the child born of her from that [other man] is without a share; there is no entitlement to his inheritance. But if the brother-in-law is absent, even a child born from another is indeed entitled to a share. 28.21.
The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and not established in life.

That which is given by the father, mother, son, or brother; that which is received in the presence of the sacred fire; and that which is obtained upon supersession by another wife—these are proclaimed as a woman’s property (strīdhana). [YDh 2.143]

Thus says Yājñavalkya: That woman’s property, upon her death, belongs to her unmarried daughters; if all are married, it belongs to those who are unsettled (without means). Among those who are married, some may be settled and others unsettled; in the case of both married and unmarried daughters being present, the unmarried one takes it; in the case of both settled and unsettled daughters being present, the unsettled one takes it. When it is property such as that received from her son and so forth, then it belongs to all of them. This is the rule for the woman’s property acquired from her father’s family after the mother’s death, while she is still living. And so Manu says:
But whatever may be the mother’s *yautaka* (separate property), that is indeed the share of the unmarried daughter.

And Vasiṣṭha says: “The women shall divide the mother’s *pāriṇeya* (marriage-portion). As for what was stated by Śākala and Khāṇḍika—“All uterine brothers and the daughters, both married and unmarried, are entitled to an equal share of the mother’s property”—that refers to daughters who have received property from their husband’s family; for regarding such married daughters, the rule of Manu is most authoritative: “But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers [shall divide it] equally.”
The mother's estate shall be divided among the uterine sisters.
"But for those who may be their daughters, something should also be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth out of affection, according to what is appropriate. (MDh 9.192–193).
Regarding that same case when the wealth is small, there is the teaching of Bṛhaspati:

"That woman's property belongs to her offspring; if there are daughters, they shall consume it. If she is unmarried, she shall receive it together with her mother; but if she is married, she shall receive it [only] along with her mother. (28.22)
The sister's dowry belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother's death. 28.23.

Regarding the property taken by the father for the purpose of giving away his daughter in the Āsura or Ārṣa forms of marriage: when he has died, that belongs to her uterine brothers alone; and while the mother is still living, it belongs to her alone, and not to the deceased father as his own property. In this regard, those brothers who are half-brothers (from different mothers) and the stepmother shall all not take a share. As for the ornaments, fields, and so forth given to the sister and others by the husband’s family or similar kin at the time of the wedding, that belongs to her alone. And when she has died childless, it is stated by Yājñavalkya: [that it goes to her husband].
Likewise, the property given by a kinsman, the nuptial fee (śulka),
and the supplementary gift (anvādheya) shall be obtained by the relatives when she has died without issue.
"By whomsoever a gift was given, he shall obtain that very thing; but when there are offspring, they themselves shall take it. || 28.23 ||
And some [hold] that it was previously [so]. 28.24.
Some maintain that even before the mother's death, the dowry for a sister belongs to the uterine brothers; this is an option depending on her conduct. (28.24)
The division of the inheritance among the hungry ghosts belongs to the eldest son. 28.25.

"Those who have not reunited" refers to brothers who have divided their property. "Vibhāgaḥ" means that which is to be divided. "Asaṃsṛṣṭivibhāgaḥ" is the division of those who have not reunited. The term "of the deceased" (*pretānām*) is an adjective qualifying even those who have not reunited, though they are here in a subordinate position. The phrase "and of one who is childless" (*anapatyasya ca*) also carries over. The teacher’s view is as follows: when brothers who have not reunited and have divided their property die childless, the portion to be divided—the wealth and so forth—belongs to the eldest brother alone, and not to the other brothers, nor to the wife, nor to the parents. Thus say Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Pitāmaha: "The property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the mother and father shall take it, or the eldest wife; or [it goes to] a fellow-student of the same lineage or a celibate student. But Manu says:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, as shall his brothers. [MDh 9.185] And Devala says:
"Thereafter, the uterine brothers shall divide the estate of one who has no son."
"Or a kinsman, or a daughter, or even a father who is still living. (28.25)
When a *saṃsṛṣṭin* has died, the *saṃsṛṣṭin* is the heir to the inheritance.
One who has reunited wealth with his brothers and others is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, one whose property is common; he is either undivided, or one who was divided but has reunited after having been separated.
Furthermore, he who, having been divided, should live again in one place with his father, brother, or paternal uncle out of affection, is called *saṃsṛṣṭa*.

Thus, from the *Bārhaspatya* [Smṛti]: the term "one who is childless" (*anapatya*) carries over. Regarding the phrase "the one associated in property" (*saṃsṛṣṭī*): when a person who was associated in property dies childless, his heir shall take his estate. In that case, if he was associated with both a uterine brother and a non-uterine brother, the uterine brother shall take it. This is because of the observation of Yājñavalkya: "But for a uterine brother, [it belongs to] the uterine brother" (YDh 2.138). Therefore, when a divided brother dies childless, his wealth goes to the eldest; in the absence of an eldest brother, it goes to the other brothers. However, if he died undivided, his share belongs to all the brothers. (28.26)
That which is born of a divided estate belongs exclusively to the father.

However, a son born after the partition—whether from that same mother or from another wife—should receive only the paternal estate. He shall inherit whatever was acquired by the father after the partition, or whatever was received at the time of partition, whether it be small or large. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"Whatever was acquired by the father himself after he had been divided from his sons, all that belongs to the son born after partition; the elder brothers are declared to have no right to it."
But when the father possesses nothing, then the Vaiṣṇava rule applies: "Those divided from the father shall give a share to one born after the partition" (ViDh 17.3). Yājñavalkya also says:
"A son born after the partition from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share;
or his share may be determined from what is visible, after deducting income and expenses" (YDh 2.122).

On this point, Manu and Nārada state: "But one born after partition shall inherit the paternal wealth alone; or, those who have reunited with him, he shall divide it together with them" (MDh 9.216). 28.27.
A physician may, at his own discretion, not give what he has earned himself to those who are unlearned in the science. || 28.28 ||

One who has studied knowledge is called a *vaidya* (learned man). He may, at his pleasure, not give what he has earned by his own effort to brothers who lack learning; for there is no sin in not giving, while there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) in giving. [28.28]
Those who are unlearned shall divide [the estate] equally. 28.29.

But when all the brothers are unlearned, they should divide equally whatever they acquire through agriculture and other such means. Even that which is acquired by one learned brother through agriculture and the like—provided it was not obtained through learning and does not conflict with the paternal estate—is subject to equal division. Both of these two sūtras refer specifically to the case of brothers. However, while the father is alive, whatever is acquired by one who is undivided, whether he be learned or unlearned, belongs to the father alone.
"Wife, son, and slave—these three are declared to be without property.
Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. (MDh 8.416)
Thus says Manu (28.29).
The Teacher has stated that "sons shall divide the inheritance," but he says this so that there may be no misconception that only *aurasa* (body-born) sons are intended; [therefore he specifies]:
"Sons—the *aurasa*, the *kṣetraja*, the *dattaka*, the *kṛtrima*, the *gūḍhotpanna*, and the *apaviddha*—are the sharers of the inheritance. (28.30)
The *aurasa* son is one born of a lawful wife. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"A son procreated by means of *niyoga* in the field of another by a man who has no son is, according to dharma, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both. (YDh 2.127)

This [son] belongs only to the one who procreates him, and not to the biological father or the husband. Regarding the son given (*datta*), Vasiṣṭha states: “One should neither give nor receive an eldest son; for he is for the continuation of the lineage of the ancestors. A woman should neither give nor receive a son without the permission of her husband. One intending to adopt a son, having summoned his kinsmen and announced it to the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras in the middle of the house, should adopt a boy who is not too distant and who is closely related to his own kin. He is the "given" (*datta*) son. Regarding the "made" (*kṛtrima*) son, Manu says:
But he whom one may make similar, who is free from [the father's] virtues and defects,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son, is to be known as the *kṛtrima* (adopted) son.
He who is born in a man's house, yet whose parentage is not known, [is the son of unknown origin].
He who is born secretly in the house shall belong to him whose wife gave birth to him.

"A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is known as an *apaviddha* (cast-off). [MDh 9.169–171] These six sons are heirs to the inheritance. 28.30.

The son born of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the son of a remarried woman, the son of an appointed daughter, the son given by himself, and the son bought are sharers of the family name. || 28.31 ||

"A son whom a maiden bears here in her father's house, one should call him by the name Kānīna (the maiden-born), produced from the maiden, not from the husband. Thus [says Manu, MDh 9.172]. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:

"If an unmarried daughter should obtain a son from one who is weighed [in the balance], by that grandson the maternal grandfather becomes a *pautrin*; he shall offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherit the wealth. Thus [says] Vaśiṣṭha (VaDh 17.23). Yājñavalkya says:

"A *kānīna* is one born of an unmarried girl (*kanyakā*), since he is the son of his maternal grandfather. [YDh 2.129] In that regard, if she dies while still unmarried, he is the son or grandson of the maternal grandfather; if she is married, he is the son of the husband. On this point, Manu says:
"If a woman who is already pregnant is wedded, whether her condition be known or unknown..."
That fetus becomes the carrier [of the child] and is called "saḥoḍha" (the one carried).

One who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, produces offspring through her own will after becoming a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman), is called *paunarbhava*. The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) has already been mentioned previously. — Manu.
One who is deprived of his mother and father, or who has been abandoned without cause,
and who offers himself to someone— that person is known as *svayaṃdatta* (self-given).

“He who may purchase from his mother and father a son for the sake of offspring—whether he be similar or dissimilar to them—that son is his *krītaka* (purchased) son. [MDh 9.174, 177] These [sons], however, are *gotrabhāj* (inheritors of the lineage); they inherit the lineage alone, not the estate. The former [sons], on the other hand, are *rikthabhāj* (inheritors of the estate) as well as *gotrabhāj*, because they are mentioned together with the *aurasa* (legitimate) son. And all these [sons] belong to the same caste (*sajātīya*).
"This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste," according to the statement of Yājñavalkya (YDh 2.133). 28.31.
Those entitled to a fourth share [receive it] in the absence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the others.

Alternatively, these sons—the *kānīna* and the others—are neither excluded from inheritance nor are they entitled to the entire estate; rather, they are entitled to a fourth share. They shall take a fourth part of the father’s wealth in the absence of the six previously mentioned sons, beginning with the *aurasa*. However, if those [six] are present, they themselves shall take the inheritance. As for the remainder beyond the fourth share, the *sapiṇḍas* shall take it. Regarding the fact that the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) is stated here to be entitled to a fourth share even in the absence of the *aurasa* and other sons, this refers to the case of an inferior *putrikāputra*. The meaning is that this applies to the son of one who designates a daughter as an *appointed daughter* (*putrikā*) through a mere agreement with a wife of a lower caste; it concerns such a son. On this point, Manu says:
