"But if a son is born after a daughter has been appointed as an heir, the division of the property shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. (MDh 9.134) Thus it is said.
When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja),
or even a fifth share.
“The two sons, the *aurasa* and the *kṣetraja*, are sharers of the father’s inheritance;
but ten others, in their respective order, are sharers of the lineage and the portion of the inheritance” (MDh 9.164–165).

Regarding this, after mentioning the adoption of a son (*dattaputra*), Vasiṣṭha states: “If, after he has been adopted, a biological son (*aurasa*) is born, [the adopted son] shall be entitled to a fourth share. On this point, Kātyāyana says:

"But when a legitimate son (aurasa) has been born, sons of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a third part [of the estate], while those of a different caste (asavarṇa) shall be entitled only to food and clothing. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
The legitimate son of the body alone is declared the sole owner of the paternal wealth;
the son of an appointed daughter is equal to him, while all others are recorded as being entitled only to maintenance.
"Other sons, such as the *kṣetraja* and the rest, are entitled to five, six, seven, or eight shares," so it is said.

Hārīta states: "When about to divide the inheritance, one should give twenty-one parts to the *kānīna*, twenty to the *paunarbhava*, nineteen to the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, eighteen to the *kṣetraja*, seventeen to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), and the remainder to the legitimate son (*aurasa*). Yājñavalkya, having enumerated the twelve types of sons, says: "Among these, each subsequent one offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share in the absence of the preceding. (YDh 2.132)
Manu also says: "In the absence of each superior [heir], the next younger one is entitled to the inheritance" (MDh 9.184). Nārada also says:
"These [categories] proceed in order regarding the wealth of one whose father has died;
in the absence of each elder [heir], the next younger one shall obtain it.
Vasiṣṭha also states: "But for one who has no heir among his ancestors, these [others] shall take his inheritance" (VaDh 17.39).

Having enumerated the sons in order as the legitimate son (*aurasa*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*), the son begotten on a wife (*kṣetraja*), the maiden-born son (*kānīna*), the secretly born son (*guḍhotpanna*), the abandoned son (*apaviddha*), the son received with a bride (*sahoḍha*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the adopted son (*datta*), the son who has come of his own accord (*svayam-upāgata*), the made son (*kṛtaka*), and the bought son (*krīta*), Devala states:
"These twelve sons have been declared for the sake of continuity— those born of oneself, those born of another, and likewise those obtained by chance."
Of these, six are kinsmen and heirs, as were previously mentioned in relation to the father alone;
furthermore, among sons, the distinction is determined by their specific order of precedence.
All these sons of one who has no legitimate son (aurasa) are declared to be heirs to the inheritance;
however, once a legitimate son is born, they no longer receive the status of the eldest.
"Those sons of theirs who are of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a third share;
those of lower caste shall subsist [on the estate], provided with food and clothing.

Regarding the term *bandhudāyādāḥ*, these [sons] may inherit the property not only from the father but also from their paternal kinsmen (*bandhu*), that is, their *sapiṇḍas*; others [however] inherit from the father alone. This is precisely the meaning of the term *bandhudāyāda* in other Smṛtis as well. Thus it is:

The legitimate son (aurasa), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā), the sons of the seed-owner and the field-owner (bījikṣetriṇau), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with a wife (sahoḍha), and the son born in secret (gūḍhasambhava).
The son given, the son bought, the son self-given, the adopted son, the son cast off,
and the son begotten on a woman by another— these are the fifteen known as sons.

"In this very sequence, in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person is the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and the taker of the inheritance; thus is established the order according to their qualities. (28.32)

The division of property among sons born of wives of the same caste has been stated. Now, he describes the specific rule regarding sons of different castes born from marriages in the prescribed order:
"The son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya wife, if he is the eldest and endowed with good qualities, shall receive an equal share. (28.33)

If a son born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is endowed with excellent qualities and is the eldest, then he shares equally with the younger son of the Brāhmaṇa wife; for the seniority of one is by age, while that of the other is by birth. (28.33)
The other [shares] are diminished by the eldest's portion. 28.34.

It is understood from the context that one should divide everything other than that "extra portion" (uddhāra) previously mentioned—such as "a twentieth part for the eldest"—among the rest. Regarding an eldest son who is devoid of good qualities or is the son of a *rājanya* mother, the law of Manu applies: "Or, having divided the entire estate here into ten parts, one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous division according to the following rule."
"A Brahmin son shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share" (MDh 9.152–153).
In a case where there is a gathering of sons born of a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman, it is the same as with the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman. || 28.35 ||

When the son of the Brāhmaṇī is not present, then the son of the Rājanyā shares equally with the son of the Brāhmaṇī; likewise, the son of the Vaiśyā shares equally with the son of the Kṣatriyā. || 28.35 ||
If [the woman] is a Kṣatriya. 28.36.

The word *ca* has the sense of *ca* (and). When there is a concurrence of two sons born from a Kṣatriya—one being the son of a Vaiśya and the other the son of a Kṣatriya—the son of the Vaiśya, even if he is the elder, shares equally with the younger son of the Kṣatriya provided he is endowed with good qualities. Some maintain that this same principle should be understood to apply to the son of a Śūdra born from a Vaiśya; others say no, because it has not been so stated. (28.36)
Even the son of a Śūdra woman, if he is obedient, may receive a means of subsistence from a childless man according to the rule for a pupil.

The term "of the Brāhmaṇa" continues [from the previous rule]. Even the son of a Śūdra woman may obtain the means of subsistence for a Brāhmaṇa who is childless—that is, one who has no son of the twice-born caste. He shall receive as much as he is capable of performing work such as agriculture and so forth, provided that he serves according to the rules for a resident pupil (*antevāsin*); that is, if he serves just as a student serves his teacher. In this same manner, even the son of a Śūdra woman from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya father may obtain the means of subsistence. (28.37)
According to some, even the son of a woman of the same caste does not receive [the inheritance] if he behaves improperly.

However, some hold the opinion that one who behaves unjustly and acquires property through unrighteous means, or bestows it upon prostitutes and the like—even if he is the son of a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*), and even if he is the eldest—shall not receive an inheritance. Thus says Āpastamba: "But one who acquires property through unrighteousness, even if he is the eldest, they shall exclude him from his share" (ĀpDh 2.14.15). || 28.38 ||
The Vedic scholars (śrotriya) shall divide the inheritance of a childless Brāhmaṇa.

The mention of "offspring" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the lineage (gotra), the ancestral sages (ṛṣi), and other such connections. For a Brāhmaṇa who is childless and thus possesses no wealth, the learned (śrotriya) [kinsmen] shall indeed divide the inheritance. (28.39)
For others than the king. || 28.40 ||
The king shall take the inheritance of other [classes], such as Kṣatriyas and so forth, who die without offspring. || 28.40 ||
The dull-witted and the impotent should be maintained. || 28.41 ||
The "insane" (jaḍa) is one whose mind is lost; the "impotent" (klība) is one of the third gender. These two must be maintained by providing food and clothing. Manu, however, states:

"The impotent, the outcast, those born blind or deaf, as well as the insane, the mentally deficient, the mute, and whoever lacks their [sexual] organs, do not receive a share of the inheritance. (MDh 9.201) || 28.41 ||
The offspring of a fool is entitled to a share. || 28.42 ||
If, however, a son is born to one who is impotent (*jaḍa*), then he is entitled to a share; that share should be given to him by his father. On this point, Manu says:
"But if, in any way, there should be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and the like, their offspring, having produced progeny, shall be entitled to the inheritance" (MDh 9.203). 28.42.
But those born in the inverse order [of castes] are like the sons of a Śūdra woman.

Even for those born in the reverse order, such as the Sūta and others, if they are distinguished by superior qualities, the means of subsistence should be provided just as it is for the son of a Śūdra.
There shall be no division of food prepared for the sake of water and security. || 28.44 ||
Water refers to wells and the like. Yoga and kṣema refer to *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable works). Thus says Laugākṣi:
"The seers of truth say that *yoga* is *pūrta* and *kṣema* is *iṣṭā*;
these two are declared to be indivisible, as are the bed and food."

But regarding prepared food at festivals and the like, even when it has been prepared in abundance, no division should be made among these [co-heirs]; rather, they should enjoy it exactly as it stands, according to their respective shares. 28.44.
And [the same applies] when women are engaged [in sexual intercourse]. || 28.45 ||

And those women who are female slaves, having been joined with a brother or others by someone and taken for enjoyment, belong to him alone. If there are other [slaves], they shall be a share for the others; if there are none, then equality must be established through property. But when there is only one female slave and she is joined [to him], then let her perform work in turn. 28.45.
When a matter is not clearly understood, it should be performed as recommended by at least ten learned men who are knowledgeable in the Vedic hymns (ūha) and free from greed. 28.46.

That which is known as if it were unknown is "anājñāta" (unrecognized). The opposite of that is "ajñāta. When a matter has not been understood as it truly is, or is subject to doubt, regarding that unrecognized matter, the decision is made by at least ten learned men (*śiṣṭa*), no fewer than ten. Those Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Veda along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*) according to the law are to be known as *śiṣṭas*, for they are the authorities based on direct revelation (*śruti*). *Yair dharmeṇādhigato vedas tu saparibṛṃhaṇaḥ |* *Te śiṣṭā brāhmaṇā jñeyāḥ śrutipratyakṣahetavaḥ ||* (MDh 12.109)

Thus it is stated by Manu: that which is praised—commended as "this is appropriate here"—by Brahmins who are learned in *ūha* (adaptation), skilled in reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*), and free from greed, having no desire for bribes and the like; such a thing is fit to be done. 28.46.
Who, then, are those "at least ten"? He says:
four who have mastered the four Vedas; three of the [other] stages of life prior to the last one;
and three who know the Dharma individually—these are the "at least ten."
They call it the assembly. 28.47

Those who have mastered the four Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), as well as those who know their meaning—four such persons constitute a *cāturvidya*, not just one. Regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*), three were mentioned in the third chapter: the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) or forest-dweller (*vāikhānasa*). Among these, the three stages preceding the highest, the *vāikhānasa*, are each experts in the treatises on Dharma. They are mentioned separately so that there might not be an inclusion of only three persons who know a single treatise on Dharma. Those who know the Dharma call this assembly of at least ten persons a *pariṣad*. (28.47)
But in the absence of these, whatever a learned Vedic scholar who is disciplined says when there is a conflict of opinions [is authoritative]. 28.48.

In the absence of many such persons—whether individually or collectively—one who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*), one who knows the Veda, that is, one who understands its meaning, and one who is disciplined, being devoted to his own duty—even such a single person, when he declares in a matter of dispute, "This is proper here; this must be done," that is what should be done. And so Manu says:

"Even a single person who knows the Veda, if he determines the Dharma with a concentrated mind—that Dharma should be known as supreme; it is not that which is proclaimed by thousands of ignorant men. (MDh 12.113)
But why must one follow the word of even a single learned man, a Vedic scholar who is refined? To this he says:
"Because he has no power over beings in matters of harming or favoring.

"Prabhava" means that from which something originates; it is a cause. That which lacks such a [worldly] cause is "aprabhava. Because this person is not perceived to have any worldly cause for his actions regarding the infliction of harm or the conferring of favor upon living beings—such as punishment or penance—but is instead guided solely by the scripture, therefore even the word of a single such person is to be carried out. Another says: "Prabhava" is the act of originating, that is, sovereignty. He who does not possess that is "aprabhava. For he does not independently bestow favor or inflict harm on anyone without regard for the scripture. Therefore, his word is to be carried out. (28.49)
Now, he says that one who practices after having understood [the Dharma] is superior to those who merely practice the Dharma:
"The knower of Dharma attains the heavenly world especially through his excellence as a practitioner, by means of both knowledge and resolute application. (28.50)

Those who possess the qualities of their respective duties are the *dhārmikas*. Among them, he who knows the Dharma—that is, one who has studied the treatises on Dharma according to their meaning and understands the Dharma in its true essence—is distinguished by both knowledge and application. Knowledge is a competent understanding; application is practice with total dedication. Through such knowledge and application, he attains the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) more excellently than those who merely perform the rites. (28.50)
Thus, this is the Dharma, the Dharma. || 28.51 ||

Thus, beginning from the very first statement that "the Veda is the root of Dharma" (GDh 1.1), the Dharma has been declared up to this point. The repetition [of the final words] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the treatise. 28.51.
In this commentary composed by Haradatta on the Dharmaśāstra spoken by Gautama,
this twenty-eighth chapter, concerning inheritance, is completed.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Śrīgautamīya composed by Haradatta.
This work is completed.
